uni-bsc-phy-electricity-magnetism.title: B.Sc. Physics · Electricity & Magnetism
uni-bsc-phy-electricity-magnetism.description: Vector calculus for fields, electrostatics and Gauss's law, potential, capacitors and dielectrics, magnetostatics with Biot–Savart and Ampère's laws, magnetic materials, electromagnetic induction and transients, Maxwell's equations and EM waves, with standard practicals and exam practice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc. Physics (Hons./Programme) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Vector Calculus & Electrostatics
courses.summary: Gradient, divergence, curl and the integral theorems, Coulomb's law and superposition, Gauss's law in integral and differential form with standard applications, conductors and electrostatic energy density.
outcomes: Compute gradient, divergence and curl and apply Gauss's and Stokes' theorems
Find fields of point charges and dipoles by superposition
Use Gauss's law for line, sheet and spherical charge distributions
Describe fields at conductors and compute field energy

scenes.text: Around a tap, water spreads outward; in a whirlpool it circles.
Divergence measures spreading from a point; curl measures swirling. Electric and magnetic fields are described by exactly these.

steps.title: Operators
steps.body: ∇ = x̂ ∂/∂x + ŷ ∂/∂y + ẑ ∂/∂z. Gradient ∇f points along steepest increase of a scalar f. Divergence ∇ · A = ∂Aₓ/∂x + ∂A_y/∂y + ∂A_z/∂z measures net outflow per unit volume. Curl ∇ × A measures circulation per unit area. Identities: ∇ × (∇f) = 0; ∇ · (∇ × A) = 0.

steps.title: Integral theorems
steps.body: Gauss (divergence) theorem: ∮_S A · da = ∫_V (∇ · A) dτ. Stokes' theorem: ∮_C A · dl = ∫_S (∇ × A) · da. Fundamental theorem for gradients: ∫ₐᵇ ∇f · dl = f(b) − f(a).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A = r = (x, y, z): ∇ · A = 3. Flux through a sphere of radius R: ∮ r · da = R × 4πR² = 4πR³, and ∫3 dτ = 3 × (4/3)πR³ = 4πR³ ✓. B = (−y, x, 0): ∇ × B = 2ẑ; around a circle of radius R, ∮B · dl = 2πR², equal to 2 × πR² ✓.

steps.title: Worked example: gradient
steps.body: f = x²y + z: ∇f = (2xy, x², 1). At (1, 2, 0): (4, 1, 1), magnitude √18 ≈ 4.24 — the maximum rate of change of f there.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating ∇ · A as a vector or ∇ × A as a scalar; forgetting that Stokes' theorem needs consistent orientation (right-hand rule) of the surface and its boundary.

activity.prompt: Match each expression to its result.

quiz.q: The divergence theorem relates:
options: Surface flux to volume integral of divergence
quiz.why: ∮ A · da = ∫ (∇ · A) dτ connects closed-surface flux with the enclosed divergence.

quiz.q: The curl of any gradient is:
quiz.why: Mixed partial derivatives commute, so ∇ × ∇f = 0 identically.

quiz.q: ∇f points in the direction of:
quiz.why: The directional derivative ∇f · û is largest when û is along ∇f.

scenes.text: Rub a balloon on your hair and it sticks to the wall.
A tiny transfer of electrons — nanocoulombs — produces forces big enough to beat gravity on the balloon.

steps.title: Coulomb's law
steps.body: F = (1/4πε₀) q₁q₂ r̂/r², with 1/4πε₀ = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻². Field E = F/q₀; for continuous charge E = (1/4πε₀)∫ dq r̂/r². Superposition: fields add as vectors.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 1 μC and 2 μC, 3 cm apart: F = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻¹²/(9 × 10⁻⁴) = 20 N (repulsive). Field at the midpoint of +4 μC and −4 μC separated by 0.2 m: each gives 9 × 10⁹ × 4 × 10⁻⁶/0.01 = 3.6 × 10⁶ N/C toward the negative charge, total 7.2 × 10⁶ N/C. For two EQUAL like charges the midpoint field is zero.

steps.title: Electric dipole
steps.body: Dipole moment p = qd (from − to +). Far field on the axis: E = 2kp/r³; on the perpendicular bisector: kp/r³ (opposite to p). Torque in uniform E: τ = p × E; potential energy U = −p · E. Dipole fields fall as 1/r³.

steps.title: Worked example: water molecule
steps.body: A water molecule has p ≈ 6.2 × 10⁻³⁰ C m. In E = 10⁵ N/C at 90°: τ = pE = 6.2 × 10⁻²⁵ N m. Work to rotate it from aligned (0°) to antiparallel (180°): 2pE = 1.24 × 10⁻²⁴ J — tiny compared with thermal energy kT ≈ 4 × 10⁻²¹ J at room temperature, so alignment is only partial.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Adding field magnitudes without directions; using r instead of r² in Coulomb's law; forgetting that a dipole in a uniform field feels torque but no net force.

activity.prompt: Charges +3 μC and −3 μC sit 0.3 m apart. Electric field magnitude at the midpoint, in units of 10⁶ N/C?

quiz.q: Doubling the distance between two charges changes force by:
quiz.why: F ∝ 1/r².

quiz.q: Axial field of a short dipole varies as:
quiz.why: The fields of the two opposite charges nearly cancel, leaving a 1/r³ term proportional to p.

quiz.q: Net force on a dipole in a uniform field is:
quiz.why: Forces +qE and −qE are equal and opposite; only a torque remains.

scenes.text: Wrap any closed bubble around a charge: the number of field lines piercing it never changes.
With a clever choice of bubble, symmetric fields can be found in one line.

steps.title: Statement
steps.body: Integral form: ∮ E · da = Q_enc/ε₀. Using the divergence theorem: ∇ · E = ρ/ε₀ (differential form). Gauss's law always holds, but it gives E directly only for highly symmetric distributions (spherical, cylindrical, planar).

steps.title: Infinite line charge
steps.body: Coaxial cylinder radius r, length L: E × 2πrL = λL/ε₀ → E = λ/(2πε₀r). For λ = 10⁻⁸ C/m at r = 0.1 m: E = 2 × 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁸/0.1 = 1800 N/C.

steps.title: Infinite sheet & uniform sphere
steps.body: Sheet (surface density σ), pillbox: 2EA = σA/ε₀ → E = σ/(2ε₀), independent of distance. Uniform sphere (charge Q, radius R): outside E = Q/(4πε₀r²); inside, Q_enc = Q r³/R³ → E = Qr/(4πε₀R³), linear in r.

steps.title: Choosing a Gaussian surface
steps.body: Pick a surface where E is either parallel to da with constant magnitude, or perpendicular to da (zero flux). If the symmetry is broken (e.g. a finite rod), Gauss's law is true but not useful — integrate Coulomb's law instead.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Including charges outside the surface in Q_enc; using σ/ε₀ for an isolated sheet (that is for a conductor surface); claiming E = 0 wherever flux is zero.

activity.prompt: An infinite non-conducting sheet has σ = 8.85 × 10⁻⁹ C/m². Field near it (N/C)?

quiz.q: Field of an infinite line charge varies as:
quiz.why: Gauss's law over a cylinder gives E = λ/(2πε₀r).

quiz.q: Differential form of Gauss's law:
quiz.why: Applying the divergence theorem to the integral form gives ∇ · E = ρ/ε₀.

quiz.q: Inside a uniformly charged solid sphere, E at r = R/2 compared with the surface value:
quiz.why: Inside, E ∝ r, so at R/2 it is half the surface field.

scenes.text: During a thunderstorm, the safest place outdoors is inside a metal-bodied car.
The metal shell keeps the field inside near zero — a Faraday cage.

steps.title: Conductors in equilibrium
steps.body: E = 0 inside the material; ρ = 0 inside (excess charge on the surface); the conductor is an equipotential; just outside, E is normal to the surface with magnitude σ/ε₀. A charge-free cavity has E = 0 regardless of outside fields (shielding). Charge density is higher at sharp points (lightning rods, corona discharge).

steps.title: Field energy
steps.body: Work to assemble charges W = ½∫ρV dτ = (ε₀/2)∫E² dτ over all space. Energy density u = ½ε₀E². Pressure on a charged conductor surface: σ²/(2ε₀), outward.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Air breaks down near E = 3 × 10⁶ V/m: u = ½ × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 9 × 10¹² ≈ 39.8 J/m³. Energy of a sphere (radius R, charge Q, conductor): W = Q²/(8πε₀R). For Q = 1 μC, R = 0.1 m: W = 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻¹²/(2 × 0.1) = 0.045 J.

steps.title: Shielding in practice
steps.body: MRI rooms, coaxial cables and microwave oven doors use conducting enclosures or meshes to keep external fields out or internal fields in.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying the potential inside a conductor is zero (it is constant, not necessarily zero); forgetting that a charge placed INSIDE a cavity induces charge on the cavity wall and appears on the outer surface.

activity.prompt: Energy density (J/m³) of an electric field of 3 × 10⁶ V/m in air (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹²)?

quiz.q: Field just outside a conductor with surface charge σ:
quiz.why: A pillbox with one face inside (E = 0) gives EA = σA/ε₀.

quiz.q: Excess charge on a conductor resides:
quiz.why: Any interior charge would create a field inside, so it moves to the surface.

quiz.q: Electrostatic energy density is:
quiz.why: Writing W = ½∫ρV dτ in terms of fields gives u = ½ε₀E².

Field between two infinite parallel sheets with +σ and −σ:
questions.why: Each sheet gives σ/2ε₀, adding between the sheets and cancelling outside.

questions.q: In a charge-free region, the potential satisfies:
questions.why: With ρ = 0, Poisson's equation reduces to Laplace's equation.

questions.q: Electrostatic pressure on a conductor surface with σ:
questions.why: Force per area = σ × (average field σ/2ε₀) = σ²/2ε₀.

options: Charge density and field are largest at sharp points
questions.why: High surface fields at sharp tips ionise air and discharge charge gradually.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Potential, Capacitors & Dielectrics
courses.summary: Electric potential and its relation to field, Poisson and Laplace equations, capacitance of parallel-plate, spherical and cylindrical capacitors, energy stored and charge sharing, and dielectrics with polarisation, displacement D and partially filled capacitors.
outcomes: Compute potentials of point charges, dipoles and charge systems
Derive capacitance of standard geometries
Calculate stored energy and losses on charge sharing
Use P, D and εr to analyse capacitors with dielectrics

scenes.text: A trekking map shows height contours; water flows straight downhill, across the contours.
Equipotentials are electric contours — and field lines cut them at right angles, pointing downhill in V.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: Because ∇ × E = 0 in electrostatics, E = −∇V. V(P) = −∫_∞^P E · dl (reference at infinity). Point charge: V = kq/r. Superposition: V = Σkqᵢ/rᵢ — scalars, much easier than adding vectors. Work to bring q₀ from infinity: W = q₀V.

steps.title: Poisson & Laplace
steps.body: Combining ∇ · E = ρ/ε₀ with E = −∇V: ∇²V = −ρ/ε₀ (Poisson); in charge-free regions ∇²V = 0 (Laplace). Solutions of Laplace's equation have no local maxima or minima — hence no stable electrostatic equilibrium for a charge (Earnshaw's theorem).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 2 nC at 0.3 m: V = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁹/0.3 = 60 V. Bringing 1 μC from infinity needs 60 μJ. Dipole potential: V = kp cosθ/r²; on the bisector (θ = 90°) V = 0, though E ≠ 0 there.

steps.title: Worked example: field from V
steps.body: V = 5x²y (volts, metres). E = −∇V = (−10xy, −5x², 0). At (1, 2, 0): E = (−20, −5, 0) V/m, magnitude ≈ 20.6 V/m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming E = 0 wherever V = 0 (or vice versa); dropping the minus sign in E = −∇V; adding potentials as vectors.

activity.prompt: Four +1 nC charges sit at the corners of a square of side 0.2 m. Potential at the centre (V)?

quiz.q: E and V are related by:
quiz.why: The field points toward decreasing potential, E = −∇V.

quiz.q: On the perpendicular bisector of a dipole:
quiz.why: Contributions of ±q cancel in V but their field vectors add to a non-zero field parallel to −p.

quiz.q: Laplace's equation applies where:
quiz.why: Poisson's equation ∇²V = −ρ/ε₀ reduces to ∇²V = 0 in charge-free space.

scenes.text: A camera flash whines as it charges, then dumps its stored energy in a millisecond.
The capacitor's geometry sets how much charge it can hold per volt.

steps.title: Definition & method
steps.body: C = Q/V. Method: assume ±Q on the conductors, find E by Gauss's law, integrate to get V, divide.

steps.title: Spherical & cylindrical
steps.body: Concentric spheres a < b: V = kQ(1/a − 1/b) → C = 4πε₀ab/(b − a); isolated sphere (b → ∞): 4πε₀a (Earth ≈ 711 μF). Coaxial cylinders, length L: V = (λ/2πε₀) ln(b/a) → C = 2πε₀L/ln(b/a); about 55.6 pF per metre when b/a = e.

steps.title: Combinations
steps.body: Parallel: C = C₁ + C₂ (same V). Series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ (same Q). Example: 4 μF and 12 μF in series → 3 μF; on 16 V each carries 48 μC.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating capacitor combinations like resistors (they are the reverse); using ln(a/b) (negative) for the cylindrical capacitor; forgetting C depends only on geometry and medium, not on Q or V.

activity.prompt: A 2 m coaxial cable has inner radius 0.5 mm and outer radius 2 mm (vacuum between). Capacitance in pF?

quiz.q: Capacitance of an isolated sphere of radius R:
quiz.why: Letting b → ∞ in 4πε₀ab/(b − a) gives 4πε₀a.

quiz.q: Halving plate separation of a parallel-plate capacitor:
quiz.why: C = ε₀A/d is inversely proportional to d.

quiz.q: Two equal capacitors C in series give:

scenes.text: A charged capacitor is connected to an identical empty one. Charge is conserved and shares equally.
Yet half the stored energy vanishes — into heat and radiation in the connecting wires.

steps.title: Stored energy
steps.body: Work to charge: W = ∫V dq = ∫(q/C) dq = Q²/2C = ½CV² = ½QV. Equivalently u = ½ε₀E² integrated over the field volume: for a parallel plate ½ε₀(V/d)² × Ad = ½CV² ✓.

steps.title: Charge sharing
steps.body: Connecting C₁ (at V₁) to C₂ (at V₂): common potential V = (C₁V₁ + C₂V₂)/(C₁ + C₂). Energy loss ΔU = C₁C₂(V₁ − V₂)²/(2(C₁ + C₂)) — always positive.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 4 μF at 100 V joined to an uncharged 4 μF: V = 50 V. Initial energy ½ × 4 × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁴ = 20 mJ; final ½ × 8 × 10⁻⁶ × 2500 = 10 mJ. Loss 10 mJ — exactly half, independent of wire resistance.

steps.title: Force between plates
steps.body: F = Q²/(2ε₀A) (attractive). For A = 0.01 m², Q = 10⁻⁷ C: F = 10⁻¹⁴/(2 × 8.85 × 10⁻¹⁴) ≈ 0.056 N.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using QV instead of ½QV; assuming energy is conserved in charge sharing; forgetting that with the battery connected V is fixed, while with it disconnected Q is fixed.

activity.prompt: A 2 μF capacitor charged to 200 V is connected across an uncharged 6 μF capacitor. Energy lost (mJ)?

quiz.q: Energy stored in a capacitor is:
quiz.why: Charging from 0 to V requires average potential V/2 per unit charge.

quiz.q: Common potential after joining C₁ at V₁ to uncharged C₂:
quiz.why: Charge C₁V₁ is shared over total capacitance C₁ + C₂.

quiz.q: With a battery connected, inserting a dielectric:
options: Keeps V fixed and increases Q
quiz.why: The battery maintains V while C rises, drawing more charge.

scenes.text: Old radio capacitors used thin sheets of mica between metal foils.
The mica's molecules polarise, partly cancelling the field and letting the capacitor store more charge per volt.

steps.title: Polarisation
steps.body: In a field, molecules acquire or align dipoles; dipole moment per unit volume is P. Bound charges: σ_b = P · n̂ on surfaces, ρ_b = −∇ · P inside. For linear dielectrics P = ε₀χₑE.

steps.title: Displacement D
steps.body: D = ε₀E + P = ε₀(1 + χₑ)E = εE, εᵣ = 1 + χₑ. Gauss's law in matter: ∇ · D = ρ_free, ∮ D · da = Q_free. Boundary conditions: D⊥ continuous (no free surface charge); E∥ continuous. Filling a capacitor completely: C = εᵣC₀.

steps.title: Worked example: partial slab
steps.body: Plates A = 0.01 m², gap d = 2 mm, with a slab of thickness t = 1 mm, εᵣ = 4. C = ε₀A/(d − t + t/εᵣ) = 8.85 × 10⁻¹⁴/(1.25 × 10⁻³) ≈ 70.8 pF (vs 44.3 pF empty).

steps.title: Worked example: bound charge
steps.body: Isolated capacitor with free σ_f; dielectric εᵣ = 5 fills it. E = σ_f/(ε₀εᵣ); P = ε₀(εᵣ − 1)E = (4/5)σ_f, so bound surface charge is 80% of the free charge, opposite in sign.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using ∇ · E = ρ_free/ε₀ in matter (it should be total charge, or use D with free charge); assuming D is always ∥ E (true only for isotropic linear media).

activity.prompt: Plate area 0.02 m², gap 3 mm, a 2 mm slab of εᵣ = 5 inserted. Capacitance (pF)? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹²)

quiz.q: D = ε₀E + P. Its divergence equals:
quiz.why: Bound charge is absorbed into P, leaving ∇ · D = ρ_free.

quiz.q: Relative permittivity εᵣ equals:
quiz.why: D = ε₀(1 + χₑ)E, so εᵣ = 1 + χₑ.

quiz.q: At a dielectric boundary with no free charge, which is continuous?
quiz.why: Gauss's law for D on a thin pillbox gives continuity of its normal component.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Magnetostatics & Magnetic Materials
courses.summary: Lorentz force and forces on currents, the Biot–Savart law for wires and loops, Ampère's law with solenoids and toroids, divergence and curl of B, and magnetisation, H, susceptibility and the classes of magnetic materials with hysteresis.
outcomes: Compute motion of charges and forces between currents in magnetic fields
Use Biot–Savart for straight wires and circular loops
Apply Ampère's law to solenoids, toroids and thick wires
Relate B, H and M and classify magnetic materials

scenes.text: In a cyclotron, ions spiral outward in a strong magnetic field, kicked by an alternating voltage each half-turn.
The magic: the orbit time doesn't depend on speed, so one fixed radio frequency keeps them in step.

steps.title: Lorentz force
steps.body: F = q(E + v × B). The magnetic part is perpendicular to v, so it does no work and cannot change speed. In uniform B, a charge moves in a circle: r = mv/(qB), angular frequency ω = qB/m, cyclotron frequency f = qB/(2πm), independent of v (non-relativistic).

steps.title: Force on currents
steps.body: dF = I dl × B; straight wire F = BIL sinθ. Parallel wires: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd), attractive for parallel currents. Torque on a coil: τ = m × B with m = NIA — the basis of motors and moving-coil galvanometers.

steps.title: Worked example: galvanometer coil
steps.body: N = 100, A = 2 cm², I = 1 mA, radial B = 0.2 T: deflecting torque τ = NIAB = 100 × 10⁻³ × 2 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.2 = 4 × 10⁻⁶ N m. With suspension torsion constant C = 2 × 10⁻⁵ N m/rad, the steady deflection is θ = NIAB/C = 0.2 rad ≈ 11.5°. Current sensitivity θ/I = NAB/C.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the sign of q (electrons curve the opposite way); claiming B does work on charges; using μ₀I/2πd for force per length without multiplying by the second current.

activity.prompt: Two long parallel wires 5 cm apart each carry 10 A in the same direction. Force per metre, in units of 10⁻⁴ N/m?

quiz.q: The magnetic force on a moving charge does no work because:
quiz.why: F = qv × B is always ⊥ v, so F · v = 0.

quiz.q: Cyclotron frequency depends on:
quiz.why: f = qB/(2πm) contains no speed or radius.

quiz.q: Two wires with currents in opposite directions:
quiz.why: Each wire's field acting on the other's antiparallel current gives a repulsive force.

scenes.text: A compass at the centre of a vertical coil is deflected when current flows.
Balancing the coil's field against Earth's horizontal field gives a way to measure current — and Earth's field.

steps.title: The law
steps.body: dB = (μ₀/4π) I dl × r̂/r², μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A. Like Coulomb's law, it gives fields by integration and superposition.

steps.title: Straight wire
steps.body: Segment seen at angles θ₁, θ₂ from perpendicular distance s: B = (μ₀I/4πs)(sinθ₂ − sinθ₁). Infinite wire (θ → ±90°): B = μ₀I/(2πs). For I = 10 A, s = 5 cm: B = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 10/0.05 = 40 μT.

steps.title: Circular loop
steps.body: On the axis at distance x from the centre: B = μ₀IR²/(2(R² + x²)^(3/2)); at the centre μ₀I/(2R). Coil of N = 50 turns, R = 0.1 m, I = 5 A: B = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 250/0.2 ≈ 1.57 mT. Far away the loop is a magnetic dipole: B ≈ μ₀m/(2πx³).

steps.title: Tangent galvanometer
steps.body: With the coil in the magnetic meridian, B_coil = B_H tanθ, so I = (2RB_H/μ₀N) tanθ. Best sensitivity near θ = 45°.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using μ₀I/2R for points off-centre; forgetting the factor N for multi-turn coils; confusing axial distance x with radius R.

activity.prompt: A single loop of radius 5 cm carries 10 A. Field on its axis at a distance equal to its radius, in μT?

quiz.q: Field at the centre of a circular loop:
quiz.why: Every element is at distance R and perpendicular to r̂, giving (μ₀I/4πR²)(2πR) = μ₀I/2R.

quiz.q: Field of an infinite wire varies as:
quiz.why: B = μ₀I/(2πs).

quiz.q: Far along the axis, a current loop's field falls as:
quiz.why: For x ≫ R, B ≈ μ₀IR²/(2x³), a dipole field.

scenes.text: An MRI magnet is essentially a huge superconducting solenoid.
Inside it the field is strong and nearly uniform; outside it is weak — exactly what Ampère's law predicts.

steps.title: Laws of magnetostatics
steps.body: ∮ B · dl = μ₀I_enc (Ampère), or ∇ × B = μ₀J. ∇ · B = 0: no magnetic monopoles, field lines close on themselves. B can be written as ∇ × A (vector potential).

steps.title: Long solenoid
steps.body: Rectangular Amperian loop with one side inside: BL = μ₀nLI → B = μ₀nI (n = turns per metre), uniform inside, ≈ 0 outside. n = 1000 m⁻¹, I = 2 A: B = 4π × 10⁻⁴ × 2 ≈ 2.51 mT.

steps.title: Toroid and thick wire
steps.body: Toroid (N turns): circle of radius r inside the core: B × 2πr = μ₀NI → B = μ₀NI/(2πr); zero outside. Thick wire radius a with uniform J: inside B = μ₀Is/(2πa²) (∝ s), outside μ₀I/(2πs).

steps.title: When Ampère works
steps.body: Like Gauss's law, it gives B directly only with symmetry: infinite lines, planes, solenoids, toroids. For a finite segment use Biot–Savart.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using total turns N instead of n = N/L for a solenoid; forgetting the Amperian loop must be closed; applying the static law to circuits with charging capacitors (needs displacement current, Unit 5).

activity.prompt: A toroid of 500 turns carries 3 A. Field at mean radius 10 cm (mT)?

quiz.q: ∇ · B = 0 means:
quiz.why: Zero divergence means no sources or sinks of B — field lines never start or end.

quiz.q: Field inside a long solenoid depends on:
quiz.why: B = μ₀nI is independent of radius and uniform away from the ends.

quiz.q: Inside a thick wire with uniform current, B at s = a/2:
quiz.why: Inside, B ∝ s.

story.title: The fridge magnet and the frog

scenes.text: Iron sticks to a magnet strongly; aluminium barely notices it.
In a 16 T magnet, even water — and a live frog — is weakly repelled and can levitate: diamagnetism.

steps.title: M, H, B
steps.body: Magnetisation M = magnetic moment per unit volume. Bound currents: J_b = ∇ × M, K_b = M × n̂. Define H = B/μ₀ − M, so ∇ × H = J_free and ∮ H · dl = I_free. Linear media: M = χₘH, B = μ₀(1 + χₘ)H = μH, μᵣ = 1 + χₘ.

steps.title: Classes of materials
steps.body: Diamagnetic (χₘ small negative, ~ −10⁻⁵; Bi, Cu, water): induced moments oppose B. Paramagnetic (χₘ small positive, ~10⁻⁵–10⁻³; Al, O₂): permanent moments partly align, Curie's law χ = C/T. Ferromagnetic (Fe, Co, Ni): domains, χ ≫ 1, nonlinear with hysteresis; above the Curie temperature (Fe ≈ 1043 K) they become paramagnetic.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A solenoid with n = 1000 m⁻¹, I = 2 A has H = nI = 2000 A/m. Filled with a paramagnet of χₘ = 2 × 10⁻⁵: M = 0.04 A/m and B rises by only 0.002%. With soft iron (μᵣ ≈ 2000 in this range): B ≈ μ₀μᵣH ≈ 5 T — in practice iron saturates near 2 T, showing μᵣ is not constant.

steps.title: Hysteresis
steps.body: The B–H loop shows retentivity (B remaining at H = 0) and coercivity (H needed to remove it). Loop area = energy lost per cycle per unit volume. Soft iron (narrow loop) for transformer cores; hard steel/alloys (wide loop, high coercivity) for permanent magnets.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating H and B as interchangeable inside matter; assuming ferromagnets have a fixed μᵣ; confusing retentivity with coercivity.

activity.prompt: Classify each material or property.

quiz.why: Soft iron has high permeability and a narrow loop, minimising hysteresis loss.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Electromagnetic Induction & Circuit Transients
courses.summary: Faraday's and Lenz's laws, motional emf and AC generators, self and mutual inductance with magnetic energy, growth and decay of charge in RC circuits and of current in LR circuits, and AC fundamentals with impedance and power factor.
outcomes: Calculate induced emf from changing flux and motion
Derive inductance of solenoids and stored magnetic energy
Solve RC and LR transients and use time constants
Analyse series AC circuits with impedance and power factor

scenes.text: An induction cooktop stays cool, yet a steel pan on it gets hot within seconds.
A rapidly changing magnetic field induces swirling currents in the pan's base — Faraday's law at work.

steps.title: Faraday & Lenz
steps.body: emf = −dΦ_B/dt, Φ_B = ∫B · da (N turns: −N dΦ/dt). The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change producing it — a consequence of energy conservation. Differential form: ∇ × E = −∂B/∂t; induced electric fields are non-conservative.

steps.title: Motional emf
steps.body: A rod of length L moving at v ⊥ B: emf = BLv (from the magnetic force on its charges). L = 0.5 m, v = 4 m/s, B = 0.2 T → 0.4 V. With circuit resistance R = 2 Ω, I = 0.2 A and the retarding force BIL = 0.02 N must be supplied to keep v constant — mechanical power 0.08 W = I²R.

steps.title: AC generator
steps.body: Coil of N turns, area A, rotating at ω in B: Φ = NBA cos ωt → emf = NBAω sin ωt. N = 200, A = 0.01 m², B = 0.5 T, f = 50 Hz (ω = 100π): peak emf = 200 × 0.5 × 0.01 × 314.2 ≈ 314 V; rms ≈ 222 V.

steps.title: Eddy currents
steps.body: Induced currents in bulk conductors cause heating and drag: used in induction furnaces, cooktops, electromagnetic brakes and damping of galvanometers; minimised in transformer cores by laminating them.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying emf is proportional to flux (it is proportional to its rate of change); getting the current direction wrong — apply Lenz's law by asking what the induced field must do to oppose the change.

activity.prompt: A 100-turn coil's flux changes from 5 mWb to 1 mWb per turn in 0.02 s. Magnitude of average induced emf (V)?

quiz.q: Lenz's law is a consequence of:
quiz.why: If induced currents aided the change, energy would grow without input — a perpetual motion machine.

quiz.q: Peak emf of a rotating coil is:
quiz.why: Differentiating NBA cos ωt gives amplitude NBAω.

quiz.q: Transformer cores are laminated to reduce:
quiz.why: Thin insulated sheets break up the large loops in which eddy currents would flow.

scenes.text: Switching off a large motor often produces a spark at the switch contacts.
The coil's stored magnetic energy fights the sudden drop in current, driving a high voltage across the gap.

steps.title: Self inductance
steps.body: Φ_total = LI, emf = −L dI/dt. Long solenoid (n turns/m, area A, length l): B = μ₀nI, Φ = (nl)(μ₀nIA) → L = μ₀n²Al. Unit: henry (H).

steps.title: Mutual inductance
steps.body: Φ₂ = MI₁, emf₂ = −M dI₁/dt, and M₁₂ = M₂₁ (Neumann). Coaxial solenoids (outer n₁, inner N₂ turns, area A₂): M = μ₀n₁N₂A₂. Coupling: M = k√(L₁L₂), 0 ≤ k ≤ 1.

steps.title: Magnetic energy
steps.body: W = ½LI²; energy density u = B²/(2μ₀). For B = 1 T, u ≈ 4 × 10⁵ J/m³ — far more than an electric field at air breakdown (≈ 40 J/m³).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using N instead of n in L = μ₀n²Al; thinking inductance depends on current (it depends only on geometry and core, if linear).

quiz.why: Both B and the number of linked turns are proportional to n.

quiz.why: From ½LI² for a solenoid divided by its volume, u = B²/(2μ₀).

quiz.q: Coefficient of coupling k = 1 means:
options: All flux of one coil links the other
quiz.why: M = √(L₁L₂) is the maximum possible, achieved with perfect flux linkage.

scenes.text: Roadside warning lights blink on a steady rhythm without any microchip.

steps.title: Charging
steps.body: Kirchhoff: E = IR + q/C with I = dq/dt. Solution: q = CE(1 − e^{−t/RC}), I = (E/R)e^{−t/RC}. Time constant τ = RC: after τ, q reaches 63.2% of its final value; after 5τ, over 99%.

steps.title: Discharging
steps.body: q = Q₀e^{−t/RC}, I = −(Q₀/RC)e^{−t/RC}. Half-life t½ = RC ln2 ≈ 0.693RC. Energy dissipated in R during charging equals the energy stored, ½CE² — the battery supplies CE².

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 μF: τ = 1 s. Time to reach 90%: e^{−t} = 0.1 → t = ln10 ≈ 2.30 s. Initial current with E = 12 V: 1.2 mA.

steps.title: Lab: measuring τ
steps.body: Discharge a capacitor through a large resistor, record V every few seconds, plot ln V vs t: slope = −1/RC. A leakage-free capacitor and a voltmeter with resistance ≫ R are needed — or include the meter's resistance in parallel.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using τ = R/C; forgetting the current decays during charging (it is maximum at t = 0, not at the end).

activity.prompt: A 5 μF capacitor discharges through 2 MΩ. Time for its voltage to fall to half (s)?

quiz.why: From dq/dt = −q/RC, the exponential has time constant RC.

quiz.q: After one time constant of charging, the capacitor holds:

quiz.why: The battery supplies CE², half stored (½CE²) and half dissipated, independent of R.

scenes.text: Old fan regulators used a choke coil rather than a resistor to reduce speed.
An inductor limits AC current without wasting much power as heat — reactance, not resistance.

steps.title: Growth and decay in LR
steps.body: E = IR + L dI/dt → I = (E/R)(1 − e^{−Rt/L}); τ = L/R. Decay: I = I₀e^{−Rt/L}. Example L = 0.5 H, R = 10 Ω: τ = 0.05 s; after 0.05 s the current is 63.2% of E/R.

steps.title: AC fundamentals
steps.body: V = V₀ sin ωt; V_rms = V₀/√2 (230 V mains → peak ≈ 325 V). Reactances X_L = ωL, X_C = 1/(ωC). Series LCR impedance Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²), phase tanφ = (X_L − X_C)/R. Average power P = V_rms I_rms cosφ; cosφ = R/Z is the power factor.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: R = 30 Ω in series with X_L = 40 Ω on 230 V rms: Z = 50 Ω, I = 4.6 A, cosφ = 0.6, P = 230 × 4.6 × 0.6 ≈ 635 W (= I²R = 21.16 × 30 ✓). Current lags voltage by 53.1°.

steps.title: Wattless current
steps.body: In a pure inductor or capacitor, φ = 90° and average power is zero — current flows but no net energy is consumed. That is why a choke wastes far less power than a resistor regulator.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Adding R and X arithmetically; using peak values in P = V I cosφ without dividing by 2; forgetting X_C decreases with frequency while X_L increases.

quiz.why: From L dI/dt + IR = E, the exponential has τ = L/R.

quiz.why: φ = 90° and cos90° = 0.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Maxwell's Equations & Electromagnetic Waves
courses.summary: Displacement current and the complete Maxwell equations, the electromagnetic wave equation and plane waves, energy flow by the Poynting vector, intensity and radiation pressure, and waves in conductors with skin depth.
outcomes: Explain why Maxwell added displacement current and write all four equations
Derive the wave equation and c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀)
Compute Poynting vector, intensity and radiation pressure
Estimate skin depth in conductors

scenes.text: Current flows into a charging capacitor, but no charge crosses the gap between the plates.
Ampère's law gives different answers for two surfaces with the same boundary — until Maxwell adds the changing E field.

steps.title: The inconsistency
steps.body: Taking the divergence of ∇ × B = μ₀J gives ∇ · J = 0, which contradicts the continuity equation ∇ · J = −∂ρ/∂t whenever charge accumulates. Using ρ = ε₀∇ · E, Maxwell added J_d = ε₀ ∂E/∂t (displacement current density) to make the equations consistent.

steps.title: Maxwell's equations (vacuum, with sources)
steps.body: ∇ · E = ρ/ε₀ (Gauss). ∇ · B = 0 (no monopoles). ∇ × E = −∂B/∂t (Faraday). ∇ × B = μ₀J + μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t (Ampère–Maxwell). In matter: ∇ · D = ρ_f, ∇ × H = J_f + ∂D/∂t. Together with the Lorentz force they describe all classical electromagnetism.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Parallel-plate capacitor (A = 0.01 m²) with field rising at dE/dt = 10¹² V m⁻¹ s⁻¹: I_d = ε₀A dE/dt = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 0.01 × 10¹² = 0.0885 A — exactly equal to the conduction current in the wires, restoring continuity.

steps.title: B between capacitor plates
steps.body: Circular plates of radius R, charging current I: at radius r < R inside the gap, ∮B · dl = μ₀I_d(r²/R²) → B = μ₀Ir/(2πR²). With I = 1 A, R = 5 cm, r = 2.5 cm: B = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 0.025/(2π × 0.0025) = 2 μT.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking displacement current is a flow of charge (it is a changing field); omitting it in quasi-static problems is fine, but not for capacitors or waves.

activity.prompt: Plates of area 0.01 m²; E between them rises at 10¹² V/(m·s). Displacement current in mA?

quiz.q: Displacement current density is:
quiz.why: Maxwell's correction term to Ampère's law is μ₀ times ε₀ ∂E/∂t.

quiz.q: Which Maxwell equation expresses the absence of magnetic monopoles?
quiz.why: Zero divergence of B means no isolated magnetic charges.

quiz.q: Without displacement current, Ampère's law contradicts:
quiz.why: It would force ∇ · J = 0, which fails when charge builds up.

scenes.text: Maxwell computed the speed of his predicted waves from electrical constants measured on lab benches.
It came out at the measured speed of light. Light, he concluded, is an electromagnetic wave.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body: In vacuum without sources, take the curl of Faraday's law: ∇ × (∇ × E) = −∂(∇ × B)/∂t. Using ∇ × (∇ × E) = ∇(∇ · E) − ∇²E with ∇ · E = 0 and Ampère–Maxwell: ∇²E = μ₀ε₀ ∂²E/∂t². Same for B. Wave speed c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) = 1/√(4π × 10⁻⁷ × 8.854 × 10⁻¹²) ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.

steps.title: Plane waves
steps.body: E = E₀ sin(kz − ωt) x̂, B = B₀ sin(kz − ωt) ŷ. Transverse: E ⊥ B ⊥ direction of travel (E × B points along propagation). In phase, with E₀ = cB₀. In a linear medium v = 1/√(με) = c/n, n = √(εᵣμᵣ).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: E₀ = 300 V/m → B₀ = 300/3 × 10⁸ = 1 μT. For a 100 MHz FM wave: λ = 3 m, k = 2.09 rad/m.

steps.title: Water's two refractive indices
steps.body: Water's static εᵣ ≈ 80 would give n ≈ 9, yet optical n = 1.33: εᵣ depends strongly on frequency because molecular dipoles cannot reorient at optical frequencies (dispersion).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming E and B are 90° out of phase in a travelling plane wave (they are in phase); writing B₀ = E₀c instead of E₀/c.

activity.prompt: A plane EM wave in vacuum has E₀ = 600 V/m. Amplitude of B in μT?

quiz.why: The wave equation's coefficient μ₀ε₀ equals 1/v².

quiz.q: In a plane EM wave, E and B are:
quiz.why: Faraday's law forces B ⊥ E with the same phase for a travelling plane wave.

scenes.text: Japan's IKAROS spacecraft unfurled a thin sail in 2010 and was pushed by sunlight alone.
Light carries energy AND momentum — the push is tiny but never stops.

steps.title: Poynting's theorem
steps.body: Energy density u = ½(ε₀E² + B²/μ₀). Energy flux (power per area) S = (1/μ₀) E × B. Poynting's theorem: −∂u/∂t = ∇ · S + J · E — field energy lost locally either flows away or does work on charges.

steps.title: Intensity and pressure
steps.body: For a plane wave, electric and magnetic energy densities are equal. Intensity I = ⟨S⟩ = ½ε₀cE₀² = E₀²/(2μ₀c). Momentum density S/c²; radiation pressure I/c on a perfect absorber, 2I/c on a perfect reflector.

steps.title: Worked example: sunlight
steps.body: Solar constant I = 1361 W/m² above the atmosphere. E₀ = √(2I/(ε₀c)) = √(2722/2.655 × 10⁻³) ≈ 1.01 × 10³ V/m; B₀ ≈ 3.4 μT. Pressure on an absorber: 1361/3 × 10⁸ ≈ 4.5 × 10⁻⁶ Pa.

steps.title: Worked example: wire
steps.body: For a resistor carrying I with voltage V, S points radially INTO the wire; integrated over its surface it gives exactly VI = I²R — the energy enters the wire from the surrounding fields.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the ½ for time-averaged intensity; using I/c for a reflector (it is 2I/c).

activity.prompt: A 1 mW laser beam has cross-section 1 mm² (uniform). Peak electric field amplitude (V/m)?

quiz.q: The Poynting vector is:
quiz.why: S = (1/μ₀)E × B gives power per unit area and direction of energy flow.

quiz.q: Radiation pressure on a perfect reflector of intensity I:
quiz.why: Reversing the momentum doubles the transfer compared with absorption.

quiz.q: In a vacuum plane wave, magnetic energy density is:
quiz.why: With B = E/c, B²/2μ₀ = ε₀E²/2.

lessons.title: EM waves in conductors & the spectrum

story.title: Why submarines use very low frequencies

scenes.text: Ordinary radio waves cannot reach a submerged submarine: seawater conducts.
Navies use VLF and ELF signals, whose skin depths in seawater reach metres to tens of metres.

steps.title: Skin depth
steps.body: In a good conductor (σ ≫ ωε), fields decay as e^{−z/δ} with skin depth δ = √(2/(μσω)). Currents at high frequency crowd near the surface, raising effective resistance; waves are strongly reflected (metals are shiny).

steps.title: Worked example: copper
steps.body: σ = 5.96 × 10⁷ S/m. At 50 Hz: μσω = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 5.96 × 10⁷ × 314.2 ≈ 2.35 × 10⁴ m⁻², δ = √(2/2.35 × 10⁴) ≈ 9.2 mm — so thick busbars gain little. At 1 MHz: δ scales by √(50/10⁶), giving ≈ 65 μm.

steps.title: The spectrum
steps.body: Radio (> 1 m) → microwaves (1 mm–1 m) → infrared → visible (≈ 400–700 nm) → ultraviolet → X-rays → gamma rays. All travel at c in vacuum; they differ in frequency, photon energy (E = hf) and interaction with matter.

steps.title: Shielding and Litz wire
steps.body: Thin metal coatings block radio frequencies because δ is micrometres; high-frequency coils use Litz wire (many thin insulated strands) to beat the skin effect.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting δ ∝ 1/√f (not 1/f); assuming visible light penetrates metals as deeply as in glass.

activity.prompt: Using δ ≈ 9.2 mm for copper at 50 Hz and δ ∝ 1/√f, skin depth at 1 MHz in μm?

Metals reflect light strongly because:

quiz.why: Free electrons respond to the field, cancelling it within a skin depth and re-radiating a reflected wave.

quiz.q: Which has the longest wavelength?
quiz.why: Microwaves (mm to m) are far longer than visible (≈ 0.5 μm), UV or X-rays.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Revision, Practicals & Exam
courses.summary: A formula sheet for Electricity & Magnetism and the standard practicals — Carey Foster's bridge, verification of Thevenin's and maximum power transfer theorems, and the ballistic galvanometer — with procedures, calculations, viva points and a mixed exam.
outcomes: Recall the key laws and formulas of all units
Measure low resistance and resistivity with a Carey Foster bridge
Verify Thevenin's theorem and maximum power transfer

scenes.text: Rohan notices that almost every chapter is one of Maxwell's four equations seen from a new angle.
He organises his revision sheet around them.

steps.title: Electrostatics
steps.body: ∇ · E = ρ/ε₀; E = −∇V; ∇²V = −ρ/ε₀. Line λ/2πε₀r; sheet σ/2ε₀; conductor surface σ/ε₀; dipole axis 2kp/r³. u = ½ε₀E².

steps.title: Capacitors & dielectrics
steps.body: Parallel plate ε₀A/d; sphere 4πε₀ab/(b − a); cylinder 2πε₀L/ln(b/a). W = ½CV². Sharing loss C₁C₂(V₁ − V₂)²/2(C₁ + C₂). D = ε₀E + P; ∇ · D = ρ_f; slab C = ε₀A/(d − t + t/εᵣ).

steps.title: Magnetostatics
steps.body: F = q(E + v × B); r = mv/qB. Wire μ₀I/2πs; loop centre μ₀I/2R; axis μ₀IR²/2(R² + x²)^(3/2); solenoid μ₀nI; toroid μ₀NI/2πr. H = B/μ₀ − M; Curie χ = C/T.

steps.title: Induction & circuits
steps.body: emf = −dΦ/dt; BLv; NBAω. L = μ₀n²Al; W = ½LI²; u = B²/2μ₀. τ_RC = RC; τ_LR = L/R. Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²); P = V_rms I_rms cosφ.

steps.title: Maxwell & waves
steps.body: J_d = ε₀∂E/∂t. c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀); E₀ = cB₀; S = E × B/μ₀; I = ½ε₀cE₀²; pressure I/c (absorb), 2I/c (reflect). δ = √(2/μσω).

quiz.q: Which law contains Lenz's minus sign?
quiz.why: emf = −dΦ/dt, where the minus sign expresses opposition to change.

quiz.q: Capacitors in series share the same:
quiz.why: The same charge flows onto each plate pair in series.

quiz.q: The E–B amplitude relation in vacuum is:
quiz.why: Faraday's law for a plane wave gives E₀ = cB₀.

lessons.title: Lab: Carey Foster's bridge — low resistance & resistivity

scenes.text: A metre bridge cannot measure small resistances well: end resistances and contacts spoil it.
Carey Foster's trick — swap the two resistors and measure the SHIFT of the balance point — cancels those errors.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: P and Q (nearly equal) form the ratio arms; X and Y sit in the outer gaps of a wire of resistance ρ per cm. Balance at l₁; interchange X and Y, balance at l₂. Then X − Y = ρ(l₁ − l₂) (sign set by which gap X occupies first). End resistances and contact errors cancel in the difference.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Calibrate ρ: put a known Y (e.g. 0.5 Ω) in one gap and a thick copper strip (X ≈ 0) in the other; find l₁ and l₂; ρ = Y/(l₂ − l₁) in magnitude. 2) Replace the strip with the unknown X; find new l₁, l₂; X = Y + ρ(l₁ − l₂). 3) Measure wire length L and diameter for resistivity ρ_wire = Xπr²/L.

steps.title: Worked calculation
steps.body: Calibration: Y = 0.5 Ω gives a 25 cm shift → ρ = 0.02 Ω/cm. Unknown with Y = 1.0 Ω: shift 15 cm with X > Y → X = 1.0 + 0.02 × 15 = 1.30 Ω. If X is a 0.5 m wire of radius 0.2 mm: resistivity = 1.3 × π × 4 × 10⁻⁸/0.5 ≈ 3.3 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Loose connections; heating from leaving current on (use a tap key); P and Q not nearly equal; null point near the ends of the wire.

steps.title: Viva points
steps.body: Why is it better than a metre bridge for low resistance? (End corrections cancel.) Why should P ≈ Q? (Balance points then lie near the centre, maximising sensitivity.)

activity.prompt: Carey Foster bridge: ρ = 0.02 Ω/cm, Y = 1.0 Ω, balance-point shift 15 cm with X > Y. Unknown X (Ω)?

quiz.q: Carey Foster's bridge eliminates:
quiz.why: Interchanging X and Y and using the difference l₁ − l₂ cancels end corrections.

quiz.q: ρ (resistance per cm) is found using:
options: A known resistor and a copper strip of negligible resistance
quiz.why: With X ≈ 0, Y = ρ × shift directly gives ρ.

quiz.q: Why use a tap key for the battery?
options: To avoid heating the wire and resistors
quiz.why: Continuous current heats the bridge wire, changing its resistance.

lessons.title: Lab: Thevenin's & maximum power transfer theorems

scenes.text: An amplifier delivers the most power when the speaker's resistance matches the amplifier's output resistance.
Thevenin's theorem reduces the amplifier to one source and one resistor, making this obvious.

steps.title: Theorems
steps.body: Thevenin: any linear two-terminal network = V_th (open-circuit voltage) in series with R_th (resistance seen with sources replaced by their internal resistances). Norton: I_N = V_th/R_th in parallel with R_th. Maximum power transfer: load power is largest when R_L = R_th, P_max = V_th²/(4R_th), at 50% efficiency.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 12 V source with R₁ = 4 Ω, then R₂ = 12 Ω across the output terminals. V_th = 12 × 12/16 = 9 V; R_th = 4 × 12/16 = 3 Ω. With R_L = 6 Ω: I = 9/9 = 1 A. At R_L = 3 Ω: P_max = 81/12 = 6.75 W.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Build the network on a breadboard; connect R_L and measure I_L. 2) Remove R_L; measure open-circuit voltage (V_th) with a high-resistance voltmeter. 3) Replace the source by a short (if ideal) and measure R_th with a multimeter. 4) Build the Thevenin equivalent from a variable supply and resistor; confirm the same I_L. 5) Vary R_L, record V and I, plot P = VI vs R_L; peak at R_L = R_th.

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Voltmeter loading when measuring V_th; source internal resistance ignored; resistor tolerances (±5%).

steps.title: Viva points
steps.body: Why is efficiency only 50% at maximum power? (Equal power is dissipated in R_th.) Why don't power grids match impedances? (They want high efficiency, not maximum power.)

activity.prompt: For the network with V_th = 9 V and R_th = 3 Ω, what is the maximum power deliverable to a load (W)?

quiz.q: R_th is found by:
options: Replacing ideal voltage sources with shorts and finding resistance across the terminals
quiz.why: Independent sources are deactivated (voltage → short, current → open) to find the equivalent resistance.

quiz.q: Maximum power transfer occurs at:
quiz.why: dP/dR_L = 0 for P = V_th²R_L/(R_th + R_L)² gives R_L = R_th.

quiz.q: Efficiency at maximum power transfer:
quiz.why: Equal currents through equal resistances dissipate equal power in R_th and R_L.

scenes.text: A capacitor discharges through a galvanometer in a few milliseconds — far shorter than the coil's swing period.
The coil gets a sudden kick, and its first throw is proportional to the charge that passed.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: A ballistic galvanometer has a heavy coil with a long period T, so the whole charge q passes before it moves appreciably. Angular impulse NBAq gives the coil KE, converted to torsional energy: q = (CT/(2πNBA)) θ = Kθ. Damping correction: q = Kθ₁(1 + λ/2), where λ is the logarithmic decrement of successive throws.

steps.title: Comparing capacitances
steps.body: Charge C₁ from a battery V, discharge through the BG, note first throw θ₁. Repeat with C₂ at the same V: θ₂. Since q = CV ∝ θ: C₁/C₂ = θ₁/θ₂ (damping corrections cancel for the same instrument). De Sauty's bridge is an alternative null method.

steps.title: Worked calculation
steps.body: θ₁ = 12.0 cm (scale), θ₂ = 8.0 cm with C₂ = 2 μF: C₁ = 2 × 12/8 = 3 μF. If successive throws are 12.0, 10.8 cm: λ = ln(12/10.8) ≈ 0.105, correction factor 1.053.

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Capacitor leakage (discharge promptly); slow discharge compared with T; charging to slightly different voltages; parallax in reading the lamp-and-scale.

steps.title: Viva points
steps.body: Why must T be long? (So the coil is effectively at rest during the charge pulse.) Why is the coil damped little? (To get a measurable throw; correct with λ.) How is a BG brought to rest quickly? (Short-circuit its terminals — electromagnetic damping.)

activity.prompt: Ballistic throws: 12 cm for an unknown C₁ and 8 cm for C₂ = 2 μF at the same voltage. C₁ (μF)?

quiz.q: A ballistic galvanometer's first throw is proportional to:
quiz.why: The coil receives an angular impulse NBAq, so its throw scales with q.

quiz.q: The period of a BG coil must be:
options: Long compared with the discharge time
Short compared with the discharge time
quiz.why: All charge must pass before the coil moves appreciably for the impulse approximation to hold.

quiz.q: Damping correction factor for small λ:
quiz.why: The first throw is reduced by about half a decrement, so q = Kθ₁(1 + λ/2).

questions.q: Potential at the centre of a ring of radius R with charge Q:
questions.why: Every element is at distance R, so V = kQ/R.

questions.why: Q is fixed and C triples, so V = Q/C drops by 3.

uni-bsc-phy-electronics.title: B.Sc Physics · Analog & Digital Electronics
uni-bsc-phy-electronics.description: Diodes and power supplies, transistor biasing and amplifiers, op-amps and oscillators, number systems and Boolean algebra, and combinational and sequential logic with ADC/DAC, with solved circuit numericals and unit exams. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Physics (Hons) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Diodes, rectifiers and regulated power supplies
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Analog and Digital Electronics)
courses.summary: The p–n junction and its I–V characteristic, half-wave and full-wave rectifiers with their figures of merit, capacitor filters and ripple, Zener voltage regulation, and special diodes such as LEDs and photodiodes.
outcomes: Explain the depletion region, barrier potential and the diode equation
Calculate dynamic resistance of a diode at a given current
Find V_dc, ripple factor, efficiency and PIV of half-wave and full-wave rectifiers
Design a capacitor filter for a given ripple
Design and analyse a Zener shunt regulator

scenes.text: Karan puts the batteries of his torch in the wrong way round. The LED stays dark.
A diode lets current flow only one way, like a one-way street. The physics lives in a thin depletion layer.

steps.title: Junction formation
steps.body:
When p- and n-type silicon meet, electrons and holes diffuse across and recombine, leaving fixed ions. This **depletion region** has an electric field and a **barrier potential** V₀ ≈ 0.7 V for Si and 0.3 V for Ge.

- Forward bias lowers the barrier; current rises sharply after the knee (cut-in) voltage.
- Reverse bias widens the region; only a tiny saturation current I_s flows until breakdown.

steps.title: Shockley diode equation
steps.body:
I = I_s [exp(V/ηV_T) − 1]

- V_T = kT/q ≈ 25.9 mV at 300 K (often taken as 26 mV)
- η ≈ 1 for Ge, 1–2 for Si
- **Dynamic resistance** r_d = ηV_T/I ≈ 26 mV/I for η = 1

steps.title: Solved: dynamic resistance
steps.body:
A diode (η = 1) carries 2 mA at 300 K.

- r_d = 26 mV/2 mA = **13 Ω**

At 20 mA it falls to 1.3 Ω: the diode looks more and more like a short circuit as current rises.

steps.title: Solved: series resistor
steps.body:
A 5 V supply drives a Si diode through R = 1 kΩ. Using the constant-drop model (0.7 V):

- I = (5 − 0.7)/1000 = **4.3 mA**

steps.title: Temperature
steps.body: I_s roughly doubles every 10 °C, and the forward drop at fixed current falls by about 2 mV/°C. Ignoring this causes thermal runaway in poorly designed circuits.

activity.prompt: Find the dynamic resistance of a diode (η = 1, V_T = 26 mV) at a forward current of 0.5 mA, in Ω.

quiz.q: The barrier potential of a silicon junction is about:
quiz.why: Silicon's larger band gap gives a built-in potential of about 0.7 V, compared with 0.3 V for germanium.

quiz.q: In reverse bias, the depletion region:
quiz.why: Reverse bias adds to the barrier, pulling carriers away from the junction and widening the depletion layer.

quiz.q: Dynamic resistance r_d varies with current as:
quiz.why: Differentiating the diode equation gives r_d = ηV_T/I, inversely proportional to current.

scenes.text: Indian mains is 230 V AC at 50 Hz, but a phone battery needs steady DC.
The first job of every charger is rectification: turning both halves of the AC wave into one direction.

steps.title: Half-wave rectifier
steps.body:
One diode passes only the positive half-cycle (V_m = peak).

- V_dc = V_m/π = 0.318 V_m
- V_rms = V_m/2
- Ripple factor r = √[(V_rms/V_dc)² − 1] = **1.21**
- Maximum efficiency **40.6%**
- PIV = V_m

steps.title: Full-wave rectifiers
steps.body:
Centre-tapped (2 diodes) or bridge (4 diodes):

- V_dc = 2V_m/π = 0.637 V_m
- V_rms = V_m/√2
- Ripple factor **0.482**
- Maximum efficiency **81.2%**
- Ripple frequency = 2f = 100 Hz in India
- PIV: 2V_m for centre-tapped, V_m for bridge

steps.title: Solved: comparing outputs
steps.body:
Secondary peak V_m = 20 V (ideal diodes).

- Half-wave: V_dc = 20/π = **6.37 V**
- Full-wave: V_dc = 40/π = **12.73 V**
- For a bridge with Si diodes, two diodes conduct at once, so the peak falls to 20 − 1.4 = 18.6 V and V_dc ≈ 11.8 V.

steps.title: Why bridges dominate
steps.body: A bridge needs no centre-tapped transformer and has half the PIV of a centre-tapped circuit, so it is the standard choice in power supplies.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Never probe mains-side circuits without isolation. Practise rectifier labs with a step-down transformer of 6–12 V.

activity.prompt: A full-wave rectifier with ideal diodes has V_m = 15 V. Find V_dc = 2V_m/π in V (two decimals).

quiz.q: The ripple factor of a half-wave rectifier is:
quiz.why: Using V_rms = V_m/2 and V_dc = V_m/π, r = √[(π/2)² − 1] ≈ 1.21.

quiz.q: The ripple frequency of a full-wave rectifier on 50 Hz mains is:
quiz.why: Both half-cycles produce an output pulse, so there are 100 pulses per second.

quiz.q: The PIV across each diode in a bridge rectifier is:
quiz.why: In a bridge, a non-conducting diode is effectively in parallel with the secondary through a conducting diode, so it sees about V_m.

scenes.text: A home-made amplifier hums loudly at 100 Hz. Sana's teacher points at the tiny filter capacitor.
A larger capacitor stores more charge between peaks, so the output dips less. The hum fades.

steps.title: Capacitor (shunt) filter
steps.body:
The capacitor charges to V_m at each peak and discharges through the load between peaks.

For a full-wave rectifier:

- Peak-to-peak ripple **V_r ≈ I_dc/(2fC)**
- V_dc ≈ V_m − V_r/2
- Ripple factor r = 1/(4√3 fR_LC)

For half-wave, replace 2f with f.

steps.title: Solved: ripple voltage
steps.body:
Full-wave, f = 50 Hz, I_dc = 100 mA, C = 1000 μF.

- V_r = 0.1/(2 × 50 × 1000 × 10⁻⁶) = **1.0 V** peak-to-peak
- If V_m = 12 V, V_dc ≈ 11.5 V.

steps.title: Solved: choosing C
steps.body:
Need V_r ≤ 0.5 V at 200 mA, full-wave, 50 Hz.

- C ≥ I/(2fV_r) = 0.2/(100 × 0.5) = 4.0 × 10⁻³ F
- Choose **4700 μF** (next standard value)

steps.title: Other filters
steps.body:
- **Inductor (choke) filter**: ripple falls as load current rises; good for heavy loads.
- **LC (L-section) filter**: ripple nearly independent of load.
- **π (CLC) filter**: very low ripple but poorer regulation.

steps.title: Surge current
steps.body: A large discharged capacitor draws a big inrush current at switch-on. Diodes must be rated for this surge, or a small series resistor or NTC thermistor is added.

activity.prompt: A full-wave rectifier on 50 Hz mains supplies 200 mA through a 2200 μF filter capacitor. Find the peak-to-peak ripple V_r = I/(2fC) in V (two decimals).

quiz.q: Increasing the filter capacitance:
quiz.why: V_r = I/(2fC), so a larger C discharges less between peaks.

quiz.q: An inductor filter works best when the load current is:
quiz.why: An inductor opposes changes in current, and its smoothing improves as load current rises (ripple ∝ 1/ωL relative to R_L).

quiz.q: For the same C and load, a half-wave rectifier's ripple compared with full-wave is:
quiz.why: The capacitor discharges for a whole period 1/f instead of 1/2f, doubling the ripple.

scenes.text: In a village workshop, the mains voltage swings between 190 V and 250 V through the day.
A Zener diode at the end of the supply holds the output close to 5.1 V anyway.

steps.title: Zener breakdown
steps.body: A heavily doped diode in reverse bias breaks down at a sharp voltage V_Z and keeps nearly that voltage over a wide current range. Below about 5 V the mechanism is Zener (tunnelling); above about 6 V it is avalanche.

steps.title: Shunt regulator
steps.body:
V_in → series resistor R_S → Zener in parallel with load R_L.

- I_S = (V_in − V_Z)/R_S
- I_L = V_Z/R_L
- **I_Z = I_S − I_L**
- Need I_Z > I_Z(min) at minimum V_in and maximum load, and P_Z = V_Z I_Z below rating at maximum V_in and no load.

steps.title: Special diodes
steps.body:
- **LED**: forward-biased direct-gap semiconductor emits light; colour set by band gap (red ≈ 1.8 V, blue ≈ 3 V forward drop).
- **Photodiode**: reverse-biased; current ∝ light intensity.
- **Solar cell**: unbiased junction; light generates power (Si: V_oc ≈ 0.6 V).
- **Varactor**: reverse-biased junction capacitance tunes radios.

steps.title: Modern practice
steps.body: Today most supplies use IC regulators like the 7805 (5 V) or switching regulators, but the Zener shunt still appears as a reference and in lab exams.

activity.prompt: V_in = 12 V, V_Z = 5.1 V, R_S = 150 Ω, R_L = 510 Ω. Find the Zener current I_Z in mA.

quiz.q: A Zener diode is used as a regulator in:
quiz.why: In reverse breakdown the voltage across a Zener stays nearly constant over a wide current range.

quiz.q: In a shunt regulator, if the load current rises, the Zener current:
quiz.why: I_S is fixed by V_in and R_S, so I_Z = I_S − I_L falls when the load takes more.

quiz.q: A photodiode is normally operated in:
quiz.why: In reverse bias the dark current is tiny, so the light-generated current dominates and is proportional to intensity.

questions.q: V_T = kT/q at 300 K is about:
A Si diode in series with 2.2 kΩ across 9 V passes about:
questions.why: I = (9 − 0.7)/2200 ≈ 3.8 mA using the constant-drop model.

questions.q: The maximum efficiency of a full-wave rectifier is:
A half-wave rectifier with V_m = 31.4 V gives V_dc of:
The PIV across a diode in a centre-tapped full-wave rectifier is:
questions.why: The non-conducting diode sees the full secondary, which is twice the half-winding peak.

questions.q: The ripple factor of an unfiltered full-wave rectifier is:
questions.why: With V_rms = V_m/√2 and V_dc = 2V_m/π, r = √[(π²/8) − 1] ≈ 0.482.

questions.q: Full-wave, 50 Hz, I_dc = 50 mA, C = 500 μF. Peak-to-peak ripple is:
An L-section filter is preferred because:
options: ripple is nearly independent of load
questions.why: The inductor's effect improves with load while the capacitor's worsens, so together they keep ripple roughly constant.

questions.q: Regulator: V_in = 20 V, V_Z = 10 V, R_S = 250 Ω, no load. Zener power is:
Zener breakdown at low voltages (< 5 V) is mainly due to:
options: quantum tunnelling across a thin junction
questions.why: Heavy doping makes the depletion layer so thin that electrons tunnel directly from valence to conduction band.

questions.q: A blue LED has a higher forward voltage than a red LED because:
options: blue light needs a larger band gap
questions.why: Photon energy equals roughly the band gap, and blue photons (≈ 2.7 eV) carry more energy than red (≈ 1.9 eV).

questions.q: For R_S = 100 Ω, V_Z = 5 V, V_in = 9 V and I_Z(min) = 5 mA, the minimum allowed R_L is about:

courses.title: Unit 2 · Bipolar transistors, biasing and amplifiers; FETs
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Analog and Digital Electronics)
courses.summary: How a BJT works, its CB, CE and CC configurations, current gains α and β, DC load lines and biasing for stability, small-signal analysis of the CE amplifier, and the JFET and MOSFET as voltage-controlled devices.
outcomes: Relate I_E, I_B, I_C, α and β for a BJT
Draw a DC load line and locate the Q-point for fixed and voltage-divider bias
Explain bias stability and why voltage-divider bias is preferred
Calculate voltage gain of a CE amplifier using the r_e model
Use Shockley's equation and transconductance for a JFET; compare JFET and MOSFET

scenes.text: A small turn of a tap controls a big flow of water from the overhead tank.
In a transistor, a small base current controls a collector current a hundred times larger.

steps.title: Structure and action
steps.body: An npn transistor has a thin, lightly doped base between a heavily doped emitter and a collector. In the **active region**: emitter–base junction forward biased, collector–base junction reverse biased. Electrons injected from the emitter mostly cross the thin base and are swept into the collector.

steps.title: Current relations
steps.body:
- I_E = I_B + I_C
- α = I_C/I_E (CB gain, 0.95–0.995)
- β = I_C/I_B (CE gain, 50–300)
- **β = α/(1 − α)**, α = β/(1 + β)
- Leakage: I_CEO = (1 + β)I_CBO

steps.title: Three configurations
steps.body:
| | CB | CE | CC (emitter follower) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current gain | α < 1 | β high | 1 + β |
| Voltage gain | high | high | ≈ 1 |
| Input resistance | low | medium | high |
| Output resistance | high | medium | low |
| Phase shift | 0° | 180° | 0° |

CE is the usual amplifier; CC is a buffer.

steps.title: Regions
steps.body: Cut-off (both junctions reverse): switch OFF. Saturation (both forward, V_CE ≈ 0.2 V): switch ON. Active: amplifier.

activity.prompt: A transistor has α = 0.995. Find β = α/(1 − α).

quiz.q: In the active region, the collector–base junction is:
quiz.why: A reverse-biased collector junction sweeps electrons arriving from the base into the collector.

quiz.q: The emitter follower (CC) has a voltage gain of about:
quiz.why: The emitter follows the base voltage minus about 0.7 V, so small-signal voltage gain is close to 1.

quiz.q: If β = 100, α is:

scenes.text: Varun's amplifier sounds fine in the morning but distorts by afternoon when the lab gets hot.
His fixed-bias design lets the Q-point wander with β and temperature. Voltage-divider bias would hold it still.

steps.title: DC load line
steps.body:
For a CE stage: V_CE = V_CC − I_C R_C (plus R_E if present).

- Saturation end: I_C = V_CC/R_C at V_CE = 0
- Cut-off end: V_CE = V_CC at I_C = 0

The operating (Q) point should sit near the middle for maximum symmetrical swing.

steps.title: Solved: fixed bias
steps.body:
V_CC = 12 V, R_B = 470 kΩ, R_C = 2.2 kΩ, β = 100.

- I_B = (12 − 0.7)/470 k = 24.0 μA
- I_C = 2.40 mA
- V_CE = 12 − 2.40 × 2.2 = **6.7 V**

But I_C ∝ β, so a transistor with β = 200 would saturate.

steps.title: Voltage-divider bias
steps.body:
R₁ and R₂ set V_B; an emitter resistor R_E gives negative feedback.

- V_TH = V_CC R₂/(R₁ + R₂)
- If βR_E ≫ R_TH: I_E ≈ (V_TH − 0.7)/R_E, nearly independent of β.

steps.title: Stability factor
steps.body: S = ∂I_C/∂I_CBO. Fixed bias: S = 1 + β (poor). Voltage-divider bias with R_E: S can be brought close to 1, because a rising I_C raises V_E and reduces V_BE.

activity.prompt: Fixed bias: V_CC = 9 V, R_B = 330 kΩ, R_C = 1 kΩ, β = 150, V_BE = 0.7 V. Find V_CE in V (two decimals).

quiz.q: The saturation end of the load line is at:
quiz.why: Setting V_CE = 0 in V_CE = V_CC − I_C R_C gives the maximum collector current V_CC/R_C.

quiz.q: Voltage-divider bias is more stable than fixed bias because:
options: R_E provides negative feedback making I_C nearly independent of β
quiz.why: A rise in I_C raises V_E, which lowers V_BE and pulls I_C back.

quiz.q: For fixed bias, the stability factor S is about:
quiz.why: With no feedback, any leakage change is amplified by (1 + β), so S = 1 + β.

scenes.text: A dynamic microphone produces only a few millivolts. Diya's speaker needs volts.
A single CE stage with a gain of about 200 bridges much of that gap.

steps.title: r_e model
steps.body:
For small signals the base–emitter junction acts like a resistance

**r_e = 26 mV/I_E**

Input resistance at the base: r_π = βr_e.

steps.title: Voltage gain
steps.body:
- R_E bypassed by a capacitor: **A_v = −R_C/r_e** (with load: −(R_C ∥ R_L)/r_e)
- R_E unbypassed: A_v ≈ −R_C/(r_e + R_E) ≈ −R_C/R_E, lower but stable
- Minus sign: 180° phase inversion

steps.title: Solved: gain
steps.body:
Continue the voltage-divider design: I_E = 1.41 mA, R_C = 4.7 kΩ, R_E bypassed.

- r_e = 26/1.41 = 18.4 Ω
- A_v = −4700/18.4 = **−255**
- With R_L = 4.7 kΩ: R_C ∥ R_L = 2.35 kΩ, A_v = −128

steps.title: h-parameters
steps.body: Many textbooks use the hybrid model: h_ie (input resistance ≈ βr_e), h_fe (≈ β), h_re and h_oe (often neglected). Approximate CE results: A_i ≈ −h_fe, A_v ≈ −h_fe R_L/h_ie, Z_i ≈ h_ie.

steps.title: Frequency response
steps.body: Coupling and bypass capacitors set a lower cut-off f_L; junction and stray capacitances set an upper cut-off f_H. Bandwidth = f_H − f_L, measured at the −3 dB (0.707) points. Gain–bandwidth is roughly constant for a given device.

steps.title: Common slip
steps.body: r_e depends on the DC emitter current, so always find the Q-point first, then the AC gain.

activity.prompt: A CE amplifier has I_E = 2.0 mA, R_C = 3.3 kΩ and a fully bypassed R_E, with no load. Find the magnitude of voltage gain |A_v| = R_C/r_e (r_e = 26 mV/I_E), nearest whole number.

quiz.q: r_e of a BJT at I_E = 1 mA is about:
quiz.why: r_e = 26 mV/1 mA = 26 Ω.

quiz.q: The phase shift between input and output of a CE amplifier is:
quiz.why: A rising base voltage increases I_C, increasing the drop across R_C and lowering the collector voltage.

quiz.q: Removing the bypass capacitor across R_E:
quiz.why: The unbypassed R_E adds AC negative feedback, so gain falls to about R_C/R_E but becomes less dependent on the transistor.

scenes.text: The processor in Meena's phone contains billions of MOSFETs, each switching billions of times a second.
They are controlled by voltage, not current, so their gates draw almost no current when idle.

steps.title: JFET
steps.body:
An n-channel JFET is a bar of n-silicon with p-gate regions. Reverse-biasing the gate widens depletion layers and narrows the channel.

**I_D = I_DSS (1 − V_GS/V_P)²**

V_P = pinch-off voltage (negative for n-channel), I_DSS = drain current at V_GS = 0. Input resistance is very high (≈ 10⁹ Ω).

steps.title: Solved: drain current and g_m
steps.body:
I_DSS = 10 mA, V_P = −4 V, V_GS = −2 V.

- I_D = 10 × (1 − 0.5)² = **2.5 mA**
- g_m0 = 2I_DSS/|V_P| = 5 mS
- g_m = g_m0 (1 − V_GS/V_P) = **2.5 mS**
- Common-source gain with R_D = 4 kΩ: A_v = −g_m R_D = −10

steps.title: MOSFET
steps.body:
The gate is insulated by a thin oxide (SiO₂ or high-k).

- **Enhancement** MOSFET: no channel at V_GS = 0; channel forms above threshold V_T. I_D = K(V_GS − V_T)² in saturation.
- **Depletion** MOSFET: channel exists at V_GS = 0.
- CMOS logic pairs n- and p-MOSFETs so that almost no current flows in either steady state.

steps.title: BJT vs FET
steps.body:
| | BJT | FET |
|---|---|---|
| Control | current (bipolar) | voltage (unipolar) |
| Input resistance | kΩ | MΩ–GΩ |
| Gain per stage | higher | lower |
| Noise | more | less |
| Thermal runaway | possible | resistant |

steps.title: Handling MOSFETs
steps.body: The gate oxide is only nanometres thick and can be destroyed by static discharge. Use a wrist strap and anti-static foam in the lab.

activity.prompt: An n-channel JFET has I_DSS = 8 mA and V_P = −4 V. Find I_D at V_GS = −1 V, in mA.

quiz.why: At pinch-off the channel is closed, so (1 − V_GS/V_P)² = 0.

quiz.q: An enhancement MOSFET conducts only when:
quiz.why: Without enough gate voltage there is no inversion layer, so no channel exists.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Operational amplifiers, feedback and oscillators
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Analog and Digital Electronics)
courses.summary: The ideal op-amp and its golden rules, inverting and non-inverting amplifiers, summing amplifiers, integrators and differentiators, real op-amp limits such as CMRR and slew rate, negative and positive feedback, and RC phase-shift and Wien-bridge oscillators.
outcomes: Apply the virtual-short rules to analyse op-amp circuits
Design inverting, non-inverting and summing amplifiers for a given gain
Analyse integrators and differentiators in time and frequency
Use CMRR and slew rate to judge real op-amp performance
State the Barkhausen criterion and design RC phase-shift and Wien-bridge oscillators

lessons.title: Ideal op-amp: inverting and non-inverting amplifiers

scenes.text: At Lamington Road in Mumbai, Rohan buys a 741 op-amp for about the price of a cup of tea.
With two resistors it becomes an amplifier with any gain he wants. Feedback does the work.

steps.title: Ideal op-amp
steps.body:
Open-loop gain A → ∞, input resistance → ∞, output resistance → 0, infinite bandwidth.

**Golden rules with negative feedback:**
1. No current flows into the inputs.
2. The output adjusts so that V₊ = V₋ (virtual short).

steps.title: Two basic amplifiers
steps.body:
- **Inverting**: input through R₁ to V₋, R_f from output to V₋, V₊ grounded.
  **A_v = −R_f/R₁**, input resistance = R₁. V₋ is a *virtual ground*.
- **Non-inverting**: input to V₊, R₁ from V₋ to ground, R_f to output.
  **A_v = 1 + R_f/R₁**, input resistance very high.
- **Voltage follower**: R_f = 0, R₁ = ∞, A_v = 1.

steps.title: Solved: inverting amplifier
steps.body:
R₁ = 10 kΩ, R_f = 100 kΩ, V_in = 0.5 V.

- A_v = −100/10 = −10
- V_out = **−5 V**

With ±12 V supplies, V_in = 1.5 V would ask for −15 V, so the output saturates near −11 V.

steps.title: Solved: designing a gain of 21
steps.body: Non-inverting: 1 + R_f/R₁ = 21, so R_f/R₁ = 20. Choose R₁ = 1 kΩ and **R_f = 20 kΩ**.

steps.title: Saturation
steps.body: An op-amp output cannot exceed its supply rails (for a 741, about 1–2 V less than the rails). Always check that the calculated output is within range.

activity.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier uses R₁ = 4.7 kΩ and R_f = 47 kΩ. Find V_out for V_in = 0.30 V, in V.

quiz.q: The gain of an inverting amplifier is:
quiz.why: With V₋ at virtual ground, the input current V_in/R₁ flows through R_f, giving V_out = −(R_f/R₁)V_in.

quiz.q: A voltage follower has gain:
quiz.why: With full feedback, V₋ = V_out and V₊ = V_in, so V_out = V_in.

quiz.q: The 'virtual ground' in an inverting amplifier means:
options: V₋ ≈ 0 V but no current flows to ground there
quiz.why: Negative feedback holds V₋ equal to the grounded V₊, yet no current enters the input.

scenes.text: Before digital computers, engineers solved differential equations for rockets with racks of op-amps.
Op-amps could add, integrate and differentiate, which is where the name 'operational' amplifier comes from.

steps.title: Summing amplifier
steps.body:
Several inputs through R₁, R₂, R₃ into the virtual ground:

V_out = −R_f (V₁/R₁ + V₂/R₂ + V₃/R₃)

With all resistors equal: V_out = −(V₁ + V₂ + V₃). Weighted resistors (R, 2R, 4R, 8R) make a simple DAC.

steps.title: Integrator
steps.body:
Replace R_f with C:

**V_out = −(1/RC)∫V_in dt**

- A constant input gives a ramp.
- A square wave gives a triangle wave.
- Practical circuits add a large resistor across C to stop drift into saturation.

steps.title: Solved: ramp
steps.body:
V_in = +1 V (constant), R = 10 kΩ, C = 1 μF, starting at 0 V.

- RC = 0.01 s, slope = −1/0.01 = −100 V/s
- After 50 ms: V_out = **−5 V**

steps.title: Differentiator
steps.body:
Swap R and C: **V_out = −RC dV_in/dt**.

- A triangle wave gives a square wave.
- Gain rises with frequency, so noise is amplified; practical versions add a small series resistor with C.

activity.prompt: An integrator has R = 100 kΩ and C = 0.1 μF and starts at 0 V. A constant +2 V input is applied for 20 ms. Find V_out in V.

quiz.q: A square wave into an integrator produces:
quiz.why: Integrating a constant level gives a linear ramp, so alternating levels give alternating ramps: a triangle.

quiz.q: A differentiator's gain increases with:
quiz.why: V_out = −RC dV/dt, so for a sine wave the gain magnitude is ωRC, which rises with frequency.

quiz.q: Three equal inputs of 1 V into a summing amplifier with all resistors equal give:
quiz.why: V_out = −(V₁ + V₂ + V₃) = −3 V for equal resistors.

lessons.title: Real op-amps: CMRR, offset and slew rate

scenes.text: An ECG picks up a 1 mV heart signal, but the patient's body also carries about 1 V of 50 Hz mains hum.
The hum is common to both electrodes. A differential amplifier with high CMRR removes it and keeps the heartbeat.

steps.title: Differential and common-mode gain
steps.body:
V_out = A_d(V₁ − V₂) + A_cm(V₁ + V₂)/2

**CMRR = A_d/A_cm**, in dB: 20 log(A_d/A_cm). The 741 has typical CMRR ≈ 90 dB. Instrumentation amplifiers reach 120 dB or more.

steps.title: Slew rate
steps.body:
The maximum rate of change of output voltage. For a sine of peak V_p:

**f_max = SR/(2πV_p)**

741: SR ≈ 0.5 V/μs. TL081: about 13 V/μs.

steps.title: Solved: slew-limited frequency
steps.body:
741 (0.5 V/μs), V_p = 10 V.

- f_max = 0.5 × 10⁶/(2π × 10) = **7.96 kHz**

Above this a sine output turns into a triangle.

steps.title: Other non-idealities
steps.body:
- **Input offset voltage** (741: ≈ 1 mV) appears at the output multiplied by (1 + R_f/R₁).
- **Input bias current**: add a resistor R₁ ∥ R_f at V₊ to cancel its effect.
- **Gain–bandwidth product**: 741 ≈ 1 MHz. A gain-of-100 stage has only about 10 kHz bandwidth.

activity.prompt: A TL081 op-amp has slew rate 13 V/μs. Find the highest frequency for an undistorted 10 V peak sine output, in kHz (nearest whole number).

quiz.q: An ideal op-amp has CMRR of:
quiz.why: An ideal differential amplifier rejects common-mode signals completely, so A_cm = 0 and CMRR is infinite.

quiz.q: Slew rate limits:
options: how fast the output can change
quiz.why: Slew rate is the maximum dV_out/dt, set by internal compensation capacitance.

quiz.q: A 741 with GBW = 1 MHz in a gain-of-50 stage has bandwidth about:
quiz.why: Bandwidth ≈ GBW/gain = 1 MHz/50 = 20 kHz.

scenes.text: At a college fest, the microphone is pointed at a speaker and a loud squeal fills the hall.
Sound loops round with enough gain and the right phase. That accidental oscillator follows the same rule as a designed one.

steps.title: Negative feedback
steps.body: With open-loop gain A and feedback fraction β: **A_f = A/(1 + Aβ)**. For Aβ ≫ 1, A_f ≈ 1/β. Benefits: stable gain, wider bandwidth, less distortion, controlled input and output impedances.

steps.title: Barkhausen criterion
steps.body:
Sustained oscillation needs, at one frequency:

1. Loop gain |Aβ| = 1
2. Total loop phase shift = 0° or 360°

In practice |Aβ| is made slightly above 1 to start, and limited by non-linearity or an automatic gain control.

steps.title: RC phase-shift oscillator
steps.body:
Three RC sections give 180°; an inverting amplifier gives another 180°.

- **f = 1/(2π√6 RC)**
- Amplifier gain needed: **|A| ≥ 29**

steps.title: Wien-bridge oscillator
steps.body:
A series RC and parallel RC network gives 0° phase shift at

- **f = 1/(2πRC)**, where β = 1/3
- Non-inverting gain needed: **A = 3**, i.e. R_f = 2R₁

Used in audio signal generators. LC (Hartley, Colpitts) and crystal oscillators are used at radio frequencies.

steps.title: Solved: frequencies
steps.body:
R = 10 kΩ, C = 10 nF, RC = 10⁻⁴ s.

- Wien bridge: f = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁴) = **1.59 kHz**
- Phase shift: f = 1592/√6 = **650 Hz**

activity.prompt: A Wien-bridge oscillator uses R = 4.7 kΩ and C = 22 nF. Find f = 1/(2πRC) in Hz (nearest 5 Hz).

quiz.q: The Barkhausen criterion requires a loop phase shift of:
quiz.why: The fed-back signal must arrive in phase with the original so it reinforces itself.

quiz.q: A Wien-bridge oscillator needs an amplifier gain of:
quiz.why: At the oscillation frequency the Wien network passes 1/3 of the signal, so the amplifier must supply a gain of 3.

quiz.q: Negative feedback with Aβ ≫ 1 makes the closed-loop gain about:
quiz.why: A_f = A/(1 + Aβ) → 1/β, which depends only on the passive feedback network.

A non-inverting amplifier with R_f = 9 kΩ and R₁ = 1 kΩ has gain:

questions.why: The input sees R₁ connected to a virtual ground.

An integrator with RC = 1 ms and constant input −0.5 V ramps at:
A triangle wave into a differentiator gives:
questions.why: The slope of a triangle alternates between two constants, so its derivative is a square wave.

A 741 (0.5 V/μs) must output 5 V peak. The maximum sine frequency is about:
An RC phase-shift oscillator needs a minimum amplifier gain of:
questions.why: The three-section RC network attenuates by a factor of 29 at the frequency where it gives 180°.

With A = 10⁵ and β = 0.01, the closed-loop gain is about:

questions.why: Input offset is amplified by the noise gain 1 + R_f/R₁ = 101, giving 101 mV.
