courses.title: Unit 4 · Number systems, logic gates and Boolean algebra
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Analog and Digital Electronics)
courses.summary: Binary, octal, hexadecimal and BCD; Gray code and two's-complement arithmetic; basic and universal logic gates; Boolean laws and De Morgan's theorems; SOP and POS forms and Karnaugh-map minimisation up to four variables.
outcomes: Convert between decimal, binary, octal, hexadecimal and BCD
Perform binary subtraction using two's complement
Write truth tables for AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR, and build any gate from NAND or NOR
Simplify expressions with Boolean laws and De Morgan's theorems
Minimise functions of up to four variables with Karnaugh maps, including don't-cares

scenes.text: Pooja designs a website and types #FF8800 for orange. Her friend asks what those letters mean.
It is hexadecimal: FF = 255 red, 88 = 136 green, 00 = 0 blue. Every digital system speaks in bases.

steps.title: Positional systems
steps.body:
A number in base r: d_n…d₁d₀ = Σ dᵢ rⁱ.

- Binary (r = 2), octal (8), decimal (10), hexadecimal (16, digits 0–9, A–F).
- Decimal → binary: divide by 2 repeatedly, read remainders bottom-up.
- Binary → hex: group 4 bits from the right; binary → octal: group 3 bits.

steps.title: Two's complement
steps.body:
For an n-bit number, −X is represented as 2ⁿ − X: invert all bits and add 1. Range for 8 bits: −128 to +127.

Subtraction A − B = A + (two's complement of B); discard the final carry.

steps.title: Codes
steps.body:
- **BCD (8421)**: each decimal digit in 4 bits; 59 = 0101 1001.
- **Gray code**: successive values differ in one bit (used in rotary encoders). Binary → Gray: g₃ = b₃, gᵢ = bᵢ₊₁ ⊕ bᵢ. Example: 0111 → 0100.
- **ASCII**: 7-bit text code; 'A' = 65 = 41₁₆.

activity.prompt: Convert the binary number 11010110 to decimal.

quiz.q: The hexadecimal number 3F equals in decimal:
The 8-bit two's complement of 00000110 is:
quiz.why: Invert to 11111001, then add 1 to get 11111010, which represents −6.

quiz.q: Gray code is useful because:
options: adjacent values differ in only one bit
quiz.why: A single bit change between neighbours avoids glitches when a shaft encoder passes between positions.

scenes.text: A car alarm sounds if the door opens AND the alarm is armed, OR if the glass breaks.
That sentence is already a logic circuit: two inputs into an AND, its output and a third into an OR.

steps.title: Universal gates
steps.body:
NAND alone (or NOR alone) can build every logic function.

- NOT from NAND: tie both inputs, (A·A)′ = A′
- AND: NAND followed by NAND-as-NOT (2 gates)
- OR: invert each input with NAND, then NAND: (A′B′)′ = A + B (3 gates)
- XOR: **4 NAND gates**

steps.title: Logic families
steps.body: TTL (74xx) runs on 5 V; CMOS (4000, 74HC) uses less power. Popular ICs: 7400 quad NAND, 7402 quad NOR, 7408 quad AND, 7432 quad OR, 7486 quad XOR.

steps.title: Lab tip
steps.body: Unused TTL inputs float high but pick up noise; tie them to V_CC or ground. Never leave CMOS inputs floating.

activity.prompt: What is the minimum number of 2-input NAND gates needed to build a 2-input OR gate?

quiz.q: The output of a NOR gate is 1 only when:
quiz.why: NOR is the inverse of OR, and OR is 0 only when all inputs are 0.

quiz.q: XOR gives output 1 when:
quiz.why: A ⊕ B = A′B + AB′ is 1 exactly when one input is 1 and the other 0.

quiz.q: Why are NAND and NOR called universal gates?
options: any Boolean function can be built from either alone
quiz.why: Each can make NOT, AND and OR, which together can express any logic function.

lessons.title: Boolean algebra and De Morgan's theorems

scenes.text: A start-up in Bengaluru needs to cut the cost of a controller board by removing chips.
Simplifying the logic expression by Boolean algebra removes two gates before any soldering starts.

steps.title: Key laws
steps.body:
- Identity: A + 0 = A, A·1 = A
- Null: A + 1 = 1, A·0 = 0
- Idempotent: A + A = A, A·A = A
- Complement: A + A′ = 1, A·A′ = 0
- Involution: (A′)′ = A
- Absorption: A + AB = A, A(A + B) = A
- **A + A′B = A + B**
- Distributive: A + BC = (A + B)(A + C)

steps.title: De Morgan's theorems
steps.body:
**(A + B)′ = A′B′** and **(AB)′ = A′ + B′**.

Rule: break the bar, change the operator. This is why a NAND is equivalent to an OR with inverted inputs (bubbled OR).

steps.title: Solved: simplification
steps.body:
Y = AB + AB′ + A′B

- AB + AB′ = A(B + B′) = A
- Y = A + A′B = **A + B**

Three AND terms and an OR become one OR gate.

steps.title: Solved: De Morgan
steps.body:
Y = ((A + B)′ + C)′

- = (A + B)·C′ (break outer bar)
- = **AC′ + BC′**

steps.title: SOP and POS
steps.body:
- **Sum of products (minterms)**: F = Σm(…), one term for each 1 in the truth table.
- **Product of sums (maxterms)**: F = ΠM(…), one term for each 0.
- Example: F(A, B) = Σm(1, 2) = A′B + AB′ = A ⊕ B.

activity.prompt: Evaluate Y = (A + B′)·(A′ + C) for A = 1, B = 1, C = 0. Enter 0 or 1.

quiz.q: A + A′B simplifies to:
quiz.why: A + A′B = (A + A′)(A + B) = A + B by the distributive law.

quiz.q: By De Morgan, (AB)′ equals:
quiz.why: Breaking the bar over a product turns AND into OR and complements each variable.

quiz.q: A(A + B) simplifies to:
quiz.why: By absorption, A·A + AB = A + AB = A(1 + B) = A.

scenes.text: Algebra can get messy with four variables. Maurice Karnaugh, in 1953, drew the truth table as a grid instead.
Neighbouring 1s show up as rectangles, and each rectangle is one simple term.

steps.title: The map
steps.body: Cells are arranged in **Gray-code order** (00, 01, 11, 10), so neighbours differ in one variable. A 4-variable map has 16 cells; edges wrap around like a torus.

steps.title: Grouping rules
steps.body:
1. Group 1s in rectangles of 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells.
2. Make groups as large as possible.
3. Use as few groups as possible; groups may overlap.
4. A group of 2ᵏ cells removes k variables.
5. Don't-care cells (X) may be used as 1s if they help.

steps.title: Solved: three variables
steps.body:
F(A, B, C) = Σm(1, 3, 5, 7).

- All four cells have C = 1.
- One group of 4 → **F = C**

steps.title: Solved: corners
steps.body:
F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 2, 8, 10).

- These are the four corners: B = 0 and D = 0 in all of them.
- Corners wrap around to form one group of 4 → **F = B′D′**

steps.title: Solved: with don't-cares
steps.body:
BCD digit is 5 or more: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(5, 6, 7, 8, 9), d(10–15).

- Group m8, m9 with d10–d15 → **A**
- Group m5, m7 with d13, d15 → **BD**
- Group m6, m7 with d14, d15 → **BC**
- F = **A + BD + BC**

activity.prompt: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 1, 2, 3, 8, 9, 10, 11). How many literals are in the minimal SOP expression?

quiz.q: K-map cells are ordered in Gray code so that:
options: adjacent cells differ in exactly one variable
quiz.why: One-bit differences between neighbours let us combine adjacent 1s using A + A′ = 1.

quiz.q: A group of 8 cells in a 4-variable K-map gives a term with how many literals?
quiz.why: A group of 2³ cells eliminates 3 of the 4 variables, leaving one literal.

quiz.q: Don't-care conditions:
options: can be taken as 1 or 0, whichever simplifies more
quiz.why: Those input combinations never occur, so their outputs can be chosen freely to enlarge groups.

questions.q: 25₁₀ in binary is:
The octal equivalent of 111 010₂ is:
BCD for 93 is:
questions.why: Each decimal digit is coded separately: 9 = 1001 and 3 = 0011.

questions.q: In 8-bit two's complement, 11111111 represents:
questions.why: Inverting gives 00000000, adding 1 gives 1, so the value is −1.

questions.q: Gray code for binary 1011 is:
Which gate gives 1 only when both inputs are equal?
questions.why: XNOR is the complement of XOR, so it is 1 when inputs match.

questions.q: How many 2-input NAND gates make an XOR gate (minimum)?
questions.why: The standard construction uses one NAND for (AB)′ and three more, four in total.

questions.q: AB + A′C + BC simplifies (consensus theorem) to:
questions.why: BC is the consensus of AB and A′C and is redundant.

questions.q: (A′ + B′)′ equals:
questions.why: By De Morgan, (A′ + B′)′ = A″B″ = AB.

questions.q: F(A, B, C) = Σm(0, 2, 4, 6) minimises to:
questions.why: All four minterms have C = 0, so one group of four gives C′.

questions.q: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(5, 7, 13, 15) minimises to:
questions.why: These four cells share B = 1 and D = 1 and form one group of four.

questions.q: Using the K-map, F(A, B, C) = Σm(1, 2, 3, 5, 7) minimises to:
questions.why: m1, m3, m5, m7 group to C; m2 with m3 groups to A′B; so F = C + A′B.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Combinational and sequential logic, DAC and ADC
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Analog and Digital Electronics)
courses.summary: Half and full adders, multiplexers, decoders and encoders; SR, JK, D and T flip-flops; ripple and synchronous counters and shift registers; and the R-2R ladder DAC with successive-approximation and flash ADCs.
outcomes: Design half and full adders and a 4-bit parallel adder
Use multiplexers, demultiplexers, decoders and encoders
Explain SR, JK, D and T flip-flops, race-around and master–slave operation
Design ripple counters of any modulus and use shift registers
Calculate DAC output and resolution and compare ADC types

scenes.text: Aman presses 7 + 6 on a basic calculator and 13 appears instantly.
Inside, a chain of full adders adds the binary digits column by column, passing carries along.

steps.title: Half adder
steps.body:
Adds two bits A and B.

- Sum S = A ⊕ B
- Carry C = AB

One XOR and one AND gate.

steps.title: Full adder
steps.body:
Adds A, B and carry-in C_in.

- **S = A ⊕ B ⊕ C_in**
- **C_out = AB + C_in(A ⊕ B)**

Two half adders and an OR gate. Chaining n full adders gives an n-bit **ripple-carry adder** (IC 7483). Carry-look-ahead adders avoid the ripple delay.

steps.title: Subtractors
steps.body: Half subtractor: D = A ⊕ B, Borrow = A′B. In practice, an adder with XOR gates on the B inputs and C_in = 1 computes A − B using two's complement. One control line then selects add or subtract.

steps.title: Check by truth table
steps.body: For a full adder, C_out is 1 whenever at least two of the three inputs are 1, which is the majority function.

activity.prompt: A 4-bit adder adds 1001 and 0101 with C_in = 0. What is the decimal value of the 4-bit sum (ignoring C_out)?

quiz.q: The sum output of a half adder is:
quiz.why: The sum bit is 1 when exactly one input is 1, which is XOR.

quiz.q: For a full adder with A = 1, B = 1, C_in = 1:
quiz.why: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 = 11₂, so the sum bit is 1 and the carry is 1.

quiz.q: The main drawback of a ripple-carry adder is:
options: delay grows with the number of bits
quiz.why: Each stage must wait for the previous carry, so the worst-case delay increases linearly with word length.

scenes.text: The TV remote's channel button picks one of many inputs to show on screen.
A multiplexer does the same in hardware: select lines choose which input reaches the single output.

steps.title: Multiplexer (data selector)
steps.body:
2ⁿ inputs, n select lines, 1 output. 4:1 MUX:

Y = S₁′S₀′I₀ + S₁′S₀I₁ + S₁S₀′I₂ + S₁S₀I₃

A 2ⁿ:1 MUX can implement any n-variable function: put the truth-table outputs on the inputs. ICs: 74151 (8:1), 74153 (dual 4:1).

steps.title: Demultiplexer and decoder
steps.body:
- **DEMUX**: one input routed to one of 2ⁿ outputs.
- **Decoder** n-to-2ⁿ: exactly one output active for each input code (74138 is 3-to-8). A decoder with an enable input acts as a DEMUX.
- **BCD to 7-segment decoder** (7447) drives displays.

steps.title: Encoders
steps.body: 2ⁿ inputs → n-bit code. A **priority encoder** (74148) outputs the code of the highest-priority active input, used for keyboard and interrupt handling.

steps.title: Solved: XOR with a 4:1 MUX
steps.body: Use A, B as select lines. The XOR truth table is 0, 1, 1, 0, so set I₀ = 0, I₁ = 1, I₂ = 1, I₃ = 0. The output is A ⊕ B.

steps.title: Counting select lines
steps.body: Select lines = log₂(number of inputs). 8:1 needs 3, 16:1 needs 4, 32:1 needs 5.

activity.prompt: How many select lines does a 16-to-1 multiplexer need?

quiz.q: A 3-to-8 decoder has how many outputs?
quiz.why: An n-input decoder has 2ⁿ outputs, and 2³ = 8.

quiz.q: A priority encoder outputs:
options: the code of the highest-priority active input
quiz.why: When several inputs are active, it encodes only the one with highest priority.

quiz.q: Which device sends one input to one of many outputs?
quiz.why: A demultiplexer distributes a single data line to an output chosen by its select lines.

scenes.text: Press a doorbell latch button once and the light stays on even after you let go.
That memory comes from feedback between two gates: a flip-flop, the basic one-bit store.

steps.title: SR latch
steps.body:
Two cross-coupled NOR (or NAND) gates.

| S R | Q(next) |
|---|---|
| 0 0 | Q (hold) |
| 0 1 | 0 (reset) |
| 1 0 | 1 (set) |
| 1 1 | invalid (NOR latch) |

Adding a clock enable gives a clocked SR flip-flop.

steps.title: JK, D and T
steps.body:
- **JK**: like SR, but J = K = 1 **toggles** Q.
- **D**: Q(next) = D; stores a bit; used in registers.
- **T**: T = 1 toggles, T = 0 holds; a JK with J = K = T.

Characteristic equation of JK: Q⁺ = JQ′ + K′Q.

steps.title: Race-around
steps.body: In a level-triggered JK with J = K = 1, Q may toggle many times while the clock is high. Fixes: **master–slave** JK (master follows on high, slave on low) or **edge triggering**.

steps.title: Solved: frequency division
steps.body:
A T flip-flop with T = 1 toggles on every clock edge, so its output has half the clock frequency.

Three T flip-flops in cascade on an 8 kHz clock: 8 → 4 → 2 → **1 kHz**.

steps.title: Timing
steps.body: Setup time and hold time are the windows before and after the clock edge when D must be steady. Violating them can cause metastability.

activity.prompt: A 32 kHz clock drives a chain of 5 toggle flip-flops. What is the output frequency of the last flip-flop, in kHz?

quiz.q: In a JK flip-flop, J = K = 1 causes:
quiz.why: With both inputs 1, the next state is the complement of the present state.

quiz.q: A D flip-flop's output after the clock edge equals:
quiz.why: The characteristic equation of a D flip-flop is Q⁺ = D.

quiz.q: Master–slave construction removes:
quiz.why: The slave updates only after the master is disabled, so the output changes once per clock cycle.

scenes.text: A wall clock counts seconds 0 to 59, then rolls over and bumps the minutes.
Inside, a mod-10 counter and a mod-6 counter do the seconds. Counters are flip-flops wired together.

steps.title: Ripple (asynchronous) counter
steps.body:
Each flip-flop's output clocks the next. n flip-flops count 0 to 2ⁿ − 1 (mod 2ⁿ).

- Simple, but delay accumulates down the chain.
- **Mod-N counter**: use enough flip-flops (2ⁿ ≥ N) and reset when the count reaches N. Mod-10 (decade): reset at 1010 using a NAND on Q₃ and Q₁ (IC 7490).

steps.title: Synchronous counter
steps.body: All flip-flops share the clock; logic sets J, K inputs. No ripple delay, so they are faster and glitch-free. Up/down counters (74193) and ring and Johnson counters are common variants. A Johnson counter with n flip-flops has 2n states.

steps.title: Shift registers
steps.body:
A chain of D flip-flops that moves data one position per clock.

- SISO, SIPO, PISO, PIPO modes.
- SIPO converts serial data to parallel (as in UART receivers).
- Shifting left multiplies a binary number by 2; shifting right divides by 2.

steps.title: Solved: design
steps.body:
Need a mod-12 counter.

- 2³ = 8 < 12 ≤ 16 = 2⁴, so **4 flip-flops**
- Reset at 12 = 1100, so NAND Q₃ and Q₂ into the clear inputs.
- A 4-bit counter on a 1 MHz clock gives a mod-16 output of 62.5 kHz.

steps.title: Timing diagram habit
steps.body: Draw the clock and every Q waveform one below the other; each stage toggles on the falling edge of the one above (for negative-edge ripple counters).

activity.prompt: What is the minimum number of flip-flops needed for a mod-50 counter?

quiz.q: A 3-bit ripple counter counts from 0 to:
quiz.why: Three flip-flops give 2³ = 8 states, from 0 to 7.

quiz.q: Synchronous counters are faster than ripple counters because:
quiz.why: With a common clock, all outputs change after one flip-flop delay instead of accumulated ripple delays.

quiz.q: Shifting the binary number 0011 left by one place gives:
quiz.why: Each left shift multiplies by 2, so 3 becomes 6.

scenes.text: A temperature sensor in a lab gives a smooth voltage. The laptop only understands numbers.
An ADC turns the voltage into a binary number; later a DAC turns numbers back into sound or a control voltage.

steps.title: R-2R ladder DAC
steps.body:
Uses only two resistor values, so it is easy to make accurately. For an n-bit input D (decimal value):

**V_out = V_ref × D/2ⁿ**

(for the common inverted form, with a sign change). Resolution (one LSB) = V_ref/2ⁿ.

steps.title: Solved: DAC output
steps.body:
4-bit R-2R, V_ref = 10 V, input 1010 (10).

- V_out = 10 × 10/16 = **6.25 V**
- Step size = 10/16 = 0.625 V

An 8-bit DAC with 5 V reference has step 5/256 ≈ 19.5 mV.

steps.title: ADC types
steps.body:
- **Flash**: 2ⁿ − 1 comparators, fastest; an 8-bit flash needs 255 comparators.
- **Successive approximation (SAR)**: binary search, n clock cycles per conversion; most common in microcontrollers.
- **Dual-slope**: integrates input then a reference; slow but very accurate and rejects mains noise; used in digital multimeters.
- **Counter (ramp) type**: up to 2ⁿ cycles; simple but slow.

steps.title: Sampling
steps.body: The Nyquist theorem: sample at more than twice the highest signal frequency. Audio CDs sample at 44.1 kHz for signals up to about 20 kHz. Quantisation error is ±½ LSB.

steps.title: Solved: SAR timing
steps.body: A 10-bit SAR ADC with a 1 MHz clock needs about 10 cycles: **10 μs** per conversion, so up to about 100,000 samples per second.

activity.prompt: An 8-bit R-2R DAC has V_ref = 5.12 V. Find V_out for the input 10000000 using V_out = V_ref × D/256, in V.

quiz.q: The resolution of a 10-bit DAC with V_ref = 10.24 V is:
The fastest ADC type is:
quiz.why: A flash ADC compares the input with all levels at once using 2ⁿ − 1 comparators.

quiz.q: Digital multimeters usually use dual-slope ADCs because they:
quiz.why: Integrating over a fixed time averages out noise such as 50 Hz hum and gives high accuracy.

questions.q: The carry output of a half adder is:
questions.why: A carry occurs only when both bits are 1.

questions.q: How many full adders are needed to add two 8-bit numbers in a ripple-carry adder?
questions.why: One full adder per bit position is used, so 8 are needed (the first may be a half adder).

questions.q: A 4:1 MUX has how many select lines?
The IC 74138 is a:
questions.why: The 74138 decodes a 3-bit input to one of 8 active-low outputs.

questions.q: The NOR SR latch is invalid when:
questions.why: Both outputs are forced to 0, so Q and Q′ are no longer complements.

questions.q: The JK characteristic equation is:
questions.why: It reproduces hold, set, reset and toggle for the four J, K combinations.

questions.q: A mod-10 counter needs at least:
A 4-flip-flop Johnson counter has how many states?
questions.why: A Johnson (twisted-ring) counter with n flip-flops cycles through 2n states.

questions.q: An 8-bit flash ADC needs how many comparators?
questions.why: A flash ADC uses 2ⁿ − 1 comparators, which is 255 for n = 8.

questions.q: A 4-bit R-2R DAC with V_ref = 8 V and input 0110 outputs:
A 12-bit SAR ADC with a 2 MHz clock needs about how long per conversion?
questions.why: 12 clock cycles at 0.5 μs each take 6 μs.

questions.q: A 10 kHz signal must be sampled at more than:
questions.why: The Nyquist criterion requires a sampling rate above twice the highest frequency.

questions.q: A ripple counter of 4 flip-flops, each with 20 ns delay, has a worst-case settling time of:
questions.why: In a ripple counter delays add along the chain: 4 × 20 ns = 80 ns.

uni-bsc-phy-mathematical-physics.title: B.Sc Physics · Mathematical Physics I–III
uni-bsc-phy-mathematical-physics.description: The three Mathematical Physics papers in one pack: vector calculus, differential equations, Fourier series and transforms, special functions, complex analysis, matrices and partial differential equations — each with solved problems physicists actually use. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Physics (Hons) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Vector calculus
courses.summary: Scalar and vector fields, gradient, divergence and curl with their physical meaning, vector identities, line, surface and volume integrals, Gauss's divergence theorem, Stokes' theorem and Green's theorem, and orthogonal curvilinear coordinates.
outcomes: Compute gradient, divergence and curl and interpret them physically
Use standard vector identities such as ∇×∇φ = 0 and ∇·(∇×A) = 0
Evaluate line, surface and volume integrals and recognise conservative fields
Apply Gauss's and Stokes' theorems to verify or simplify integrals
Write grad, div, curl and Laplacian in cylindrical and spherical coordinates

scenes.text: On a contour map, Arun wants the steepest path up. The gradient of height points exactly that way.
Down at the river, divergence tells where water springs out and curl tells where it swirls.

steps.title: The del operator
steps.body:
∇ = î ∂/∂x + ĵ ∂/∂y + k̂ ∂/∂z.
- **Gradient** ∇φ: vector pointing along the fastest increase of φ; |∇φ| is that rate. Directional derivative along unit n̂: n̂·∇φ. ∇φ is normal to the level surfaces φ = const.
- **Divergence** ∇·A = ∂Aₓ/∂x + ∂A_y/∂y + ∂A_z/∂z: net outflow per unit volume (source density).
- **Curl** ∇×A = determinant of (î ĵ k̂; ∂ₓ ∂_y ∂_z; Aₓ A_y A_z): circulation per unit area (rotation).

steps.title: Solved: div and curl
steps.body:
(a) r = (x, y, z): ∇·r = 3, ∇×r = 0 (radial field, pure source).
(b) v = (−y, x, 0) (rigid rotation, ω = 1): ∇·v = 0, ∇×v = (0, 0, 2) = 2ω. Curl equals twice the angular velocity.

steps.title: Key identities
steps.body:
- ∇×(∇φ) = 0 (gradients are curl-free)
- ∇·(∇×A) = 0 (curls are divergence-free)
- ∇·(φA) = φ∇·A + A·∇φ
- ∇×(∇×A) = ∇(∇·A) − ∇²A
- ∇²(1/r) = 0 for r ≠ 0; ∇·(r̂/r²) = 4πδ³(r)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to normalise the direction vector in a directional derivative.
- Treating ∇·A as a vector or ∇×A as a scalar.
- Concluding a field with curved field lines must have non-zero curl: v = r̂/r (2-D, φ̂/r) can have zero curl away from the axis.

activity.prompt: Find the divergence of F = (x², y², z²) at the point (1, 2, 3).

quiz.q: ∇φ at a point is:
quiz.why: Moving along a level surface does not change φ, so dφ = ∇φ·dr = 0 for tangential dr, which means ∇φ is normal to the surface.

quiz.q: For v = (−y, x, 0), ∇×v is:
quiz.why: The z-component is ∂(x)/∂x − ∂(−y)/∂y = 1 + 1 = 2, i.e. twice the angular velocity of rotation.

quiz.q: ∇·(∇×A) equals:
quiz.why: Mixed partial derivatives cancel in pairs, so the divergence of any curl vanishes identically.

story.title: Carrying a bucket up the stairs

scenes.text: Whether Leela takes the lift or the stairs, gravity does the same work on the bucket.
That path independence is the signature of a conservative field.

steps.title: Line integrals
steps.body:
∫_C F·dr = ∫ (Fₓ dx + F_y dy + F_z dz) along curve C (parametrise x(t), y(t), z(t)). Physically: work done.

**Conservative field**: the following are equivalent (simply connected region): ∮F·dr = 0; ∫F·dr path independent; F = ∇φ; ∇×F = 0. Then ∫_A^B F·dr = φ(B) − φ(A).

steps.title: Surface and volume integrals
steps.body:
- Flux: ∬_S F·dA with dA = n̂ dA. For a closed surface n̂ points outward.
- Volume integral: ∭_V ρ dV (e.g. total charge or mass).
- Area elements: plane z = const: dA = dx dy k̂; sphere radius R: dA = R² sinθ dθ dφ r̂.

steps.title: Solved: path independence
steps.body:
F = (y, x, 0) from (0,0) to (1,2).
- ∇×F = (0, 0, 1 − 1) = 0 → conservative, φ = xy.
- ∫F·dr = φ(1,2) − φ(0,0) = **2**.
Check along y = 2x: x = t, y = 2t: ∫₀¹ (2t·1 + t·2) dt = ∫₀¹ 4t dt = 2 ✓

steps.title: Solved: non-conservative circulation
steps.body:
F = (−y, x, 0) around the unit circle (x = cos t, y = sin t):
∮F·dr = ∫₀^{2π} (sin²t + cos²t) dt = **2π** ≠ 0 → not conservative (∇×F = 2k̂).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring orientation: reversing a path flips the sign of a line integral.
- Using ∇×F = 0 to claim conservative in a region with a hole (e.g. F = φ̂/r around the z-axis has zero curl but ∮ = 2π).
- Forgetting the R² sinθ factor on a sphere.

activity.prompt: Evaluate ∫ F·dr for F = (2x, 3y², 0) from (0, 0, 0) to (1, 2, 0) along any path.

quiz.q: A field F is conservative in a simply connected region if:
quiz.why: Zero curl in a simply connected region guarantees F = ∇φ and path-independent line integrals.

quiz.q: ∮F·dr for F = (−y, x, 0) round the unit circle anticlockwise is:
quiz.why: The integrand reduces to sin²t + cos²t = 1, and integrating over t from 0 to 2π gives 2π.

quiz.q: The area element on a sphere of radius R is:
quiz.why: A patch has sides R dθ and R sinθ dφ, giving R² sinθ dθ dφ.

scenes.text: To know how many people are inside a stadium, you can count inside — or just count the net number crossing the gates.
Gauss's theorem says the same of any field: inside sources equal net outward flux.

steps.title: Statements
steps.body:
- **Gauss (divergence)**: ∭_V (∇·F) dV = ∯_S F·dA (S closed, outward normal).
- **Stokes**: ∬_S (∇×F)·dA = ∮_C F·dr (C bounds S; right-hand rule fixes orientation).
- **Green (plane)**: ∮_C (P dx + Q dy) = ∬_R (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dx dy.
In physics: Gauss's law ∇·E = ρ/ε₀ ⇔ ∯E·dA = Q/ε₀; Ampère ∇×B = μ₀J ⇔ ∮B·dl = μ₀I.

steps.title: Solved: Gauss for F = r on a sphere
steps.body:
Sphere radius R = 2.
- Volume side: ∇·r = 3 → 3 × (4/3)πR³ = 4πR³ = **32π ≈ 100.5**
- Surface side: r·r̂ = R on the surface → R × 4πR² = 4πR³ = 32π ✓

steps.title: Solved: Stokes on a disc
steps.body:
F = (−y, x, 0), C = circle of radius a in the xy-plane.
- ∇×F = (0, 0, 2); ∬ 2 dA = 2πa².
- ∮F·dr = 2πa² as well (a = 1 gives the 2π of the previous lesson) ✓
Green's corollary: area = (1/2)∮(x dy − y dx).

steps.title: When to use which
steps.body: Hard surface integral over a closed surface → convert to a volume integral of the divergence. Hard line integral round a loop → convert to flux of the curl over any convenient surface bounded by it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Gauss's theorem to an open surface (it needs a closed one).
- Forgetting the singularity at r = 0 for fields like r̂/r²: its divergence is 4πδ³(r), not 0.
- Mismatching orientation of C and n̂ in Stokes' theorem.

activity.prompt: Use Gauss's theorem to find the outward flux of F = (x, y, z) through the surface of the unit cube 0 ≤ x, y, z ≤ 1.

quiz.q: Gauss's divergence theorem relates:
options: a line integral to a surface integral
a volume integral of div F to flux through the closed boundary
quiz.why: It equates ∭∇·F dV over a region with the outward flux ∯F·dA through its closed boundary.

quiz.q: Area enclosed by a curve C can be written as:
quiz.why: Green's theorem with P = −y/2 and Q = x/2 gives ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = 1, so the double integral equals the area.

quiz.q: ∯ (r̂/r²)·dA over any sphere centred at the origin is:
quiz.why: The field has magnitude 1/R² on a sphere of area 4πR², giving 4π regardless of R, matching its delta-function divergence.

story.title: Why the hydrogen atom uses spheres

scenes.text: In x, y, z the hydrogen atom's Schrödinger equation is a mess. In r, θ, φ it separates cleanly.
Choosing coordinates that match the symmetry is half the battle.

steps.title: Scale factors
steps.body:
For coordinates (u₁,u₂,u₃) with ds² = h₁²du₁² + h₂²du₂² + h₃²du₃²:
- Cylindrical (ρ, φ, z): h = (1, ρ, 1); dV = ρ dρ dφ dz
- Spherical (r, θ, φ): h = (1, r, r sinθ); dV = r² sinθ dr dθ dφ

∇f = Σ (1/hᵢ)(∂f/∂uᵢ) êᵢ;
∇·A = (1/h₁h₂h₃)[∂(h₂h₃A₁)/∂u₁ + cyclic].

steps.title: Laplacian in spherical coordinates
steps.body:
∇²f = (1/r²) ∂/∂r(r² ∂f/∂r) + (1/(r² sinθ)) ∂/∂θ(sinθ ∂f/∂θ) + (1/(r² sin²θ)) ∂²f/∂φ²

Cylindrical: ∇²f = (1/ρ) ∂/∂ρ(ρ ∂f/∂ρ) + (1/ρ²) ∂²f/∂φ² + ∂²f/∂z².

steps.title: Solved: Laplacian of 1/r and r²
steps.body:
(a) f = 1/r: r² ∂f/∂r = −1, derivative 0 → ∇²(1/r) = **0** (r ≠ 0) — the Coulomb potential is harmonic.
(b) f = r²: r² × 2r = 2r³ → ∂/∂r = 6r² → (1/r²)(6r²) = **6** (check in Cartesian: ∇²(x²+y²+z²) = 6 ✓).

steps.title: Solved: volume of a sphere
steps.body: V = ∫₀^R r² dr ∫₀^π sinθ dθ ∫₀^{2π} dφ = (R³/3)(2)(2π) = **(4/3)πR³** ✓

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing ∇² in spherical coordinates as ∂²/∂r² + ∂²/∂θ² + ∂²/∂φ².
- Treating unit vectors r̂, θ̂, φ̂ as constant — they change with position, so they cannot be pulled out of derivatives.
- Swapping θ (polar, 0 to π) and φ (azimuthal, 0 to 2π) limits.

activity.prompt: Using the spherical Laplacian, evaluate ∇²(r³) at r = 2 (answer = 12r).

quiz.q: Scale factors in spherical coordinates (r, θ, φ) are:
quiz.why: Line elements are dr, r dθ and r sinθ dφ, so h_r = 1, h_θ = r and h_φ = r sinθ.

quiz.q: The volume element in cylindrical coordinates is:
quiz.why: The product of scale factors (1)(ρ)(1) multiplies dρ dφ dz.

quiz.q: ∇²(1/r) for r ≠ 0 is:
quiz.why: r²∂(1/r)/∂r = −1 is constant, so its r-derivative is zero and the Laplacian vanishes away from the origin.

questions.why: The curl of any gradient vanishes because mixed partial derivatives are equal.

questions.q: Directional derivative of φ = x²y + yz at (1,2,−1) along (1,2,2):
∇·r in three dimensions equals:
Stokes' theorem converts:
options: line integral round C to flux of curl through S
questions.why: ∮_C F·dr = ∬_S (∇×F)·dA for S bounded by C.

questions.q: Flux of F = r through a sphere of radius 2 is:
∫F·dr for F = (y, x, 0) from (0,0) to (1,2):
questions.why: F = ∇(xy), so the integral is xy evaluated at (1,2), which is 2.

questions.q: Which identity is correct?
questions.why: The curl of curl expands as grad(div) minus the vector Laplacian.

questions.q: ∇·(r̂/r²) everywhere including the origin is:
questions.why: It is zero for r ≠ 0, but the 4π flux through any sphere requires a delta function at the origin.

questions.q: The h_φ scale factor in cylindrical coordinates is:
questions.why: An arc of angle dφ at radius ρ has length ρ dφ.

questions.q: Circulation of (−y, x, 0) around a circle of radius 3 is:
∇²(x² + y² + z²) equals:
A field with ∇·F = 0 everywhere is called:
questions.why: Divergence-free fields such as B are solenoidal and can be written as the curl of a vector potential.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Ordinary differential equations
courses.summary: First-order equations (separable, linear with integrating factor, exact), second-order linear equations with constant coefficients, complementary function and particular integral, damped and forced oscillations with resonance, and circuit applications.
outcomes: Solve separable, linear and exact first-order ODEs
Write the general solution of homogeneous second-order equations from the auxiliary equation
Find particular integrals by undetermined coefficients and the D-operator method
Classify damping and compute damped frequency and resonance
Model RC and LCR circuits as ODEs and extract τ, f₀ and Q

scenes.text: Your chai cools fast at first, then slowly. Newton noticed the rate is proportional to the temperature gap.
That one sentence is a first-order ODE: dT/dt = −k(T − T₀).

steps.title: Separable equations
steps.body:
dy/dx = f(x)g(y) → ∫dy/g(y) = ∫f(x)dx.
Examples: radioactive decay dN/dt = −λN → N = N₀e^(−λt), half-life t½ = ln2/λ. Newton's cooling: T − T₀ = (T_i − T₀)e^(−kt).

steps.title: Linear first-order: integrating factor
steps.body:
dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x). Multiply by μ = e^(∫P dx): d(μy)/dx = μQ → y = (1/μ)[∫μQ dx + C].

**Exact** equations M dx + N dy = 0 with ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x: solution F(x,y) = C where ∂F/∂x = M, ∂F/∂y = N.

steps.title: Solved: dy/dx + y = x
steps.body:
μ = eˣ. d(eˣy)/dx = xeˣ → eˣy = (x − 1)eˣ + C → **y = x − 1 + Ce^(−x)**.
With y(0) = 0: C = 1, so y = x − 1 + e^(−x).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dropping the constant of integration, or adding it only at the very end after dividing by μ incorrectly.
- Forgetting that ∫P dx in μ needs no constant (any one works).
- Dividing by g(y) and losing solutions where g(y) = 0 (e.g. y = 0 for dy/dx = y).

activity.prompt: A capacitor charges through a resistor from zero. What percentage of its final charge does it hold after three time constants (t = 3RC)? Give one decimal place.

quiz.q: Integrating factor for dy/dx + 2y = eˣ is:
quiz.why: With P(x) = 2, the integrating factor is e^(∫2dx) = e^(2x).

quiz.q: Half-life for decay constant λ is:
quiz.why: Setting N₀/2 = N₀e^(−λt) gives t = ln2/λ.

quiz.q: M dx + N dy = 0 is exact when:
quiz.why: Exactness means M dx + N dy is dF for some F, which requires equal mixed partials ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x.

scenes.text: After a speed-breaker, a good car settles at once; a car with worn shocks bounces several times.
Engineers tune the damping to be close to 'critical'. The auxiliary equation tells us what that means.

steps.title: Auxiliary equation
steps.body:
a y'' + b y' + c y = 0. Try y = e^(mx): am² + bm + c = 0.
- Real distinct roots m₁, m₂: y = Ae^(m₁x) + Be^(m₂x)
- Repeated root m: y = (A + Bx)e^(mx)
- Complex α ± iβ: y = e^(αx)(A cos βx + B sin βx)

steps.title: Damped oscillator
steps.body:
m ẍ + b ẋ + k x = 0 → ẍ + 2γẋ + ω₀²x = 0 with γ = b/2m, ω₀ = √(k/m).
- γ < ω₀ underdamped: x = Ae^(−γt) cos(ω_d t + φ), ω_d = √(ω₀² − γ²)
- γ = ω₀ critical: fastest return without oscillation (b_c = 2√(mk))
- γ > ω₀ overdamped: slow non-oscillatory return

steps.title: Solved: spring–mass–damper
steps.body:
m = 0.5 kg, k = 50 N/m, b = 2 kg/s.
- ω₀ = √(50/0.5) = 10 rad/s; γ = 2/(2 × 0.5) = 2 s⁻¹
- Underdamped: ω_d = √(100 − 4) = **9.80 rad/s**; amplitude falls by e every 0.5 s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing Ae^(mx) + Be^(mx) for a repeated root — that is only one independent solution; multiply the second by x.
- Confusing γ = b/2m with b/m.
- Thinking critical damping oscillates once; it does not cross equilibrium more than once at most.

activity.prompt: For m = 0.5 kg and k = 50 N/m, what damping constant b (kg/s) gives critical damping?

quiz.q: General solution of y'' + 9y = 0 is:
quiz.why: The auxiliary equation m² + 9 = 0 gives m = ±3i, which produces cosine and sine of 3x.

quiz.q: A damped oscillator with γ > ω₀ is:
quiz.why: When the damping rate exceeds the natural frequency the roots are real and negative, giving a slow non-oscillatory decay.

quiz.q: Repeated root m = −2 gives the solution:
quiz.why: For a double root the second independent solution is x e^(mx), so y = (A + Bx)e^(−2x).

lessons.title: Inhomogeneous equations, forced oscillations and resonance

scenes.text: Small pushes, timed exactly with the swing, make it go higher and higher.
That is resonance: a driving frequency matching the natural one.

steps.title: General solution = CF + PI
steps.body:
For a y'' + b y' + c y = f(x): y = y_c (complementary function, solves the homogeneous equation) + y_p (any particular integral).

Undetermined coefficients — trial y_p:
- f = constant → y_p = constant
- f = e^(kx) → Ae^(kx) (multiply by x if k is a root)
- f = cos ωx or sin ωx → A cos ωx + B sin ωx
- f = polynomial → polynomial of same degree

steps.title: Solved: exponential forcing
steps.body:
y'' + y = e^(2x). Try y_p = Ae^(2x): 4A + A = 1 → A = 1/5.
y = A cos x + B sin x + **e^(2x)/5**.
D-operator check: y_p = e^(2x)/(D² + 1) = e^(2x)/(4 + 1) ✓

steps.title: Forced damped oscillator
steps.body:
ẍ + 2γẋ + ω₀²x = (F₀/m) cos ωt. Steady state x = A cos(ωt − δ):

A = (F₀/m)/√[(ω₀² − ω²)² + 4γ²ω²], tan δ = 2γω/(ω₀² − ω²).

Amplitude peaks at ω_r = √(ω₀² − 2γ²); phase lag is 90° at ω = ω₀. Quality factor Q = ω₀/(2γ): sharpness of resonance. The transient (CF) dies out as e^(−γt).

steps.title: Solved: resonance numbers
steps.body: ω₀ = 10 rad/s, γ = 2 s⁻¹: ω_r = √(100 − 8) = **9.59 rad/s**, Q = 10/4 = **2.5** (broad resonance). Halving γ to 1 s⁻¹ raises Q to 5 and the peak gets taller and sharper.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to add the CF — y_p alone is not the general solution and cannot satisfy initial conditions.
- Using trial Ae^(kx) when k is already a root of the auxiliary equation (use Axe^(kx)).
- Assuming amplitude peaks exactly at ω₀ for a damped system; it peaks slightly below.

activity.prompt: Find the constant particular integral of y'' + 3y' + 2y = 4.

quiz.q: PI of y'' − y = e^(2x) is:
quiz.why: Substituting Ae^(2x) gives 4A − A = 1, so A = 1/3.

quiz.q: At ω = ω₀ the phase lag of a forced damped oscillator is:
quiz.why: tan δ = 2γω/(ω₀² − ω²) becomes infinite when ω = ω₀, so δ = 90°.

quiz.q: Quality factor of an oscillator is:
quiz.why: Q = ω₀/(2γ) measures how many radians of oscillation occur per e-fold of energy decay, i.e. the sharpness of resonance.

lessons.title: Lab: LCR series resonance as a second-order ODE

scenes.text: Turning the tuning knob changes a capacitor until the LCR circuit resonates with one station.
Same equation as the damped spring — just with L, R and 1/C.

steps.title: Mapping
steps.body:
L q̈ + R q̇ + q/C = V₀ cos ωt.
Compare with m ẍ + b ẋ + kx: m ↔ L, b ↔ R, k ↔ 1/C.
- ω₀ = 1/√(LC), f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC))
- γ = R/2L; Q = ω₀L/R = (1/R)√(L/C)
- Bandwidth Δf = f₀/Q (between half-power points)

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Connect R, L, C in series with a signal generator and an ammeter/CRO across R.
2. Vary frequency in steps from well below to well above expected f₀; keep source amplitude fixed.
3. Record current I at each frequency.
4. Plot I vs f; read f₀ at the peak and the frequencies f₁, f₂ where I = I_max/√2.
5. Q_exp = f₀/(f₂ − f₁); compare with (1/R)√(L/C).

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- Why is current maximum at f₀? Inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, so impedance = R.
- What sets the sharpness? Q; lower R gives sharper resonance.
- Why include the coil's own resistance? It adds to R and lowers Q.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ω₀ when f₀ is asked (factor 2π).
- Taking too coarse frequency steps near the peak.
- Letting the generator amplitude drift as frequency changes.

quiz.why: Q = ω₀L/R with ω₀ = 1/√(LC) simplifies to (1/R)√(L/C).

quiz.why: Inductive and capacitive reactances cancel at f₀, leaving only the resistance.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Fourier series, Fourier and Laplace transforms
courses.summary: Periodic functions and Dirichlet conditions, Fourier coefficients, odd/even and half-range series, Parseval's identity and summing series, Gibbs phenomenon; Fourier transform and its properties, convolution; Laplace transform, Dirac delta and solving ODEs with transforms.
outcomes: Compute Fourier coefficients of standard waveforms
Use symmetry and half-range expansions to simplify series
Apply Parseval's identity to sum series such as Σ1/n²
Compute Fourier transforms of pulses and Gaussians and state the uncertainty trade-off
Use Laplace transforms to solve linear ODEs with initial conditions

story.title: A tabla and a sitar playing the same note

scenes.text: Both play 'Sa' at the same pitch, yet you instantly tell them apart.
Their waveforms contain different mixtures of harmonics — exactly what a Fourier series lists.

steps.title: Definition (period 2π)
steps.body:
f(x) = a₀/2 + Σ_{n=1}^∞ (aₙ cos nx + bₙ sin nx), with
aₙ = (1/π)∫_{−π}^{π} f(x) cos nx dx, bₙ = (1/π)∫_{−π}^{π} f(x) sin nx dx.

For period 2L replace nx by nπx/L and 1/π by 1/L.
**Dirichlet conditions** (finite number of maxima, minima and finite jumps, absolutely integrable): the series converges to f(x) where continuous and to the mid-point [f(x⁺) + f(x⁻)]/2 at a jump.

steps.title: Symmetry shortcuts
steps.body:
- Even f (f(−x) = f(x)): bₙ = 0, cosine series only.
- Odd f: aₙ = 0 (including a₀), sine series only.
Orthogonality: ∫_{−π}^{π} sin mx sin nx dx = π δₘₙ, same for cos; sin·cos integrals vanish.

steps.title: Solved: square wave
steps.body:
f = −1 on (−π, 0), +1 on (0, π) — odd.
bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π sin nx dx = (2/nπ)(1 − cos nπ) = 4/(nπ) for odd n, 0 for even n.
f(x) = (4/π)[sin x + (sin 3x)/3 + (sin 5x)/5 + …]
At x = π/2: 1 = (4/π)(1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − …) → **1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − … = π/4** (Leibniz).

steps.title: Solved: f(x) = x² on (−π, π)
steps.body:
Even. a₀ = (2/π)∫₀^π x² dx = 2π²/3. aₙ = 4(−1)ⁿ/n² (two integrations by parts).
x² = π²/3 + 4Σ(−1)ⁿ cos nx/n².
At x = 0: 0 = π²/3 + 4Σ(−1)ⁿ/n² → **Σ(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n² = π²/12**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 1/2 in front of a₀ (or doubling it twice).
- Claiming the series equals f at a jump; it gives the average of the two one-sided limits.
- Integrating only over (0, π) without doubling for even/odd integrands.

activity.prompt: For the square wave of amplitude 1 (−1 on (−π,0), +1 on (0,π)), give the coefficient b₁ = 4/π to three decimals.

quiz.q: The Fourier series of an odd function contains:
quiz.why: For an odd f, f(x)cos nx is odd and integrates to zero, so all aₙ vanish and only sine terms remain.

quiz.q: At a jump discontinuity the Fourier series converges to:
options: the average of left and right limits
quiz.why: Dirichlet's theorem guarantees convergence to [f(x⁺) + f(x⁻)]/2 at a finite jump.

quiz.q: The square wave contains harmonics:
quiz.why: bₙ = (2/nπ)(1 − cos nπ) is zero for even n, so only odd harmonics appear.

lessons.title: Half-range series, Parseval's identity and Gibbs phenomenon

scenes.text: A string fixed at both ends is defined only on 0 < x < L, yet we expand its shape in sines.
That is a half-range sine series — and Parseval tells how energy is shared among harmonics.

steps.title: Half-range expansions
steps.body:
A function given on (0, L) can be extended as odd (sine series) or even (cosine series):
- Sine: bₙ = (2/L)∫₀^L f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx
- Cosine: aₙ = (2/L)∫₀^L f(x) cos(nπx/L) dx
Choose by boundary conditions: fixed ends (f = 0) → sine series.

steps.title: Parseval's identity
steps.body:
(1/π)∫_{−π}^{π} f² dx = a₀²/2 + Σ(aₙ² + bₙ²).
Physically: mean power of a signal = sum of powers in its harmonics.

steps.title: Solved: Basel sum from f(x) = x
steps.body:
x on (−π, π): bₙ = 2(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n.
Left side: (1/π)∫x² dx = (1/π)(2π³/3) = 2π²/3.
Right side: Σ 4/n².
→ **Σ 1/n² = π²/6 ≈ 1.645**.

steps.title: Gibbs phenomenon
steps.body: Near a jump, partial sums overshoot by about 9 % of the jump size, and the overshoot does not shrink as more terms are added — it just narrows. For the square wave (jump 2) the peaks reach about 1.18 instead of 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the full-range formula 1/L on a half-range problem (should be 2/L).
- Forgetting a₀²/2 (not a₀²) in Parseval.
- Believing Gibbs overshoot disappears with enough terms.

activity.prompt: Using Parseval's identity on f(x) = x, the sum Σ 1/n² over n = 1, 2, 3, … equals π²/6. Give its value to three decimals.

quiz.q: Displacement of a string fixed at x = 0 and x = L is best expanded in:
quiz.why: Each sin(nπx/L) vanishes at both ends, matching the fixed-end boundary conditions.

quiz.q: Gibbs overshoot near a jump is roughly:
quiz.why: Partial Fourier sums overshoot by about 9 % of the jump, and the overshoot persists as terms are added.

quiz.q: Parseval's identity expresses:
options: mean square of f as sum of squared coefficients
quiz.why: It equates the mean of f² over a period to a₀²/2 plus the sum of aₙ² + bₙ².

scenes.text: A camera flash lasts microseconds; a laser for eye surgery fires femtosecond pulses.
The shorter the pulse in time, the wider its frequency spread — the Fourier transform shows why.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
F(k) = ∫_{−∞}^{∞} f(x) e^(−ikx) dx, f(x) = (1/2π)∫ F(k) e^(ikx) dk.
(Other books put 1/√(2π) in both; be consistent.)
Properties: linearity; shift f(x − a) → e^(−ika)F(k); scaling f(ax) → (1/|a|)F(k/a); derivative f′ → ikF(k); **convolution** (f*g) → F·G.

steps.title: Solved: rectangular pulse
steps.body:
f = 1 for |x| < a, 0 otherwise.
F(k) = ∫_{−a}^{a} e^(−ikx) dx = **2 sin(ka)/k** (a sinc). F(0) = 2a (area). First zeros at k = ±π/a: the narrower the pulse (small a), the wider the spectrum.

steps.title: Solved: Gaussian
steps.body:
f = e^(−x²/2σ²) → F(k) = σ√(2π) e^(−σ²k²/2).
A Gaussian transforms into a Gaussian of width 1/σ: Δx·Δk is fixed. In quantum mechanics with p = ħk this underlies Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2 (equality for Gaussians).

steps.title: Where it is used
steps.body: MRI scanners record signals in k-space and inverse-Fourier-transform them into images; spectrum analysers, JPEG/MP3 compression (cosine transforms) and X-ray crystallography all rely on Fourier analysis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing conventions (2π placement, sign of exponent) between forward and inverse transforms.
- Forgetting the 1/|a| factor in scaling.
- Treating F(k) as always real; it is real only for even real f.

activity.prompt: A rectangular pulse f(x) = 1 for |x| < 1.5 (0 elsewhere). With F(k) = ∫f e^(−ikx)dx, what is F(0)?

quiz.q: The Fourier transform of a convolution f*g is:
quiz.why: The convolution theorem turns convolution in x-space into simple multiplication in k-space.

quiz.q: The FT of a Gaussian is:
quiz.why: Completing the square in the exponent shows the transform of e^(−x²/2σ²) is again a Gaussian, with width 1/σ.

quiz.q: Shifting f(x) to f(x − a) multiplies F(k) by:
quiz.why: Substituting x′ = x − a in the integral pulls out the phase factor e^(−ika).

lessons.title: Laplace transforms and the Dirac delta

scenes.text: At t = 0 an engineer flips a switch. The circuit's ODE has initial conditions, not boundary conditions.
The Laplace transform turns that ODE into algebra, initial conditions included.

steps.title: Definition and table
steps.body:
L{f}(s) = F(s) = ∫₀^∞ f(t) e^(−st) dt.
- L{1} = 1/s; L{tⁿ} = n!/s^(n+1)
- L{e^(at)} = 1/(s − a)
- L{sin ωt} = ω/(s² + ω²); L{cos ωt} = s/(s² + ω²)
- L{f′} = sF − f(0); L{f″} = s²F − s f(0) − f′(0)
- First shift: L{e^(at)f(t)} = F(s − a)

steps.title: Dirac delta
steps.body: δ(x − a) = 0 for x ≠ a, ∫δ(x − a)dx = 1, and **∫f(x)δ(x − a)dx = f(a)** (sifting). L{δ(t − a)} = e^(−as); FT of δ(x) = 1 (all frequencies equally). Models point charges, impulses and sharp kicks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dropping the initial-value terms in L{f′} and L{f″}.
- Inverting without partial fractions.
- Writing L{tⁿ} = n!/sⁿ (the power is n + 1).

activity.prompt: Evaluate the Laplace transform of t² at s = 2 (L{t²} = 2/s³).

quiz.why: The sifting property picks out cos π = −1.

quiz.q: L{f″} equals:
quiz.why: Applying the derivative rule twice gives s²F − s f(0) − f′(0), which builds the initial conditions into the algebra.

questions.why: Integrating x sin nx by parts gives bₙ = 2(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n.

questions.q: An even function's Fourier series has:
questions.why: The sine coefficients of an even function vanish.

questions.why: Parseval applied to f = x gives 4Σ1/n² = 2π²/3.
The square-wave series evaluated at x = π/2 gives this sum.

questions.why: The scaling property spreads F(k) as f is compressed (Δx·Δk fixed).

questions.why: L{sin ωt} = ω/(s² + ω²) with ω = 2.

questions.why: Sifting gives ∫δ(x)e^(−ikx)dx = e⁰ = 1 for all k.

questions.why: The overshoot height converges to a fixed fraction of the jump while its width shrinks.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Series solutions and special functions
courses.summary: Ordinary and regular singular points, power-series and Frobenius methods; Legendre polynomials (Rodrigues formula, generating function, recurrence, orthogonality); Bessel functions; Hermite polynomials; Gamma and Beta functions.
outcomes: Classify singular points and apply the Frobenius method
Generate Legendre polynomials and use their orthogonality to expand functions
State key properties of Bessel functions and where they arise in physics
Use Hermite polynomials and recognise their role in the quantum oscillator
Evaluate integrals with Gamma and Beta functions

lessons.title: Power series, Frobenius method and the Legendre equation

scenes.text: Some ODEs from physics have no answer in sines, exponentials or logs.
So we build the solution brick by brick as a power series — and name the useful ones.

steps.title: Singular points
steps.body:
Write y″ + P(x)y′ + Q(x)y = 0.
- x₀ is **ordinary** if P and Q are analytic there → y = Σaₙ(x − x₀)ⁿ.
- **Regular singular** if (x − x₀)P and (x − x₀)²Q are analytic → Frobenius: y = Σaₙ(x − x₀)^(n+r).
- Otherwise irregular.
The lowest-power coefficient gives the **indicial equation** for r.

steps.title: Legendre's equation
steps.body:
(1 − x²)y″ − 2xy′ + l(l + 1)y = 0 (from ∇² in spherical coordinates). x = 0 is ordinary.
Substituting y = Σaₙxⁿ gives the recurrence
**a_{n+2} = [n(n + 1) − l(l + 1)] a_n / [(n + 1)(n + 2)]**.
For integer l one series terminates → Legendre polynomial P_l(x), normalised so P_l(1) = 1. The other series diverges at x = ±1, so physics keeps only P_l.

steps.title: Solved: building P₂
steps.body:
l = 2, start with a₀ = 1, a₁ = 0.
a₂ = [0 − 6]a₀/2 = −3; a₄ = [6 − 6]a₂/12 = 0 → stops.
y = 1 − 3x². Normalise so y(1) = 1: divide by −2 → **P₂ = (3x² − 1)/2**.
List: P₀ = 1, P₁ = x, P₂ = (3x² − 1)/2, P₃ = (5x³ − 3x)/2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a plain power series at a regular singular point (Bessel's equation at x = 0) — Frobenius is needed.
- Forgetting to normalise P_l(1) = 1.
- Index shifting errors when collecting powers of x; write the recurrence carefully.

activity.prompt: Evaluate P₃(0.5), where P₃(x) = (5x³ − 3x)/2.

quiz.q: x = 0 for Legendre's equation is:
quiz.why: Dividing by (1 − x²) gives P and Q analytic at x = 0, so it is an ordinary point.

quiz.q: P_l(1) equals:
quiz.why: Legendre polynomials are normalised by the convention P_l(1) = 1.

quiz.q: The Frobenius method is needed at:
quiz.why: At a regular singular point solutions may behave like x^r with non-integer r, which a plain Taylor series cannot capture.

lessons.title: Legendre polynomials: Rodrigues, generating function and orthogonality

scenes.text: The potential at r from a charge at distance a along z involves 1/|r − a|.
Expanding it in powers of a/r produces exactly the Legendre polynomials — the multipole expansion.

steps.title: Rodrigues' formula and generating function
steps.body:
P_l(x) = (1/(2^l l!)) d^l/dx^l (x² − 1)^l.

Generating function: 1/√(1 − 2xt + t²) = Σ_{l=0}^∞ P_l(x) t^l (|t| < 1).
With x = cosθ, t = a/r: 1/|r − a| = (1/r)Σ(a/r)^l P_l(cosθ) — the multipole expansion.

steps.title: Recurrence and orthogonality
steps.body:
Bonnet: (l + 1)P_{l+1} = (2l + 1)xP_l − lP_{l−1}.
Orthogonality: ∫_{−1}^{1} P_m P_n dx = **2/(2n + 1) δ_mn**.
Expansion: f(x) = Σ c_l P_l(x), c_l = (2l + 1)/2 ∫_{−1}^{1} f P_l dx.

steps.title: Solved: expand x² in Legendre polynomials
steps.body:
From P₂ = (3x² − 1)/2: x² = (2P₂ + 1)/3 = **(1/3)P₀ + (2/3)P₂**.
Check via the formula: c₀ = (1/2)∫x² dx = 1/3 ✓.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the norm as 2/(2n − 1) or 1/(2n + 1).
- Forgetting the (2l + 1)/2 factor in expansion coefficients.
- Applying the generating function for |t| ≥ 1, where it does not converge.

activity.prompt: Using orthogonality, evaluate ∫_{−1}^{1} [P₃(x)]² dx (= 2/7). Give three decimals.

quiz.q: ∫_{−1}^{1} P₂ P₃ dx equals:
quiz.why: Different Legendre polynomials are orthogonal on [−1, 1], so the integral is zero.

quiz.q: In the expansion x² = c₀P₀ + c₂P₂, c₂ is:
quiz.why: Rearranging P₂ = (3x² − 1)/2 gives x² = 1/3 + (2/3)P₂.

quiz.q: The generating function of Legendre polynomials is:
quiz.why: Expanding (1 − 2xt + t²)^(−1/2) in powers of t gives P_l(x) as coefficients; e^(2xt − t²) generates Hermite polynomials.

story.title: The drum and the quantum spring

scenes.text: The vibration patterns of a circular mridangam head are Bessel functions.
The wavefunctions of a quantum harmonic oscillator carry Hermite polynomials. Two special functions, two everyday physics problems.

steps.title: Bessel's equation
steps.body:
x²y″ + xy′ + (x² − n²)y = 0 (from ∇² in cylindrical coordinates). x = 0 is regular singular; Frobenius gives r = ±n and
J_n(x) = Σ_{k=0}^∞ (−1)^k (x/2)^(2k+n) / [k! Γ(k + n + 1)].
J₀(0) = 1, J_n(0) = 0 for n ≥ 1. Zeros of J₀: 2.405, 5.520, 8.654, …
Recurrences: J_{n−1} + J_{n+1} = (2n/x)J_n; J_{n−1} − J_{n+1} = 2J_n′; J₀′ = −J₁.
Generating function: e^((x/2)(t − 1/t)) = Σ J_n(x)tⁿ.

steps.title: Hermite polynomials
steps.body:
y″ − 2xy′ + 2ny = 0. Generating function e^(2xt − t²) = Σ H_n(x)tⁿ/n!.
H₀ = 1, H₁ = 2x, H₂ = 4x² − 2, H₃ = 8x³ − 12x.
Recurrence H_{n+1} = 2xH_n − 2nH_{n−1}.
Orthogonality: ∫_{−∞}^{∞} e^(−x²) H_m H_n dx = 2ⁿ n! √π δ_mn.
Quantum oscillator: ψ_n ∝ H_n(ξ)e^(−ξ²/2), ξ = x√(mω/ħ).

steps.title: Solved: drum fundamental
steps.body: A circular membrane of radius a vibrates in its lowest mode as J₀(kr) with J₀(ka) = 0 → ka = 2.405. With wave speed v, f = v k/(2π) = 2.405v/(2πa). For v = 100 m/s, a = 0.10 m: f = 240.5/0.628 = **383 Hz**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking Bessel zeros as multiples of π like sine zeros; they are not equally spaced at small x.
- Mixing physicists' Hermite H_n with probabilists' He_n (different scaling).
- Forgetting the weight e^(−x²) in Hermite orthogonality.

quiz.q: Hermite polynomials appear in the wavefunctions of:
quiz.why: Solving the oscillator Schrödinger equation leads to Hermite's equation, so ψ_n contains H_n times a Gaussian.

quiz.why: From the recurrence J_{n−1} − J_{n+1} = 2J_n′ with n = 0 and J_{−1} = −J₁, we get J₀′ = −J₁.

scenes.text: Can you compute (1/2)! ? It sounds absurd, yet physicists need it for Gaussian integrals.
The Gamma function extends the factorial — and (1/2)! = √π/2.

steps.title: Gamma function
steps.body:
Γ(n) = ∫₀^∞ x^(n−1) e^(−x) dx (n > 0).
- Γ(n + 1) = nΓ(n); Γ(n + 1) = n! for integers
- Γ(1) = 1, **Γ(1/2) = √π**
- Reflection: Γ(z)Γ(1 − z) = π/sin(πz)
- Gaussian link: ∫₀^∞ e^(−x²) dx = Γ(1/2)/2 = √π/2

steps.title: Beta function
steps.body:
B(m, n) = ∫₀¹ x^(m−1)(1 − x)^(n−1) dx = **Γ(m)Γ(n)/Γ(m + n)**.
Trigonometric form: ∫₀^{π/2} sin^(2m−1)θ cos^(2n−1)θ dθ = B(m, n)/2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing Γ(n) = n! (it is (n − 1)!).
- Forgetting the 1/2 in the trigonometric Beta form.
- Using Γ for non-positive integers, where it has poles.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Complex analysis
courses.summary: Complex numbers and functions, analyticity and Cauchy–Riemann conditions, harmonic functions, contour integrals, Cauchy's theorem and integral formula, Taylor and Laurent series, singularities and residues, and evaluation of real integrals by contour integration.
outcomes: Test analyticity with the Cauchy–Riemann equations and find harmonic conjugates
Evaluate contour integrals using Cauchy's theorem and integral formula
Expand functions in Laurent series and classify singularities
Compute residues at simple and higher-order poles
Evaluate real definite integrals with the residue theorem

scenes.text: Engineers sketch smooth streamlines of the Ganga flowing past a pillar.
Those streamlines and equipotentials come from one analytic function: its real and imaginary parts.

steps.title: Complex numbers recap
steps.body: z = x + iy = re^(iθ), r = |z|, θ = arg z. Euler: e^(iθ) = cosθ + i sinθ. De Moivre: (cosθ + i sinθ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ. nth roots of unity: e^(2πik/n), k = 0 … n − 1.

steps.title: Analyticity
steps.body:
f(z) = u(x,y) + iv(x,y) is **analytic** in a region if f′(z) exists at every point there (same limit from every direction). Necessary conditions (sufficient if partials are continuous) — the **Cauchy–Riemann equations**:

∂u/∂x = ∂v/∂y, ∂u/∂y = −∂v/∂x.

Consequence: ∇²u = ∇²v = 0 (both are harmonic) and level curves of u and v cross at right angles.

steps.title: Solved: f = z²
steps.body:
z² = (x² − y²) + i(2xy): u = x² − y², v = 2xy.
uₓ = 2x = v_y ✓; u_y = −2y = −vₓ ✓ → analytic everywhere, f′ = 2z.
By contrast f = z̄ = x − iy: uₓ = 1, v_y = −1 ✗ → nowhere analytic.

steps.title: Solved: harmonic conjugate
steps.body:
Given u = x³ − 3xy². Check ∇²u = 6x − 6x = 0 ✓.
v_y = uₓ = 3x² − 3y² → v = 3x²y − y³ + g(x).
vₓ = 6xy + g′ = −u_y = 6xy → g′ = 0.
v = 3x²y − y³, so f = **z³**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign error in the second CR equation (u_y = −vₓ).
- Treating |z|² as analytic; it satisfies CR only at z = 0.
- Forgetting the integration 'constant' g(x) when constructing v.

activity.prompt: Compute |(3 + 4i)²|.

quiz.q: Which function is analytic everywhere?
quiz.why: eᶻ = eˣ(cos y + i sin y) satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations at every point, while the others fail them.

quiz.q: The real part of an analytic function is:
quiz.why: Differentiating the Cauchy–Riemann equations shows uₓₓ + u_yy = 0, so u is harmonic.

quiz.q: For u = x² − y², the harmonic conjugate v is:
quiz.why: u + iv = z² requires v = 2xy, which satisfies both CR equations.

lessons.title: Contour integrals, Cauchy's theorem and integral formula

story.title: A loop that knows what's inside

scenes.text: Integrate an analytic function around a closed loop: you get zero, however wiggly the loop.
Put a singularity inside and the loop 'feels' it — Cauchy's formula reads off the function's value there.

steps.title: Contour integrals
steps.body:
∫_C f(z) dz = ∫ f(z(t)) z′(t) dt for a parametrised path.
Key example: on |z| = R, z = Re^(iθ):
∮ zⁿ dz = 0 for n ≠ −1 and **∮ dz/z = 2πi**.
ML-inequality: |∫_C f dz| ≤ M·L (M = max|f| on C, L = length).

steps.title: Cauchy's theorem and integral formula
steps.body:
**Cauchy–Goursat**: if f is analytic on and inside a simple closed contour C, ∮_C f dz = 0.
**Integral formula**: for z₀ inside C,
f(z₀) = (1/2πi)∮ f(z)/(z − z₀) dz,
f⁽ⁿ⁾(z₀) = (n!/2πi)∮ f(z)/(z − z₀)^(n+1) dz.
An analytic function is infinitely differentiable; bounded entire functions are constant (Liouville).

steps.title: Solved: integral formula
steps.body:
∮_{|z|=2} eᶻ/(z − 1) dz: z₀ = 1 is inside, f = eᶻ analytic → = 2πi e¹ = **2πie**.
∮_{|z|=2} eᶻ/(z − 3) dz = **0** (z = 3 outside).

steps.title: Solved: derivative form
steps.body: ∮_{|z|=1} cos z / z³ dz: n = 2, f = cos z → (2πi/2!) f″(0) = πi(−cos 0) = **−πi**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Cauchy's theorem when a singularity lies inside the contour.
- Forgetting the n! in the derivative formula.
- Ignoring orientation: clockwise contours flip the sign.

activity.prompt: ∮ dz/(z − 0.5) taken anticlockwise round |z| = 1 equals 2πi. Give the imaginary part to three decimals.

quiz.q: ∮_{|z|=1} z² dz equals:
quiz.why: z² is analytic everywhere, so Cauchy's theorem gives zero for any closed contour.

quiz.q: ∮_{|z|=2} eᶻ/(z − 1) dz equals:
quiz.why: By Cauchy's integral formula the integral is 2πi times eᶻ evaluated at z = 1.

quiz.q: Liouville's theorem states that a bounded entire function is:
quiz.why: Cauchy's estimate forces f′ = 0 everywhere for a bounded entire function, so it must be constant.

scenes.text: A Laurent series may have infinitely many terms, but for integrals only one survives.
The coefficient of 1/(z − z₀) — the residue — carries all the information.

steps.title: Laurent series
steps.body:
In an annulus around z₀: f(z) = Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} aₙ(z − z₀)ⁿ.
The negative-power part is the **principal part**.
- Removable singularity: no negative powers (sin z/z at 0)
- Pole of order m: lowest power (z − z₀)^(−m)
- Essential: infinitely many negative powers (e^(1/z) at 0)
**Residue** = a₋₁.

steps.title: Computing residues
steps.body:
- Simple pole: Res = lim_{z→z₀} (z − z₀) f(z); if f = p/q with q(z₀) = 0, q′(z₀) ≠ 0: Res = p(z₀)/q′(z₀).
- Pole of order m: Res = (1/(m − 1)!) lim d^(m−1)/dz^(m−1) [(z − z₀)^m f(z)].
**Residue theorem**: ∮_C f dz = 2πi Σ residues inside C.

steps.title: Solved: Laurent in an annulus
steps.body:
f = 1/[z(1 − z)] for 0 < |z| < 1: 1/(1 − z) = Σzⁿ → f = 1/z + 1 + z + z² + …
Simple pole at 0, residue 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the simple-pole formula at a double pole.
- Including residues of poles outside the contour.
- Thinking sin z/z has a pole at 0 — the singularity is removable.

activity.prompt: Find the residue of f(z) = 1/[z(z − 2)] at z = 2.

quiz.q: e^(1/z) at z = 0 has:
quiz.why: Its Laurent series Σ z^(−n)/n! has infinitely many negative powers, which defines an essential singularity.

quiz.q: Residue of eᶻ/z³ at 0 is:
quiz.why: The z² term of eᶻ is z²/2, which divided by z³ gives (1/2)/z, so the residue is 1/2.

quiz.q: The residue theorem says ∮f dz equals:
quiz.why: Each enclosed singularity contributes 2πi times its residue to the contour integral.

lessons.title: Evaluating real integrals by contour integration

story.title: An integral with no antiderivative trick

scenes.text: ∫ dθ/(2 + cos θ) over a full turn defeats most substitution tricks.
Map the circle into the complex plane and a single residue finishes it in three lines.

steps.title: Type I: trigonometric integrals over 0 to 2π
steps.body: Put z = e^(iθ): cosθ = (z + 1/z)/2, sinθ = (z − 1/z)/(2i), dθ = dz/(iz). The integral becomes a contour integral round |z| = 1.

steps.title: Type II: ∫_{−∞}^{∞} of rational functions
steps.body:
If f = P/Q with deg Q ≥ deg P + 2 and no real poles, close the contour with a large upper semicircle (its contribution → 0 by the ML-inequality):
∫_{−∞}^{∞} f(x) dx = 2πi Σ residues in the upper half-plane.
(Jordan's lemma extends this to f(x)e^(ikx) with deg Q ≥ deg P + 1.)

steps.title: Solved: ∫ dx/(x² + 1)
steps.body:
Upper pole z = i, Res = 1/(2i). Integral = 2πi/(2i) = **π** (= [arctan x] from −∞ to ∞ ✓).
Similarly ∫_{−∞}^{∞} dx/(x² + 1)² = 2πi × Res at i of 1/(z+i)²(z−i)² = 2πi × [−2/(2i)³] = **π/2**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including lower-half-plane poles when closing upward.
- Forgetting dθ = dz/(iz).
- Using the semicircle method when deg Q < deg P + 2 without checking the arc vanishes.

activity.prompt: Evaluate ∫_{−∞}^{∞} dx/(x² + 4) by residues (answer π/2). Give three decimals.

quiz.q: In Type I integrals, dθ is replaced by:
quiz.why: z = e^(iθ) gives dz = iz dθ, so dθ = dz/(iz).
The only upper-half-plane pole is z = i with residue 1/(2i), and 2πi/(2i) = π.

quiz.q: ∫₀^{2π} dθ/(2 + cosθ) equals:
quiz.why: Only the root −2 + √3 lies inside the unit circle, and its residue 1/(i√3) gives 2π/√3.

questions.q: Cauchy–Riemann equations are:
questions.why: Equating the derivative along x and along y gives uₓ = v_y and u_y = −vₓ.

questions.q: f = z̄ is:
questions.why: uₓ = 1 but v_y = −1, so CR fails everywhere.

questions.q: Harmonic conjugate of u = x³ − 3xy²:
questions.why: u + iv = z³ gives v = 3x²y − y³.
With z = e^(iθ), dz/z = i dθ, integrating to 2πi.

questions.q: ∮_{|z|=1} cos z/z³ dz:
questions.why: (2πi/2!) times the second derivative of cos z at 0, which is −1.

questions.q: sin z/z at z = 0 has:
questions.why: sin z/z = 1 − z²/6 + …, with no negative powers.

questions.q: Residue of 1/(z² + 1) at z = i:

questions.why: The double-pole residue at i is −i/4, and 2πi(−i/4) = π/2.

questions.q: ∫₀^{2π} dθ/(2 + cosθ):
An analytic function's real part satisfies:
Cube roots of unity are:
questions.why: The roots of z³ = 1 are e^(2πik/3) for k = 0, 1, 2.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Matrices, partial differential equations, revision & exam
courses.summary: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors, Hermitian and unitary matrices, diagonalisation and Cayley–Hamilton theorem; separation of variables for the wave, heat and Laplace equations with boundary conditions; and a formula sheet with previous-year-style problems and a full-paper exam covering all three Mathematical Physics papers.
outcomes: Find eigenvalues/eigenvectors and diagonalise 2×2 and 3×3 matrices
State properties of Hermitian and unitary matrices used in quantum mechanics
Solve the 1-D wave equation for a string with fixed ends
Solve the 1-D heat equation and the 2-D Laplace equation by separation of variables
Revise all Mathematical Physics formulas and solve mixed exam problems

scenes.text: Two pendulums joined by a spring swap energy back and forth in a puzzling pattern.
Diagonalise the coupling matrix and the motion splits into two simple 'normal modes'.

steps.title: Eigenvalue problem
steps.body:
Av = λv with v ≠ 0 → det(A − λI) = 0 (characteristic equation).
For 2×2: λ² − (tr A)λ + det A = 0. In general Σλ = trace, Πλ = determinant.
**Diagonalisation**: if A has n independent eigenvectors, P⁻¹AP = D (columns of P = eigenvectors).
**Cayley–Hamilton**: every matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation.

steps.title: Special matrices
steps.body:
- Hermitian A† = A: real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors (observables in QM).
- Unitary U†U = I: |λ| = 1, preserves lengths (time evolution, rotations).
- Real symmetric = real Hermitian; orthogonal = real unitary.
- Pauli matrices σₓ, σ_y, σ_z are Hermitian and unitary with eigenvalues ±1.

steps.title: Solved: coupled pendulums
steps.body: Equal pendulums (ω₀² = g/l) coupled by spring κ: ẍ = −M x with M = [[ω₀² + κ, −κ], [−κ, ω₀² + κ]]. Eigenvalues ω₀² (in-phase, (1,1)) and ω₀² + 2κ (anti-phase, (1,−1)). Energy swaps with beat frequency equal to the difference of the two normal-mode frequencies.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Normalising eigenvectors incorrectly for complex vectors (use v†v = 1).
- Assuming every matrix is diagonalisable ([[1,1],[0,1]] is not).
- Taking transpose instead of conjugate transpose for Hermitian tests.

activity.prompt: Find the larger eigenvalue of the matrix [[4, 1], [2, 3]].

quiz.q: Eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix are:
quiz.why: For Av = λv, v†Av is real when A is Hermitian, which forces λ to be real.

quiz.q: The sum of eigenvalues equals:
quiz.why: Comparing coefficients of the characteristic polynomial shows Σλ equals the trace.

quiz.q: For a unitary matrix, every eigenvalue satisfies:
quiz.why: Unitary matrices preserve norms, so |Uv| = |λ||v| = |v| gives |λ| = 1.

scenes.text: Pressing a fret shortens the vibrating length and raises the pitch.
Separation of variables on the wave equation gives f = n v/(2L) — the whole story of frets.

steps.title: Separation of variables
steps.body:
∂²y/∂t² = v² ∂²y/∂x², y(0,t) = y(L,t) = 0, v = √(T/μ).
Try y = X(x)T(t): X″/X = T̈/(v²T) = −k².
X = sin kx with kL = nπ → **kₙ = nπ/L**, ωₙ = vkₙ, fₙ = nv/(2L).
y(x,t) = Σ sin(nπx/L)[Aₙ cos ωₙt + Bₙ sin ωₙt].

steps.title: Using initial conditions
steps.body:
Initial shape y(x,0) = f(x) → Aₙ = (2/L)∫₀^L f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx (half-range sine series).
Initial velocity g(x) → Bₙωₙ = (2/L)∫₀^L g(x) sin(nπx/L) dx.
Plucked at the middle: only odd harmonics appear (the middle is an antinode for odd n).

steps.title: d'Alembert's solution
steps.body: The general solution of the 1-D wave equation is y = F(x − vt) + G(x + vt): two shapes travelling in opposite directions. Standing waves are their superposition.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing a positive separation constant, which gives exponentials that cannot satisfy two fixed ends.
- Using μ in g/m with T in N.
- Forgetting that plucking at a node of harmonic n removes that harmonic.

activity.prompt: A string of length 0.50 m, tension 100 N and linear density 1.0 g/m is fixed at both ends. Find its fundamental frequency in Hz.

quiz.q: For a string fixed at both ends, allowed wavenumbers are:
quiz.why: sin kL = 0 at the far end requires kL = nπ.

quiz.q: Doubling string tension multiplies f₁ by:
quiz.why: f₁ = (1/2L)√(T/μ), so doubling T multiplies the frequency by √2.

quiz.q: A string plucked at its midpoint lacks:
quiz.why: Even harmonics have a node at the midpoint, so a pluck there does not excite them.

scenes.text: A rod taken from the forge has its ends dipped in ice water. Sharp kinks in its temperature profile smooth out first.
Each Fourier mode dies at its own rate — high harmonics fastest.

steps.title: 1-D heat equation
steps.body:
∂u/∂t = α ∂²u/∂x², u(0,t) = u(L,t) = 0.
Separation: u = Σ bₙ sin(nπx/L) exp(−n²π²αt/L²), bₙ from the initial profile (sine series).
Mode n decays with time constant τₙ = L²/(n²π²α): the n = 3 mode dies 9 times faster than n = 1.

steps.title: 2-D Laplace equation
steps.body:
∇²u = 0 in a rectangle 0 < x < a, 0 < y < b with u = 0 on three sides and u(x, b) = f(x):
u = Σ cₙ sin(nπx/a) sinh(nπy/a), with cₙ sinh(nπb/a) = (2/a)∫₀^a f(x) sin(nπx/a) dx.
Maximum principle: a harmonic function takes its max and min on the boundary.

steps.title: Solved: decay time of a copper rod
steps.body:
L = 1.0 m, α(copper) ≈ 1.1×10⁻⁴ m²/s.
τ₁ = L²/(π²α) = 1/(9.87 × 1.1×10⁻⁴) = **≈ 920 s** (about 15 min). The n = 2 mode: τ₂ = 230 s.

steps.title: Solved: initial profile with one mode
steps.body: If u(x, 0) = 50 sin(πx/L) °C, then u(x, t) = 50 sin(πx/L) e^(−t/τ₁). After t = τ₁ ln 2 the centre has fallen to 25 °C.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing e^(−nπαt/L) (the n and π are squared).
- Using sinh where cosh fits the boundary condition, or vice versa — check u at y = 0.
- Forgetting to shift to zero boundary values when ends are held at non-zero temperatures (subtract the steady linear profile first).

activity.prompt: For a rod of length 0.50 m with diffusivity α = 1.0×10⁻⁴ m²/s and ends at 0 °C, find the decay time constant τ₁ = L²/(π²α) of the fundamental mode, in seconds.

quiz.q: In the heat equation solution, mode n decays as:
quiz.why: Substituting sin(nπx/L) into ∂u/∂t = α∂²u/∂x² gives a decay rate proportional to n².

quiz.q: A harmonic function in a region attains its maximum:
quiz.why: The maximum principle states a non-constant harmonic function has no interior maxima, so extrema lie on the boundary.

quiz.q: Laplace's equation in a rectangle with data on the top edge uses in y:
quiz.why: With the x-part oscillatory, the y-part must satisfy Y″ = k²Y, and sinh(ky) vanishes at y = 0 as required.

lessons.title: Revision: formula sheet and previous-year-style problems

scenes.text: Mathematical Physics I, II and III together look enormous the week before exams.
Grouped by idea, the essential formulas fit on two cards.

steps.title: Sheet I — vectors, ODEs, Fourier
steps.body:
- ∇×∇φ = 0; ∇·∇×A = 0; Gauss ∭∇·F dV = ∯F·dA; Stokes ∬(∇×F)·dA = ∮F·dr
- Spherical: dV = r² sinθ dr dθ dφ; ∇² radial part (1/r²)∂ᵣ(r²∂ᵣ)
- μ = e^(∫P dx); auxiliary roots → e^(mx), (A + Bx)e^(mx), e^(αx)(cos, sin)
- ω_d = √(ω₀² − γ²); Q = ω₀/2γ
- aₙ, bₙ = (1/π)∫f cos/sin nx; Parseval; Σ1/n² = π²/6

steps.body:
- P₂ = (3x² − 1)/2; ∫P_mP_n = 2δ/(2n + 1); Γ(1/2) = √π; B = ΓΓ/Γ
- CR: uₓ = v_y, u_y = −vₓ; f(z₀) = (1/2πi)∮f/(z − z₀); ∮ = 2πiΣRes
- Σλ = trace, Πλ = det; Hermitian → real λ
- String fₙ = nv/2L; heat τₙ = L²/(n²π²α)

steps.title: Problem 1 (5 marks)
steps.body:
Verify Stokes' theorem for F = (−y, x, 0) over the disc x² + y² ≤ 4.
- Curl = 2k̂; flux = 2 × π(4) = 8π
- Line integral with z = 2e^(iθ): ∮(−y dx + x dy) = ∫₀^{2π} 4 dθ = 8π ✓

steps.title: Problem 2 (5 marks)
steps.body:
Find eigenvalues of σ_y = [[0, −i], [i, 0]].
λ² − (0)λ + (0 − (−i)(i)) = λ² − 1 = 0 → **λ = ±1** (real, as σ_y is Hermitian).
