uni-bsc-phy-mechanics.title: B.Sc. Physics · Mechanics
uni-bsc-phy-mechanics.description: Full first-semester Mechanics: frames of reference, Newton's laws, work–energy, momentum and collisions, rotational dynamics, gravitation and central forces, elasticity and special relativity, with lab experiments and exam practice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc. Physics (Hons./Programme) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Frames of Reference & Newton's Laws
courses.summary: Inertial and non-inertial frames, Galilean transformation, Newton's laws applied to connected bodies, pseudo forces, and the centrifugal and Coriolis forces of a rotating Earth.
outcomes: Apply Galilean transformations to positions, velocities and accelerations
Solve connected-body problems with free-body diagrams
Use pseudo forces correctly in linearly accelerating frames
Derive and estimate centrifugal and Coriolis accelerations on Earth

scenes.text: Riya sits in a train moving at 20 m/s and rolls a ball forward at 5 m/s along the aisle.
Arjun on the platform sees the same ball moving at 25 m/s. Both are right — they use different frames.

steps.title: Frame of reference
steps.body: A frame of reference is a coordinate system plus a clock used to describe motion. An inertial frame is one in which a free particle (no net force) moves with constant velocity; Newton's first law effectively defines such frames. Any frame moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is also inertial.

steps.title: Galilean transformation
steps.body: Let frame S′ move with constant velocity V along +x relative to S, origins coinciding at t = 0. Then x′ = x − Vt, y′ = y, z′ = z, t′ = t. Differentiating: u′ = u − V (velocity addition). Differentiating again: a′ = a, so acceleration — and hence F = ma — is the same in all inertial frames. This is Galilean invariance of Newton's laws.

steps.title: Worked example: velocity addition
steps.body: Train (S′) moves at V = 20 m/s; ball moves at u′ = +5 m/s in the train. Ground velocity u = u′ + V = 25 m/s. If thrown backward (u′ = −5 m/s), u = 15 m/s. Acceleration of a ball dropped in the train is g in both frames.

steps.title: Worked example: rain and umbrella
steps.body: Rain falls vertically at 6 m/s; a cyclist moves at 8 m/s. Rain velocity relative to cyclist = (−8, −6) m/s, magnitude √(64 + 36) = 10 m/s, at tan⁻¹(8/6) ≈ 53° from the vertical, coming from the front. Tilt the umbrella forward by 53°.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Galilean transformation assumes t′ = t and holds only for speeds much less than c; at relativistic speeds use the Lorentz transformation (Unit 6). Also, velocity changes between frames but acceleration does not — students often 'transform' accelerations by subtracting V.

steps.title: Is the Earth inertial?
steps.body: Only approximately: its rotation gives a centripetal acceleration of about 0.034 m/s² at the equator. For most lab problems we neglect this; for winds, ocean currents and long-range projectiles we cannot.

activity.prompt: A boat moves at 4 m/s relative to water straight across a river flowing at 3 m/s. What is the boat's speed relative to the bank (m/s)?

quiz.q: Under a Galilean transformation between two inertial frames, which quantity is unchanged?
quiz.why: Because V is constant, differentiating u′ = u − V gives a′ = a, so acceleration is invariant.

quiz.q: A frame in which a free particle moves with constant velocity is:
quiz.why: That is the definition of an inertial frame, the frame in which Newton's first law holds.

quiz.q: Galilean transformation fails when:
quiz.why: It assumes absolute time, which experiments show is wrong at speeds comparable to light, where Lorentz transformations apply.

scenes.text: A student stands on a bathroom scale in a lift. As the lift starts upward the reading jumps; as it slows near the top it drops.
The scale reads the normal force N, not the weight mg — and N depends on the acceleration.

steps.title: The three laws
steps.body: First law: a body continues in uniform motion unless acted on by a net force (defines inertial frames). Second law: F_net = dp/dt; for constant mass F_net = ma. Third law: forces come in equal and opposite pairs acting on DIFFERENT bodies, so action–reaction pairs never cancel on one free-body diagram.

steps.title: Method: free-body diagrams
steps.body: 1) Isolate each body. 2) Draw every external force (weight, normal, tension, friction). 3) Choose axes along the expected acceleration. 4) Write ΣF = ma for each body. 5) Add constraint equations (inextensible string → equal accelerations). 6) Solve simultaneously.

steps.title: Worked example: lift
steps.body: m = 60 kg, lift accelerates upward at 2 m/s², g = 9.8 m/s². N − mg = ma → N = m(g + a) = 60 × 11.8 = 708 N. Moving down with a = 2 m/s² downward: N = 60 × 7.8 = 468 N. In free fall (a = g) N = 0: apparent weightlessness.

steps.title: Worked example: Atwood machine
steps.body: Masses m₁ = 3 kg and m₂ = 2 kg over a light frictionless pulley. For m₁ (going down): m₁g − T = m₁a. For m₂: T − m₂g = m₂a. Adding: a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂) = (1/5)(9.8) = 1.96 m/s². Tension T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) = 2(3)(2)(9.8)/5 = 23.52 N.

steps.title: Worked example: friction on an incline
steps.body: A 5 kg block on a 30° incline, μ_k = 0.2. a = g(sin30° − μ cos30°) = 9.8(0.5 − 0.2 × 0.866) = 9.8 × 0.3268 ≈ 3.20 m/s² down the slope.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Putting both members of an action–reaction pair on one body; using N = mg on inclines (it is mg cosθ) or in accelerating lifts; forgetting that static friction is ≤ μ_s N, not always equal to it.

activity.prompt: Atwood machine with 5 kg and 3 kg masses, g = 9.8 m/s². What is the tension in the string (N)?

quiz.q: A 50 kg person in a lift accelerating downward at 1.8 m/s² (g = 9.8). Scale reads:
quiz.why: N = m(g − a) = 50 × 8.0 = 400 N, because a downward acceleration reduces the required normal force.

quiz.q: Action and reaction forces:
options: Act on the same body and cancel
quiz.why: Newton's third-law pairs act on two different bodies, so they never cancel in a single body's force balance.

quiz.q: Acceleration of an Atwood machine with equal masses is:
quiz.why: a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂) vanishes when the masses are equal, so the system stays at rest or moves uniformly.

quiz.q: On an incline of angle θ the normal force on a block (no other push) is:
quiz.why: Only the component of weight perpendicular to the surface, mg cosθ, is balanced by the normal force.

scenes.text: A pendulum hangs from the mirror of a car. When the car accelerates, the bob swings back and stays tilted.
Inside the car nothing pushes the bob backward — yet Newton's law seems to need a force. Enter the pseudo force.

steps.title: Pseudo (fictitious) force
steps.body: In a frame accelerating with a₀ relative to an inertial frame, a particle obeys m a′ = F_real − m a₀. The term −m a₀ is a pseudo force: it has no source body and no reaction partner, but it lets us use Newton's second law inside the accelerating frame.

steps.title: Worked example: pendulum in a car
steps.body: Car acceleration a₀. In the car frame the bob is in equilibrium under T, mg (down) and m a₀ (backward). T sinθ = m a₀ and T cosθ = mg, so tanθ = a₀/g. For θ = 30°: a₀ = 9.8 × tan30° = 9.8 × 0.577 ≈ 5.66 m/s². T = m√(g² + a₀²).

steps.title: Worked example: block on an accelerating wedge
steps.body: A smooth wedge of angle θ is pushed horizontally with acceleration a₀. For the block to stay at rest on it (wedge frame), the pseudo force m a₀ along the push must balance gravity's component along the slope: m a₀ cosθ = mg sinθ → a₀ = g tanθ. For θ = 45°, a₀ = 9.8 m/s².

steps.title: Choose one frame and stick to it
steps.body: Either solve in the ground frame with no pseudo forces, or in the accelerating frame with pseudo forces. Mixing the two is the commonest source of double-counting.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Adding a pseudo force when working in the ground frame; pointing it along a₀ instead of opposite; looking for its third-law reaction (there is none).

activity.prompt: Classify each force.

items.text: Centrifugal force in a rotating frame
−m a₀ in an accelerating lift frame

quiz.q: A pendulum in a car accelerating at a₀ hangs at angle θ with tanθ equal to:
quiz.why: Balancing the horizontal pseudo force m a₀ against the vertical weight mg in the car frame gives tanθ = a₀/g.

quiz.q: A pseudo force has:
quiz.why: It arises from the frame's acceleration rather than from an interaction, so Newton's third law does not apply to it.

quiz.q: The pseudo force in a frame with acceleration a₀ is:
quiz.why: It is −m a₀, directed opposite to the acceleration of the frame.

scenes.text: In 1851 Léon Foucault hung a long pendulum in the Panthéon; its swing plane slowly turned through the day.
The pendulum wasn't turning — the Earth was turning under it. The Coriolis force explains the rate.

steps.title: Equation of motion in a rotating frame
steps.body: For a frame rotating with constant angular velocity ω about a fixed axis: m a_rot = F − 2m(ω × v_rot) − m ω × (ω × r). The second term is the Coriolis force, the third the centrifugal force (magnitude mω²ρ, directed away from the axis, ρ = distance from axis).

steps.title: Effects on Earth
steps.body: ω = 2π/86164 s ≈ 7.29 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s. Centrifugal acceleration at latitude λ is ω²R cosλ; at the equator ω²R = (7.29 × 10⁻⁵)² × 6.37 × 10⁶ ≈ 0.034 m/s², so effective g is smallest there. The horizontal Coriolis acceleration for horizontal motion is 2ωv sinλ, deflecting moving bodies to the right in the northern hemisphere.

steps.title: Worked example: Coriolis deflection
steps.body: A projectile moves horizontally at 500 m/s at latitude 30° N. a_c = 2ωv sinλ = 2 × 7.29 × 10⁻⁵ × 500 × 0.5 ≈ 0.0365 m/s², to the right of its motion.

steps.title: Worked example: Foucault pendulum
steps.body: The swing plane rotates with angular speed ω sinλ, so it completes one turn in T = 24 h / sinλ (using the sidereal day ≈ 23.93 h gives a slightly smaller value). At the pole λ = 90°: 24 h. At 30°: 24/0.5 = 48 h. At the equator the plane does not rotate.

steps.title: Cyclones
steps.body: Air moving toward a low-pressure centre is deflected right in the northern hemisphere, producing anticlockwise cyclones in the Bay of Bengal and clockwise ones south of the equator. Coriolis force is far too weak to set the swirl direction of a sink drain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using cosλ instead of sinλ for the horizontal Coriolis component; forgetting the factor 2; applying the Coriolis force to a body at rest in the rotating frame (it is zero when v_rot = 0).

activity.prompt: Using T = 24 h / sinλ, how many hours does a Foucault pendulum at latitude 30° take for one full rotation of its plane?

quiz.q: The Coriolis force on a particle is:
quiz.why: The Coriolis term is −2m(ω × v_rot), depending on the velocity measured in the rotating frame.

quiz.q: Effective g on Earth is least at:
quiz.why: Centrifugal acceleration ω²R cosλ is largest at the equator and the equatorial radius is also largest, so g_eff is smallest there.

quiz.q: In the northern hemisphere a moving body is deflected:
quiz.why: With ω pointing north out of the ground, −2ω × v gives a rightward deflection for horizontal motion in the northern hemisphere.

questions.q: x′ = x − Vt, t′ = t is the:
questions.why: These are the Galilean equations for frames in uniform relative motion along x.

questions.q: Newton's second law holds unchanged in all inertial frames because:
questions.why: Under a Galilean transformation a′ = a, and mass and force are frame-independent, so F = ma keeps its form.

questions.q: Rain falls vertically at 3 m/s; you walk at 4 m/s. Rain speed relative to you:
questions.why: Relative velocity is the vector difference, √(3² + 4²) = 5 m/s.

questions.q: A 70 kg man in a lift accelerating upward at 1.2 m/s² (g = 9.8). Normal force:
Atwood masses 4 kg and 1 kg: acceleration (g = 9.8):
In free fall, a person's apparent weight is:
questions.why: With a = g downward, N = m(g − g) = 0, giving apparent weightlessness.

questions.q: A pendulum in a car hangs at 45° from vertical. Car's acceleration is:
questions.why: tanθ = a₀/g and tan45° = 1, so a₀ = g.

questions.q: Centrifugal force on a body at rest in a frame rotating at ω, distance ρ from axis:
questions.why: The centrifugal force −mω × (ω × r) has magnitude mω²ρ and points away from the rotation axis.

questions.q: Earth's angular speed is about:
Horizontal Coriolis acceleration of a car at 30 m/s at latitude 30° is about:
A Foucault pendulum's plane does NOT rotate at:
questions.why: The rotation rate is ω sinλ, which is zero at the equator where λ = 0.

questions.q: For a block to stay at rest on a smooth wedge of angle θ, the wedge's horizontal acceleration must be:
questions.why: In the wedge frame m a₀ cosθ = mg sinθ along the slope, giving a₀ = g tanθ.

questions.q: A 5 kg block slides down a 30° incline with μ_k = 0.2 (g = 9.8). Acceleration ≈
questions.why: a = g(sin30° − 0.2 cos30°) = 9.8 × 0.327 ≈ 3.20 m/s²; the mass cancels.

questions.q: Northern-hemisphere cyclones rotate anticlockwise mainly because of:
questions.why: Air rushing toward low pressure is deflected to the right, which sets up an anticlockwise circulation around the low.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Work, Energy, Momentum & Collisions
courses.summary: Work–energy theorem, conservative forces and potential energy, equilibrium from potential curves, centre of mass, variable-mass (rocket) motion and elastic/inelastic collisions in lab and CM frames.
outcomes: Test whether a force is conservative and find its potential
Locate and classify equilibrium points from U(x)
Derive and apply the rocket equation
Solve 1-D elastic and inelastic collisions and use the coefficient of restitution

scenes.text: Two hikers climb the same 100 m hill — one by the steep path, one by the long winding road.
Gravity does the same work on both: −mgh. That path-independence is what makes gravity conservative.

steps.title: Work and the work–energy theorem
steps.body: Work done by a force along a path: W = ∫ F · dr. Using F = m dv/dt, the net work equals the change in kinetic energy: W_net = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i². This holds for any force, conservative or not.

steps.title: Conservative forces
steps.body: A force is conservative if its work between two points is path-independent — equivalently ∮ F · dr = 0, or ∇ × F = 0 in a simply connected region. Then a potential energy exists with F = −∇U, and E = K + U is conserved. Friction and air drag are non-conservative: they convert mechanical energy to heat.

steps.title: Worked example: testing a force
steps.body: F = (2xy, x²). ∂F_y/∂x = 2x and ∂F_x/∂y = 2x, so (∇ × F)_z = 0 → conservative. Find U: −∂U/∂x = 2xy → U = −x²y + f(y); −∂U/∂y = x² − f′(y) must equal x², so f is constant. U = −x²y + C.

steps.title: Worked example: spring launcher
steps.body: k = 200 N/m, compression 0.1 m, block 0.25 kg, smooth floor. Stored energy ½kx² = ½ × 200 × 0.01 = 1 J. Launch speed v = √(2E/m) = √(2/0.25) = √8 ≈ 2.83 m/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Sign of the potential: F = −dU/dx, so the force points downhill on the U curve. Normal forces do no work when perpendicular to motion; static friction on a rolling wheel does no work either.

activity.prompt: A spring (k = 400 N/m) is compressed 5 cm and launches a 0.5 kg block on a smooth floor. Launch speed in m/s?

quiz.q: A force is conservative in a simply connected region if:
options: F is constant in time only
quiz.why: Zero curl guarantees path-independent work in a simply connected region, so a potential U with F = −∇U exists.

quiz.q: Which force is non-conservative?
quiz.why: Work done by kinetic friction depends on path length and turns mechanical energy into heat, so no potential exists.

quiz.q: For U = −x²y, the x-component of force is:

story.title: A marble on a curved track

scenes.text: A marble on a wavy track settles at the bottom of a valley; balanced on a hilltop, the slightest nudge sends it rolling.
Reading U(x) tells you where a particle can be, where it balances, and how it oscillates.

steps.title: Reading U(x)
steps.body: F(x) = −dU/dx. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0. Stable if d²U/dx² > 0 (minimum), unstable if < 0 (maximum), neutral if U is flat. With total energy E, motion is allowed only where U(x) ≤ E; points with U = E are turning points.

steps.title: Small oscillations
steps.body: Near a minimum x₀, U ≈ U(x₀) + ½U″(x₀)(x − x₀)². This is a spring with effective k = U″(x₀), so the particle performs SHM with ω = √(U″(x₀)/m). Every stable equilibrium is locally harmonic.

steps.title: Worked example: cubic potential
steps.body: U = x³ − 3x (SI units). U′ = 3x² − 3 = 0 → x = ±1. U″ = 6x: at x = 1, U″ = 6 > 0 → stable; at x = −1, U″ = −6 → unstable. For m = 1.5 kg at x = 1: ω = √(6/1.5) = 2 rad/s, period T = π ≈ 3.14 s.

steps.title: Worked example: molecular bond
steps.body: The Lennard-Jones potential U = 4ε[(σ/r)¹² − (σ/r)⁶] has its minimum where dU/dr = 0: r₀ = 2^(1/6) σ ≈ 1.12σ, with depth −ε. The curvature at r₀ sets the molecular vibration frequency.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing 'U is zero' with equilibrium — equilibrium needs zero slope, not zero value. Also ω uses U″, not U.

activity.prompt: For U(x) = x³ − 3x, classify each point.

quiz.q: Stable equilibrium corresponds to U(x) having a:
quiz.why: At a minimum, a displacement produces a restoring force −dU/dx back toward the point.

quiz.q: Near a minimum the angular frequency of small oscillations is:
quiz.why: Expanding U to second order gives an effective spring constant k = U″(x₀), so ω = √(U″/m).

quiz.q: Turning points of motion with energy E occur where:
quiz.why: Where U = E the kinetic energy is zero, so the particle momentarily stops and reverses.

lessons.title: Centre of mass & the rocket equation

scenes.text: A launch vehicle burns most of its mass in minutes, throwing hot gas backward at kilometres per second.
With nothing to push against in space, momentum conservation alone sets its speed gain.

steps.title: Centre of mass
steps.body: R_cm = Σmᵢrᵢ / M. Total momentum P = M V_cm and M A_cm = F_ext: internal forces cannot move the CM. If F_ext = 0, P is conserved. Example: 2 kg at x = 0 and 3 kg at x = 5 m → x_cm = 15/5 = 3 m.

steps.title: Deriving the rocket equation
steps.body: A rocket of mass m and velocity v ejects mass −dm with exhaust speed u relative to it. Momentum before: mv. After dt: (m + dm)(v + dv) + (−dm)(v − u). Setting them equal and dropping second-order terms: m dv = −u dm. Integrating from m₀ to m: Δv = u ln(m₀/m) (no gravity). With gravity during a vertical burn: Δv = u ln(m₀/m) − g t.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: u = 2000 m/s, mass ratio m₀/m = 4. Δv = 2000 × ln4 = 2000 × 1.386 ≈ 2773 m/s. Thrust = u |dm/dt|: burning 100 kg/s gives 2 × 10⁵ N.

steps.title: Why multistage rockets
steps.body: Δv grows only logarithmically with mass ratio, so dropping empty tanks (staging) is far more effective than carrying them — each stage starts with a fresh, high mass ratio.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using exhaust speed relative to the ground instead of relative to the rocket; writing ln(m/m₀) (negative) instead of ln(m₀/m).

activity.prompt: Exhaust speed 2500 m/s, mass ratio m₀/m = 3, no gravity. Speed gained (m/s)?

quiz.q: The CM of an isolated system:
quiz.why: With no external force, M A_cm = 0 so the CM velocity is constant.

quiz.q: The rocket equation (no gravity) is:
quiz.why: Integrating m dv = −u dm from m₀ to m gives Δv = u ln(m₀/m).

quiz.q: Rocket thrust equals:
quiz.why: Momentum carried away per second by the exhaust is u|dm/dt|, which is the thrust force.

scenes.text: A forensic lab fires a bullet into a hanging wooden block and measures how high it swings.
Momentum during the hit, energy during the swing — two conservation laws give the bullet's speed.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body: Momentum is conserved in every collision with negligible external impulse. Elastic: KE also conserved. Inelastic: KE lost. Perfectly inelastic: bodies stick (maximum KE loss consistent with momentum). Coefficient of restitution e = (v₂ − v₁)/(u₁ − u₂): e = 1 elastic, e = 0 perfectly inelastic.

steps.title: 1-D elastic results
steps.body: With m₂ initially at rest: v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u₁/(m₁ + m₂), v₂ = 2m₁u₁/(m₁ + m₂). Equal masses exchange velocities; a light ball bouncing off a heavy one reverses with nearly the same speed. In the CM frame the velocities simply reverse in an elastic collision.

steps.title: Worked example: elastic
steps.body: m₁ = 2 kg at 3 m/s hits m₂ = 1 kg at rest. v₁ = (1/3)(3) = 1 m/s, v₂ = (4/3)(3) = 4 m/s. Check KE: before ½·2·9 = 9 J; after ½·2·1 + ½·1·16 = 1 + 8 = 9 J. ✓

steps.title: Worked example: perfectly inelastic
steps.body: Same masses stick: V = 2 × 3/3 = 2 m/s. KE after = ½ × 3 × 4 = 6 J, so 3 J (one third) is lost to heat and deformation.

steps.title: Worked example: ballistic pendulum
steps.body: Bullet 10 g at 400 m/s into a 2 kg block. V = (0.01 × 400)/2.01 ≈ 1.99 m/s. Rise h = V²/2g = 3.96/19.6 ≈ 0.20 m. Energy is NOT conserved during impact, only during the swing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using energy conservation across a sticking collision; mixing signs for velocities in opposite directions; assuming e is a property of one body (it belongs to the pair of surfaces).

activity.prompt: A 10 g bullet at 400 m/s embeds in a 2 kg block at rest. Speed of block + bullet just after impact (m/s)?

quiz.q: In a 1-D elastic collision of equal masses (one at rest):
quiz.why: With m₁ = m₂ the formulas give v₁ = 0 and v₂ = u₁, an exchange of velocities.

quiz.q: Coefficient of restitution for a perfectly inelastic collision is:
quiz.why: The bodies move together, so their relative velocity of separation is zero and e = 0.

quiz.q: In a ballistic pendulum, the conservation law used during the impact is:
quiz.why: The impact is perfectly inelastic, so only linear momentum is conserved during it; energy is used afterward for the swing.

quiz.q: A 2 kg ball at 3 m/s sticks to a 1 kg ball at rest. Fraction of KE lost:
quiz.why: KE drops from 9 J to 6 J, so 3/9 = 1/3 is lost, equal to m₂/(m₁ + m₂).

questions.why: Integrating F = m dv/dt along the path gives W_net = ΔK for any combination of forces.

questions.q: F = (y, x) is:
questions.why: ∂F_y/∂x = 1 = ∂F_x/∂y so the curl vanishes, and F = −∇(−xy).

questions.why: dU/dx = 4x − 8 = 0 gives x = 2, and U″ = 4 > 0 makes it stable.

questions.why: x_cm = (0 + 40)/5 = 8 m, closer to the heavier mass.

questions.why: Total momentum is zero in the CM frame, and conserving KE then requires each velocity simply to reverse.

questions.q: Why are rockets multistage?
options: Because Δv depends only logarithmically on mass ratio, so shedding dead mass helps
questions.why: Dropping empty structure raises the effective mass ratio of later stages, increasing total Δv.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Rotational Dynamics
courses.summary: Torque and angular momentum, their conservation, moments of inertia by integration, parallel and perpendicular axis theorems, rolling motion and the flywheel.
outcomes: Relate torque to rate of change of angular momentum
Compute moments of inertia of rods, rings, discs and spheres
Apply parallel and perpendicular axis theorems
Solve rolling-without-slipping and flywheel problems

scenes.text: A figure skater spins slowly with arms outstretched, then pulls them in and blurs into a fast spin.
No torque acted — she just redistributed her mass. Angular momentum stayed fixed.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: Angular momentum of a particle about origin O: L = r × p. Torque: τ = r × F. Differentiating L: dL/dt = v × mv + r × F = τ. For a system, internal forces obeying the strong form of Newton's third law contribute no net torque, so dL/dt = τ_ext.

steps.title: Conservation
steps.body: If τ_ext = 0, L is constant. For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, L = Iω, so I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂. Central forces (directed along r) exert zero torque about the centre — hence planets conserve L (Unit 4).

steps.title: Worked example: skater
steps.body: I₁ = 4.0 kg m², ω₁ = 2 rev/s. Arms in: I₂ = 1.6 kg m². ω₂ = I₁ω₁/I₂ = 8/1.6 = 5 rev/s. KE ratio K₂/K₁ = ω₂/ω₁ = 2.5 — the extra energy comes from the work her muscles do pulling the arms in.

steps.title: Worked example: clay on a turntable
steps.body: Turntable I = 0.02 kg m² at 3 rad/s; 0.1 kg of clay lands 0.2 m from the axis, adding mr² = 0.004 kg m². ω = (0.02 × 3)/0.024 = 2.5 rad/s. KE falls from 0.09 J to 0.075 J — an inelastic rotational 'collision'.

steps.title: Worked example: torque on a wrench
steps.body: A 40 N force at 0.25 m from the bolt, at 60° to the handle: τ = rF sin60° = 0.25 × 40 × 0.866 ≈ 8.66 N m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming kinetic energy is conserved whenever L is; quoting L without stating the reference point; using r instead of the perpendicular distance r sinθ.

activity.prompt: A turntable (I = 0.03 kg m²) spins at 4 rad/s. A 0.2 kg lump of clay drops onto it 0.3 m from the axis. New angular speed (rad/s)?

quiz.q: dL/dt equals:
quiz.why: Differentiating L = r × p gives r × F, which is the torque about the same origin.

story.title: Why the door handle is far from the hinge

scenes.text: Pushing a door near its hinge is hard work; pushing at the handle is easy.
Distance from the axis matters twice over — in torque and in moment of inertia, which grows as r².

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: I = Σmᵢrᵢ² = ∫ r² dm, where r is the perpendicular distance from the axis. Radius of gyration k: I = Mk². Rotational KE = ½Iω², L = Iω about a symmetry axis.

steps.title: Derivation: thin rod about its centre
steps.body: Rod of mass M, length L, density λ = M/L. dm = λ dx, x from −L/2 to L/2. I = ∫ x² λ dx = λ [x³/3] = λ (L³/12) = ML²/12. About one end (x from 0 to L): ML²/3.

steps.title: Derivation: uniform disc about its axis
steps.body: Rings of radius r, width dr: dm = (M/πR²) 2πr dr. I = ∫₀ᴿ r² (2M r/R²) dr = (2M/R²)(R⁴/4) = MR²/2.

steps.title: Axis theorems
steps.body: Parallel axis: I = I_cm + Md² (d = distance between parallel axes). Perpendicular axis (planar lamina only): I_z = I_x + I_y. Disc about a diameter: I_x = I_y, I_z = MR²/2 → I_diameter = MR²/4. Rod about end: ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/3. ✓

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Rod 2 kg, 1.2 m about one end: I = ML²/3 = 2 × 1.44/3 = 0.96 kg m². Solid sphere (2MR²/5), M = 5 kg, R = 0.1 m, about a tangent: 2(5)(0.01)/5 + 5(0.01) = 0.02 + 0.05 = 0.07 kg m².

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The parallel axis theorem must start from the axis through the CM — you cannot jump between two arbitrary axes by adding Md². The perpendicular axis theorem does not apply to 3-D bodies such as spheres.

activity.prompt: Match each body with its moment of inertia.

quiz.q: I of a rod (M, L) about its centre, perpendicular to length:
quiz.why: Integrating x² λ dx from −L/2 to L/2 gives ML²/12.

quiz.q: The perpendicular axis theorem applies to:
quiz.why: Its proof uses r² = x² + y² with z = 0, which is valid only for bodies lying in a plane.

quiz.q: Moment of inertia of a ring about a tangent in its plane:
quiz.why: About a diameter I = MR²/2 (perpendicular axis theorem), and the parallel shift adds MR², giving 3MR²/2.

quiz.q: Radius of gyration of a disc about its axis:
quiz.why: Mk² = MR²/2 gives k = R/√2.

scenes.text: A ring, a disc and a solid ball are released together down the same ramp.
The ball always wins and the ring always loses — mass and radius don't matter, only shape.

steps.title: Rolling condition
steps.body: Rolling without slipping: v_cm = ωR and a_cm = αR. The contact point is momentarily at rest, so static friction does no work and mechanical energy is conserved. KE = ½Mv² + ½Iω² = ½Mv²(1 + k²/R²).

steps.title: Down an incline
steps.body: Energy: Mgh = ½Mv²(1 + k²/R²) → v = √(2gh/(1 + k²/R²)). Dynamics: a = g sinθ/(1 + k²/R²). Ring (k²/R² = 1): a = g sinθ/2. Disc (½): 2g sinθ/3. Solid sphere (2/5): 5g sinθ/7. Friction needed f = Ma k²/R², which must be ≤ μ_s Mg cosθ.

steps.title: Worked example: sphere
steps.body: Solid sphere on 30° incline: a = (5/7)(9.8)(0.5) = 3.5 m/s². Starting from rest and dropping h = 1.4 m: v = √(10gh/7) = √(10 × 9.8 × 1.4/7) = √19.6 ≈ 4.43 m/s.

steps.title: Worked example: share of KE
steps.body: For a rolling disc, rotational KE / total KE = (k²/R²)/(1 + k²/R²) = (1/2)/(3/2) = 1/3. For a ring it is 1/2; for a sphere 2/7.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using v = √(2gh) for rolling bodies (that is sliding without friction); thinking friction always opposes motion — on an incline it acts up the slope and provides the torque for spinning up.

activity.prompt: A uniform disc rolls without slipping from rest down a height of 3 m (g = 9.8). Speed at the bottom (m/s)?

quiz.q: Which reaches the bottom first?
quiz.why: The solid sphere has the smallest k²/R² (2/5), so the least energy goes into rotation and it accelerates fastest.

quiz.q: Acceleration of a rolling ring on incline θ:
quiz.why: For a ring k²/R² = 1, so a = g sinθ/(1 + 1) = g sinθ/2.

quiz.q: For rolling without slipping, static friction:
quiz.why: It acts at the contact point, which has zero instantaneous velocity, so no work is done.

scenes.text: A village potter kicks a heavy stone wheel a few times and then shapes clay for minutes while it keeps spinning.
The heavy rim stores energy — the same idea as the flywheel on an engine or the lab flywheel experiment.

steps.title: Equations
steps.body: τ = Iα (fixed axis). Work W = ∫ τ dθ = Δ(½Iω²). Power P = τω. Kinematics mirror linear motion: ω = ω₀ + αt, θ = ω₀t + ½αt², ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ.

steps.title: Worked example: stopping a flywheel
steps.body: I = 0.5 kg m² at ω = 100 rad/s. KE = ½ × 0.5 × 10⁴ = 2500 J. To stop it in 10 s: α = 10 rad/s², τ = Iα = 5 N m. Angle turned = ω₀t/2 = 500 rad ≈ 80 revolutions.

steps.title: Lab: flywheel moment of inertia
steps.body: A mass m on a cord wound n₁ times on an axle of radius r falls and detaches; the wheel then makes n₂ further turns in time t before stopping. Energy: mgh = ½mv² + ½Iω² + n₁W_f, with friction per turn W_f = ½Iω²/n₂ and v = ωr. Combining: I = (2mgh − mω²r²) / (ω²(1 + n₁/n₂)), where h = 2πr n₁ and ω = 4πn₂/t (uniform deceleration: initial ω is twice the average).

steps.title: Energy storage
steps.body: Flywheels store energy as ½Iω²; doubling ω quadruples storage, so modern ones spin fast in vacuum on magnetic bearings, limited by rim tensile strength.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mixing rev/min with rad/s (multiply rpm by 2π/60); forgetting frictional losses in the flywheel experiment.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Gravitation, Central Forces & Elasticity
courses.summary: Gravitational field and potential of shells and spheres, central-force motion and Kepler's laws, satellite orbits, and elastic moduli with torsion and bending.
outcomes: Use the shell theorem to find field and potential inside and outside spheres
Derive Kepler's second and third laws from central-force motion
Compute orbital speeds, energies and the geostationary radius
Relate Y, η, K and σ and apply torsion and cantilever formulas

scenes.text: Imagine dropping a stone down a tunnel bored straight through the Earth.
As it falls, the shell above it pulls with zero net force — only the mass beneath counts, so g falls linearly to zero at the centre.

steps.title: Field and potential
steps.body: Newton: F = GMm/r², G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Field g = −(GM/r²) r̂; potential V = −GM/r (zero at infinity), g = −∇V. Potential energy U = mV.

steps.title: Shell theorem
steps.body: For a thin uniform shell of mass M and radius R: outside (r > R) the field and potential are those of a point mass at the centre, V = −GM/r; inside (r < R) the field is zero and V = −GM/R (constant). For a uniform solid sphere, inside g(r) = GMr/R³ and V(r) = −GM(3R² − r²)/(2R³).

steps.title: Worked example: g at depth
steps.body: g(d) = g(1 − d/R) for a uniform Earth. At d = R/2: g = 4.9 m/s². Above the surface g(h) = g R²/(R + h)²; at h = R, g/4 = 2.45 m/s².

steps.title: Worked example: escape speed
steps.body: Set ½mv² − GMm/R = 0: v_e = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR) = √(2 × 9.8 × 6.37 × 10⁶) ≈ √(1.25 × 10⁸) ≈ 1.12 × 10⁴ m/s = 11.2 km/s. It is independent of the launch direction and of m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using g(h) ≈ g(1 − 2h/R) for large heights (valid only for h ≪ R); forgetting that potential is negative and maximum (zero) at infinity; claiming the field inside a shell is zero because the potential is zero — the potential is constant, not zero.

activity.prompt: Taking a uniform Earth with surface g = 9.8 m/s², what is g at a depth of one quarter of the Earth's radius (m/s²)?

quiz.q: Field inside a uniform spherical shell is:
quiz.why: Contributions from opposite parts of the shell cancel exactly because area grows as r² while force falls as 1/r².

quiz.q: Inside a uniform solid sphere, g varies as:
quiz.why: Only the enclosed mass M(r/R)³ pulls, giving g = GMr/R³ ∝ r.

quiz.q: Escape speed from Earth is about:
quiz.why: v_e = √(2gR) ≈ 11.2 km/s, which is √2 times the low orbital speed of 7.9 km/s.

scenes.text: Kepler spent years fitting Tycho Brahe's precise Mars data and found ellipses, equal areas and a T²–a³ rule.
Decades later Newton showed all three follow from an inverse-square central force.

steps.title: Two-body reduction
steps.body: Two bodies interacting by a central force reduce to one body of reduced mass μ = m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂) moving about the CM. Because torque about the centre is zero, L = μr²θ̇ is constant and motion lies in a plane.

steps.title: Kepler's second law
steps.body: Area swept in dt: dA = ½r²dθ, so dA/dt = ½r²θ̇ = L/(2μ) = constant. Equal areas in equal times is conservation of angular momentum — true for ANY central force.

steps.title: Effective potential and orbits
steps.body: E = ½μṙ² + L²/(2μr²) − k/r with k = Gm₁m₂. The term L²/(2μr²) acts as a centrifugal barrier. E < 0: bound ellipse (circle at the minimum of U_eff); E = 0: parabola; E > 0: hyperbola. Orbit equation: 1/r = (μk/L²)(1 + e cosθ).

steps.title: Kepler's third law
steps.body: For a circular orbit, GMm/r² = m(4π²/T²)r → T² = (4π²/GM) r³; the same holds for ellipses with r replaced by the semi-major axis a. In years and AU around the Sun, T² = a³: a planet at 4 AU has T = √64 = 8 years.

steps.title: Worked example: perihelion speed
steps.body: Angular momentum conservation: v_p r_p = v_a r_a. A comet with r_p = 1 AU and r_a = 9 AU moves 9 times faster at perihelion than at aphelion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Claiming the second law needs an inverse-square force (it doesn't — only the third and the elliptical shape do); forgetting that the Sun sits at a focus, not the centre, of the ellipse.

activity.prompt: An asteroid orbits the Sun with semi-major axis 2.5 AU. Using T² = a³, its period in years?

quiz.q: Kepler's second law follows from conservation of:
quiz.why: dA/dt = L/(2μ), which is constant because a central force exerts no torque.

quiz.q: An orbit with total energy E = 0 is a:
quiz.why: E = 0 is the borderline between bound (E < 0) and unbound hyperbolic (E > 0) orbits, which is a parabola.

quiz.q: Reduced mass of two equal masses m:

scenes.text: INSAT and GSAT communication satellites appear fixed in the sky, so dish antennas never need to track them.
That works only at one radius, about 42,000 km from Earth's centre, over the equator.

steps.title: Circular orbits
steps.body: GMm/r² = mv²/r → v = √(GM/r). KE = GMm/(2r), PE = −GMm/r, E = −GMm/(2r) = −KE. Lower orbits are faster; to climb to a higher orbit you must add energy, yet you end up moving slower.

steps.title: Worked example: geostationary radius
steps.body: T = sidereal day = 86164 s. r³ = GM T²/4π² = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ × 7.424 × 10⁹ / 39.48 ≈ 7.50 × 10²² m³ → r ≈ 4.22 × 10⁷ m = 42,200 km, i.e. about 35,800 km above the surface, in the equatorial plane.

steps.title: Energy to change orbit
steps.body: Raising a 1000 kg satellite from r₁ to r₂ needs ΔE = (GMm/2)(1/r₁ − 1/r₂). Transfer orbits (Hohmann) do this with two engine burns, the strategy used by Indian lunar and Mars missions with repeated orbit-raising burns.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using height above surface instead of r from Earth's centre; using the solar day 86400 s gives a slightly wrong geostationary radius; geostationary orbits must be equatorial.

activity.prompt: GM_E = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s². Orbital speed of a satellite at r = 8000 km from Earth's centre (km/s)?

quiz.q: Total energy of a satellite in a circular orbit is:
quiz.why: E = KE + PE = GMm/2r − GMm/r = −GMm/2r.

quiz.q: Moving to a higher circular orbit, a satellite's speed:
quiz.why: v = √(GM/r) decreases with r even though total energy increases.

quiz.q: A geostationary satellite orbits at about:
quiz.why: Matching a one-sidereal-day period requires r ≈ 42,200 km, i.e. ≈ 35,800 km above the surface.

story.title: The torsion pendulum in the lab

scenes.text: A heavy disc hangs from a thin steel wire; twisted slightly, it oscillates slowly back and forth.
From the period, the wire's radius and length, you can measure the steel's rigidity modulus.

steps.title: Stress, strain and moduli
steps.body: Hooke's law (within the elastic limit): stress ∝ strain. Young's modulus Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L); rigidity modulus η = shear stress/shear angle; bulk modulus K = −ΔP/(ΔV/V). Poisson's ratio σ = −(lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain).

steps.title: Relations
steps.body: Y = 2η(1 + σ) = 3K(1 − 2σ), and 9/Y = 1/K + 3/η. Since K and η are positive, −1 < σ < 0.5; real materials have 0 < σ < 0.5 (about 0.3 for steel, near 0.5 for rubber).

steps.title: Worked example: wire extension
steps.body: Steel wire, L = 2 m, diameter 1 mm, load 10 kg, Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa. A = π(0.5 × 10⁻³)² = 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m². Stress = 98/7.85 × 10⁻⁷ ≈ 1.25 × 10⁸ Pa. Strain = 6.24 × 10⁻⁴. ΔL ≈ 1.25 mm.

steps.title: Torsion of a cylinder
steps.body: Couple per unit twist of a wire of radius r, length l: C = πηr⁴/(2l). Torsion pendulum period T = 2π√(I/C), so η = 8πIl/(r⁴T²). The r⁴ dependence means radius must be measured most carefully (screw gauge, many readings).

steps.title: Worked example: torsion constant
steps.body: η = 8 × 10¹⁰ Pa, r = 0.5 mm, l = 1 m: r⁴ = 6.25 × 10⁻¹⁴ m⁴. C = π × 8 × 10¹⁰ × 6.25 × 10⁻¹⁴/2 ≈ 7.85 × 10⁻³ N m/rad. Bending: a cantilever of length L with end load W deflects δ = WL³/(3YI_g), where I_g is the geometric moment of the cross-section (bd³/12 for a rectangle).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using diameter for r in r⁴ formulas (a 16× error); forgetting to convert the load in kg to newtons; quoting σ > 0.5 as physical.

activity.prompt: A metal has Y = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa and Poisson's ratio 0.3. Its rigidity modulus in GPa?

quiz.q: Y, η and σ are related by:
quiz.why: Analysing a cube under combined stretch and shear gives Y = 2η(1 + σ).

quiz.q: Theoretical limits of Poisson's ratio:
quiz.why: Positive η requires σ > −1 and positive K requires σ < 0.5.

quiz.q: Torsional couple per unit twist depends on radius as:
quiz.why: Integrating shear stress over the cross-section gives C = πηr⁴/(2l).

questions.q: Gravitational potential of a point mass M at distance r:
questions.why: Taking V = 0 at infinity, the work per unit mass to bring a test mass from infinity is −GM/r.

questions.q: Potential inside a thin uniform shell (radius R):
questions.why: With zero field inside, the potential stays equal to its surface value −GM/R.

questions.q: g at height h = R above Earth's surface:
questions.why: g(h) = gR²/(R + h)² = g/4 at h = R.

questions.q: Escape speed from a planet with twice Earth's mass and twice its radius:
questions.why: v_e = √(2GM/R) is unchanged when M and R both double.

questions.q: Areal velocity of a planet equals:

questions.why: v_a = v_p r_p/r_a = 40/5 = 8 km/s by angular momentum conservation.

questions.q: For a satellite, KE : PE in a circular orbit is:
questions.why: KE = GMm/2r and PE = −GMm/r, giving the ratio 1 : −2.

questions.q: Orbital period at r = 4R_E compared with r = R_E:

questions.why: Y = 3K(1 − 2σ) with σ = 0.5 requires K → ∞, i.e. no volume change.

Torsion pendulum formula for η:
questions.why: Combining T = 2π√(I/C) with C = πηr⁴/2l gives η = 8πIl/(r⁴T²).

questions.q: Cantilever end deflection depends on length as:
questions.why: δ = WL³/(3YI_g), so doubling length gives eight times the deflection.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Special Theory of Relativity
courses.summary: Michelson–Morley experiment, Einstein's postulates, Lorentz transformation, time dilation and length contraction, relativistic velocity addition, momentum and mass–energy equivalence.
outcomes: Explain the null result of Michelson–Morley and state the postulates
Derive time dilation and length contraction from the Lorentz transformation
Add velocities relativistically
Compute relativistic momentum, kinetic energy and rest-mass energy

scenes.text: In 1887 Michelson and Morley floated a sensitive interferometer on mercury, expecting fringe shifts as Earth ploughed through the 'ether'.
They saw essentially nothing. Light's speed did not depend on Earth's motion.

steps.title: The experiment
steps.body: A beam is split into two perpendicular arms of length L, reflected back and recombined. If Earth moved at v through an ether, the round-trip times would differ by Δt ≈ (L/c)(v²/c²). Rotating the apparatus by 90° should swap the arms and shift the fringes by ΔN ≈ 2Lv²/(λc²).

steps.title: Worked example: expected shift
steps.body: Effective L = 11 m, λ = 500 nm, v = 3 × 10⁴ m/s (Earth's orbital speed), v²/c² = 10⁻⁸. ΔN ≈ 2 × 11 × 10⁻⁸/(5 × 10⁻⁷) = 0.44 fringe. The apparatus could detect about 0.01 fringe, yet the observed shift was far smaller than 0.44 — a null result.

steps.title: Einstein's postulates (1905)
steps.body: 1) The laws of physics have the same form in all inertial frames. 2) The speed of light in vacuum, c, is the same in all inertial frames, independent of the motion of source or observer. Together they abolish absolute simultaneity and require the Lorentz transformation.

steps.title: Relativity of simultaneity
steps.body: Two flashes simultaneous for a platform observer, at the ends of a moving train, are not simultaneous for a passenger at the train's centre: she moves toward one flash and sees it first, and since c is the same for her, she concludes it happened first.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying relativity claims 'everything is relative' — c and physical laws are absolute. Also, the null result rules out a simple ether wind; it does not by itself prove the second postulate.

activity.prompt: Order the logic of the Michelson–Morley argument.
items: Assume light moves at c relative to a stationary ether
Earth's motion should make the two arm travel times differ
Recombining the beams gives an interference pattern
Rotating the apparatus by 90° should shift the fringes
The simple ether picture is rejected

quiz.q: The Michelson–Morley experiment found:
quiz.why: The observed shift was much smaller than predicted, indicating no detectable ether wind.

quiz.q: Einstein's second postulate states that:
options: c is the same in all inertial frames
quiz.why: It asserts the invariance of the speed of light regardless of source or observer motion.

quiz.q: The expected time difference in the ether picture scales as:
quiz.why: The effect is second order in v/c, which is why such a sensitive interferometer was needed.

lessons.title: Lorentz transformation, time dilation & length contraction

story.title: Muons that shouldn't reach the ground

scenes.text: Cosmic rays create muons about 10 km up. Muons live only 2.2 μs on average — at nearly c they should travel just 660 m.
Yet many reach sea level. Their clocks run slow in our frame.

steps.title: Lorentz transformation
steps.body: For S′ moving at v along x: x′ = γ(x − vt), t′ = γ(t − vx/c²), y′ = y, z′ = z, with γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) ≥ 1. For v ≪ c, γ → 1 and it reduces to the Galilean transformation. The interval c²t² − x² − y² − z² is invariant.

steps.title: Time dilation
steps.body: A clock at rest in S′ ticks Δt′ = Δτ (proper time). From the inverse transformation t = γ(t′ + vx′/c²) with Δx′ = 0: Δt = γΔτ. Moving clocks run slow.

steps.title: Length contraction
steps.body: A rod at rest in S′ has proper length L₀ = Δx′. Measuring both ends at the same time in S (Δt = 0): Δx′ = γΔx → L = L₀/γ. Only lengths along the motion contract.

steps.title: Worked example: muons
steps.body: v = 0.998c: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.996) = 1/√0.003996 ≈ 15.8. Dilated lifetime = 15.8 × 2.2 μs ≈ 34.8 μs, distance ≈ 0.998 × 3 × 10⁸ × 34.8 × 10⁻⁶ ≈ 10.4 km. In the muon's frame instead, the 10 km atmosphere contracts to about 0.63 km — both views agree.

steps.title: Worked example: rod
steps.body: A 1 m rod moves at 0.6c: γ = 1/√0.64 = 1.25, so its length is 0.8 m in the lab. At 0.8c, γ = 1/0.6 ≈ 1.667 and L = 0.6 m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Putting γ on the wrong side: proper time is the SHORTEST elapsed time, proper length the LONGEST length. Identify which frame has the clock at rest or the rod at rest first.

activity.prompt: A spaceship passes Earth at 0.6c. One hour passes on the ship's clock. How many minutes pass on Earth's clocks?

quiz.q: γ for v = 0.8c is:
Proper time is measured by a clock that is:
options: At rest relative to the events' location
quiz.why: Proper time is recorded in the frame where both events occur at the same place, where the clock is at rest.

quiz.q: Length contraction occurs:
options: Along the direction of motion only
quiz.why: y′ = y and z′ = z, so only the dimension along v contracts.

scenes.text: A train at 0.5c switches on its headlight. Galileo would predict the light leaves at 1.5c relative to the ground.
Measured from the ground, it still moves at exactly c.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body: Differentiate the Lorentz transformation: dx′ = γ(dx − v dt), dt′ = γ(dt − v dx/c²). Dividing: u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²). Inverse: u = (u′ + v)/(1 + u′v/c²).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Two rockets each move at 0.6c relative to Earth in opposite directions. Speed of one relative to the other: (0.6 + 0.6)c/(1 + 0.36) = 1.2c/1.36 ≈ 0.882c, not 1.2c.

steps.title: Worked example: light
steps.body: u′ = c in the train: u = (c + v)/(1 + v/c) = c. Light's speed is unchanged, consistent with the second postulate.

steps.title: Sanity checks
steps.body: For u′, v ≪ c the denominator → 1 and you recover u = u′ + v. Combining any two speeds below c always gives a speed below c.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Sign errors: use u′v with signs (opposite directions give negative products). The formula above applies to velocity components along v; transverse components transform differently.

activity.prompt: A spaceship moving at 0.5c fires a probe forward at 0.5c relative to the ship. Probe speed relative to Earth, as a fraction of c?

quiz.q: Relativistic addition of u′ and v gives:
quiz.why: This follows from dividing the transformed dx by dt using the Lorentz transformation.

quiz.q: 0.9c added to 0.9c (same direction) gives about:

steps.body: Relativistic momentum p = γm₀v (conserved in all frames). Total energy E = γm₀c², rest energy E₀ = m₀c², kinetic energy K = (γ − 1)m₀c². Energy–momentum relation: E² = p²c² + m₀²c⁴; for a photon (m₀ = 0) E = pc. For v ≪ c, K → ½m₀v².

courses.title: Unit 6 · Revision, Practicals & Exam
courses.summary: A one-page formula sheet for Mechanics, the standard practicals — bar pendulum, Searle's apparatus, flywheel and torsion pendulum — with procedures, observation calculations and viva points, plus previous-year-style questions.
outcomes: Recall the key results of every Mechanics unit
Perform and analyse the bar pendulum and Searle's experiments
Plan the flywheel and torsion pendulum experiments and estimate errors
Answer typical viva and long-answer exam questions

scenes.text: Meera has five units of notes and one evening left.
She condenses them to one page of results and the conditions under which each holds.

steps.title: Frames
steps.body: Galilean: x′ = x − Vt, u′ = u − V, a′ = a. Pseudo force −m a₀. Rotating frame: Coriolis −2m ω × v, centrifugal mω²ρ outward. Foucault rotation rate ω sinλ.

steps.title: Energy & momentum
steps.body: W_net = ΔK; conservative ⇔ ∇ × F = 0, F = −∇U. Small oscillations ω = √(U″/m). Rocket Δv = u ln(m₀/m), thrust u|dm/dt|. Elastic (m₂ at rest): v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u/(m₁ + m₂), v₂ = 2m₁u/(m₁ + m₂). e = separation/approach speed.

steps.title: Rotation
steps.body: τ = dL/dt, L = Iω. I: rod ML²/12 (centre), ML²/3 (end); ring MR²; disc MR²/2; solid sphere 2MR²/5; shell 2MR²/3. Parallel axis I_cm + Md²; perpendicular axis I_z = I_x + I_y. Rolling a = g sinθ/(1 + k²/R²). P = τω.

steps.title: Gravitation & elasticity
steps.body: V = −GM/r; inside shell V = −GM/R; inside solid sphere g ∝ r. v_e = √(2GM/R); v_orb = √(GM/r); E = −GMm/2r; T² = 4π²a³/GM. Y = 2η(1 + σ) = 3K(1 − 2σ); C = πηr⁴/2l; cantilever δ = WL³/3YI_g.

steps.title: Relativity
steps.body: γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²); Δt = γΔτ; L = L₀/γ; u = (u′ + v)/(1 + u′v/c²); p = γm₀v; K = (γ − 1)m₀c²; E² = p²c² + m₀²c⁴.

steps.title: Long-answer strategy
steps.body: Derivations earn most marks: state assumptions, draw the diagram, write the starting law, show each step, box the result and add one line on its physical meaning or limiting case.

quiz.q: Which result needs a conservative force?
quiz.why: A potential energy function exists only for conservative forces, whereas the work–energy theorem holds generally.

quiz.q: Which body rolls down an incline slowest?
quiz.why: The ring has the largest k²/R² = 1, so it accelerates least.

quiz.q: Total energy of a circular orbit is equal to:
quiz.why: E = −GMm/2r, which is the negative of KE = GMm/2r.

lessons.title: Lab: Bar (compound) pendulum — g and radius of gyration

scenes.text: A metre-long steel bar has holes drilled every few centimetres; it can hang from a knife edge through any of them.
Plotting period against distance from the CG gives a W-shaped curve — and g with it.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: For suspension at distance h from the CG: T = 2π√((k² + h²)/(gh)), where k is the radius of gyration about the CG. The equivalent simple pendulum length is L = h + k²/h. For a given T there are two points h₁, h₂ on each side with h₁h₂ = k² and L = h₁ + h₂. Then g = 4π²L/T². T is minimum at h = k.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Locate the CG by balancing on a knife edge. 2) Suspend from the hole nearest one end, displace by a small angle (< 5°), time 20 oscillations twice. 3) Repeat for each hole on both sides. 4) Plot T against h (taking one side negative). 5) Draw a horizontal line cutting the curve at four points; read off L = (AC + BD)/2 for that T. 6) k = √(h₁h₂).

steps.title: Worked calculation
steps.body: From the graph, at T = 2.006 s the line meets the curve with L = 1.000 m. g = 4π² × 1.000/(2.006)² = 39.478/4.024 ≈ 9.81 m/s². If h₁ = 0.20 m and h₂ = 0.80 m, k = √0.16 = 0.40 m.

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Large amplitudes (period grows); knife edge not horizontal; starting the stopwatch at the extreme instead of the mean position; timing too few oscillations.

steps.title: Viva points
steps.body: Why is it called compound? (Mass is distributed, not a point.) Centre of oscillation and suspension are interchangeable (Kater's reversible pendulum uses this). Where is T infinite? (Suspended at the CG, h = 0.)

activity.prompt: Observation: for a period of 1.85 s the graph gives an equivalent length L = 0.85 m. Calculate g (m/s²).

quiz.q: The period of a bar pendulum is minimum when h equals:
quiz.why: Setting dT/dh = 0 in T = 2π√((k² + h²)/gh) gives h = k.

quiz.q: For the two points with equal period, h₁h₂ equals:
quiz.why: Equal periods require h + k²/h to be equal, whose two roots multiply to k².

quiz.q: Small amplitude is required because:
options: The SHM formula assumes sinθ ≈ θ
quiz.why: The derived period holds for small angles, where the restoring torque is proportional to θ.

lessons.title: Lab: Young's modulus by Searle's method

story.title: Two wires and a spirit level

scenes.text: Two identical wires hang from one beam; a spirit level bridges them on a frame.
Loading the experimental wire tilts the level; a micrometer screw restoring it reads the tiny extension.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: Y = (Mg/πr²)/(l/L) = MgL/(πr²l), with L the original length, r the wire radius and l the extension under load M. The reference wire cancels effects of temperature changes and support yielding.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Measure L with a metre scale and diameter at several points with a screw gauge (mutually perpendicular readings). 2) Hang a dead load to straighten the wire; level the bubble and record the micrometer reading. 3) Add 0.5 kg steps up to the limit, recording readings each time after levelling. 4) Unload in the same steps and record. 5) Average loading/unloading; plot extension vs load — the slope gives l/M.

steps.title: Common errors
steps.body: Exceeding the elastic limit (loading and unloading readings disagree); measuring diameter at one place only; screw-gauge zero error and backlash. Since Y ∝ 1/r², a 1% error in r gives a 2% error in Y.

steps.title: Viva points
steps.body: Why two wires? Why wait after each load? (Elastic after-effect.) Why is the wire long and thin? (Larger, measurable extension.)

activity.prompt: Searle's data: M = 3 kg, L = 1.5 m, r = 0.5 mm, extension l = 0.30 mm, g = 9.8 m/s². Y in GPa?

quiz.q: The reference wire in Searle's apparatus compensates for:
quiz.why: Both wires experience the same temperature and support sag, so only the load-induced extension tilts the level.

quiz.q: The quantity needing the most precise measurement is:
quiz.why: r is small and appears squared, so its relative error is doubled in Y.

quiz.q: Readings on unloading differ from loading if:
quiz.why: Permanent set beyond the elastic limit prevents the wire returning to its original length.

steps.title: Flywheel procedure
steps.body: 1) Measure axle radius r. 2) Wind the cord n₁ turns with mass m; release and start the stopwatch the instant the cord detaches. 3) Count n₂ turns and time t until the wheel stops. 4) ω = 4πn₂/t. 5) I = (2mgh − mω²r²)/(ω²(1 + n₁/n₂)) with h = 2πrn₁. Repeat for 2–3 masses.

steps.title: Torsion pendulum procedure
steps.body: 1) Suspend a disc of known I = MR²/2 by the wire; measure wire length l and radius r (screw gauge). 2) Twist slightly and time 20 oscillations: T = 2π√(I/C). 3) η = 8πIl/(r⁴T²). Adding two identical masses at distance d (Maxwell's needle method) removes the need to know I exactly.

steps.title: Common errors
steps.body: Cord slipping on the axle; counting n₂ inaccurately; wire kinks in torsion pendulum; disc swinging sideways rather than twisting purely.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Special theory of relativity
courses.summary: Michelson–Morley experiment and Einstein's postulates, Lorentz transformations, relativity of simultaneity, time dilation and length contraction, relativistic velocity addition and Doppler effect, relativistic momentum and energy, E = mc² and mass–energy equivalence.
outcomes: Explain the null result of Michelson–Morley and state Einstein's postulates
Derive and apply the Lorentz transformation equations
Compute time dilation and length contraction and resolve standard paradoxes
Add velocities relativistically and use the relativistic Doppler formula

scenes.text: At sixteen Einstein wondered: if I rode alongside a light wave, would I see a frozen wave?
Maxwell's equations said no frozen light exists. Einstein trusted Maxwell — and rebuilt space and time.

steps.title: Michelson–Morley (1887)
steps.body: An interferometer with perpendicular arms was rotated to detect Earth's motion through the supposed ether. Expected fringe shift ≈ 0.4 fringe; observed: essentially zero. Conclusion: no detectable ether wind — the speed of light is the same in all directions for a moving observer.

steps.title: Einstein's postulates (1905)
steps.body:
1. The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames.
2. The speed of light in vacuum, c, is the same for all inertial observers, independent of the source's motion.

Galilean x′ = x − vt, t′ = t violates postulate 2.

steps.title: Lorentz transformation
steps.body:
Frame S′ moves at v along x relative to S; γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²).
x′ = γ(x − vt), y′ = y, z′ = z, t′ = γ(t − vx/c²).
Inverse: x = γ(x′ + vt′), t = γ(t′ + vx′/c²).
Invariant interval: s² = c²t² − x² − y² − z² is the same in all frames. For v ≪ c, γ → 1 and the Galilean form returns.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the vx/c² term in t′ — it is the origin of relativity of simultaneity.
- Applying γ to transverse coordinates y, z (they are unchanged).
- Thinking relativity says 'everything is relative': c and the interval are absolute.

activity.prompt: Compute the Lorentz factor γ for a spacecraft moving at v = 0.6c.

quiz.q: The Michelson–Morley experiment showed:
quiz.why: Rotating the interferometer produced no significant fringe shift, so no motion through an ether was detected.

quiz.q: In the Lorentz transformation, t′ =
quiz.why: Time in S′ depends on both t and the position x through the term vx/c², scaled by γ.

quiz.q: Which quantity is the same in all inertial frames?
quiz.why: The Lorentz transformation leaves c²t² − x² − y² − z² unchanged, making the interval invariant.

lessons.title: Time dilation, length contraction and simultaneity

story.title: Muons that shouldn't reach the ground

scenes.text: Cosmic rays create muons about 10 km up. Muons live only 2.2 µs — barely enough to travel 660 m.
Yet detectors at sea level count plenty of them. Their clocks run slow in our frame.

steps.title: Time dilation
steps.body: Proper time τ₀ is measured by a clock at rest relative to the events (same place). Any other inertial observer measures Δt = γτ₀ ≥ τ₀. 'Moving clocks run slow.'

steps.title: Length contraction
steps.body: Proper length L₀ is measured in the object's rest frame. Along the direction of motion, L = L₀/γ. Perpendicular lengths are unchanged. Simultaneity: events simultaneous in S at different x are not simultaneous in S′ (Δt′ = −γvΔx/c²).

steps.title: Solved: muons
steps.body:
τ₀ = 2.2 µs, v = 0.995c → γ = 1/√(1 − 0.990) = **10.0**.
- Earth frame: lifetime 22 µs, distance = 0.995 × 3×10⁸ × 22×10⁻⁶ ≈ **6.6 km**.
- Muon frame: the 10 km atmosphere contracts to ≈ 1.0 km. Both frames agree on how many muons arrive.

steps.title: Solved: contraction
steps.body: A 1.0 m rod moves along its length at 0.8c (γ = 5/3): L = 1.0 × 0.6 = **0.60 m**.

steps.title: Twin paradox
steps.body: The travelling twin changes inertial frames at turnaround, so the situation is not symmetric; she ages less. This has been confirmed with atomic clocks flown on aircraft (Hafele–Keating, 1971) and is routinely corrected for in GPS satellites (along with gravitational effects).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using L₀/γ when the given length is already the contracted one.
- Calling any measured time 'proper' — it is proper only if both events occur at the same place in that frame.
- Believing contraction is an optical illusion; it is a real difference in measured length.

activity.prompt: A rod of proper length 2.0 m moves along its length at 0.6c. What length (m) do lab observers measure?

quiz.q: Proper time is measured by a clock that is:
options: at rest relative to both events
quiz.why: Proper time is the interval recorded by a clock present at both events, i.e. at rest in their frame, and it is the shortest.

quiz.q: At 0.8c a 1 m rod measures:
quiz.why: γ = 5/3 at 0.8c, so the length is 1/γ = 0.6 m.

quiz.q: Muons reach sea level mainly because:
options: time dilation extends their lifetime in our frame
they are created at sea level
quiz.why: With γ ≈ 10 their 2.2 µs proper lifetime becomes about 22 µs in the Earth frame, enough to cover several kilometres.

lessons.title: Velocity addition and the relativistic Doppler effect

scenes.text: A train moving at 0.6c switches on its headlight. Do platform observers see the light at 1.6c?
No: still c. Velocities don't simply add.

steps.title: Velocity addition
steps.body:
If an object moves at u′ in S′ (along x) and S′ moves at v relative to S:

**u = (u′ + v)/(1 + u′v/c²)**

If u′ = c then u = c for any v — the speed of light is invariant. Transverse components: u_y = u′_y/[γ(1 + u′ₓv/c²)].

steps.title: Solved: two spacecraft
steps.body:
Ship A leaves Earth at 0.6c and fires a probe forward at 0.8c relative to itself.
u = (0.6 + 0.8)c/(1 + 0.48) = 1.4c/1.48 = **0.946c** (< c).

steps.title: Relativistic Doppler effect
steps.body:
Source and observer receding at speed v (β = v/c):
f_obs = f_src √[(1 − β)/(1 + β)] (redshift). Approaching: swap signs (blueshift).
Unlike sound, there is a transverse Doppler shift f_obs = f_src/γ — pure time dilation.

steps.title: Solved: receding galaxy
steps.body:
Light of λ = 500 nm from a galaxy receding at 0.1c:
λ_obs = λ√[(1 + β)/(1 − β)] = 500 × √(1.1/0.9) = 500 × 1.1055 = **553 nm**; redshift z = 0.106.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding velocities linearly at high speeds.
- Using the sound-Doppler formula for light.
- Mixing frequency and wavelength forms (they are reciprocals).

quiz.why: Putting u′ = c in the addition formula always returns c, as the second postulate demands.

quiz.why: For a receding source the observed frequency is lowered by √[(1 − β)/(1 + β)], shifting it towards red.

quiz.q: Transverse Doppler shift is due to:
quiz.why: When motion is perpendicular to the line of sight, the only effect is the slower ticking of the source's clock, f/γ.

steps.title: Momentum and energy
steps.body:
p = γmv (m = rest mass). Total energy E = γmc²; rest energy E₀ = mc²; kinetic energy K = (γ − 1)mc².
Energy–momentum relation: **E² = (pc)² + (mc²)²**. For a photon m = 0: E = pc.
Useful units: electron mc² = 0.511 MeV, proton 938.3 MeV; p in MeV/c.

steps.body:
(a) 1 g of mass fully converted: E = 10⁻³ × 9×10¹⁶ = **9×10¹³ J** (≈ 21 kilotonnes of TNT).

steps.title: When to use relativity
