story.title: Solar calculator under a tube light

scenes.text: Riya's solar calculator works under a dim white LED but not under a bright deep-red lamp.
Light is delivered in packets; each packet must carry enough energy on its own. Brightness only adds more packets.

steps.title: Experimental facts
steps.body:
Light on a clean metal in vacuum ejects electrons (Hertz, Lenard). Observations:
1. No emission below a threshold frequency ν₀, however intense the light.
2. Maximum KE depends linearly on ν, not on intensity.
3. Photocurrent (number of electrons) ∝ intensity.
4. Emission is instantaneous (< 10⁻⁹ s) even at very low intensity.
Classical waves predict the opposite of 1, 2 and 4.

steps.title: Einstein's explanation (1905)
steps.body:
Light consists of photons of energy E = hν. One photon gives all its energy to one electron:
**K_max = hν − φ = eV₀**, where φ = hν₀ is the work function and V₀ the stopping potential.
Plot V₀ vs ν: straight line, slope h/e, intercept −φ/e. Millikan (1916) confirmed it and measured h.
Shortcut: E(eV) = 1240/λ(nm).

steps.title: Solved: stopping potential
steps.body:
Metal with φ = 2.3 eV lit by 400 nm light.
- E = 1240/400 = 3.10 eV
- K_max = 3.10 − 2.30 = **0.80 eV**, V₀ = 0.80 V
- Threshold λ₀ = 1240/2.3 = **539 nm** (green): red light cannot eject electrons.

steps.title: Solved: photon count
steps.body:
A 1 mW laser at 632.8 nm emits photons of E = 1240/632.8 = 1.96 eV = 3.14×10⁻¹⁹ J.
Photons per second = 10⁻³/3.14×10⁻¹⁹ = **3.2×10¹⁵ s⁻¹**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying brighter light gives faster electrons; it gives more electrons.
- Mixing eV and J: K_max in eV equals V₀ in volts numerically.
- Forgetting that K_max is a maximum — electrons from deeper levels emerge slower.

activity.prompt: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 300 nm falls on a metal with work function 2.3 eV. Find the stopping potential in volts (use E = 1240/λ eV·nm).

quiz.q: Increasing light intensity at fixed frequency (above threshold) increases:
quiz.why: More intense light carries more photons per second, so more electrons are ejected, but each still has the same maximum energy.

quiz.q: Slope of the V₀ versus ν graph is:
quiz.why: eV₀ = hν − φ gives V₀ = (h/e)ν − φ/e, so the slope is h/e.

quiz.q: Threshold wavelength for φ = 2.48 eV is:

scenes.text: In 1923 Arthur Compton fired X-rays at graphite and found the scattered rays had a longer wavelength.
The shift matched a collision between a photon 'ball' and an electron, with energy and momentum both conserved.

steps.title: Derivation outline
steps.body:
Photon (E = hc/λ, p = h/λ) hits a free electron at rest. Conserve energy and both momentum components, using relativistic electron energy E² = p²c² + m²c⁴. Eliminating the electron's recoil angle gives

**Δλ = λ′ − λ = (h/mₑc)(1 − cos θ)**

Compton wavelength h/mₑc = 2.426 pm. Δλ depends only on θ, not on λ or the material.

steps.title: Observations explained
steps.body:
- Two peaks in scattered radiation: unshifted λ (scattering from tightly bound electrons; effectively the whole atom recoils, so h/Mc is tiny) and shifted λ′.
- Effect is noticeable only for short λ (X-rays, γ-rays): Δλ/λ is small for visible light.

steps.title: Where it matters
steps.body: Compton scattering dominates photon interactions in soft tissue for diagnostic and therapy energies (roughly 0.1–10 MeV), so it governs scatter dose in radiotherapy and image fog in X-ray imaging.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the electron rest mass in eV directly without c: h/mₑc = 2.426×10⁻¹² m.
- Thinking Δλ depends on the incident wavelength.
- Using 1 + cos θ instead of 1 − cos θ.

activity.prompt: Find the Compton shift (in pm) for X-rays scattered at θ = 60° (h/mₑc = 2.426 pm).

quiz.q: Compton shift at θ = 180° is:
quiz.why: With cos 180° = −1, Δλ = 2h/mₑc ≈ 4.85 pm, the largest possible shift.

quiz.q: The unshifted line in Compton's data comes from:
quiz.why: When the photon scatters off a strongly bound electron the entire atom recoils, and the large mass makes the shift negligible.

quiz.q: The Compton effect is hard to see with visible light because:
quiz.why: A 2.4 pm shift against a 500 nm wavelength is a relative change of about 5×10⁻⁶, far too small to notice easily.

lessons.title: X-rays: spectra, Bragg's law and Moseley's law

scenes.text: A dental X-ray tube runs at about 60–70 kV. Why that number?
The voltage sets the shortest wavelength produced — and the target metal sets the sharp characteristic lines.

steps.title: Continuous spectrum
steps.body:
Electrons accelerated through V decelerate in the target, emitting bremsstrahlung with a continuous spread. Shortest wavelength (all KE → one photon), the **Duane–Hunt law**:
λ_min = hc/(eV) → λ_min(nm) = 1.240/V(kV).
λ_min depends only on V, not on the target.

steps.title: Characteristic lines and Moseley's law
steps.body:
A fast electron knocks out a K-shell electron; an L electron drops in emitting Kα (M → K gives Kβ). Lines are fixed by the target element.
**Moseley**: √ν ∝ (Z − σ); for Kα, E ≈ 10.2 eV × (Z − 1)². Moseley used this (1913) to order elements by atomic number, not mass, and to predict missing elements.

steps.title: Bragg's law
steps.body:
X-rays reflect from parallel crystal planes of spacing d. Constructive interference:
**2d sin θ = nλ** (θ measured from the planes). Used both to measure λ (known crystal) and to find d (known λ) — the basis of X-ray crystallography.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Measuring θ from the normal in Bragg's law (it is the glancing angle).
- Thinking λ_min depends on the target metal.
- Using Z instead of Z − 1 in Moseley's Kα formula (one K electron screens the nucleus).

activity.prompt: An X-ray tube operates at 40 kV. Find the cut-off wavelength λ_min in pm.

quiz.q: The Duane–Hunt limit depends on:
quiz.why: λ_min = hc/eV comes from converting the full electron KE eV into one photon, so only V matters.

quiz.q: Moseley's law showed elements should be ordered by:
quiz.why: Characteristic X-ray frequencies vary smoothly with Z, revealing atomic number as the true ordering principle.

quiz.q: In Bragg's law, θ is the angle:
options: of the detector from the tube
quiz.why: Bragg's construction measures the glancing angle between the incident ray and the reflecting planes.

scenes.text: Red, orange, yellow, green and blue LEDs each start glowing at a different voltage.
Plot that voltage against 1/λ and the slope gives Planck's constant to within a few percent.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Connect each LED in series with a 1 kΩ resistor and a variable DC supply; voltmeter across the LED.
2. Increase voltage slowly; note the knee (turn-on) voltage V where current starts rising sharply (or extrapolate the linear I–V part to I = 0).
3. Take the peak wavelength λ from the datasheet or a spectrometer.
4. Theory: eV ≈ hc/λ (photon energy ≈ band-gap energy).
5. Plot V vs 1/λ; slope = hc/e → h = e × slope/c.

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- Why is the method approximate? The knee voltage includes resistive drops and the emission band has finite width.
- Why use a series resistor? To limit current and protect the LED.
- What does the photocell method measure instead? Stopping potential vs frequency (slope h/e).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading voltage across the resistor+LED instead of the LED alone.
- Using nm without converting to m.
- Pushing current above the LED rating and burning it out.

activity.prompt: A green LED (λ = 525 nm) turns on at 2.36 V. Compute h = eVλ/c and give the coefficient of 10⁻³⁴ J·s (e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C, c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s).

quiz.q: In the LED method, eV is approximately equal to:
quiz.why: An electron crossing the junction gives up roughly the band-gap energy as one photon of energy hc/λ.

quiz.q: Slope of V versus 1/λ equals:
quiz.why: V = (hc/e)(1/λ), so the graph's slope is hc/e.

quiz.q: A blue LED needs a higher turn-on voltage than red because:
quiz.why: Shorter wavelength means higher photon energy, which requires a larger band gap and hence a larger voltage.

questions.q: Einstein's photoelectric equation:
questions.why: Photon energy minus work function equals the maximum electron KE.

questions.q: K_max for 400 nm light on a φ = 2.3 eV metal:
Compton wavelength of the electron:
71.0 pm X-rays scattered at 90° have wavelength:
λ_min for a 30 kV tube:
Moseley estimate of copper Kα energy (Z = 29):
First-order Bragg angle for 0.154 nm X-rays on d = 0.282 nm:
Photons per second from a 1 mW, 633 nm laser:
questions.why: 10⁻³ W divided by 3.14×10⁻¹⁹ J per photon ≈ 3.2×10¹⁵.

questions.q: Which observation cannot be explained by wave theory?
questions.why: Waves of any frequency should eventually eject electrons, so a sharp threshold demands photons.

questions.q: In Compton scattering Δλ depends on:
Planck's constant from a red LED (630 nm, 1.95 V) is about:
Kα X-ray emission involves an electron moving from:
questions.why: After a K vacancy is created, an L electron drops into it.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Matter waves and the uncertainty principle
courses.summary: De Broglie hypothesis and wavelengths of electrons, neutrons and everyday objects; Davisson–Germer and G. P. Thomson experiments; wave packets, phase and group velocity; Heisenberg's uncertainty relations and their applications (no electrons in the nucleus, spectral line width, ground-state energies).
outcomes: Compute de Broglie wavelengths, including λ = 1.226/√V nm for electrons
Explain how Davisson–Germer confirmed matter waves
Distinguish phase and group velocity and show v_g equals the particle velocity
State position–momentum and energy–time uncertainty relations
Use uncertainty estimates to reason about atoms, nuclei and line widths

story.title: A PhD thesis that convinced Einstein

scenes.text: In 1924 Louis de Broglie proposed that if light waves act like particles, particles should act like waves.
His examiners were unsure — until Einstein read it and called it 'a first feeble ray of light'.

steps.title: The relation
steps.body:
λ = h/p = h/(mv) for non-relativistic particles.
For kinetic energy K: λ = h/√(2mK).
Electron accelerated through V volts: **λ = h/√(2meV) = 1.226/√V nm** (non-relativistic).

steps.title: Solved: electron vs cricket ball
steps.body:
(a) Electron through 100 V: λ = 1.226/10 = **0.123 nm** — comparable to atomic spacings, so crystals diffract electrons.
(b) Cricket ball 0.16 kg at 40 m/s: λ = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/6.4 = **1.0×10⁻³⁴ m** — far too small to ever observe.

steps.title: Solved: thermal neutron
steps.body:
K = 0.025 eV = 4.0×10⁻²¹ J, mₙ = 1.675×10⁻²⁷ kg.
λ = h/√(2mK) = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/√(1.34×10⁻⁴⁷) = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/3.66×10⁻²⁴ = **0.18 nm** — ideal for neutron diffraction from crystals.

steps.title: Bohr orbits as standing waves
steps.body: If an electron wave fits round an orbit, 2πr = nλ = nh/(mv) → mvr = nh/2π — exactly Bohr's angular-momentum quantisation, now with a physical picture.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using λ = 1.226/√V for protons (the constant depends on mass).
- Using non-relativistic formulas for electrons above ~50 kV (error > 2 %).
- Thinking matter waves are electromagnetic; they are probability-amplitude waves.

activity.prompt: Find the de Broglie wavelength (nm) of an electron accelerated from rest through 150 V.

quiz.q: De Broglie wavelength is:
quiz.why: De Broglie proposed λ = h/p, the same relation that holds for photons.

quiz.q: Doubling an electron's accelerating voltage changes λ by a factor:
quiz.why: λ ∝ 1/√V, so doubling V reduces λ by a factor √2.

quiz.q: Why don't we notice the wave nature of a cricket ball?
options: its λ is ~10⁻³⁴ m, immeasurably small
quiz.why: With such a tiny wavelength, no slit or obstacle could ever produce observable diffraction.

story.title: An accident with a nickel target

scenes.text: In 1925 a vacuum leak oxidised Davisson and Germer's nickel target. Heating it to clean it fused it into large crystals.
Suddenly the scattered electrons showed a sharp peak at 50° — the fingerprint of diffraction.

steps.title: The experiment
steps.body:
An electron gun fires electrons at 54 eV normally onto a nickel crystal. A movable detector records intensity vs scattering angle φ. A strong peak appears at φ ≈ 50°.
The crystal surface acts as a reflection grating with atomic row spacing d = 0.215 nm: **d sin φ = nλ**.

steps.title: Solved: checking de Broglie
steps.body:
- Predicted: λ = 1.226/√54 = 1.226/7.35 = **0.167 nm**
- From diffraction: λ = d sin φ = 0.215 × sin 50° = 0.215 × 0.766 = **0.165 nm**
Agreement within about 1 % — direct proof of matter waves.

steps.title: G. P. Thomson's experiment
steps.body: Thomson (1927) sent faster electrons (tens of keV) through thin metal foils and photographed concentric rings like X-ray powder patterns. Ring radii scale as 1/√V, as de Broglie predicts. (Irony: J. J. Thomson showed the electron is a particle; his son G. P. Thomson showed it is a wave.)

steps.title: Electron microscopes
steps.body: With λ of a few pm at 100 kV, transmission electron microscopes resolve atomic columns, far beyond optical microscopes limited by λ ≈ 500 nm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the Bragg form with the wrong angle; in Davisson–Germer's surface-grating view use d sin φ = nλ with φ the scattering angle.
- Forgetting the electron energy is kinetic energy eV, not total energy.
- Thinking the peak comes from reflection like a mirror — it exists only at specific energy–angle combinations.

activity.prompt: What accelerating voltage (V) gives electrons a de Broglie wavelength of 0.050 nm? Use λ = 1.226/√V nm.

quiz.q: In the Davisson–Germer experiment the diffraction peak for 54 eV electrons was at about:
quiz.why: The intensity maximum appeared at about 50°, which with d = 0.215 nm gives λ ≈ 0.165 nm.

quiz.q: G. P. Thomson observed electron diffraction using:
quiz.why: Electrons passing through thin metal foils produced ring patterns like X-ray powder diffraction.

quiz.q: An electron microscope beats an optical one in resolution because:
quiz.why: Resolution is limited by wavelength, and fast electrons have picometre wavelengths compared with ~500 nm for light.

lessons.title: Wave packets, phase velocity and group velocity

scenes.text: De Broglie waves of an electron have phase velocity c²/v — faster than light!
No paradox: information and the particle travel with the packet's envelope, the group velocity, which is v.

steps.title: Two velocities
steps.body:
For a wave e^(i(kx − ωt)):
- Phase velocity v_p = ω/k (speed of crests)
- Group velocity v_g = dω/dk (speed of the envelope of a packet built from nearby k)
Relation: v_g = v_p + k dv_p/dk = v_p − λ dv_p/dλ. If v_p does not depend on k (non-dispersive), v_g = v_p.

steps.title: For de Broglie waves
steps.body:
E = ħω = γmc², p = ħk = γmv.
- v_p = ω/k = E/p = **c²/v** > c
- v_g = dE/dp = pc²/E = **v** (use E² = p²c² + m²c⁴)
So v_p v_g = c². Non-relativistic: ω = ħk²/2m → v_g = ħk/m = v, v_p = v/2 (when the rest energy is excluded).

steps.title: Solved: superposing two waves
steps.body:
y = A cos(k₁x − ω₁t) + A cos(k₂x − ω₂t) = 2A cos(Δk x/2 − Δω t/2) cos(k̄x − ω̄t).
The envelope moves at Δω/Δk → dω/dk = v_g; the carrier moves at ω̄/k̄ = v_p. Beats in sound are the time-domain version.

steps.title: Solved: water waves
steps.body: Deep-water waves: ω = √(gk) → v_p = √(g/k), v_g = (1/2)√(g/k) = v_p/2. Watch a boat's wake: individual crests run forward through the group and vanish at its front.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming v_p > c violates relativity; phase velocity carries no information.
- Computing v_g as ω/k.
- Forgetting that a single infinite plane wave has no group, hence no localisation.

activity.prompt: An electron moves at v = 0.5c. What is the phase velocity of its de Broglie wave, in units of c?

quiz.q: Group velocity is defined as:
quiz.why: The envelope of a packet built from nearby wavenumbers travels at dω/dk.

quiz.q: For a de Broglie wave, v_p·v_g equals:
quiz.why: v_p = c²/v and v_g = v, so their product is c².

quiz.q: In a non-dispersive medium:
quiz.why: If ω is proportional to k, dω/dk = ω/k, so group and phase velocities coincide.

lessons.title: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and its applications

scenes.text: Heisenberg imagined locating an electron with a microscope. Sharper images need shorter-wavelength light.
But shorter wavelength photons kick the electron harder. Position and momentum cannot both be pinned down.

steps.title: The relations
steps.body:
Δx Δpₓ ≥ ħ/2, ΔE Δt ≳ ħ/2 (ħ = h/2π = 1.055×10⁻³⁴ J·s).
These follow from the wave nature: a packet localised within Δx needs a spread of wavenumbers Δk ≳ 1/(2Δx). They are a property of nature, not of clumsy instruments.

steps.title: Solved: no electrons inside nuclei
steps.body:
Confine an electron to Δx = 10⁻¹⁴ m (nuclear size):
- Δp ≥ ħ/2Δx = 1.055×10⁻³⁴/(2×10⁻¹⁴) = 5.3×10⁻²¹ kg·m/s
- pc ≈ 5.3×10⁻²¹ × 3×10⁸ = 1.6×10⁻¹² J ≈ **10 MeV**
β-decay electrons have only ~1 MeV, and no force could hold a 10 MeV electron in the nucleus — so β electrons are created at the moment of decay.

steps.title: Solved: atom-sized box
steps.body: Electron in Δx = 0.1 nm: Δp ≥ 5.3×10⁻²⁵ kg·m/s → E ≈ Δp²/2m = (5.3×10⁻²⁵)²/(2 × 9.11×10⁻³¹) = 1.5×10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ **1 eV** — the right order of magnitude for atomic energies (hydrogen: 13.6 eV with fuller estimates).

steps.title: Solved: natural line width
steps.body: An excited state lives τ = 10 ns: ΔE ≥ ħ/2τ = 1.055×10⁻³⁴/(2×10⁻⁸) = 5.3×10⁻²⁷ J ≈ **3.3×10⁻⁸ eV**. Spectral lines therefore have a minimum width; short-lived particles (resonances) appear as broad peaks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using h instead of ħ/2 (gives estimates 4π too large; fine for order of magnitude, wrong for 'minimum').
- Thinking better instruments could beat the limit.
- Applying Δx Δp to perpendicular components (Δx Δp_y has no lower bound).

activity.prompt: An electron is confined to a region Δx = 1.0 nm. Using Δp = ħ/(2Δx), find the minimum velocity uncertainty in km/s (ħ = 1.055×10⁻³⁴ J·s, mₑ = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg).

quiz.q: The position–momentum uncertainty relation is:
quiz.why: Heisenberg's relation sets ħ/2 as the minimum product of the standard deviations of x and p.

quiz.q: A short-lived excited state produces a spectral line that is:
quiz.why: ΔE ≳ ħ/2τ, so a smaller lifetime τ means a larger energy spread and a broader line.

quiz.q: The uncertainty argument shows electrons cannot reside in nuclei because:
quiz.why: Squeezing an electron into 10⁻¹⁴ m forces momentum of order 10 MeV/c, far above observed β energies.

questions.q: λ of an electron through 100 V:
λ of a thermal neutron (0.025 eV):
Davisson–Germer used:
questions.why: Low-energy electrons scattered from a nickel crystal showed a diffraction peak.

questions.q: d sin φ with d = 0.215 nm and φ = 50° gives λ ≈
Group velocity of a de Broglie wave equals:
Deep-water waves have v_g =
Bohr's quantisation follows from fitting:
questions.why: 2πr = nλ with λ = h/mv gives mvr = nħ.

questions.q: Electron confined to 0.1 nm has energy of order:
questions.why: Δp²/2m with Δp = ħ/2Δx gives ≈ 1.5×10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 1 eV.

questions.q: Natural width of a level with τ = 10 ns:
Phase velocity of a de Broglie wave is:
questions.why: v_p = c²/v exceeds c since v < c.

questions.q: Voltage for λ = 0.05 nm electrons:
The uncertainty principle is a consequence of:
questions.why: A localised wave packet must contain a spread of wavenumbers, hence of momenta.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Atomic structure and spectra
courses.summary: Rutherford scattering and the nuclear atom, Bohr's model of hydrogen and hydrogen-like ions, spectral series and the Rydberg constant, reduced-mass correction, Franck–Hertz experiment, quantum numbers, electron spin, Stern–Gerlach and the Pauli principle; spectrometer lab on the hydrogen spectrum.
outcomes: Explain Rutherford's scattering results and compute distance of closest approach
Derive Bohr radii and energy levels and apply them to H, He⁺ and Li²⁺
Calculate wavelengths of Lyman, Balmer and Paschen lines
Interpret the Franck–Hertz experiment as evidence for discrete levels
Use the four quantum numbers and the Pauli principle to build shell structure
Measure Balmer wavelengths with a diffraction grating and find R_H

story.title: A shell bouncing off tissue paper

scenes.text: Rutherford said it was 'as if you fired a 15-inch shell at tissue paper and it came back and hit you'.
A few alpha particles bounced straight back from gold foil — the atom's mass and positive charge sit in a tiny nucleus.

steps.title: Rutherford's experiment (Geiger–Marsden, 1909)
steps.body:
α particles (~5 MeV) on thin gold foil: most pass undeflected, a few scatter through large angles, about 1 in 8000 by more than 90°. Thomson's 'plum pudding' could not produce large angles. Rutherford's formula: number scattered ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2).
Distance of closest approach (head-on): d = (1/4πε₀)(2Ze²)/K.

steps.title: Solved: closest approach
steps.body:
5.0 MeV α on gold (Z = 79), using e²/4πε₀ = 1.44 MeV·fm:
d = 1.44 × 2 × 79/5.0 = **45.5 fm** — larger than the gold nucleus (~7 fm), so the pure Coulomb picture holds.

steps.title: Bohr's postulates (1913)
steps.body:
1. Electrons move in certain stationary circular orbits without radiating.
2. Angular momentum is quantised: mvr = nħ.
3. Radiation is emitted when jumping between orbits: hν = E_i − E_f.
Combining with mv²/r = kZe²/r²:
r_n = (0.0529 nm) n²/Z, v_n = (αc)Z/n, **E_n = −13.6 Z²/n² eV**.

steps.title: Solved: hydrogen-like ions
steps.body:
- H, n = 2: E = −3.40 eV, r = 0.212 nm
- He⁺ ground state: E = −13.6 × 4 = **−54.4 eV**
- Li²⁺ ground state: −13.6 × 9 = −122.4 eV
- Ionisation energy of H from n = 1: 13.6 eV.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Bohr's formulas to multi-electron atoms like He (only one-electron ions).
- Forgetting Z² in energies and Z in radii.
- Thinking the Bohr model is the final word; quantum mechanics replaces orbits with orbitals, though the energies agree for hydrogen.

activity.prompt: How much energy (eV) is needed to ionise a hydrogen atom whose electron is in the n = 3 level?

quiz.q: Large-angle α scattering proved that:
options: positive charge is concentrated in a tiny nucleus
quiz.why: Only a compact, massive positive nucleus can produce the strong Coulomb force needed to turn α particles back.

quiz.q: Energy of the n = 2 level of hydrogen is:
Ground-state energy of He⁺ is:
quiz.why: For a hydrogen-like ion E₁ = −13.6Z² eV, and Z = 2 gives −54.4 eV.

lessons.title: Hydrogen spectrum and the Rydberg formula

scenes.text: In 1885 Johann Balmer, a schoolteacher, found a formula fitting four hydrogen lines to amazing precision.
Bohr later showed the formula was simply the difference of two energy levels.

steps.title: Rydberg formula
steps.body:
1/λ = R Z² (1/n_f² − 1/n_i²), R_H = 1.097×10⁷ m⁻¹.
Series by final level:
- Lyman (n_f = 1): ultraviolet, 91.2–121.5 nm
- Balmer (n_f = 2): visible, 364.6–656.3 nm
- Paschen (n_f = 3): infrared
- Brackett (4), Pfund (5): far IR

steps.title: Reduced-mass correction
steps.body: The nucleus is not infinitely heavy: replace mₑ with μ = mₑM/(mₑ + M). R_M = R_∞/(1 + mₑ/M). Deuterium lines are shifted by about 0.18 nm from hydrogen's Hα — how Urey discovered deuterium in 1931.

steps.title: Solved: Lyman α and photon energy
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping n_i and n_f (giving negative 1/λ).
- Forgetting Z² for ions (He⁺ lines are four times the H wavenumbers).
- Calling the series limit a line — it is the edge where lines crowd together.

activity.prompt: Using R = 1.097×10⁷ m⁻¹, find the wavelength in nm of the hydrogen line emitted in the n = 5 → n = 2 transition (Hγ).

quiz.q: The Balmer series ends on level:
quiz.why: Balmer lines arise from transitions ending on n = 2, which places them in the visible region.

quiz.q: Lyman α photon energy is:
quiz.why: It is the n = 2 to n = 1 energy difference, −3.4 − (−13.6) = 10.2 eV.

quiz.q: Deuterium lines differ from hydrogen's because of:
quiz.why: The heavier deuteron makes the reduced mass slightly larger, shifting the Rydberg constant and the line wavelengths.

lessons.title: Franck–Hertz, quantum numbers and electron spin

scenes.text: Franck and Hertz (1914) sent electrons through mercury vapour and saw the current drop sharply every 4.9 V.
Mercury atoms accept energy only in tickets of 4.9 eV — direct proof of discrete levels without any optics.

steps.title: Franck–Hertz experiment
steps.body: Electrons accelerated by V pass through Hg vapour to an anode held slightly negative (retarding potential). When eV reaches 4.9 eV electrons excite Hg atoms inelastically, lose their energy, and cannot reach the anode → current falls. Dips repeat at 9.8, 14.7 V … (multiple excitations). Excited Hg emits UV at λ = 1240/4.9 = **253 nm**, which is observed.

steps.title: Four quantum numbers
steps.body:
- n = 1, 2, 3, … (shell, energy)
- l = 0 … n − 1 (s, p, d, f; |L| = √(l(l+1)) ħ)
- m_l = −l … +l (L_z = m_l ħ)
- m_s = ±1/2 (spin)
**Pauli exclusion**: no two electrons share all four. Shell capacity 2n²: 2, 8, 18, 32.

steps.title: Stern–Gerlach and spin
steps.body: A beam of silver atoms through a non-uniform magnetic field split into **two** spots (1922). Orbital angular momentum l would give 2l + 1 (an odd number) of spots, so two spots revealed an intrinsic angular momentum s = 1/2: electron spin (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925). Spin also explains fine-structure doublets such as the sodium D lines (589.0 and 589.6 nm).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Allowing l = n (l goes only up to n − 1).
- Saying |L| = lħ; it is √(l(l+1)) ħ.
- Explaining Franck–Hertz dips as ionisation; they are excitation (ionisation of Hg needs 10.4 eV).

activity.prompt: In a Franck–Hertz tube with neon, the current dips are spaced about 18.7 V apart. What wavelength (nm) corresponds to an 18.7 eV photon? (Use 1240 eV·nm; note that neon actually de-excites in steps, mostly giving visible light.)

quiz.q: Franck–Hertz dips in mercury occur every:
quiz.why: Mercury's first excitation energy is 4.9 eV, so electrons lose energy inelastically every 4.9 V of acceleration.

quiz.q: Maximum number of electrons in the n = 3 shell:
quiz.why: 2n² = 18, from 9 orbital states each holding two spin orientations.

quiz.q: Stern–Gerlach splitting of silver into two beams shows:
quiz.why: Two components mean 2s + 1 = 2, so s = 1/2, which cannot come from orbital angular momentum.

lessons.title: Lab: Balmer lines and the Rydberg constant with a grating

story.title: A pink glow through a grating

scenes.text: A hydrogen discharge tube glows pink. Through a grating spectrometer it splits into red, blue-green and violet lines.
Measure three angles and you can recover R_H to better than 1 %.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Level the spectrometer; focus the telescope for parallel light (Schuster's method) and set the collimator slit narrow.
2. Set the grating normal to the incident beam.
3. Find the first-order lines on both sides; record vernier readings.
4. θ = half the angle between left and right positions.
5. λ = d sin θ, d = 1/N (N = lines per metre).
6. For each line compute R = 1/[λ(1/4 − 1/n²)] and average.

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- Why measure both sides? It cancels small errors in setting the grating normal.
- Why is the slit narrow? Broad slits give wide lines and poor angle readings.
- Why can't you see Lyman lines? They are ultraviolet and absorbed by glass.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using lines/mm directly as d (d is the reciprocal).
- Forgetting to halve the angle between the two first-order positions.
- Reading the vernier across the 360° → 0° wrap incorrectly.

quiz.q: Measuring the line on both sides of the central image helps to:
quiz.why: Averaging left and right angles removes the first-order error from a grating not exactly normal to the beam.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Nuclear physics, radioactivity, practicals & exam
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Modern Physics / Nuclear Physics)
courses.summary: Nuclear size, density, mass defect and binding energy, the binding-energy curve and semi-empirical mass formula; radioactive decay law, half-life, activity, α, β and γ decay and radiocarbon dating; fission and fusion energetics; GM-counter practical; formula sheet and a full-paper exam.
outcomes: Compute nuclear radii, mass defects and binding energy per nucleon
Explain the binding-energy curve and the terms of the semi-empirical mass formula
Apply N = N₀e^(−λt), t½ = ln2/λ and A = λN including dating problems
Describe α, β and γ decays with conservation laws and the role of the neutrino
Calculate energy released in fission and fusion
Determine a half-life from GM-counter data with background correction

scenes.text: Weigh two protons and two neutrons separately, then weigh a helium nucleus: the nucleus is lighter by about 0.75 %.
That missing mass is the binding energy that holds it together — and powers the stars.

steps.title: Size and density
steps.body:
Nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3), R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm. Volume ∝ A, so nuclear density is nearly constant ≈ 2.3×10¹⁷ kg/m³ — nuclear matter is incompressible-ish, like a liquid drop.
¹A_Z X notation: A nucleons, Z protons, N = A − Z neutrons. Isotopes: same Z; isobars: same A; isotones: same N.

steps.title: Mass defect and binding energy
steps.body:
Δm = Z m_H + N m_n − M_atom (atomic masses, electrons cancel).
B = Δm c²; 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c².
Binding energy per nucleon B/A rises to a peak ≈ 8.8 MeV near ⁵⁶Fe/⁶²Ni and falls slowly for heavy nuclei → fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both release energy.

steps.title: Semi-empirical mass formula (liquid drop)
steps.body:
B = a_v A − a_s A^(2/3) − a_c Z(Z−1)/A^(1/3) − a_a (A − 2Z)²/A ± δ
Volume, surface, Coulomb, asymmetry and pairing terms (typical a_v ≈ 15.8, a_s ≈ 18.3, a_c ≈ 0.71, a_a ≈ 23.2 MeV). Explains the B/A curve and the valley of stability (N > Z for heavy nuclei).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing nuclear and atomic masses (use m_H, not m_p, with atomic masses).
- Saying iron has the largest total binding energy; it has (nearly) the largest B per nucleon.
- Forgetting R ∝ A^(1/3), not A.

activity.prompt: Using m_H = 1.007825 u, m_n = 1.008665 u and M(²H) = 2.014102 u, compute the deuteron binding energy in MeV (1 u = 931.5 MeV/c²).

quiz.q: Radius of a nucleus with A = 64 is about:
B/A is largest near:
quiz.why: The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve peaks around A ≈ 56–62, near iron and nickel.

quiz.q: The Coulomb term in the SEMF reduces binding because:
quiz.why: Electrostatic repulsion among Z protons lowers the binding and grows roughly as Z²/A^(1/3).

story.title: The age of a temple beam

scenes.text: Archaeologists find a wooden beam in an old temple. How old is it?
Its carbon-14 has been decaying since the tree died. Measure what's left and the clock reads out the age.

steps.title: Decay law
steps.body:
dN/dt = −λN → N = N₀e^(−λt).
Half-life t½ = ln2/λ = 0.693/λ; mean life τ = 1/λ = 1.443 t½.
Activity A = λN (Bq = 1 decay/s; 1 Ci = 3.7×10¹⁰ Bq).
After n half-lives N = N₀/2ⁿ.

steps.title: Types of decay
steps.body:
- **α**: ᴬ_Z X → ᴬ⁻⁴_(Z−2) Y + ⁴He; discrete energies; explained by quantum tunnelling (Gamow).
- **β⁻**: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ; continuous electron spectrum — the antineutrino carries the missing energy and angular momentum (Pauli, 1930).
- **β⁺**: p → n + e⁺ + νₑ; electron capture competes.
- **γ**: excited nucleus → ground state + photon; A, Z unchanged.
Natural series: ²³⁸U → … → ²⁰⁶Pb (8 α, 6 β⁻).

steps.title: Solved: radiocarbon dating
steps.body:
t½(¹⁴C) = 5730 y. A sample's ¹⁴C activity is 60 % of living wood.
t = (t½/ln2) ln(A₀/A) = (5730/0.693) × ln(1/0.6) = 8267 × 0.511 = **≈ 4220 years**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing mean life with half-life.
- Using log₁₀ instead of ln in t = ln(N₀/N)/λ.
- Thinking a single nucleus 'half decays' — decay is random; the law is statistical.

activity.prompt: A sample's activity falls from 800 counts/min to 200 counts/min (background already subtracted) in 30 minutes. What is its half-life in minutes?

quiz.q: After three half-lives the fraction remaining is:
quiz.why: Each half-life halves the amount, so (1/2)³ = 1/8 remains.

quiz.q: The continuous β-spectrum led Pauli to propose:
quiz.why: A third, nearly undetectable particle carrying variable energy explained why electron energies are spread continuously.

quiz.q: In α decay, Z and A change by:
quiz.why: Emitting a helium nucleus removes 2 protons and 4 nucleons.

scenes.text: India's first nuclear power station at Tarapur splits uranium nuclei.
The Sun does the opposite — fusing hydrogen. Both climb the binding-energy curve towards iron.

steps.title: Fission
steps.body:
²³⁵U + n → ²³⁶U* → two fragments + 2–3 neutrons + ≈ 200 MeV, e.g. ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n.
Estimate from the curve: B/A ≈ 7.6 MeV (A ≈ 236) → ≈ 8.5 MeV (fragments) gives ≈ 236 × 0.9 ≈ 210 MeV.
Chain reaction: multiplication factor k = 1 critical; moderators (water, heavy water, graphite) slow neutrons; control rods (cadmium, boron) absorb them. India's PHWRs use natural uranium with heavy water.

steps.title: Fusion
steps.body: D + T → ⁴He + n + **17.6 MeV**. Needs ~10⁸ K to overcome Coulomb repulsion (tunnelling helps). In the Sun the proton–proton chain converts 4 ¹H → ⁴He + 2e⁺ + 2ν, releasing 26.7 MeV in total. Lawson criterion (nτ above a threshold) sets the confinement requirement for reactors such as tokamaks (ITER, where India is a partner).

steps.title: Solved: energy per kilogram of ²³⁵U
steps.body:
Nuclei in 1 kg: (1000/235) × 6.022×10²³ = 2.56×10²⁴.
E = 2.56×10²⁴ × 200 MeV × 1.602×10⁻¹³ J/MeV = **8.2×10¹³ J** — about 2.7 million times the ~3×10⁷ J from burning 1 kg of coal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying fission of iron releases energy (it would absorb energy).
- Confusing moderator (slows neutrons) with control rods (absorb them).
- Forgetting that most fusion energy in D–T is carried by the neutron (14.1 MeV).

activity.prompt: Assuming 200 MeV per fission, find the energy released by fission of all nuclei in 1 kg of ²³⁵U, in units of 10¹³ J.

quiz.q: Energy per ²³⁵U fission is about:
quiz.why: Fragments sit about 0.9 MeV per nucleon higher on the binding curve, giving roughly 200 MeV for 236 nucleons.

quiz.q: A moderator in a thermal reactor:
quiz.why: Moderators such as heavy water reduce neutron speeds so that ²³⁵U captures them efficiently.

quiz.q: D–T fusion releases:
quiz.why: The mass deficit of 0.0189 u corresponds to 17.6 MeV.

lessons.title: Lab: GM counter, half-life, and the formula sheet

scenes.text: Even with no source the GM counter clicks — cosmic rays and natural radioactivity.
Subtract that background, plot ln(count rate) against time, and the slope gives λ.

steps.title: Procedure: GM plateau and half-life
steps.body:
1. Plot counts vs tube voltage; choose the operating voltage in the middle of the plateau (where counts change least).
2. Record background for 5 min without the source.
3. Place the short-lived source (e.g. a ¹³⁷Ba* generator, t½ ≈ 2.55 min); record counts per 30 s interval.
4. Subtract background; plot ln(R) vs t — a straight line of slope −λ.
5. t½ = 0.693/λ. Statistical uncertainty of N counts ≈ √N.

steps.title: Formula sheet — whole paper
steps.body:
- γ = 1/√(1 − β²); Δt = γτ₀; L = L₀/γ; u = (u′+v)/(1+u′v/c²); E² = p²c² + m²c⁴
- K_max = hν − φ; Δλ = (h/mₑc)(1 − cos θ); λ_min = 1.240/V(kV) nm; 2d sin θ = nλ
- λ = h/p = 1.226/√V nm; ΔxΔp ≥ ħ/2
- E_n = −13.6Z²/n² eV; 1/λ = RZ²(1/n_f² − 1/n_i²)
- R = 1.2A^(1/3) fm; B = Δm × 931.5 MeV; N = N₀e^(−λt); t½ = 0.693/λ

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- What is dead time? The interval after a pulse when the GM tube cannot register another (~100 µs).
- Why work on the plateau? Small voltage drifts then barely change the count rate.
- Why does the error fall with longer counting? Relative error √N/N = 1/√N.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not subtracting background before taking logs.
- Using too short counting intervals so statistical scatter dominates.
- Operating near the discharge region at the end of the plateau, which can damage the tube.

activity.prompt: After background correction, a source gives 960 counts per minute initially and 240 counts per minute after 10 minutes. What is its decay constant λ in min⁻¹? (λ = ln(960/240)/10)

quiz.q: A GM tube should be operated:
options: in the middle of the plateau
quiz.why: On the plateau the count rate is nearly independent of voltage, giving stable and reproducible readings.

quiz.q: The statistical uncertainty in N = 10 000 counts is about:
quiz.why: √10 000 = 100, which is 1 % of the total, following Poisson statistics.

quiz.q: Plotting ln R vs t gives a line of slope:
quiz.why: ln R = ln R₀ − λt, so the slope is −λ.

curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Nuclear and Particle Physics)
courses.summary: Size, density, mass and spin of nuclei; mass defect and the binding-energy curve; the liquid-drop model and semi-empirical mass formula; properties of the nuclear force and the shell model with magic numbers.
outcomes: Estimate nuclear radius and density using R = R₀A^(1/3)
Calculate mass defect and binding energy from atomic masses

lessons.title: Size, density and composition of nuclei

scenes.text: Tanvi reads that a teaspoon of neutron-star matter would weigh about as much as a mountain.
Her professor smiles: every nucleus on Earth has nearly that density already. Electron scattering proves it.

steps.title: Notation
steps.body:
A nucleus ᴬ_ZX has Z protons, N = A − Z neutrons, mass number A.

- **Isotopes**: same Z (¹²C, ¹⁴C).
- **Isobars**: same A (¹⁴C, ¹⁴N).
- **Isotones**: same N (¹³C, ¹⁴N).
- Atomic mass unit: 1 u = 1.6605 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931.5 MeV/c².

steps.title: Nuclear radius
steps.body: High-energy electron scattering shows **R = R₀A^(1/3)** with R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm (1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m). So volume ∝ A: nucleons pack like drops of an incompressible liquid.

steps.title: Solved: nuclear density
steps.body:
- Mass ≈ A × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg
- Volume = (4/3)πR₀³A = 7.24 × 10⁻⁴⁵ A m³
- ρ = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷/7.24 × 10⁻⁴⁵ = **2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³**, independent of A

steps.title: Solved: radius ratio
steps.body:
Compare ²⁷Al and ²¹⁶Po.

- R(Al) = 1.2 × 27^(1/3) = 1.2 × 3 = 3.6 fm
- R(Po) = 1.2 × 216^(1/3) = 1.2 × 6 = 7.2 fm
- Ratio = 2, although the mass ratio is 8.

steps.title: Spin and moments
steps.body: Nuclei have spin I (integer for even A, half-integer for odd A), magnetic moments measured in nuclear magnetons μ_N = eħ/2m_p (1836 times smaller than μ_B), and some have electric quadrupole moments showing they are not spherical. MRI uses the spin of the proton.

activity.prompt: Using R = 1.2 A^(1/3) fm, find the radius of ²³⁸U in fm (two decimals; 238^(1/3) ≈ 6.197).

quiz.q: Nuclear density:
options: is roughly the same for all nuclei
quiz.why: Since R³ ∝ A, both mass and volume scale with A, so density stays about 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³.

quiz.q: ¹⁴C and ¹⁴N are:
quiz.why: They have the same mass number A = 14 but different Z, which makes them isobars.

quiz.q: 1 u corresponds to an energy of about:
quiz.why: Using E = mc², 1.6605 × 10⁻²⁷ kg × c² equals 931.5 MeV.

scenes.text: Vivek adds the masses of 2 protons and 2 neutrons and compares with a helium-4 nucleus. Helium is lighter.
The missing mass became binding energy when the nucleus formed. To pull it apart you must pay it back.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Using atomic masses (electrons cancel):

Δm = Z M(¹H) + N m_n − M(ᴬX)

B = Δm c² = Δm (u) × 931.5 MeV

M(¹H) = 1.007825 u, m_n = 1.008665 u.

steps.title: Solved: deuteron
steps.body:
M(²H) = 2.014102 u.

- Δm = 1.007825 + 1.008665 − 2.014102 = 0.002388 u
- B = **2.22 MeV**, only 1.11 MeV per nucleon: the deuteron is loosely bound.

steps.title: The B/A curve
steps.body:
- B/A rises fast for light nuclei, with peaks at ⁴He, ¹²C, ¹⁶O.
- Maximum near ⁵⁶Fe/⁶²Ni at about 8.8 MeV.
- Falls slowly to about 7.6 MeV for uranium.
- **Fusion** of light nuclei and **fission** of heavy nuclei both move towards the peak and release energy.

steps.title: Exam habit
steps.body: Keep at least six decimals in atomic masses. The mass defect is a small difference of large numbers.

activity.prompt: ¹²C has atomic mass exactly 12.000000 u. Using M(¹H) = 1.007825 u and m_n = 1.008665 u, find the total binding energy of ¹²C in MeV (one decimal).

quiz.q: Binding energy per nucleon is greatest near:
quiz.why: The B/A curve peaks at about 8.8 MeV around iron and nickel, the most tightly bound nuclei.

quiz.q: Fission of uranium releases energy because:
quiz.why: Medium-mass products are more tightly bound per nucleon, so the total binding energy rises and the difference is released.

quiz.q: The deuteron's binding energy is about:
quiz.why: Its mass defect of 0.002388 u times 931.5 MeV/u gives 2.22 MeV.

lessons.title: Liquid-drop model and semi-empirical mass formula

scenes.text: A water drop wobbles and splits in two when shaken too hard.
Bohr and Wheeler used exactly this picture in 1939 to explain why uranium splits after absorbing a neutron.

steps.title: Weizsäcker formula
steps.body:
B(A, Z) = a_V A − a_S A^(2/3) − a_C Z(Z − 1)/A^(1/3) − a_A (A − 2Z)²/A + δ

Typical values (MeV): a_V ≈ 15.8, a_S ≈ 18.3, a_C ≈ 0.714, a_A ≈ 23.2. δ is + for even–even, − for odd–odd, 0 for odd A.

steps.title: Meaning of each term
steps.body:
- **Volume**: each nucleon bonds with its neighbours; B ∝ A (short-range, saturated force).
- **Surface**: surface nucleons have fewer neighbours.
- **Coulomb**: proton repulsion.
- **Asymmetry**: Pauli principle favours N ≈ Z.
- **Pairing**: paired nucleons are more tightly bound.

steps.title: Solved: Coulomb term of ⁵⁶Fe
steps.body:
Z = 26, A = 56.

- Z(Z − 1) = 650
- A^(1/3) = 3.826
- E_C = 0.714 × 650/3.826 = **121 MeV**

The total binding energy of ⁵⁶Fe is about 492 MeV, so Coulomb repulsion is a large correction.

steps.title: Most stable isobar
steps.body: Setting ∂M/∂Z = 0 gives Z₀ ≈ A/(2 + 0.0154 A^(2/3)). Heavy stable nuclei therefore have N > Z, for example ²⁰⁸Pb has 126 neutrons and 82 protons.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: The liquid-drop model fails to explain magic numbers and nuclear spins, which need the shell model.

activity.prompt: Find the asymmetry term a_A(A − 2Z)²/A for ²³⁸U (Z = 92) with a_A = 23.2 MeV, in MeV (nearest whole number).

quiz.q: The volume term being proportional to A shows that the nuclear force:
quiz.why: If each nucleon bonded with all others, B would grow as A²; B ∝ A means each nucleon bonds only with near neighbours.

quiz.q: The asymmetry term arises from:
quiz.why: Putting extra neutrons in higher levels costs energy because of Pauli exclusion, which favours N ≈ Z.

quiz.q: The pairing term is positive for:
quiz.why: Nuclei with paired protons and paired neutrons gain extra binding, so δ is positive for even–even nuclei.

lessons.title: Nuclear force and the shell model

scenes.text: In 1935 Hideki Yukawa proposed that nucleons exchange a new particle, and predicted its mass from the range of the force.
The pion was found in cosmic rays in 1947 with a mass close to his estimate.

steps.title: Properties of the nuclear force
steps.body:
- Strongest of the forces at short range, about 1–2 fm.
- Attractive, but strongly repulsive below about 0.5 fm.
- Charge independent: n–n ≈ p–p ≈ n–p.
- Saturating and spin dependent; has a non-central (tensor) part, shown by the deuteron's quadrupole moment.

steps.title: Solved: Yukawa's estimate
steps.body:
Range R ≈ ħ/(mc), so mc² ≈ ħc/R.

- ħc = 197.3 MeV fm
- R = 1.4 fm
- mc² ≈ 197.3/1.4 = **141 MeV**, close to the pion mass (about 140 MeV)

steps.title: Shell model
steps.body: Nuclei with Z or N = **2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126** (magic numbers) are especially stable: high binding, many isotopes, low neutron capture. Mayer and Jensen explained them with a strong **spin–orbit coupling** that splits levels by j = l ± ½.

steps.title: Predictions
steps.body:
- Even–even nuclei have ground-state spin 0.
- For odd A, spin and parity come from the last unpaired nucleon. Example: ¹⁷O has one neutron in d₅/₂, so I^π = 5/2⁺.
- Doubly magic nuclei: ⁴He, ¹⁶O, ⁴⁰Ca, ²⁰⁸Pb.

steps.title: Memory aid
steps.body: Magic numbers: 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126. Say it as 'two eight twenty, twenty-eight fifty, eighty-two, one twenty-six'.

activity.prompt: A force has range 2.0 fm. Using mc² ≈ ħc/R with ħc = 197.3 MeV fm, estimate the exchanged particle's mass in MeV (nearest whole number).

quiz.q: Which is a magic number?
quiz.why: 82 is one of the magic numbers 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126, as in lead with Z = 82.

quiz.q: The shell model needs strong spin–orbit coupling to explain:
quiz.why: Without spin–orbit splitting a harmonic-type potential gives 2, 8, 20, 40, 70…, which fails beyond 20.

quiz.q: Charge independence of the nuclear force means:
options: n–n, p–p and n–p forces are nearly equal
quiz.why: Apart from Coulomb effects, the strong force between any two nucleons is about the same whatever their charge.

questions.q: Nuclear radius depends on A as:
questions.why: Scattering experiments give R = R₀A^(1/3), consistent with constant density.

questions.q: The radius of ⁶⁴Cu (R₀ = 1.2 fm) is:
The binding energy of ⁴He is about:
questions.why: The mass defect 0.030377 u times 931.5 MeV/u gives 28.3 MeV; 7.07 MeV is the per-nucleon value.

questions.q: ⁷Li has atomic mass 7.016004 u. Its total binding energy is about:
Fusion of light nuclei releases energy because:
questions.why: Light nuclei sit on the rising part of the B/A curve, so combining them gives a more tightly bound product.

questions.q: The surface term in the SEMF is proportional to:
questions.why: Surface area scales as R² ∝ A^(2/3).

questions.q: Heavy stable nuclei have N > Z because:
questions.why: Coulomb repulsion grows as Z², so adding neutrons rather than protons is cheaper for large A.

questions.q: Which nucleus is doubly magic?
questions.why: ²⁰⁸Pb has Z = 82 and N = 126, both magic numbers.

questions.q: The ground-state spin of an even–even nucleus is:
questions.why: In even–even nuclei all nucleons pair up with opposite angular momenta, giving total spin 0.

questions.q: The deuteron's quadrupole moment shows that the nuclear force:
questions.why: A purely central force would give a spherical ground state; a quadrupole moment needs a tensor component.

questions.q: Using ħc = 197.3 MeV fm and R = 1.4 fm, Yukawa's meson mass is about:
questions.why: mc² ≈ ħc/R = 197.3/1.4 ≈ 141 MeV, close to the pion.

questions.q: The nuclear magneton is smaller than the Bohr magneton by about:
questions.why: μ_N = eħ/2m_p and μ_B = eħ/2m_e, so their ratio is m_p/m_e ≈ 1836.

questions.q: The Coulomb energy of ²⁰⁸Pb (Z = 82, a_C = 0.714 MeV, 208^(1/3) = 5.925) is about:

courses.summary: The exponential decay law, half-life, mean life and activity; successive decays and radioactive equilibrium; radiocarbon dating; alpha decay and Gamow's tunnelling theory; beta decay and the neutrino; gamma decay and internal conversion.
outcomes: Apply N = N₀e^(−λt) and relate λ, T½ and τ
Compute activity in Bq and Ci and use radioactive dating
Explain secular and transient equilibrium

scenes.text: At a hospital in Chennai, a patient receives iodine-131 for an overactive thyroid.
The nurse explains that half of it will have decayed in about 8 days, and most will be gone in a month.

steps.title: The law
steps.body:
Each nucleus has a constant probability λ per unit time of decaying:

dN/dt = −λN ⇒ **N = N₀e^(−λt)**

- Half-life T½ = ln2/λ = 0.693/λ
- Mean life τ = 1/λ = 1.443 T½
- Activity A = λN; 1 Bq = 1 decay/s, 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq

steps.title: Solved: activity of 1 g of radium
steps.body:
²²⁶Ra, T½ = 1600 y = 5.05 × 10¹⁰ s.

- λ = 0.693/5.05 × 10¹⁰ = 1.37 × 10⁻¹¹ s⁻¹
- N = 6.022 × 10²³/226 = 2.66 × 10²¹
- A = λN = **3.66 × 10¹⁰ Bq ≈ 1 Ci** (the curie was originally defined this way)

steps.title: Solved: fraction remaining
steps.body:
After n half-lives, N/N₀ = (½)ⁿ.

¹³¹I (T½ = 8.02 d) after 24.06 d: n = 3, so 1/8 = **12.5%** remains.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing units: λ in s⁻¹ needs T½ in seconds.
- Confusing τ and T½: τ is longer by a factor 1.443.
- Thinking a single nucleus 'ages': decay is memoryless.

steps.title: Quick log trick
steps.body: t = (T½/0.693) ln(N₀/N). For N₀/N = 10, t ≈ 3.32 T½.

activity.prompt: ⁶⁰Co has T½ = 5.27 years. Find its mean life τ = T½/0.693 in years (two decimals).

quiz.q: The relation between half-life and decay constant is:
quiz.why: Setting N = N₀/2 in N = N₀e^(−λt) gives λT½ = ln 2 = 0.693.

quiz.q: 1 curie equals:
quiz.why: The curie is defined as 3.7 × 10¹⁰ decays per second, about the activity of 1 g of radium.

quiz.q: After 5 half-lives, the fraction remaining is:
quiz.why: Each half-life halves the amount, so (½)⁵ = 1/32 remains.

story.title: The age of a temple beam

scenes.text: Archaeologists find a wooden beam in an old temple site and send a sample to a radiocarbon lab.
Its ¹⁴C activity per gram is one quarter of that of living wood. The beam is about 11,500 years old.

steps.title: Chain A → B → C
steps.body:
dN_B/dt = λ_A N_A − λ_B N_B. With N_B(0) = 0:

N_B = N_A0 λ_A/(λ_B − λ_A) [e^(−λ_A t) − e^(−λ_B t)]

steps.title: Equilibrium
steps.body:
- **Secular** (T½,A ≫ T½,B): after several T½,B, λ_A N_A = λ_B N_B; activities equal. Example: ²²⁶Ra → ²²²Rn.
- **Transient** (T½,A somewhat > T½,B): the activity ratio becomes constant, A_B/A_A = λ_B/(λ_B − λ_A). Example: ⁹⁹Mo → ⁹⁹ᵐTc generators in hospitals.
- **No equilibrium** if T½,A < T½,B.

steps.title: Solved: carbon dating
steps.body:
¹⁴C has T½ = 5730 y. A sample shows 25% of the living activity.

- 0.25 = (½)ⁿ → n = 2
- Age = 2 × 5730 = **11,460 years**

steps.title: Other clocks
steps.body: Uranium–lead (T½ of ²³⁸U = 4.47 × 10⁹ y) and potassium–argon dating are used for rocks. Radiocarbon is useful up to about 50,000 years.

activity.prompt: A bone sample has ¹⁴C activity 1/8 of living tissue (T½ = 5730 y). Find its age in years.

quiz.q: In secular equilibrium:
quiz.why: When the parent is very long-lived, the daughter decays as fast as it is produced, so the two activities are equal.

quiz.q: A ⁹⁹Mo/⁹⁹ᵐTc generator is an example of:
quiz.why: ⁹⁹Mo (66 h) is only somewhat longer-lived than ⁹⁹ᵐTc (6 h), which gives transient equilibrium.

quiz.q: Radiocarbon dating is useful up to about:
quiz.why: After about nine half-lives of 5730 years, too little ¹⁴C remains to measure reliably.

scenes.text: An α particle inside uranium has about 4 MeV, but the Coulomb barrier around the nucleus is about 30 MeV high.
Classically it can never get out. In 1928 Gamow showed it tunnels through, quantum mechanically.

steps.title: Q-value
steps.body:
For ᴬ_ZX → ᴬ⁻⁴_{Z−2}Y + ⁴He:

Q = [M(X) − M(Y) − M(⁴He)] × 931.5 MeV

By momentum conservation the α takes most of it:

**K_α = Q (A − 4)/A**

steps.title: Gamow tunnelling
steps.body: The α is pre-formed and bounces inside the nucleus about 10²¹ times per second. Each time it hits the barrier it has a small tunnelling probability T ≈ e^(−2G). G depends strongly on Q, so a small increase in Q greatly shortens the half-life.

steps.title: Geiger–Nuttall law
steps.body: log λ = a + b log R_α (or log T½ ∝ Z/√Q). α energies lie in a narrow range, about 4–9 MeV, yet half-lives range from microseconds (²¹²Po) to 10¹⁰ years (²³²Th).

steps.title: Fine structure
steps.body: Some α groups have slightly lower energies because the daughter is left in an excited state, which then emits a γ ray.

activity.prompt: ²¹⁰Po decays by α emission with Q = 5.41 MeV. Find the α kinetic energy K_α = Q(A − 4)/A in MeV (two decimals).

quiz.q: In α decay, Z and A change by:
quiz.why: An α particle is ⁴He with 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so Z falls by 2 and A by 4.

quiz.q: Gamow explained α decay by:
options: quantum tunnelling through the Coulomb barrier
quiz.why: The α energy is below the barrier top, so it can only escape by tunnelling, with probability about e^(−2G).

quiz.q: The Geiger–Nuttall law relates half-life to:
quiz.why: Higher-energy α emitters face a thinner effective barrier and so have much shorter half-lives.

lessons.title: Beta decay, neutrinos and gamma decay

scenes.text: In the 1920s, β electrons came out with a continuous range of energies. Energy seemed not to be conserved.
In 1930 Pauli proposed an invisible neutral particle carrying the missing energy. Reines and Cowan detected it in 1956.

steps.title: Three kinds of β decay
steps.body:
- **β⁻**: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄_e (neutron-rich nuclei)
- **β⁺**: p → n + e⁺ + ν_e (proton-rich; needs Q > 2m_ec² = 1.022 MeV in atomic masses)
- **Electron capture**: p + e⁻ → n + ν_e

A is unchanged; Z changes by ±1.

steps.title: Continuous spectrum
steps.body: The Q-value is shared among electron, antineutrino and recoil nucleus, so electron energies range from 0 to E_max ≈ Q. The average is about Q/3. The neutrino has spin ½, no charge, and tiny mass. Fermi's theory (1934) uses the weak interaction.

steps.title: Gamma decay
steps.body: An excited nucleus drops to a lower state by emitting a γ photon (keV to MeV). A and Z are unchanged. Alternatives: **internal conversion**, where the energy ejects an atomic electron, and long-lived **isomeric** states such as ⁹⁹ᵐTc (6 h), used in medical imaging.

steps.title: Parity violation
steps.body: Wu's 1957 ⁶⁰Co experiment showed that β electrons are emitted preferentially opposite to the nuclear spin, so the weak interaction does not conserve parity.

activity.prompt: Tritium decays: ³H → ³He + e⁻ + ν̄. Atomic masses: M(³H) = 3.016049 u, M(³He) = 3.016029 u. Find Q in keV (one decimal).

quiz.q: The β spectrum is continuous because:
options: energy is shared with an antineutrino
quiz.why: Three bodies share the decay energy, and the antineutrino takes a variable part, so electron energies are spread out.

quiz.q: In β⁺ decay:
options: Z falls by 1 and A is unchanged
quiz.why: A proton turns into a neutron, so Z decreases by 1 while the total nucleon number A is unchanged.

quiz.q: Internal conversion is:
options: ejection of an atomic electron using the nuclear excitation energy
quiz.why: Instead of a γ photon, the excited nucleus transfers its energy directly to an inner atomic electron, which is ejected.

questions.q: Mean life τ is related to T½ by:
After 4 half-lives, what percentage remains?
A source decays from 800 Bq to 100 Bq in 30 days. Its half-life is:
questions.why: 800 → 100 is a factor of 8 = 2³, so 3 half-lives take 30 days, giving 10 days each.

questions.q: Activity A = λN means a nuclide with a shorter half-life (same N) is:
questions.why: Shorter half-life means larger λ, and activity is proportional to λ.

questions.q: A wooden sample has 50% of living ¹⁴C activity. Its age is:
questions.why: Half the activity means one half-life has passed, which is 5730 years.

questions.q: In secular equilibrium with ²²⁶Ra (A = 1 Ci), the activity of ²²²Rn is:
questions.why: In secular equilibrium the daughter activity equals the parent activity.

questions.q: The α kinetic energy for Q = 6.0 MeV and A = 240 is about:
questions.why: K_α = 6.0 × 236/240 = 5.90 MeV; the recoil takes the remaining 0.1 MeV.

questions.q: α particles from heavy nuclei have energies mostly in the range:
questions.why: Observed α energies cluster between about 4 and 9 MeV even though half-lives differ hugely.

questions.q: The particle proposed by Pauli to save energy conservation in β decay is the:
questions.why: Pauli suggested a light neutral particle, later named the neutrino by Fermi.

questions.q: β⁺ decay is possible (in atomic masses) only if Q exceeds:
questions.why: Using atomic masses, β⁺ decay must also account for two electron masses, so M(parent) − M(daughter) must exceed 2m_ec² = 1.022 MeV.

questions.q: The Wu experiment demonstrated:
questions.why: Polarised ⁶⁰Co emitted electrons asymmetrically relative to spin, showing the weak force violates parity.

questions.q: 1 mg of ⁶⁰Co (T½ = 5.27 y = 1.66 × 10⁸ s) has activity about:

courses.title: Unit 3 · Nuclear reactions, fission and fusion
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Nuclear and Particle Physics)
courses.summary: Conservation laws, Q-value and threshold energy, cross-sections and the compound nucleus; fission and the chain reaction; how reactors work, with India's three-stage programme as a case study; fusion in stars and in tokamaks.
outcomes: Compute Q-values and threshold energies of nuclear reactions
Use cross-sections and reaction rates
Explain fission energy release, the multiplication factor and criticality
Describe the parts of a thermal reactor and India's three-stage programme
Explain stellar fusion, the D–T reaction and the Lawson criterion

scenes.text: In 1919 Rutherford fired α particles into nitrogen gas and detected protons coming out.
Nitrogen had turned into oxygen: ¹⁴N(α, p)¹⁷O, the first artificial nuclear reaction.

steps.title: Notation and conservation
steps.body:
a + X → Y + b, written X(a, b)Y. Conserved: charge, nucleon number, energy, linear and angular momentum, parity (strong interaction).

**Q = [(m_a + m_X) − (m_Y + m_b)] × 931.5 MeV**

Q > 0: exoergic. Q < 0: endoergic, needs a minimum projectile energy.

steps.title: Threshold energy
steps.body:
For a target at rest, part of the projectile's energy goes into centre-of-mass motion, so the non-relativistic threshold is

**K_th = −Q (1 + m_a/m_X)**

steps.title: Cross-section
steps.body:
σ is the effective target area for a reaction; unit 1 barn = 10⁻²⁸ m². Reaction rate:

R = σ Φ N

where Φ is particle flux (m⁻² s⁻¹) and N the number of target nuclei. Slow neutrons often have very large σ (¹¹³Cd capture ≈ 20,000 b), which is why cadmium is used in control rods.

steps.title: Compound nucleus
steps.body: Bohr's picture: the projectile is absorbed, its energy is shared among all nucleons, and the compound nucleus later decays in a way that 'forgets' how it was formed. Resonances in σ correspond to its excited states.

activity.prompt: ⁷Li(p, n)⁷Be has Q = −1.644 MeV. Find the threshold proton energy K_th = −Q(1 + m_p/m_Li), taking masses 1 and 7 (MeV, two decimals).

quiz.q: A reaction with Q < 0 is:
quiz.why: Negative Q means the products are heavier, so kinetic energy must be supplied: the reaction is endoergic.

quiz.q: Threshold energy is larger than |Q| because:
options: momentum conservation requires the products to keep moving
quiz.why: The total momentum is non-zero, so the products must carry kinetic energy, and the projectile must supply |Q| plus that.

quiz.q: 1 barn equals:
quiz.why: A barn is defined as 10⁻²⁸ m², roughly the geometric area of a heavy nucleus.

scenes.text: In Berlin in 1938, Hahn and Strassmann found barium in uranium bombarded with neutrons.
Meitner and Frisch realised the nucleus had split in two, releasing about 200 MeV.

steps.title: The process
steps.body:
n + ²³⁵U → ²³⁶U* → two fragments + 2–3 neutrons + ≈ 200 MeV.

Example: n + ²³⁵U → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n. Fragments are neutron-rich and β-decay further. Mass distribution is asymmetric, peaking near A ≈ 95 and 140.

steps.title: Where 200 MeV goes
steps.body: Roughly: fragment kinetic energy ≈ 165–170 MeV; prompt neutrons ≈ 5 MeV; prompt γ ≈ 7 MeV; β and γ from fragments ≈ 15 MeV; antineutrinos ≈ 10 MeV (escape).

steps.title: Solved: energy from 1 kg of ²³⁵U
steps.body:
- N = (1000/235) × 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.56 × 10²⁴ nuclei
- E = 2.56 × 10²⁴ × 200 MeV × 1.602 × 10⁻¹³ J/MeV
- E = **8.2 × 10¹³ J**, about the energy of burning 2500 tonnes of coal

steps.title: Why ²³⁵U and not ²³⁸U with slow neutrons?
steps.body: In the liquid-drop picture, fission needs the activation energy (about 6 MeV) to be supplied. Capture of a neutron by ²³⁵U (odd N) forms even–even ²³⁶U and releases about 6.5 MeV, enough. For ²³⁸U, capture releases only about 4.8 MeV, below its barrier, so fast neutrons are needed.

steps.title: Common slip
steps.body: Natural uranium is only about 0.72% ²³⁵U. Most is ²³⁸U, which is fertile (it can become fissile ²³⁹Pu) but not fissile with thermal neutrons.

activity.prompt: How many fissions per second are needed for 1 MW of thermal power at 200 MeV per fission? Give the answer in units of 10¹⁶ (two decimals).

quiz.q: Energy released per fission of ²³⁵U is about:
quiz.why: B/A rises from about 7.6 to 8.5 MeV for 236 nucleons, which gives about 200 MeV per fission.

quiz.q: Most of the fission energy appears as:
quiz.why: About 165–170 MeV of the 200 MeV goes into the kinetic energy of the two repelling fragments.

quiz.q: ²³⁸U is described as:
quiz.why: ²³⁸U captures neutrons and becomes ²³⁹Pu, which is fissile, so it is fertile material.

scenes.text: Engineering students on a visit to an Indian nuclear power station watch operators hold the reactor steady at full power.
The key number on the screen is k, the multiplication factor. It must stay at exactly 1.

steps.title: Multiplication factor
steps.body:
k = neutrons in one generation / neutrons in the previous generation.

- k < 1: subcritical, dies out
- k = 1: critical, steady power
- k > 1: supercritical, grows

Four-factor formula for an infinite thermal reactor: k∞ = ηεpf.

steps.title: Parts of a thermal reactor
steps.body:
- **Fuel**: natural or enriched uranium.
- **Moderator**: slows neutrons (heavy water, light water, graphite). Light nuclei take more energy per collision.
- **Control rods**: absorb neutrons (Cd, B, Hf).
- **Coolant**: carries heat (water, heavy water, liquid sodium).
- **Shielding**: concrete, steel, water.

Control is possible because about 0.65% of ²³⁵U fission neutrons are **delayed** by seconds.

steps.title: Solved: growth with k slightly above 1
steps.body:
With k = 1.001 and generation time 0.1 s (including delayed neutrons), after 10 s there are 100 generations.

- Power ratio = 1.001¹⁰⁰ = e^(100 × 0.0009995) ≈ **1.105**, a gentle 10% rise that operators can correct.

steps.title: India's three-stage programme
steps.body:
1. **PHWRs** burn natural uranium with heavy water, producing plutonium.
2. **Fast breeder reactors** (the Prototype FBR at Kalpakkam) use plutonium and breed more fuel.
3. **Thorium** reactors use ²³²Th → ²³³U, drawing on India's large thorium reserves.

steps.title: Moderator choice
steps.body: Heavy water absorbs very few neutrons, so it allows natural uranium fuel. Light water absorbs more, so it needs enriched fuel.

activity.prompt: A reactor has k = 1.001. By what factor does the neutron population grow after 1000 generations? (Use 1.001¹⁰⁰⁰ ≈ e^(0.9995); two decimals.)

quiz.q: A reactor at steady power has k equal to:
quiz.why: At k = 1 each generation produces exactly as many neutrons as the last, so the fission rate stays constant.

quiz.q: Reactor control is practical mainly because of:
quiz.why: Delayed neutrons, emitted seconds after fission, lengthen the effective generation time enough for control rods to act.

quiz.q: The third stage of India's nuclear programme is based on:
quiz.why: Stage three uses thorium-232 bred into fissile uranium-233, using India's large thorium reserves.

lessons.title: Nuclear fusion in stars and on Earth

scenes.text: Every second the Sun converts about 4 million tonnes of mass into energy by fusing hydrogen into helium.
On Earth, the ITER tokamak in France, with India as a partner, aims to do the same with deuterium and tritium.

steps.title: Stellar fusion
steps.body: **pp chain** (Sun): net 4¹H → ⁴He + 2e⁺ + 2ν_e + 26.7 MeV (including annihilation). Hotter, heavier stars use the **CNO cycle**, where carbon acts as a catalyst. Fusion needs high temperature (Sun's core ≈ 1.5 × 10⁷ K) and quantum tunnelling through the Coulomb barrier.

steps.title: Lawson criterion
steps.body: For net energy, the plasma must be hot enough and confined long enough. For D–T at about 10–20 keV: nτ_E ≳ 10²⁰ s m⁻³ (or the triple product nTτ_E ≳ 3 × 10²¹ keV s m⁻³).

steps.title: Confinement
steps.body:
- **Magnetic**: tokamaks such as ITER and India's SST-1 at the Institute for Plasma Research, Gandhinagar.
- **Inertial**: lasers compress a fuel pellet (NIF, USA, which reported scientific gain in 2022).

steps.title: Why fusion is attractive
steps.body: Per kilogram, D–T fusion releases about four times more energy than fission, uses abundant fuel and gives no long-lived fission products, though neutron activation of the walls must still be managed.

activity.prompt: D–T fusion releases 17.6 MeV per 5.03 u of fuel. Find the energy per kilogram of D–T fuel in units of 10¹⁴ J (two decimals).

quiz.q: Energy released in D–T fusion is about:
quiz.why: The mass defect of 0.018883 u times 931.5 MeV/u gives 17.6 MeV.

quiz.q: In D–T fusion, most energy is carried by:
quiz.why: Momentum conservation gives the light neutron about 4/5 of the energy, about 14.1 MeV.

quiz.q: The Lawson criterion concerns:
options: the product of plasma density and confinement time
quiz.why: Net fusion power needs nτ_E above a threshold at the right temperature.

questions.q: Q-value is defined as:
questions.why: Q is the rest-mass energy lost, so positive Q means energy is released.

questions.q: For Q = −3.0 MeV, m_a = 2, m_X = 10, the threshold is:
Cadmium is used in control rods because:
options: it has a very large neutron capture cross-section
questions.why: Cadmium absorbs slow neutrons very strongly, so inserting rods lowers k.

questions.q: Fissions per second for 1 W of power (200 MeV each) are about:
The best moderator, considering energy loss per collision alone, is a nucleus:
options: with mass close to the neutron's
questions.why: A neutron loses most energy in collisions with nuclei of similar mass, such as hydrogen or deuterium.

questions.q: Natural uranium contains about what percentage of ²³⁵U?
questions.why: Natural uranium is about 99.3% ²³⁸U and only 0.72% ²³⁵U.

questions.q: A reactor is supercritical when:
questions.why: With k > 1, each generation has more neutrons than the previous one, so power rises.

questions.q: The second stage of India's programme uses:
questions.why: Fast breeders use plutonium from stage one and breed more fissile material.

questions.q: The pp chain releases in total about:
questions.why: Converting four protons to helium-4 (with positron annihilation) releases 26.7 MeV.

questions.q: In D–T fusion with Q = 17.6 MeV, the α particle gets about:
questions.why: Energy splits inversely with mass, so the α (mass 4) gets 1/5 of 17.6 MeV ≈ 3.5 MeV.

questions.q: The reaction rate for σ = 2 b, Φ = 10¹⁶ m⁻² s⁻¹ and N = 10²² nuclei is:
Thermal neutrons fission ²³⁵U but not ²³⁸U because:
options: capture by ²³⁵U releases enough energy to exceed the fission barrier
questions.why: Neutron capture by odd-N ²³⁵U releases about 6.5 MeV, above its barrier, whereas ²³⁸U gains only about 4.8 MeV.

questions.q: With k = 1.0005 and an effective generation time of 0.1 s, after 100 s the power has risen by about:

courses.title: Unit 4 · Radiation detectors and particle accelerators
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Nuclear and Particle Physics)
courses.summary: How radiation interacts with matter, how gas-filled, scintillation and semiconductor detectors turn that into signals, and how Van de Graaff generators, cyclotrons, synchrotrons and colliders accelerate particles.
outcomes: Describe energy loss of charged particles and the three γ-ray interaction processes
Use the attenuation law and half-value layer
Explain the regions of a gas detector and correct GM counts for dead time
Compare scintillation and semiconductor detectors
Calculate cyclotron frequency and maximum energy; explain synchrotrons and colliders

scenes.text: At the dentist, Neha is given a heavy lead apron before her X-ray.
A few millimetres of lead absorb most of the scattered X-rays. Why lead? High Z and high density.

steps.title: Charged particles
steps.body: Heavy charged particles (α, p) lose energy mainly by ionisation and excitation. The Bethe formula gives −dE/dx ∝ z²/v² (z = charge of particle). Result: a well-defined **range** and a sharp **Bragg peak** of energy loss near the end, used in proton therapy. Electrons scatter more and also lose energy by bremsstrahlung.

steps.title: Photons: three processes
steps.body:
- **Photoelectric effect**: dominant at low energy and high Z (σ ∝ Z⁴–Z⁵).
- **Compton scattering**: dominant at medium energies (about 0.1–10 MeV in light materials).
- **Pair production**: needs E > 1.022 MeV; dominant at high energy, σ ∝ Z².

steps.title: Attenuation
steps.body:
A narrow γ beam falls off exponentially:

**I = I₀e^(−μx)**

μ is the linear attenuation coefficient. Half-value layer HVL = 0.693/μ.

steps.title: Solved: lead shielding
steps.body:
For a γ energy where lead has μ = 0.70 cm⁻¹:

- HVL = 0.693/0.70 = **0.99 cm**
- Through 3 cm: I/I₀ = e^(−2.1) = **0.12**, so about 12% passes

steps.title: Safety note
steps.body: Shielding, distance and time are the three rules of radiation protection. For a point source, intensity falls as 1/r², so doubling distance cuts dose to a quarter.

activity.prompt: A material has μ = 0.50 cm⁻¹ for a certain γ ray. Find its half-value layer in cm (two decimals).

quiz.q: Pair production requires a photon energy of at least:
quiz.why: The photon must create an electron and a positron, each of rest energy 0.511 MeV.

quiz.q: The photoelectric effect dominates at:
quiz.why: Its cross-section rises steeply with Z and falls steeply with energy.

quiz.q: The Bragg peak describes:
options: maximum energy loss near the end of a charged particle's range
quiz.why: Since dE/dx ∝ 1/v², a slowing ion loses energy fastest just before it stops.

lessons.title: Gas-filled detectors and the GM counter

scenes.text: On a field trip in Kerala, students hold a Geiger counter over monazite sand. The clicks speed up.
Each click is one ionising particle starting an avalanche in the gas tube.

steps.title: Regions of operation
steps.body:
Plot pulse size against applied voltage:

1. Recombination region
2. **Ionisation chamber**: all primary ions collected, no gain
3. **Proportional region**: gas gain 10²–10⁵, pulse ∝ deposited energy
4. Limited proportional region
5. **Geiger–Müller region**: full avalanche, same pulse for every particle
6. Continuous discharge

steps.title: Solved: ion pairs in air
steps.body:
About 34 eV is needed per ion pair in air. A 5.0 MeV α stops in an ionisation chamber.

- Pairs = 5.0 × 10⁶/34 = **1.47 × 10⁵**
- Charge = 1.47 × 10⁵ × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ C, so a sensitive amplifier is needed.

steps.title: GM counter and dead time
steps.body:
Argon with a quenching gas (alcohol or halogen). After each discharge the tube is insensitive for a **dead time** τ ≈ 100 μs. True rate:

**n = m/(1 − mτ)**, m = measured rate.

steps.title: Solved: dead-time correction
steps.body:
m = 2000 counts/s, τ = 100 μs.

- mτ = 0.2
- n = 2000/0.8 = **2500 counts/s**, so 20% of events were missed.

steps.title: Plateau
steps.body: Operate a GM tube in the middle of its plateau, where count rate barely changes with voltage. A good tube has a plateau slope below a few % per 100 V.

activity.prompt: A GM counter with dead time 50 μs records 5000 counts/s. Find the true count rate in counts/s (nearest whole number).

quiz.q: A GM counter cannot measure particle energy because:
options: every pulse is the same size
quiz.why: In the Geiger region the avalanche spreads along the whole wire, so pulse height no longer depends on the energy deposited.

quiz.q: In the proportional region, pulse size is:
quiz.why: Gas gain is fixed at a given voltage, so the output is proportional to the number of primary ion pairs.

quiz.q: The quenching gas in a GM tube:
quiz.why: Quenching molecules absorb UV photons and ion energy, ending the discharge so the tube can count again.

scenes.text: In the M.Sc lab next door, a ¹³⁷Cs source sits in front of a NaI(Tl) crystal. Its 662 keV peak is broad.
Under a cooled germanium detector, the same peak becomes a sharp spike. Resolution depends on how many charge carriers each photon makes.

steps.title: Scintillation detector
steps.body: Radiation excites a scintillator (NaI(Tl), CsI, plastic), which emits light. A **photomultiplier tube** turns the light into photoelectrons at the photocathode and multiplies them by about 10⁶ across a chain of dynodes. Output pulse ∝ energy deposited. NaI(Tl) has high Z and density, so it is very efficient for γ rays.

steps.title: Semiconductor detector
steps.body: A reverse-biased p–n or p-i-n junction forms a depletion region. Radiation creates electron–hole pairs that are swept out. Energy per pair: **Si ≈ 3.6 eV, Ge ≈ 2.9 eV**, compared with about 30 eV per ion pair in gases. HPGe must be cooled with liquid nitrogen to reduce leakage current.

steps.title: Energy resolution
steps.body:
Resolution R = FWHM/E. Statistically R ∝ 1/√N, N = number of carriers. More carriers mean sharper peaks.

At 662 keV: NaI(Tl) about 7%; HPGe about 0.2%.

steps.title: Solved: carriers in germanium
steps.body:
A 662 keV photon stops in Ge (2.9 eV per pair).

- N = 662,000/2.9 = **2.28 × 10⁵ pairs**
- Poisson limit: 1/√N ≈ 0.21%; the Fano factor makes the real figure even better.

steps.title: Spectrum features
steps.body: A γ spectrum shows the photopeak, the Compton continuum ending at the Compton edge, a backscatter peak near 200 keV, and, above 1.022 MeV, single- and double-escape peaks.

activity.prompt: A 662 keV γ ray deposits all its energy in a silicon detector (3.6 eV per pair). How many electron–hole pairs are produced? Give the answer in thousands (nearest whole number).

quiz.q: The photomultiplier tube in a scintillation detector:
options: converts light to an amplified electrical pulse
quiz.why: The photocathode releases electrons when light strikes it, and dynodes multiply them about a millionfold.

quiz.q: Germanium detectors have better resolution than NaI because:
options: each photon makes many more charge carriers
quiz.why: Only about 2.9 eV is needed per pair, so N is large and the statistical spread 1/√N is small.

quiz.q: HPGe detectors are cooled with liquid nitrogen to:
quiz.why: Ge's small band gap lets thermal electrons cross at room temperature, causing noise; cooling suppresses this.

scenes.text: The Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre in Kolkata has accelerated ions for Indian research since the late 1970s.
Hospital cyclotrons today make fluorine-18 for PET scans every morning, because its half-life is under two hours.

steps.title: Electrostatic accelerators
steps.body: **Van de Graaff**: a moving belt carries charge to a dome, reaching several MV. **Tandem** machines accelerate negative ions to the positive terminal, strip them to positive, and accelerate them again, doubling the energy. TIFR's Pelletron in Mumbai is a tandem.

steps.title: Cyclotron
steps.body:
Ions circle in a magnetic field B between two D-shaped electrodes with an AC voltage.

- Cyclotron frequency **f = qB/(2πm)**, independent of radius and speed (non-relativistic)
- Maximum kinetic energy **K = q²B²R²/(2m)**
- At high energy the mass increases and the ions fall out of step; synchrocyclotrons and isochronous cyclotrons fix this.

steps.title: Linacs, synchrotrons and colliders
steps.body:
- **Linac**: drift tubes or RF cavities in a straight line; no radiation loss from bending.
- **Synchrotron**: fixed radius; B and RF frequency rise together. Electron synchrotrons lose energy by synchrotron radiation (∝ E⁴/m⁴R), used as light sources (Indus-2, Indore).
- **Collider**: two beams collide head-on, so all beam energy is available in the centre of mass. The LHC collides protons at 13.6 TeV.

steps.title: Why colliders?
steps.body: For a fixed target, the available energy grows only as √(2Emc²). For two head-on beams of energy E each, it is 2E. That is why the Higgs boson needed a collider.

activity.prompt: Find the cyclotron frequency f = qB/(2πm) for protons in B = 1.0 T (q = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg), in MHz (two decimals).

quiz.q: The cyclotron frequency is independent of:
quiz.why: f = qB/(2πm) has no dependence on radius or speed, as long as motion is non-relativistic.

quiz.q: Synchrotron radiation losses are much larger for:
quiz.why: The loss scales as 1/m⁴, so light electrons radiate far more than protons at the same energy.

quiz.q: A tandem accelerator gains its advantage by:
options: stripping negative ions at the terminal so they are accelerated twice
quiz.why: Negative ions are pulled to the positive terminal, converted to positive ions, and then repelled, so the voltage is used twice.

questions.q: Compton scattering dominates for γ rays of about:
questions.why: At medium energies in low-Z materials, scattering from nearly free electrons is the main process.

questions.q: A shield is 3 HVL thick. The fraction transmitted is:
questions.why: Each HVL halves the intensity, so three give (½)³ = 1/8.

questions.q: With μ = 1.2 cm⁻¹, the HVL is about:
The ionisation chamber region has:
questions.why: In an ionisation chamber the field only collects the primary ions without multiplying them.

questions.q: A GM counter reads 1000 counts/s with τ = 200 μs. The true rate is:
The energy per electron–hole pair in silicon is about:
questions.why: About 3.6 eV is needed per pair in Si, roughly three times its band gap.

questions.q: Statistical energy resolution varies with the number of carriers N as:
questions.why: Carrier number follows Poisson statistics, so the relative spread is 1/√N.

questions.q: In a γ spectrum, the Compton edge is:
options: the maximum energy given to an electron in one Compton scatter
questions.why: Head-on backscattering transfers the most energy, which marks the upper end of the Compton continuum.

questions.q: Doubling B in a cyclotron (same R) multiplies the maximum proton energy by:
questions.why: K = q²B²R²/(2m) depends on B², so doubling B gives 4 times the energy.

questions.q: Colliders are preferred over fixed targets for high energies because:
options: all the beam energy is available in the centre-of-mass frame
questions.why: Head-on beams of equal energy have zero total momentum, so no energy is wasted on moving the products.

questions.q: Indus-2 at Indore is:
questions.why: Indus-2 is an electron storage ring used as a source of synchrotron radiation.
