courses.title: Unit 5 · Elementary particles and the Standard Model
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Nuclear and Particle Physics)
courses.summary: Classification of particles into leptons and hadrons, antiparticles, conservation laws including baryon number, lepton number, strangeness and isospin, the quark model with colour, the four interactions and their carriers, and the Standard Model including the Higgs boson and neutrino oscillations.
outcomes: Classify particles as leptons, mesons and baryons, fermions and bosons
Apply conservation laws to decide whether a reaction or decay is allowed
Build hadrons from quarks and find their charge, baryon number and strangeness
Compare the four interactions, their carriers and ranges
Summarise the Standard Model, the Higgs mechanism and open questions

lessons.title: The particle zoo: leptons, hadrons, antiparticles

scenes.text: Cosmic-ray muons are born about 15 km up and live only 2.2 μs. Even at light speed they should travel only about 660 m.
Yet detectors at sea level catch them all the time. Time dilation stretches their lives, a daily check of relativity.

steps.title: Fermions and bosons
steps.body:
- **Fermions** (half-integer spin) obey Pauli exclusion: quarks and leptons.
- **Bosons** (integer spin): force carriers (γ, W±, Z⁰, gluons), the Higgs, and mesons.

steps.title: Leptons and hadrons
steps.body:
- **Leptons** do not feel the strong force: e, μ, τ and their neutrinos ν_e, ν_μ, ν_τ (6 leptons + 6 antileptons).
- **Hadrons** feel the strong force:
  - **Mesons** (quark + antiquark), integer spin: π, K, η
  - **Baryons** (three quarks), half-integer spin: p, n, Λ, Σ, Ξ, Ω

steps.title: Antiparticles
steps.body: Dirac's equation (1928) predicted antiparticles: same mass, opposite charge and quantum numbers. Anderson found the positron in cosmic rays in 1932; the antiproton was made at Berkeley in 1955. A particle and its antiparticle can annihilate: e⁺ + e⁻ → 2γ (each 0.511 MeV), the basis of PET scans.

steps.title: Lifetimes
steps.body: Strong decays take about 10⁻²³ s, electromagnetic decays about 10⁻¹⁶–10⁻²⁰ s, weak decays 10⁻¹⁰ s or longer (π⁺: 26 ns; neutron: about 880 s). The lifetime is a clue to which force acts.

activity.prompt: A muon with γ = 20 (β ≈ 0.9987) has proper lifetime 2.197 μs. Find its mean decay length L = γβcτ in km (one decimal, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s).

quiz.q: The proton is a:
quiz.why: The proton is made of three quarks (uud), which makes it a baryon.

quiz.q: Which particle does NOT feel the strong force?
quiz.why: The muon is a lepton, and leptons interact only through weak, electromagnetic and gravitational forces.

quiz.q: Electron–positron annihilation at rest gives:
quiz.why: Momentum conservation needs at least two photons, which share the 1.022 MeV rest energy equally.

scenes.text: Super-Kamiokande in Japan watches 50,000 tonnes of water for a proton to decay. None has been seen.
The limit is above 10³⁴ years. Baryon number appears to be conserved very strictly.

steps.title: Always conserved
steps.body: Energy, momentum, angular momentum, electric charge, **baryon number B** (quarks +⅓, baryons +1, antibaryons −1, mesons 0), and **lepton numbers** L_e, L_μ, L_τ separately (apart from neutrino oscillations).

steps.title: Conserved by some forces
steps.body:
| Quantity | Strong | EM | Weak |
|---|---|---|---|
| Strangeness S | ✔ | ✔ | ✘ (ΔS = 0, ±1) |
| Isospin I | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ |
| Parity P | ✔ | ✔ | ✘ |
| Charge conjugation C | ✔ | ✔ | ✘ |

CP is also violated slightly in weak decays of K and B mesons.

steps.title: Solved: is it allowed?
steps.body:
1. **p → e⁺ + γ**: charge OK, but B: 1 → 0 ✘. Forbidden.
2. **μ⁻ → e⁻ + ν̄_e + ν_μ**: L_μ: 1 → 1 ✔; L_e: 0 → 1 − 1 = 0 ✔. Allowed (weak).
3. **π⁻ + p → K⁰ + Λ⁰**: S: 0 → +1 − 1 = 0 ✔. Allowed (strong, associated production).
4. **Λ⁰ → p + π⁻**: S: −1 → 0. ΔS = 1, so only weak; τ ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ s.

steps.title: Threshold for antiprotons
steps.body: p + p → p + p + p + p̄ on a fixed target. Invariant mass must reach 4m_pc², which gives a threshold kinetic energy of **6m_pc² ≈ 5.6 GeV**. The Berkeley Bevatron was built to reach about 6 GeV.

steps.title: Checklist
steps.body: For any reaction, check in order: charge, baryon number, each lepton number, then strangeness (if strong or EM). One failure means forbidden.

activity.prompt: The fixed-target threshold kinetic energy for p + p → p + p + p + p̄ is 6m_pc². With m_pc² = 0.938 GeV, find it in GeV (two decimals).

quiz.q: The decay p → π⁰ + e⁺ violates conservation of:
quiz.why: The proton has B = 1, while π⁰ and e⁺ both have B = 0.

quiz.q: Strangeness is NOT conserved in:
quiz.why: Weak decays can change a strange quark into an up quark, so ΔS = ±1 is allowed only by the weak force.

quiz.q: In μ⁻ → e⁻ + ν̄_e + ν_μ, the total electron lepton number on the right is:
quiz.why: e⁻ has L_e = +1 and ν̄_e has L_e = −1, which sum to 0, matching the muon's L_e = 0.

scenes.text: In 1962 Gell-Mann's eightfold way had a gap in its pattern of baryons. He predicted a particle with strangeness −3 and mass about 1680 MeV.
Brookhaven found the Ω⁻ in 1964 at 1672 MeV, a triumph for the quark picture.

steps.title: Six quarks
steps.body:
| Quark | Charge | Mass (approx.) |
|---|---|---|
| u (up) | +2/3 | 2 MeV |
| d (down) | −1/3 | 5 MeV |
| s (strange, S = −1) | −1/3 | 95 MeV |
| c (charm) | +2/3 | 1.27 GeV |
| b (bottom) | −1/3 | 4.2 GeV |
| t (top) | +2/3 | 173 GeV |

All have spin ½ and B = ⅓.

steps.title: Colour
steps.body: Ω⁻ (sss) and Δ⁺⁺ (uuu) with spin 3/2 would have three identical fermions in the same state, violating Pauli. Solution: each quark carries one of three **colours** (red, green, blue). Hadrons are colour-neutral. The strong force is carried by **8 gluons** that themselves carry colour (QCD).

steps.title: Confinement and asymptotic freedom
steps.body: Free quarks are never seen: the energy between quarks grows with distance, so pulling them apart makes new quark–antiquark pairs (jets). At very short distances the force becomes weak (asymptotic freedom, Nobel 2004).

steps.title: Evidence
steps.body: Deep inelastic electron–proton scattering at SLAC (1968) showed point-like constituents inside the proton. The J/ψ (cc̄) in 1974 confirmed charm.

activity.prompt: The Σ⁻ baryon has quark content dds. What is its strangeness S?

quiz.q: The quark content of the neutron is:
quiz.why: udd has charge 2/3 − 1/3 − 1/3 = 0 and baryon number 1, which matches the neutron.

quiz.q: Colour was introduced mainly to:
options: rescue the Pauli principle for states like Ω⁻ (sss)
quiz.why: Three identical s quarks in the same spin state would break Pauli exclusion unless they differ in a new quantum number, colour.

quiz.q: The charge of a meson made of cs̄ is:
quiz.why: c has +2/3 and s̄ has +1/3, which sum to +1 (this is the D_s⁺ meson).

lessons.title: Fundamental interactions and the Standard Model

scenes.text: At CERN, the ATLAS and CMS teams announce a new boson near 125 GeV. Peter Higgs wipes away tears in the audience.
Indian groups are part of CMS. The particle is named after Higgs, and the word boson honours Satyendra Nath Bose.

steps.title: Four interactions
steps.body:
| Force | Carrier | Relative strength | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| Strong | gluons (8) | 1 | ≈ 1 fm |
| Electromagnetic | photon | ≈ 1/137 | infinite |
| Weak | W±, Z⁰ | ≈ 10⁻⁶ | ≈ 10⁻³ fm |
| Gravity | graviton (not observed) | ≈ 10⁻³⁸ | infinite |

steps.title: Solved: range of the weak force
steps.body:
R ≈ ħc/(M_Wc²), M_Wc² = 80.4 GeV = 80,400 MeV.

- R = 197.3 MeV fm/80,400 MeV
- R ≈ **2.5 × 10⁻³ fm**, much smaller than a proton

steps.title: The Standard Model
steps.body:
- 3 generations of quarks and leptons (12 fermions plus antiparticles).
- Gauge group SU(3)_colour × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y.
- Electroweak unification (Glashow, Weinberg, Salam), confirmed by W and Z discovery at CERN in 1983.
- The **Higgs field** gives mass to W, Z and fermions; its boson was found at 125 GeV in 2012.

steps.title: What it does not explain
steps.body: Gravity, dark matter, dark energy, the matter–antimatter imbalance, and neutrino masses. Neutrino oscillations (Super-Kamiokande 1998, SNO 2001) prove neutrinos have mass, which the minimal Standard Model leaves out.

steps.title: India in particle physics
steps.body: Indian scientists contribute to CMS and ALICE at CERN, and the proposed India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) is designed to study atmospheric neutrinos.

activity.prompt: Estimate the range of the force carried by the Z⁰ boson (M_Zc² = 91,200 MeV) using R ≈ ħc/(Mc²), ħc = 197.3 MeV fm. Give R in units of 10⁻³ fm (two decimals).

quiz.q: The carrier of the electromagnetic force is the:
quiz.why: Electromagnetic interactions are mediated by massless photons, which is why their range is infinite.

quiz.q: The weak force is short-ranged because:
options: its carriers W and Z are very massive
quiz.why: A massive exchange particle can exist only briefly, so the range ħ/(Mc) is tiny for M ≈ 80–91 GeV.

quiz.q: Neutrino oscillations show that:
quiz.why: Flavour oscillation requires neutrino mass states with different masses, so at least some neutrinos are massive.

questions.q: Mesons consist of:
questions.why: Mesons are quark–antiquark pairs, giving integer spin and baryon number 0.

questions.q: Which is a lepton?
questions.why: The tau is a heavy charged lepton; the others are hadrons.

questions.q: The decay n → p + e⁻ is incomplete because it violates:
questions.why: The electron has L_e = +1, so an antineutrino (L_e = −1) must also be emitted.

questions.q: Λ⁰ (uds) has strangeness:
questions.why: It contains one s quark, and each s quark carries S = −1.

questions.q: The charge of the quark combination uus is:
Δ⁺⁺ = uuu with spin 3/2 needed which new quantum number?
questions.why: Three identical u quarks in a symmetric spin state need an extra antisymmetric label, colour, to satisfy Pauli.

questions.q: Which reaction is allowed by the strong interaction?
questions.why: K⁰ (S = +1) and Λ⁰ (S = −1) together conserve strangeness and charge, which is associated production.

questions.q: The relative strength of the electromagnetic force compared with the strong force is about:
questions.why: The fine-structure constant α ≈ 1/137 sets the electromagnetic coupling strength.

questions.q: The W and Z bosons were discovered at:
questions.why: The UA1 and UA2 experiments at CERN's proton–antiproton collider found the W and Z in 1983.

questions.q: The Higgs boson has a mass of about:
questions.why: ATLAS and CMS observed it at about 125 GeV in 2012.

questions.q: A pion (τ = 26 ns) travels with γ = 5 (β ≈ 0.98). Its mean decay length is about:
Which of these is NOT explained by the Standard Model?
questions.why: No Standard Model particle has the properties needed for dark matter.

questions.q: For a fixed target, the available centre-of-mass energy at high beam energy E grows roughly as:
questions.why: For a fixed target the centre-of-mass energy is about √(2Emc²) at high E, so it grows only as √E.

uni-bsc-phy-optics.title: B.Sc. Physics · Optics
uni-bsc-phy-optics.description: Geometrical optics, cardinal points and aberrations, interference by division of wavefront and amplitude, Michelson interferometer, Fraunhofer and Fresnel diffraction, gratings and resolving power, and polarisation, with the standard optics practicals and exam practice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc. Physics (Hons./Programme) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Geometrical Optics, Cardinal Points & Aberrations
courses.summary: Fermat's principle and the laws of reflection and refraction, combinations of thin lenses, cardinal points of a coaxial system, Huygens and Ramsden eyepieces, and chromatic and monochromatic aberrations with achromatic conditions.
outcomes: Derive reflection and refraction laws from Fermat's principle
Compute the equivalent focal length of separated lenses
Locate principal points and analyse eyepieces
Design achromatic combinations and name the Seidel aberrations

scenes.text: A lifeguard on the sand must reach a swimmer in the sea. Running straight wastes time in the water; she runs further on sand, then swims.
Light chooses its path between two media in exactly the same way — the path of stationary time.

steps.title: Statement
steps.body: A ray travels between two points along a path for which the optical path length L = ∫ n ds is stationary (usually a minimum) with respect to small variations. Optical path = n × geometric path; time = L/c.

steps.title: Derivation: refraction
steps.body: Points A (height a in medium n₁) and B (depth b in n₂), horizontal separation d. Ray crosses the interface at x. L = n₁√(a² + x²) + n₂√(b² + (d − x)²). dL/dx = n₁x/√(a² + x²) − n₂(d − x)/√(b² + (d − x)²) = n₁ sinθ₁ − n₂ sinθ₂ = 0 → Snell's law.

steps.title: Derivation: reflection
steps.body: For A and B on the same side of a mirror, L = √(a² + x²) + √(b² + (d − x)²). Setting dL/dx = 0 gives sin i = sin r, so i = r. Equivalently, the image of B behind the mirror lies on a straight line from A.

steps.title: Worked numerical
steps.body: Light enters glass (n = 1.5) from air at 30°: sin r = sin30°/1.5 = 0.333 → r ≈ 19.5°. Critical angle from glass to air: sin C = 1/1.5 → C ≈ 41.8°.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying light always takes the minimum-time path — for some concave mirrors it is a maximum; the principle requires only stationarity. Optical path is not the geometric length.

activity.prompt: Light passes from water (n = 1.33) into glass (n = 1.5) at an incidence angle of 45°. Angle of refraction in degrees?

quiz.q: Fermat's principle requires the optical path to be:
quiz.why: The true path makes the first variation of ∫ n ds vanish, which may be a minimum, maximum or saddle.

quiz.q: Optical path of 2 cm of glass (n = 1.5):
quiz.why: Optical path = n × d = 1.5 × 2 = 3 cm.

quiz.q: Critical angle for glass (n = 1.5) to air is about:
quiz.why: sin C = 1/n = 0.667 gives C ≈ 41.8°.

scenes.text: Zooming a camera lens slides groups of lenses closer or farther apart.
Changing their separation changes the equivalent focal length — and hence the magnification.

steps.title: Lens maker's & thin lens
steps.body: Thin lens: 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂); 1/v − 1/u = 1/f (Cartesian sign convention). Power P = 1/f (dioptres, f in metres).

steps.title: Two separated lenses
steps.body: Two thin lenses f₁, f₂ separated by d in air: 1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ − d/(f₁f₂), i.e. P = P₁ + P₂ − dP₁P₂. In contact (d = 0) powers simply add.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: f₁ = 20 cm, f₂ = 10 cm, d = 5 cm: 1/F = 0.05 + 0.1 − 5/200 = 0.125 cm⁻¹ → F = 8 cm. In contact F would be 6.67 cm.

steps.title: Worked example: lens maker
steps.body: Biconvex glass lens (n = 1.5), R₁ = +20 cm, R₂ = −20 cm: 1/f = 0.5 × (1/20 + 1/20) = 0.05 → f = 20 cm. In water (n_w = 1.33) use (n/n_w − 1) = 0.128: f ≈ 78 cm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using the contact formula for separated lenses; mixing cm and m when computing dioptres; forgetting sign conventions for concave lenses (f negative).

activity.prompt: Two convex lenses, each f = 15 cm, are separated by 10 cm. Equivalent focal length (cm)?

quiz.q: Two lenses of power +2 D and +3 D in contact give:
quiz.why: Powers of thin lenses in contact add.

quiz.q: Separating two convex lenses (d < f₁ + f₂) makes the combination:
quiz.why: The −dP₁P₂ term reduces the total power.

quiz.q: A lens with f = −25 cm has power:

story.title: A thick lens as one thin lens

scenes.text: A microscope objective has many elements, yet designers describe it by one focal length.
Six cardinal points let any coaxial system be treated as a single equivalent lens.

steps.title: The six cardinal points
steps.body: Two focal points (F₁, F₂), two principal points (H₁, H₂) — conjugate planes with unit lateral magnification — and two nodal points (N₁, N₂) — conjugate points with unit angular magnification. In a system with the same medium on both sides, nodal points coincide with principal points. Focal lengths are measured from principal points.

steps.title: Two-lens system
steps.body: For lenses f₁, f₂ separated by d: second principal point lies at distance −Fd/f₁ from the second lens (negative = toward the first lens); first principal point at +Fd/f₂ from the first lens.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: f₁ = 20, f₂ = 10, d = 5 cm → F = 8 cm. H₂ is 8 × 5/20 = 2 cm in front of (to the left of) lens 2; H₁ is 8 × 5/10 = 4 cm to the right of lens 1. Focal point F₂ is then 8 − 2 = 6 cm beyond lens 2.

steps.title: Eyepieces
steps.body: Huygens: f₁ = 3f, f₂ = f, d = 2f; satisfies d = (f₁ + f₂)/2 (free from lateral chromatic aberration); F = 1.5f; cross-wires cannot be used (the first focal plane is between the lenses). Ramsden: f₁ = f₂ = f, d = 2f/3; F = 3f/4; focal plane outside, so cross-wires can be used — used in measuring instruments like spectrometers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Measuring F from a lens instead of the principal plane; assuming nodal points differ from principal points when the media on both sides are the same.

activity.prompt: A Ramsden eyepiece uses two lenses each of focal length 4 cm separated by 2f/3. Equivalent focal length (cm)?

quiz.q: Principal planes are conjugate planes with lateral magnification:
quiz.why: By definition an object at H₁ images to H₂ with unit lateral magnification.

quiz.q: Which eyepiece allows cross-wires?
quiz.why: Ramsden's front focal plane lies outside the lenses, where cross-wires can be placed and viewed without aberration.

quiz.q: Nodal points coincide with principal points when:
options: The medium is the same on both sides
quiz.why: Nodal points shift from principal points only when object and image spaces have different refractive indices.

scenes.text: Through a cheap magnifier, white objects show red and blue edges.
Early telescopes suffered so badly that Newton built a reflector instead; later, crown–flint doublets fixed the problem.

steps.title: Chromatic aberration
steps.body: n varies with λ, so f does too. Dispersive power ω = (n_F − n_C)/(n_D − 1). Longitudinal chromatic aberration of a lens = ωf. Achromat in contact: ω₁/f₁ + ω₂/f₂ = 0 — lenses of opposite sign, from different glasses. Two separated lenses of the same glass are achromatic (for equivalent focal length) when d = (f₁ + f₂)/2.

steps.title: Worked example: doublet design
steps.body: Required F = 40 cm with crown (ω₁ = 0.02) and flint (ω₂ = 0.04). From 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ = 1/F and ω₁/f₁ = −ω₂/f₂: 1/f₁ = ω₂/((ω₂ − ω₁)F) = 0.04/0.8 = 0.05 → f₁ = +20 cm (crown, convex); 1/f₂ = −ω₁/((ω₂ − ω₁)F) = −0.025 → f₂ = −40 cm (flint, concave). Check: 1/20 − 1/40 = 1/40 ✓.

steps.title: Monochromatic (Seidel) aberrations
steps.body: Spherical aberration (marginal rays focus closer), coma (comet-shaped off-axis images), astigmatism, curvature of field, distortion (barrel/pincushion). Spherical aberration is reduced by stops, by sharing deviation between two lenses (plano-convex with curved side toward parallel light), or by aspheric surfaces; two lenses separated by d = f₁ − f₂ minimise it.

steps.title: Modern lenses
steps.body: Camera and phone lenses use many elements, aspheric moulded surfaces and low-dispersion glass to correct all seven aberrations simultaneously across the field.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Making both doublet elements of the same glass (impossible in contact); forgetting that d = (f₁ + f₂)/2 corrects equivalent focal length, not image position.

activity.prompt: Two lenses of the same glass with f₁ = 12 cm and f₂ = 4 cm are to be achromatic. Required separation (cm)?

quiz.q: Condition for an achromatic doublet in contact:
quiz.why: Requiring d(1/F)/dλ = 0 for lenses in contact gives ω₁/f₁ + ω₂/f₂ = 0.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a Seidel aberration?
quiz.why: Seidel aberrations are monochromatic; chromatic aberration arises from dispersion.

quiz.q: A plano-convex lens minimises spherical aberration when its curved face:
quiz.why: Then deviation is shared more equally between the two surfaces, reducing spherical aberration.

questions.q: Snell's law follows from Fermat's principle by:
questions.why: Requiring the optical path to be stationary with respect to the crossing point gives n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂.

questions.why: With 3f, f and 2f, d equals the mean of the focal lengths.

questions.why: Two focal, two principal and two nodal points.

Spherical aberration can be reduced by:
options: Using stops to block marginal rays
questions.why: Marginal rays cause the largest focal error, so stopping them down improves focus at the cost of brightness.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Interference by Division of Wavefront
courses.summary: Coherence and the conditions for sustained interference, intensity distribution and visibility, Young's double slit with thin-film displacement, the Fresnel biprism, and Lloyd's mirror with its phase change on reflection.
outcomes: State coherence conditions and estimate coherence length
Derive the intensity distribution and fringe width in YDSE
Determine λ with a Fresnel biprism using the displacement method
Explain the dark central fringe in Lloyd's mirror

scenes.text: Shine two torches at a wall: the light just adds — no bright and dark bands.
Split ONE beam into two and recombine it, and fringes appear. The sources must be coherent.

steps.title: Intensity of two superposed waves
steps.body: For waves of intensities I₁, I₂ and phase difference δ: I = I₁ + I₂ + 2√(I₁I₂) cosδ. Maxima (δ = 2nπ): (√I₁ + √I₂)²; minima (δ = (2n + 1)π): (√I₁ − √I₂)². For equal intensities I = 4I₀ cos²(δ/2). Phase difference δ = (2π/λ) × path difference.

steps.title: Coherence
steps.body: Sustained fringes require a constant phase relation: sources derived from one original source (division of wavefront or amplitude). Temporal coherence length l_c ≈ λ²/Δλ (path differences beyond l_c wash out fringes). Spatial coherence requires a narrow source slit.

steps.title: Worked example: coherence length
steps.body: Red LED: λ = 630 nm, Δλ = 20 nm → l_c ≈ (630 × 10⁻⁹)²/(20 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 19.8 μm. White light (λ ≈ 550 nm, Δλ ≈ 300 nm) gives about 1 μm — only a few coloured fringes are visible. A stabilised laser can have l_c of many metres.

steps.title: Worked example: visibility
steps.body: Visibility V = (I_max − I_min)/(I_max + I_min) = 2√(I₁I₂)/(I₁ + I₂). For I₁ = 4I₂: I_max = 9I₂, I_min = I₂ → V = 8/10 = 0.8.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Adding intensities instead of amplitudes for coherent waves; thinking energy is destroyed at dark fringes (it is redistributed — the average remains I₁ + I₂).

activity.prompt: Two coherent beams have intensities in the ratio 9 : 1. What is the fringe visibility?

quiz.q: For two equal coherent waves, intensity at a maximum is:
quiz.why: Amplitudes add to 2a, and intensity ∝ amplitude², giving 4I₀.

quiz.q: Coherence length is approximately:
quiz.why: The number of waves before phase drifts is λ/Δλ, so the length is λ × λ/Δλ.

quiz.q: Two independent bulbs produce no fringes because:
quiz.why: Independent atoms emit with random phases, so the interference pattern shifts too fast to observe.

scenes.text: Thomas Young passed sunlight through a pinhole, then two close pinholes, onto a screen.
Alternate bright and dark bands appeared — evidence that light is a wave.

steps.title: Path difference and fringes
steps.body: Slits separated by d, screen at D ≫ d. At height y: path difference Δ = d sinθ ≈ yd/D. Bright: yₙ = nλD/d; dark: (n + ½)λD/d. Fringe width β = λD/d, independent of n. Angular fringe width λ/d.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: λ = 600 nm, D = 1.0 m, d = 0.5 mm: β = 6 × 10⁻⁷ × 1/(5 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.2 mm. Third bright fringe at 3.6 mm from centre. In water (n = 1.33), λ and β shrink to 0.9 mm.

steps.title: Thin sheet in one beam
steps.body: A transparent sheet (index μ, thickness t) over one slit adds optical path (μ − 1)t, shifting the whole pattern by Δy = (μ − 1)tD/d toward that slit; fringe width is unchanged. The number of fringes shifted is (μ − 1)t/λ.

steps.title: Worked example: mica sheet
steps.body: Mica with μ = 1.58, t = 5 μm, λ = 580 nm: number of fringes shifted = 0.58 × 5 × 10⁻⁶/5.8 × 10⁻⁷ = 5.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using D in cm and d in mm without converting; thinking the sheet changes β; forgetting white light gives a white central fringe with coloured ones beside it.

activity.prompt: In YDSE (d = 1 mm, D = 1 m), a film of μ = 1.5 and thickness 6 μm covers one slit. By how many mm does the central fringe shift?

quiz.q: Fringe width in YDSE is:
quiz.why: Adjacent bright fringes differ in path difference by λ, which at the screen corresponds to Δy = λD/d.

quiz.q: Doubling slit separation changes fringe width by:
Placing a thin sheet over one slit:
quiz.why: It adds a constant extra optical path (μ − 1)t to one beam, displacing every fringe equally.

scenes.text: A biprism — two very thin prisms base to base — splits light from one slit into two beams.
They appear to come from two virtual slits close together, and fringes form where they overlap.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: Each half deviates light by (μ − 1)α (α = small prism angle), so a slit at distance a from the biprism yields two virtual sources separated by d = 2a(μ − 1)α. Fringes on an eyepiece at distance D from the slit: λ = βd/D.

steps.title: Measuring d: displacement method
steps.body: Place a convex lens between biprism and eyepiece (D > 4f). In two lens positions sharp images of the virtual sources appear, with separations d₁ and d₂. Then d = √(d₁d₂).

steps.title: Alignment
steps.body: Slit, biprism edge and eyepiece cross-wire must be on the same axis with the refracting edge parallel to the slit — rotate the biprism until fringes are sharpest. Remove lateral shift (eyepiece moving relative to fringes as it travels along the bench) before measuring.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using the slit-to-biprism distance instead of slit-to-eyepiece distance for D; measuring d₁, d₂ with the lens closer than 4f, where two sharp positions do not exist.

activity.prompt: Biprism data: β = 0.28 mm, d₁ = 6.4 mm, d₂ = 0.9 mm, D = 1.2 m. Wavelength in nm?

quiz.q: Virtual source separation in a biprism is:
quiz.why: Each half deviates by (μ − 1)α, displacing each virtual image by a(μ − 1)α in opposite directions.

quiz.q: In the displacement method d equals:
quiz.why: The two lens positions give magnifications m and 1/m, so d₁d₂ = d².

quiz.q: Fringes are sharpest when the biprism edge is:
quiz.why: Only then do the virtual slit images stay parallel, giving straight unblurred fringes.

lessons.title: Lloyd's mirror & phase change on reflection

scenes.text: Light from a slit grazes a flat mirror and meets direct light on a screen.
Where path difference is zero you'd expect brightness — yet the fringe at the mirror edge is dark.

steps.title: Arrangement
steps.body: A slit S close to a plane mirror; the reflected light appears to come from its image S′. S and S′ act as two coherent sources separated by d = 2h (h = slit height above mirror plane). Fringe width is again β = λD/d, but fringes lie only on one side of the mirror plane.

steps.title: Phase change
steps.body: At the point where the screen touches the mirror's plane the path difference is zero, yet the fringe is dark. Reflection from a denser medium introduces a phase change of π (an extra λ/2 path). Stokes relations derive this: r′ = −r and tt′ = 1 − r².

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: h = 0.5 mm (d = 1 mm), D = 2 m, λ = 600 nm → β = 1.2 mm. The first BRIGHT fringe is half a fringe away from the mirror plane, at 0.6 mm.

steps.title: Radio Lloyd's mirror
steps.body: Radio signals reflected from the sea surface interfere with direct signals, producing alternating strong and weak reception heights — a large-scale Lloyd's mirror.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Expecting a bright central fringe; ignoring the π phase change when reflection is from a denser medium (it does not occur for reflection from a rarer medium).

activity.prompt: Which arrangement shows each feature?

items.text: Central fringe at zero path difference is dark
Fringes on only one side of an axis

quiz.why: Stokes' treatment gives r′ = −r, equivalent to a π phase change (λ/2 extra path).

quiz.q: In Lloyd's mirror, the virtual source is formed by:
quiz.why: The mirror's image of the slit acts as the second coherent source.

quiz.q: Fringe width in Lloyd's mirror with source height h:
quiz.why: The source and its image are 2h apart, so β = λD/(2h).

questions.why: Constant phase relation is required for a stationary interference pattern.

questions.why: The wavelength in water is λ/n, so β scales by 3/4.

questions.why: Zero path difference is a maximum for all wavelengths simultaneously.

questions.why: Two conjugate lens positions exist only when object–image distance exceeds 4f.

options: π phase change on reflection from a denser medium
questions.why: Zero path difference plus a π phase shift gives destructive interference.

questions.why: cos² averages to ½, so ⟨4I₀ cos²(δ/2)⟩ = 2I₀ — energy is conserved.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Interference by Division of Amplitude
courses.summary: Thin-film interference in reflected and transmitted light, antireflection coatings, wedge-shaped films, Newton's rings and their use to find wavelength and refractive index, and the Michelson interferometer.
outcomes: Write conditions for maxima and minima in thin films including the π phase change
Use wedge fringes to measure tiny thicknesses
Determine λ and μ from Newton's rings
Use a Michelson interferometer to measure λ and Δλ

scenes.text: A drop of oil on a wet road spreads into swirls of colour.
Light reflects from the top and bottom of the film; the thickness decides which colour adds constructively.

steps.title: Path difference
steps.body: A film of index μ and thickness t, refraction angle r inside: rays reflected from the two surfaces differ in optical path by 2μt cos r. If one reflection is from a denser medium (air–film–air), add λ/2. Reflected light: bright when 2μt cos r = (n + ½)λ, dark when 2μt cos r = nλ. Transmitted light is complementary.

steps.title: Worked example: soap film
steps.body: Soap film μ = 1.33 in air, normal incidence, λ = 600 nm. Thinnest film that reflects strongly: 2μt = λ/2 → t = λ/(4μ) = 600/5.32 ≈ 113 nm. A film much thinner than λ looks black in reflection (path ≈ 0 but π shift → dark).

steps.title: Antireflection coatings
steps.body: On glass (n_g ≈ 1.5) a coating of index n_c with n_c < n_g has π shifts at BOTH surfaces, so they cancel. Destructive reflection when 2n_c t = λ/2 → t = λ/(4n_c). Complete cancellation needs n_c = √n_g ≈ 1.22; MgF₂ (1.38) is the practical choice.

steps.title: Worked example: coating
steps.body: MgF₂ (n = 1.38) for λ = 550 nm: t = 550/(4 × 1.38) ≈ 99.6 nm. Lenses with such coatings look purplish because red and blue are reflected slightly more than green.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Adding λ/2 when both reflections (or neither) are from denser media; using t cos i instead of t cos r; forgetting that transmitted fringes have the opposite condition.

activity.prompt: A quarter-wave antireflection coating (n = 1.25) is designed for λ = 600 nm. Minimum thickness in nm?

quiz.q: An air–soap–air film looks black in reflection when it is:
quiz.why: With negligible path difference, the π phase change at one surface makes the two reflections cancel.

quiz.q: For an antireflection coating on glass, the λ/2 term:
options: Cancels because both reflections have π shift
quiz.why: Both reflections are from denser media, so their phase changes cancel and only 2n_c t matters.

quiz.q: Path difference in a thin film includes the factor:
quiz.why: Geometry inside the film gives 2μt cos r, where r is the refraction angle.

scenes.text: Place a hair between the ends of two glass slides and shine sodium light from above.
Straight parallel fringes appear; their spacing reveals the hair's diameter to a fraction of a micrometre.

steps.title: Fringes in a wedge
steps.body: Film thickness t = xα at distance x from the edge (α small). Dark fringes (reflection, air wedge, normal incidence): 2μxα = nλ. Fringe width β = λ/(2μα). The contact edge is dark. Fringes are straight and parallel to the edge — contours of equal thickness.

steps.title: Worked example: thickness of a wire
steps.body: Air wedge, λ = 589 nm, slides 10 cm long, β = 0.5 mm. α = λ/(2β) = 5.89 × 10⁻⁷/10⁻³ = 5.89 × 10⁻⁴ rad. Wire thickness = αL = 5.89 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.1 ≈ 58.9 μm.

steps.title: Optical flatness testing
steps.body: Placing a test surface against a reference optical flat gives wedge fringes; straight, evenly spaced fringes mean a flat surface, while curved fringes map hills and valleys with λ/2 per fringe sensitivity.

steps.title: Liquid wedge
steps.body: Filling the wedge with a liquid of index μ reduces β by a factor μ, so μ = β_air/β_liquid.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using β = λ/α (forgetting the factor 2 for the double pass); measuring L from the wrong reference point.

activity.prompt: An air wedge 5 cm long gives fringes 0.2 mm apart with λ = 600 nm. Thickness of the spacer at the open end (μm)?

quiz.q: Fringe width in a wedge of angle α and index μ:
quiz.why: Successive dark fringes differ in thickness by λ/2μ, separated by (λ/2μ)/α.

quiz.q: The line of contact in an air wedge (reflected light) is:
quiz.why: Thickness is zero there, but the π phase change at the lower glass surface makes it dark.

quiz.q: Filling an air wedge with water (μ = 1.33):
quiz.why: β = λ/(2μα) is inversely proportional to μ.

scenes.text: A long-focus plano-convex lens rests on a glass plate under a travelling microscope lit by sodium light.
A dark centre surrounded by concentric rings appears, closer and closer together outward.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: Air film thickness at radius r: t ≈ r²/(2R), R = radius of curvature. Reflected dark rings: 2μt = nλ → r_n² = nλR/μ, or D_n² = 4nλR/μ. Bright rings: D_n² = 2(2n − 1)λR/μ. Radii ∝ √n, so rings crowd together outward. Centre is dark in reflection.

steps.title: Measuring λ
steps.body: Because the lens may not touch perfectly, use differences: λ = (D²_{n+p} − D²_n)/(4pR). R is measured with a spherometer (R = l²/6h + h/2) or by Boys' method.

steps.title: Refractive index of a liquid
steps.body: With liquid between lens and plate, D² shrinks by μ: μ = (D²_{n+p} − D²_n)_air/(D²_{n+p} − D²_n)_liquid. If the difference falls from 23.5 to 17.7 mm², μ ≈ 1.33 (water).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Measuring radii rather than diameters (centre is hard to locate precisely); not keeping the travelling microscope moving in one direction (backlash); using a short-focus lens (rings too small).

activity.prompt: Newton's rings: R = 1.0 m, D₂₀ = 6.86 mm, D₁₀ = 4.85 mm. Wavelength (nm)?

quiz.q: Diameter of the nth dark ring is proportional to:
quiz.why: D_n² = 4nλR/μ, so D_n ∝ √n.

quiz.q: The centre of Newton's rings in reflected light is:
quiz.why: At the contact point t = 0 and one reflection has a π phase change, giving darkness.

quiz.q: Introducing a liquid of index μ makes ring diameters:
quiz.why: D² ∝ 1/μ, so D shrinks by √μ.

story.title: The instrument that defined the metre

scenes.text: Michelson's interferometer splits light, sends it down two arms and recombines it.
Moving a mirror by half a wavelength makes one fringe appear or vanish — so length can be counted in wavelengths.

steps.title: Construction
steps.body: Light from an extended source hits a half-silvered beam splitter at 45°. One beam goes to fixed mirror M₂, the other to movable mirror M₁ on a precision screw. A compensating plate (same thickness as the splitter, unsilvered) equalises glass paths, essential for white-light fringes.

steps.title: Fringes
steps.body: If M₁ and the image of M₂ are parallel, they form an effective air film of thickness d: circular fringes of equal inclination, 2d cosθ = nλ. Tilted: straight fringes. Moving M₁ by λ/2 shifts one fringe: 2Δd = Nλ.

steps.title: Worked example: λ
steps.body: 200 fringes cross the field as M₁ moves 0.0589 mm. λ = 2Δd/N = 2 × 5.89 × 10⁻⁵/200 = 5.89 × 10⁻⁷ m = 589 nm.

steps.title: Worked example: sodium doublet
steps.body: Two close lines λ₁, λ₂ give fringes that fade and reappear. Mirror movement between successive positions of maximum distinctness: Δd = λ²/(2Δλ). With λ = 589.3 nm and Δλ = 0.6 nm: Δd = (589.3 × 10⁻⁹)²/(1.2 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 0.289 mm.

steps.title: Modern descendants
steps.body: LIGO's 4 km arms detect mirror motions below 10⁻¹⁸ m from gravitational waves; Fourier-transform infrared spectrometers are Michelson interferometers too.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using Δd = Nλ instead of Nλ/2; forgetting the compensating plate's role; counting fringes while turning the screw both ways (backlash).

quiz.why: The path difference changes by 2 × λ/2 = λ, one full fringe.

quiz.why: Glass is dispersive, so unequal glass paths would wash out white-light fringes; the plate equalises them for all λ.

quiz.why: For parallel mirrors each ring corresponds to a constant angle θ in 2d cosθ = nλ.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Diffraction
courses.summary: Fresnel half-period zones and the zone plate, Fraunhofer diffraction at a single slit, the plane transmission grating with missing orders, and resolving power of gratings, prisms and telescopes by Rayleigh's criterion.
outcomes: Construct half-period zones and find zone-plate focal lengths
Derive the single-slit intensity pattern and minima
Use the grating equation and identify maximum and missing orders
Compute resolving powers and the Rayleigh limit

lessons.title: Fresnel diffraction: half-period zones & zone plate

story.title: The bright spot in the shadow

scenes.text: In 1818 Poisson argued Fresnel's wave theory must be absurd: it predicted a bright spot at the centre of a disc's shadow.
Arago looked — and found the spot. Wave optics won.

steps.title: Half-period zones
steps.body: Divide a wavefront into annular zones whose distances to the observation point P increase by λ/2 each. Radius of the nth zone r_n = √(nbλ) (b = distance to P, plane wave). Zone areas are nearly equal; successive zones contribute with alternating sign and slowly decreasing amplitude. Resultant of the whole wavefront ≈ half the first zone's contribution.

steps.title: Zone plate
steps.body: Block alternate zones and the remaining ones add in phase, giving a bright focus. Primary focal length f = r₁²/λ = r_n²/(nλ). Secondary foci at f/3, f/5… Unlike a lens, a zone plate has focal length ∝ 1/λ (strong chromatic dispersion).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: r₁ = 1 mm, λ = 500 nm: f = 10⁻⁶/5 × 10⁻⁷ = 2 m. Next foci at 0.667 m and 0.4 m. For red light (700 nm) the primary focus moves to 1.43 m.

steps.title: Fresnel vs Fraunhofer
steps.body: Fresnel: source or screen at finite distance, curved wavefronts — circular aperture, straight edge. Fraunhofer: both effectively at infinity (lenses used), plane wavefronts — slits and gratings. Fresnel number a²/(Lλ) ≫ 1 → geometric shadow; ≈ 1 → Fresnel; ≪ 1 → Fraunhofer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying zone areas grow with n (they are nearly constant); confusing r_n² = nbλ with r_n = nbλ.

activity.prompt: A zone plate's first zone has radius 0.5 mm. Primary focal length for λ = 625 nm (m)?

quiz.q: Radius of the nth half-period zone is proportional to:
quiz.why: r_n² = nbλ, so r_n ∝ √n.

quiz.q: A zone plate's focal length depends on wavelength as:
quiz.why: f = r₁²/λ, so longer wavelengths focus closer.

quiz.q: Fraunhofer diffraction requires:
options: Source and screen effectively at infinity
quiz.why: Fraunhofer analysis assumes plane incident and diffracted wavefronts, achieved with lenses or large distances.

story.title: Squeeze the slit, spread the light

scenes.text: A laser pointer shone through a narrow slit made from two razor blades paints a long streak on the wall.
Narrow the slit, and the central band WIDENS — the opposite of what ray optics suggests.

steps.title: Intensity
steps.body: Slit width a, angle θ. Summing contributions across the slit (phasor arc): I = I₀ (sinβ/β)², β = πa sinθ/λ. Minima: a sinθ = nλ (n = ±1, ±2…). Secondary maxima near tanβ = β (β ≈ 1.43π, 2.46π), with intensities about 4.7% and 1.7% of I₀.

steps.title: Width of central maximum
steps.body: Angular half-width λ/a. On a screen at the focal plane of a lens of focal length f (or distance D): linear half-width λf/a, total width 2λf/a — twice the width of secondary maxima.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: a = 0.1 mm, λ = 600 nm, f = 1 m: first minima at ±6 mm, central maximum 12 mm wide. If a = 0.05 mm it doubles to 24 mm.

steps.title: Double slit (Fraunhofer)
steps.body: Two slits of width a, separation d: I = 4I₀ (sinβ/β)² cos²γ, γ = πd sinθ/λ — interference fringes modulated by the single-slit envelope. Missing orders occur where d/a is an integer ratio: if d = 3a, orders 3, 6… are missing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using a sinθ = (n + ½)λ for minima (that is YDSE dark fringe logic); assuming secondary maxima are exactly midway between minima.

activity.prompt: Single slit a = 0.2 mm, λ = 500 nm, screen 2 m away. Total width of the central maximum (mm)?

quiz.q: First minimum of a single slit occurs at:
quiz.why: Pairing the slit's two halves, path differences of λ/2 cancel pairwise when a sinθ = λ.

quiz.q: Narrowing the slit makes the central maximum:
quiz.why: Angular half-width is λ/a, inversely proportional to slit width.

quiz.q: Intensity of the first secondary maximum relative to central:

scenes.text: Tilt a CD under a lamp and rainbows flash across it.
Its closely spaced tracks act as a reflection grating, sending each colour to a different angle.

steps.title: Grating equation
steps.body: N slits with grating element d = a + b (= 1/lines per unit length). Principal maxima: d sinθ = nλ. Intensity I = I₀ (sinβ/β)² (sinNγ/sinγ)², so principal maxima grow as N² and get sharper, with N − 2 weak secondary maxima between them.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 5000 lines/cm → d = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m. λ = 589 nm: sinθ₁ = 0.2945 → θ₁ ≈ 17.1°; second order sinθ₂ = 0.589 → 36.1°. Maximum order n_max < d/λ = 3.4 → 3.

steps.title: Missing orders and overlap
steps.body: If a/d = m/n... more usefully: order n is missing when it coincides with a single-slit minimum, i.e. n = (d/a)m. For a = b (d = 2a) all even orders vanish. Spectra overlap when n₁λ₁ = n₂λ₂: e.g. 2nd-order 600 nm overlaps 3rd-order 400 nm.

steps.title: Dispersive power
steps.body: dθ/dλ = n/(d cosθ). For the first order above: 1/(2 × 10⁻⁶ × cos17.1°) ≈ 5.23 × 10⁵ rad/m, so the sodium doublet (Δλ = 0.6 nm) is separated by ≈ 3.1 × 10⁻⁴ rad ≈ 1.1 arcmin.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using lines per cm directly as d; forgetting to convert to metres; quoting n_max = d/λ when it is an exact integer (θ = 90° cannot be observed).

activity.prompt: A grating with 6000 lines/cm gives a first-order line at 20.7°. Wavelength (nm)?

quiz.q: Grating element for 4000 lines/cm:
If slit width equals opaque width (a = b), missing orders are:
quiz.why: With d = 2a, the condition n = 2m removes all even orders.

quiz.q: Increasing N (same d) makes principal maxima:
quiz.why: Peak intensity ∝ N² and angular width ∝ 1/N.

scenes.text: Sodium's yellow glow looks like one line in a cheap spectroscope.
With a good grating it splits into two lines 0.6 nm apart — 589.0 and 589.6 nm.

steps.title: Rayleigh criterion
steps.body: Two images are just resolved when the principal maximum of one falls on the first minimum of the other; the dip between them is then about 81% of the peaks. Resolving power R = λ/Δλ (spectral) or 1/θ_min (angular).

steps.title: Formulae
steps.body: Grating: R = nN (order × total illuminated lines). Prism: R = t dμ/dλ (t = base length). Telescope (circular aperture D): θ_min = 1.22λ/D. Microscope: minimum separation d = 1.22λ/(2μ sinα) = 0.61λ/NA.

steps.title: Worked example: grating
steps.body: Sodium doublet: λ/Δλ = 589.3/0.6 ≈ 982. First order needs N ≥ 982 lines illuminated; second order ≥ 491. A 2 cm-wide beam on a 5000 lines/cm grating has N = 10⁴ — easily enough.

steps.title: Worked example: telescope
steps.body: D = 10 cm, λ = 550 nm: θ_min = 1.22 × 5.5 × 10⁻⁷/0.1 ≈ 6.7 × 10⁻⁶ rad ≈ 1.4 arcsec. The eye (pupil 3 mm) manages ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻⁴ rad ≈ 46 arcsec.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using lines per cm instead of total illuminated lines for N; confusing magnification with resolution — extra magnification cannot reveal detail below the diffraction limit.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Polarisation
courses.summary: Plane polarised light and Malus's law, polarisation by reflection (Brewster), double refraction in uniaxial crystals, quarter- and half-wave plates, production and analysis of elliptical and circular light, and optical rotation with the polarimeter.
outcomes: Apply Malus's law through chains of polarisers
Derive and use Brewster's law
Explain O and E rays and design wave plates
Measure specific rotation with a half-shade polarimeter

scenes.text: Two crossed polaroid sheets block all light. Slip a third between them at 45° and light comes through.
Adding a filter lets MORE light pass — only a vector picture of polarisation explains it.

steps.title: States of polarisation
steps.body: Light is a transverse EM wave; polarisation describes the direction of E. Unpolarised light has E in rapidly varying random directions. Plane (linearly) polarised: E along one fixed direction. Circular and elliptical: E rotates. That light can be polarised at all proves it is transverse.

steps.title: Malus's law
steps.body: An ideal polariser transmits the E component along its axis: E cosθ, so I = I₀ cos²θ for polarised input. For unpolarised input, ⟨cos²θ⟩ = ½ → I = I₀/2.

steps.title: Worked example: three polarisers
steps.body: Unpolarised I₀ → polariser at 0° → I₀/2 → 45° → I₀/2 × ½ = I₀/4 → 90° → I₀/4 × ½ = I₀/8. Without the middle sheet, crossed polarisers give zero.

steps.title: Everyday polarisation
steps.body: Polaroid sunglasses block horizontally polarised glare from roads and water; LCD screens sandwich liquid crystals between crossed polarisers; photographers use polarising filters to darken skies.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using cosθ instead of cos²θ for intensity; applying Malus's law to the first polariser with unpolarised input (use ½).

activity.prompt: Unpolarised light passes polarisers with axes at 0°, 30° and 90°. What fraction of the original intensity emerges? (decimal)

quiz.q: Polarised light of intensity I₀ passes a polariser at 60°. Transmitted:
Unpolarised light through one ideal polariser:
quiz.why: Averaging cos²θ over all random orientations gives ½.

quiz.q: Polarisation shows that light waves are:
quiz.why: Only transverse vibrations have a direction perpendicular to propagation that can be selected.

scenes.text: Late afternoon glare off a lake vanishes when a fisherman puts on polaroid glasses.
At one special angle, the reflected light is completely polarised.

steps.title: Brewster's law
steps.body: When the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, the reflected light is completely polarised with E perpendicular to the plane of incidence (s-polarised). Then θ_B + r = 90°, and Snell's law gives n = sinθ_B/sin(90° − θ_B) = tanθ_B.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Glass n = 1.5: θ_B = tan⁻¹1.5 ≈ 56.3°; refraction angle r = 33.7°. Water n = 1.33: θ_B ≈ 53.1°.

steps.title: Pile of plates
steps.body: At Brewster's angle each surface reflects about 15% of the s-component and none of the p-component. A stack of 10–15 glass plates removes most s-light from the transmitted beam, leaving it largely p-polarised.

steps.title: Lasers
steps.body: Brewster windows on gas-laser tubes transmit p-polarised light with no reflection loss, so the laser output is linearly polarised.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying the REFRACTED beam is fully polarised at Brewster's angle (only partially); writing tanθ_B = 1/n for light going from air into glass.

activity.prompt: Polarising angle for light reflected from water (n = 1.33), in degrees?

quiz.q: At Brewster's angle, reflected and refracted rays are:
quiz.why: θ_B + r = 90° is the defining geometric condition.

quiz.q: Brewster's law is:
quiz.why: Combining Snell's law with θ_B + r = 90° gives tanθ_B = n.

quiz.q: Light reflected at θ_B vibrates:
options: Perpendicular to the plane of incidence
quiz.why: The p-component (in the plane) has zero reflectance at θ_B, leaving only s-polarised light.

scenes.text: Place a calcite crystal on printed text and you see the words twice.
Rotate the crystal: one image stays still, the other circles around it.

steps.title: O and E rays
steps.body: In uniaxial crystals (calcite, quartz) light splits into an ordinary ray (obeys Snell's law, index μ_o in all directions) and an extraordinary ray (index varies with direction, from μ_o along the optic axis to μ_e perpendicular to it). Both are plane polarised at right angles to each other. Along the optic axis there is no double refraction.

steps.title: Negative and positive crystals
steps.body: Calcite: μ_o = 1.658, μ_e = 1.486 (μ_e < μ_o, negative; E ray faster). Quartz: μ_o = 1.544, μ_e = 1.553 (positive). Nicol prism: a calcite rhomb cut and cemented with Canada balsam (μ ≈ 1.55) totally reflects the O ray and transmits the E ray — a polariser.

steps.title: Retardation plates
steps.body: A plate cut with the optic axis parallel to its faces introduces path difference (μ_o − μ_e)t between O and E components. Quarter-wave plate: |μ_o − μ_e|t = λ/4. Half-wave plate: λ/2 (rotates the plane of polarisation by 2θ).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Calcite, λ = 589 nm: t_QWP = 589/(4 × 0.172) ≈ 856 nm — impractically thin, so quartz or mica is used. Quartz (Δμ = 0.009): t = 589/(0.036) ≈ 16.4 μm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking a wave plate works for all wavelengths (it is designed for one λ); forgetting that O and E rays are orthogonally polarised.

activity.prompt: Thickness of a quartz quarter-wave plate (μ_e − μ_o = 0.009) for λ = 600 nm, in μm?

quiz.q: Calcite is a:
quiz.why: Its μ_e (1.486) is less than μ_o (1.658).

quiz.q: Along the optic axis of a uniaxial crystal:
quiz.why: O and E rays travel with the same speed along the optic axis.

quiz.q: A half-wave plate with its axis at θ to incident plane-polarised light:
quiz.why: A π retardation reflects the polarisation direction about the fast axis, rotating it by 2θ.

scenes.text: A sugar factory checks its syrup by shining polarised light through a tube.
The sugar rotates the plane of polarisation; the angle reveals the concentration.

steps.title: Producing and analysing
steps.body: Plane-polarised light at 45° to a QWP's axis → circular; at other angles → elliptical. Analysis with a rotating analyser: plane light shows zero minimum; circular and unpolarised show constant intensity; distinguish them by inserting a QWP first — circular becomes plane (extinction possible), unpolarised stays unpolarised.

steps.title: Optical activity
steps.body: Optically active substances (quartz along its axis, sugar solutions) rotate the plane of polarisation. Dextro = clockwise (looking toward the source), laevo = anticlockwise. Fresnel's explanation: plane light = two opposite circular components travelling at different speeds. Specific rotation [α] = θ/(l c), with l in decimetres and c in g/cm³.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: θ = 13.2° for a 2 dm tube of sugar solution with c = 0.1 g/cm³: [α] = 13.2/(2 × 0.1) = 66° dm⁻¹ (g/cm³)⁻¹, close to the accepted ≈ 66.5° for sucrose at 589 nm and 20 °C.

steps.title: Laurent's half-shade polarimeter
steps.body: A half-wave plate covers half the field, so the two halves' polarisation planes differ slightly. The analyser is set where both halves appear equally (dimly) bright — the eye judges equal brightness far more precisely than darkness. Readings with water and with solution give θ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using tube length in cm instead of dm; ignoring temperature and wavelength dependence of [α]; confusing circular with unpolarised light.

activity.prompt: Sugar solution ([α] = 66.5° dm⁻¹ (g/cm³)⁻¹) in a 2 dm tube rotates the plane by 10°. Concentration in g per 100 cm³?

quiz.why: Equal O and E amplitudes with π/2 phase difference produce circular polarisation.

quiz.q: Specific rotation uses tube length in:
quiz.why: By convention [α] = θ/(l c) with l in decimetres.

options: A quarter-wave plate before the analyser
quiz.why: A QWP turns circular light into plane light that can be extinguished, but leaves unpolarised light unpolarised.

questions.why: μ_o (1.658) > μ_balsam (1.55), so the O ray beyond the critical angle is totally reflected.

questions.why: Unequal O and E amplitudes with π/2 phase give an ellipse.

questions.why: Both unpolarised and circular light have no preferred direction for the analyser.

options: The eye judges equal brightness well
questions.why: Matching two adjacent dim fields is far more sensitive than finding a single minimum.

options: Different speeds of left and right circular components
questions.why: A phase lag between opposite circular components rotates their resultant plane vector.

questions.why: Reflection near Brewster's angle from horizontal surfaces favours horizontal E, which vertical-axis lenses block.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Revision, Practicals & Exam
courses.summary: An optics formula sheet and the standard practicals — spectrometer and prism (μ by minimum deviation), Newton's rings, diffraction grating and the half-shade polarimeter — with procedures, observation calculations and viva points, plus a mixed exam.
outcomes: Recall key formulas of geometrical and wave optics
Set up a spectrometer (Schuster's method) and find μ of a prism
Find λ with Newton's rings and a grating
Determine specific rotation with a polarimeter

scenes.text: Anjali writes every optics formula on one card with its condition in brackets.
In the exam she spends her time on derivations, not on recalling formulas.

steps.title: Geometrical
steps.body: Fermat: δ∫n ds = 0. Lens maker 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂). Two lenses 1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ − d/f₁f₂. Achromat ω₁/f₁ + ω₂/f₂ = 0; same glass d = (f₁ + f₂)/2. Huygens F = 1.5f; Ramsden F = 0.75f.

steps.title: Interference
steps.body: I = I₁ + I₂ + 2√(I₁I₂) cosδ; V = 2√(I₁I₂)/(I₁ + I₂); l_c = λ²/Δλ. YDSE β = λD/d; sheet shift (μ − 1)tD/d. Biprism d = 2a(μ − 1)α = √(d₁d₂). Film 2μt cos r = (n + ½)λ bright (reflected, π shift once). Wedge β = λ/2μα. Newton λ = (D²ₙ₊ₚ − D²ₙ)/4pR. Michelson 2Δd = Nλ; Δλ = λ²/2Δd.

steps.title: Diffraction
steps.body: Zone plate f = r₁²/λ. Single slit minima a sinθ = nλ; central width 2λf/a. Grating d sinθ = nλ; missing n = (d/a)m; R = nN. Telescope θ = 1.22λ/D.

steps.title: Polarisation
steps.body: Malus I = I₀cos²θ; Brewster tanθ_B = n; QWP Δμ t = λ/4; HWP λ/2; [α] = θ/(l c) with l in dm.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always state the sign convention; draw ray/phasor diagrams for derivations; convert all lengths to metres before substituting; quote λ in nm at the end.

quiz.q: Which experiment uses division of amplitude?
quiz.why: Newton's rings arise from partial reflection at two surfaces of an air film, splitting the amplitude.

quiz.q: Resolving power of a grating does NOT depend on:
quiz.why: R = nN; d affects which orders exist but not R for a given order and N.

quiz.q: Which eyepiece is used with cross-wires?
quiz.why: Ramsden's front focal plane lies outside the lenses.

lessons.title: Lab: Spectrometer — refractive index of a prism

scenes.text: Sodium light through a prism on the spectrometer table: as the table turns, the image moves, stops, and turns back.
That turning point is minimum deviation — and with the prism angle it gives μ.

steps.title: Adjustments
steps.body: 1) Focus the eyepiece on the cross-wires. 2) Focus the telescope for parallel rays (on a distant object, or by Schuster's method). 3) Collimator: adjust the slit until its image is sharp in the telescope. 4) Level the prism table with a spirit level. Schuster's method: with the prism near minimum deviation, focus alternately the telescope (when the table is turned toward the collimator side) and the collimator (the other side) until the image stays sharp.

steps.title: Measurements
steps.body: Angle of prism A: place the refracting edge toward the collimator, take reflected images from both faces: A = (angle between the two telescope positions)/2. Minimum deviation δ_m: locate the turning point, note reading; remove prism, note direct reading; difference = δ_m. μ = sin((A + δ_m)/2)/sin(A/2).

steps.title: Worked calculation
steps.body: A = 60°, δ_m = 38.9°: μ = sin(49.45°)/sin30° = 0.760/0.5 ≈ 1.520. Read both verniers each time and average to cancel eccentricity error.

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Prism table not levelled; slit too wide; parallax between cross-wires and image; vernier misreading across 360° → 0°.

steps.title: Viva points
steps.body: Why two verniers? (Eliminate eccentricity of the circular scale.) Why at minimum deviation? (Ray passes symmetrically; small errors in setting have least effect.) What does Cauchy's relation say? (μ = A + B/λ².)

activity.prompt: A prism with A = 60° gives minimum deviation 40° for sodium light. Refractive index?

quiz.q: At minimum deviation the ray inside the prism is:
quiz.why: Symmetric passage (i = e) makes the internal ray parallel to the base for an isosceles prism.

quiz.q: Angle of prism by the reflection method equals:
options: Half the angle between telescope positions
quiz.why: Rays reflected from two faces separated by A diverge by 2A.

quiz.q: Schuster's method is used to:
options: Focus telescope and collimator for parallel light
quiz.why: It sets both instruments for parallel rays without needing a distant object.

lessons.title: Lab: Newton's rings & the diffraction grating

story.title: Two ways to measure sodium's λ

scenes.text: On one bench, rings under a travelling microscope; on the next, coloured orders on a spectrometer.
Both should give close to 589 nm — a useful cross-check.

steps.title: Newton's rings procedure
steps.body: 1) Clean lens and plate; place under a travelling microscope with a 45° glass plate reflecting sodium light down. 2) Focus on the rings; set cross-wire tangential to, say, the 20th ring on the left; record. 3) Move inward recording rings 18, 16 … 4, then cross the centre and record 4 … 20 on the right (move in ONE direction). 4) D = difference of left and right readings. 5) Plot D² vs n: slope = 4λR. 6) Measure R with a spherometer: R = l²/6h + h/2.

steps.title: Grating procedure (normal incidence)
steps.body: 1) Adjust spectrometer. 2) Note direct reading, rotate telescope 90° and fix. 3) Rotate the table until the reflected slit image from the grating coincides with the cross-wire, then rotate the table back by 45°: grating is now normal to the beam. 4) Record first-order positions on left and right; 2θ = difference. 5) λ = sinθ/(nN), N = lines per metre.

steps.title: Worked calculation: grating
steps.body: 6000 lines/cm (N = 6 × 10⁵ m⁻¹). First-order readings differ by 39°20′ → θ = 19°40′ = 19.67°. λ = sin19.67°/(6 × 10⁵) = 0.3366/6 × 10⁵ ≈ 5.61 × 10⁻⁷ m = 561 nm (e.g. a green mercury-like line in this exercise).

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Backlash in the microscope screw; centre of rings not dark (dust — clean); grating not normal; reading only one vernier.

activity.prompt: Spherometer: distance between legs l = 4.0 cm, sagitta h = 0.027 cm. Radius of curvature R = l²/6h + h/2 (cm)?

quiz.q: In Newton's rings, the slope of D² vs n gives:
quiz.why: D_n² = 4nλR (air film), so the slope is 4λR.

quiz.q: Why record ring diameters in one direction of screw motion?
quiz.why: Reversing the screw introduces backlash, shifting readings by an unknown amount.

quiz.q: For normal incidence, the grating is set by rotating the table:
quiz.why: With the telescope at 90°, reflection occurs when the grating is at 45°; turning it 45° more makes it normal to the beam.

scenes.text: Looking into a polarimeter, the student sees a circle split into two halves of unequal brightness.
Turning the analyser until both halves match gives a sharp, repeatable reading.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Fill the tube with distilled water (no bubbles), set the analyser for equal half-shade, note reading θ₀. 2) Prepare sugar solutions of known concentrations (e.g. 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 g per 100 cm³). 3) For each, fill the tube, set equal shade, read θ. 4) Rotation = θ − θ₀. 5) Plot rotation vs c; slope = [α]l.

steps.title: Worked calculation
steps.body: Tube 2.2 dm. A 10 g/100 cm³ solution (0.10 g/cm³) gives rotation 14.6°. [α] = 14.6/(2.2 × 0.10) ≈ 66.4° dm⁻¹ (g/cm³)⁻¹.

steps.title: Sources of error
steps.body: Air bubbles in the tube; temperature differences ([α] decreases slightly as temperature rises); not using monochromatic sodium light (rotation depends strongly on λ).

steps.title: Viva points
steps.body: Why the half-wave plate in Laurent's device? (Creates two fields whose planes differ, enabling equal-shade matching.) Why sodium light? (The half-wave plate is a λ/2 plate only for its design wavelength.) What is the unit of [α]? (degrees per dm per g/cm³.)

uni-bsc-phy-quantum-mechanics.title: B.Sc Physics · Quantum Mechanics (UG paper)
uni-bsc-phy-quantum-mechanics.description: Unit-by-unit undergraduate Quantum Mechanics: the Schrödinger equation and wavefunctions, operators and postulates, one-dimensional potentials and tunnelling, the harmonic oscillator, and angular momentum with the hydrogen atom, ending with a revision unit and full exam. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc Physics (Hons) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Wavefunctions and the Schrödinger equation
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Quantum Mechanics and Applications)
courses.summary: From matter waves to the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, Born's probability interpretation and normalisation, probability current and the continuity equation, separation of variables to the time-independent equation, stationary states and admissibility conditions on ψ.
outcomes: Motivate the time-dependent Schrödinger equation from a free-particle wave
Interpret |Ψ|² as a probability density and normalise wavefunctions
Derive the continuity equation and compute probability current
Separate the time-dependent equation to obtain stationary states
State the conditions a physically acceptable wavefunction must satisfy

scenes.text: At a 1925 Zürich seminar, Peter Debye told Schrödinger: if electrons are waves, they need a wave equation.
Over a holiday in the Alps, Schrödinger found it.

steps.title: Plausibility argument
steps.body:
Free particle as a plane wave Ψ = A e^(i(kx − ωt)) with p = ħk, E = ħω (de Broglie, Einstein).
- −iħ ∂Ψ/∂x = ħkΨ = pΨ → p ↔ −iħ ∂/∂x
- iħ ∂Ψ/∂t = ħωΨ = EΨ → E ↔ iħ ∂/∂t
Insert into E = p²/2m + V:

**iħ ∂Ψ/∂t = −(ħ²/2m) ∂²Ψ/∂x² + V(x,t)Ψ**

In 3-D: iħ∂Ψ/∂t = ĤΨ with Ĥ = −(ħ²/2m)∇² + V.

steps.title: Key features
steps.body:
- First order in time: Ψ(x,0) determines Ψ at all later times.
- Linear: superpositions of solutions are solutions (interference).
- Ψ is necessarily complex (the i is essential).
- It is a postulate — justified by experiment, not derived from classical physics.

steps.title: Solved: free-particle dispersion
steps.body:
Plug Ψ = e^(i(kx − ωt)) into the free equation (V = 0): ħω = ħ²k²/2m → ω = ħk²/(2m).
Group velocity dω/dk = ħk/m = p/m = v ✓ (the particle velocity); phase velocity ω/k = v/2.

steps.title: Solved: energy of a 1 nm electron wave
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the equation without i, giving a diffusion equation.
- Taking the minus sign off the kinetic term.
- Thinking Ψ itself is measurable; only |Ψ|² and derived quantities are.

activity.prompt: An electron has de Broglie wavelength 0.5 nm. Find its kinetic energy in eV (h = 6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s, m = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg, 1 eV = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ J).

quiz.q: The momentum operator in one dimension is:
quiz.why: Acting on e^(ikx), −iħ ∂/∂x returns ħk = p, so the momentum operator is −iħ ∂/∂x.

quiz.q: Because the Schrödinger equation is linear:
quiz.why: Linearity means any combination aΨ₁ + bΨ₂ also satisfies the equation, which underlies interference effects.

quiz.q: For a free particle, ω(k) equals:
quiz.why: Substituting a plane wave into the free Schrödinger equation gives ħω = ħ²k²/2m.

scenes.text: Fire single electrons at a double slit: each lands at one random spot.
After thousands, the spots build an interference pattern. |Ψ|² is the map of where they are likely to land.

steps.title: Born's rule (1926)
steps.body:
|Ψ(x,t)|² dx = probability of finding the particle between x and x + dx at time t.
Normalisation: ∫_{−∞}^{∞} |Ψ|² dx = 1. The Schrödinger equation preserves normalisation in time (shown via the continuity equation).
Ψ and e^(iα)Ψ describe the same state (global phase is unobservable).

steps.title: Solved: parabolic wavefunction
steps.body:
ψ = A x(L − x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ L, zero outside.
∫₀^L x²(L − x)² dx = L⁵/30 → A² L⁵/30 = 1 → **A = √(30/L⁵)**.

steps.title: Square-integrable functions
steps.body: A physical ψ must have finite ∫|ψ|²dx. Plane waves e^(ikx) are not normalisable; they are idealisations, used as limits of wave packets or with box/delta normalisation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Normalising ψ instead of |ψ|² (∫ψ dx = 1 is wrong).
- Forgetting the complex conjugate: |ψ|² = ψ*ψ.
- Treating |ψ|² as a probability rather than a probability density (needs dx).

activity.prompt: For ψ = (1/√a) e^(−|x|/a), what is the probability of finding the particle with |x| < a/2? (= 1 − e^(−1)) Give three decimals.

quiz.q: |Ψ|² represents:
quiz.why: Born's rule interprets |Ψ|² dx as the probability of finding the particle in dx.

quiz.q: Normalisation constant for ψ = A x(L − x) on [0, L]:
quiz.why: The integral of x²(L − x)² over [0, L] is L⁵/30, so A² = 30/L⁵.

quiz.q: Multiplying ψ by e^(iα) (constant α):
quiz.why: A global phase cancels in ψ*ψ and in every expectation value, so it has no physical effect.

lessons.title: Probability current and the continuity equation

scenes.text: If probability decreases in one region, it must flow out through the boundary — it can't just vanish.
The Schrödinger equation guarantees this with a continuity equation, just like charge conservation.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body:
Let ρ = Ψ*Ψ. Using the Schrödinger equation and its conjugate (V real):
∂ρ/∂t = (iħ/2m)(Ψ*∂²Ψ/∂x² − Ψ∂²Ψ*/∂x²) = −∂J/∂x, with

**J = (ħ/2mi)(Ψ* ∂Ψ/∂x − Ψ ∂Ψ*/∂x) = (ħ/m) Im(Ψ* ∂Ψ/∂x)**

so ∂ρ/∂t + ∂J/∂x = 0. Integrating over all x with Ψ → 0 at ±∞: d/dt ∫ρ dx = 0 (normalisation preserved).

steps.title: Solved: plane wave
steps.body: Ψ = A e^(i(kx − ωt)): Ψ*∂Ψ/∂x = ik|A|² → J = **|A|² ħk/m = ρ v**. Probability flows at the classical speed, like a current density = density × velocity.

steps.title: Solved: real wavefunctions
steps.body: If Ψ is real (up to a global phase), Ψ*∂Ψ/∂x is real and J = 0. Bound stationary states (e.g. particle in a box) carry no net current — standing waves.

steps.title: Where it is used
steps.body: Reflection and transmission coefficients in step and barrier problems are ratios of probability currents: R = J_refl/J_inc, T = J_trans/J_inc.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dropping the factor 1/2 or i in J.
- Using J = |A|²v without remembering v depends on the region (different k on each side of a step).
- Assuming complex potentials conserve probability (they model absorption and do not).

activity.prompt: For an electron plane wave with k = 1.0×10¹⁰ m⁻¹, find the velocity ħk/m in units of 10⁶ m/s (ħ = 1.055×10⁻³⁴ J·s, m = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg).

quiz.q: The continuity equation in QM is:
quiz.why: Any decrease of probability density in a region is balanced by the outward probability current, giving ∂ρ/∂t + ∂J/∂x = 0.

quiz.q: Probability current of a real wavefunction is:
quiz.why: For real ψ, Ψ*∂Ψ/∂x is real, so its imaginary part and hence J vanish.

quiz.q: For a plane wave Ae^(ikx), J equals:
quiz.why: Evaluating (ħ/m)Im(Ψ*∂Ψ/∂x) gives |A|²ħk/m, density times velocity.

lessons.title: Time-independent Schrödinger equation and stationary states

scenes.text: A hydrogen atom in its ground state sits unchanged for ever — no glow, no collapse.
Its state is 'stationary': the wavefunction only rotates in phase, so every measurable thing stays fixed.

steps.title: Separation of variables
steps.body:
For time-independent V(x), try Ψ = ψ(x)φ(t):
iħ φ̇/φ = [−(ħ²/2m)ψ″ + Vψ]/ψ = E (constant).
- φ(t) = e^(−iEt/ħ)
- **−(ħ²/2m) ψ″ + V ψ = E ψ** (time-independent SE, an eigenvalue equation Ĥψ = Eψ).
General solution: Ψ = Σ cₙ ψₙ(x) e^(−iEₙt/ħ).

steps.title: Stationary states
steps.body: For a single energy eigenstate: |Ψ|² = |ψ|² is time independent, and so is every expectation value. A superposition of two energies has |Ψ|² oscillating at angular frequency (E₂ − E₁)/ħ — the Bohr frequency of emitted light.

steps.title: Admissible wavefunctions
steps.body: ψ must be: single-valued, finite, square-integrable, and continuous; ψ′ continuous wherever V is finite (ψ′ may jump at an infinite wall or a delta potential). These conditions are what quantise energies in bound problems.

steps.title: Solved: probability in a box
steps.body:
Ground state of an infinite well: ψ₁ = √(2/L) sin(πx/L). Probability in 0 < x < L/4:
∫₀^{L/4} (2/L) sin²(πx/L) dx = 1/4 − 1/(2π) = 0.250 − 0.159 = **0.091**.
Classically (uniform) it would be 0.25 — the particle avoids the walls.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling any solution of the TDSE 'stationary'; only single-energy states are.
- Forgetting the e^(−iEt/ħ) factors when building superpositions.
- Demanding ψ′ continuity at an infinite wall.

activity.prompt: A particle is in the ground state of an infinite well of width L. What is the probability of finding it between x = L/4 and x = 3L/4? (Use the symmetry of the 0 to L/4 result 0.091.)

quiz.why: Separating variables gives φ(t) = e^(−iEt/ħ), a pure phase rotation.

quiz.q: In a stationary state, expectation values are:
quiz.why: The phase factor cancels in ψ*Âψ, so every expectation value stays constant in time.

quiz.why: The cross term contains e^(−i(E₂−E₁)t/ħ), so the density oscillates at the Bohr frequency.

questions.why: Acting on e^(−iωt), iħ∂/∂t gives ħω = E.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Operators, expectation values and the postulates
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Quantum Mechanics and Applications)
courses.summary: Linear and Hermitian operators, eigenvalue equations and orthogonality, expectation values of position, momentum and energy, Ehrenfest's theorem, commutators and the generalised uncertainty principle, and the postulates of quantum mechanics including measurement and expansion in eigenstates.
outcomes: Identify linear and Hermitian operators and prove their eigenvalues are real
Compute expectation values ⟨x⟩, ⟨p⟩, ⟨x²⟩, ⟨p²⟩ and ⟨H⟩
State and interpret Ehrenfest's theorem
Evaluate commutators such as [x, p] = iħ and apply the generalised uncertainty relation
Use the measurement postulate to find probabilities and mean energies for superpositions

scenes.text: In quantum mechanics every measurable quantity — position, momentum, energy — becomes an operator.
The possible answers to a measurement are that operator's eigenvalues.

steps.title: Linear operators
steps.body:
An operator Â maps functions to functions; it is linear if Â(aψ + bφ) = aÂψ + bÂφ.
Standard operators: x̂ = x, p̂ = −iħ d/dx, Ĥ = −(ħ²/2m)d²/dx² + V(x), L̂_z = −iħ ∂/∂φ.
Eigenvalue equation: Âψ = aψ (ψ eigenfunction, a eigenvalue).

steps.title: Hermitian operators
steps.body:
Â is Hermitian if ∫φ*(Âψ)dx = ∫(Âφ)*ψ dx for all admissible φ, ψ.
Theorems:
1. Eigenvalues are **real** (so they can be measurement results).
2. Eigenfunctions with different eigenvalues are **orthogonal**.
3. Eigenfunctions form a complete set (expansion possible).
p̂ is Hermitian (integration by parts, boundary terms vanish); d/dx alone is not.

steps.title: Solved: eigenfunctions
steps.body:
(a) p̂ e^(ikx) = ħk e^(ikx) → eigenvalue ħk.
(b) d²/dx² sin(3x) = −9 sin(3x) → eigenvalue −9.
(c) p̂ sin(kx) = −iħk cos(kx) — not an eigenfunction of p̂ (it is a superposition of ±ħk), though it is an eigenfunction of p̂².

steps.title: Solved: proof that eigenvalues are real
steps.body: Âψ = aψ. Then ∫ψ*Âψ = a∫|ψ|², and by hermiticity ∫(Âψ)*ψ = a*∫|ψ|². Equal → a = a*: real.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting −i in p̂, making it anti-Hermitian.
- Assuming every eigenfunction of p̂² is one of p̂.
- Treating operator products as commutative: x̂p̂ ≠ p̂x̂.

activity.prompt: What is the eigenvalue of the operator d²/dx² acting on f(x) = cos(4x)?

quiz.q: Eigenvalues of a Hermitian operator are:
quiz.why: Comparing ∫ψ*Âψ with its Hermitian conjugate shows a = a*, so the eigenvalues are real.

quiz.q: e^(ikx) is an eigenfunction of p̂ with eigenvalue:
quiz.why: −iħ d/dx e^(ikx) = −iħ(ik)e^(ikx) = ħk e^(ikx).

quiz.q: Eigenfunctions of a Hermitian operator with different eigenvalues are:
quiz.why: Hermiticity gives (a₁ − a₂)∫ψ₁*ψ₂ = 0, so for a₁ ≠ a₂ the overlap integral vanishes.

scenes.text: Individual measurements on an electron are random.
Yet the average position and momentum obey Newton's laws — Ehrenfest's bridge between quantum and classical.

steps.title: Expectation value
steps.body:
⟨A⟩ = ∫ψ* Â ψ dx (ψ normalised): the average of many measurements on identically prepared systems.
Uncertainty: σ_A² = ⟨A²⟩ − ⟨A⟩².
⟨p⟩ = ∫ψ*(−iħ dψ/dx)dx. For any real bound ψ, ⟨p⟩ = 0.

steps.title: Solved: particle in a box ground state
Ehrenfest's theorem
steps.body:
d⟨x⟩/dt = ⟨p⟩/m, d⟨p⟩/dt = ⟨−dV/dx⟩.
General: d⟨A⟩/dt = (i/ħ)⟨[Ĥ, Â]⟩ + ⟨∂Â/∂t⟩.
Note ⟨−V′(x)⟩ ≠ −V′(⟨x⟩) in general, so quantum averages follow classical paths exactly only for V at most quadratic (free particle, uniform field, harmonic oscillator).

steps.title: Solved: conserved quantities
steps.body: If [Ĥ, Â] = 0 and Â has no explicit t-dependence, ⟨A⟩ is constant. Free particle: [Ĥ, p̂] = 0 → ⟨p⟩ conserved (Newton's first law, quantum version).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the operator outside: ⟨p⟩ ≠ −iħ d/dx ∫|ψ|².
- Confusing the expectation value with the most likely result.
- Forgetting to normalise ψ before computing ⟨A⟩.

activity.prompt: A particle is in the ground state of an infinite well from x = 0 to x = 2 nm. What is ⟨x⟩ in nm?

quiz.q: ⟨p⟩ for any real normalisable bound-state wavefunction is:
quiz.why: For real ψ, ∫ψ(−iħψ′)dx = −(iħ/2)[ψ²] which vanishes at the boundaries, so ⟨p⟩ = 0.

quiz.q: Ehrenfest's theorem states d⟨p⟩/dt =
quiz.why: The rate of change of mean momentum equals the average force ⟨−V′(x)⟩, not the force at the mean position.

quiz.q: σₓσ_p for the box ground state is about:
quiz.why: σₓ = 0.181L and σ_p = πħ/L multiply to about 0.568ħ, consistent with the uncertainty bound.

lessons.title: Commutators and the generalised uncertainty principle

scenes.text: Putting on socks then shoes is not the same as shoes then socks.
In quantum mechanics measuring x then p is not the same as p then x — the commutator measures the difference.

steps.title: Commutator algebra
steps.body:
[Â, B̂] = ÂB̂ − B̂Â. Act on a test function f:
[x̂, p̂]f = x(−iħf′) − (−iħ)(xf)′ = iħf → **[x̂, p̂] = iħ**.
Rules: [A, BC] = [A, B]C + B[A, C]; [x, pⁿ] = iħn pⁿ⁻¹; [x, f(p)] = iħ f′(p); [p, g(x)] = −iħ g′(x).
Angular momentum: [L_x, L_y] = iħL_z (cyclic); [L², L_z] = 0.

steps.title: Generalised uncertainty
steps.body:
For Hermitian Â, B̂: σ_A σ_B ≥ (1/2)|⟨[Â, B̂]⟩|.
- x and p: σₓσ_p ≥ ħ/2
- Commuting observables ([A, B] = 0) can have simultaneous eigenstates and be measured together sharply (compatible observables), e.g. L² and L_z, or H and p for a free particle.

steps.title: Solved: [x², p] and [H, x]
steps.body:
(a) [x², p] = x[x, p] + [x, p]x = **2iħx**.
(b) For H = p²/2m + V(x): [H, x] = (1/2m)[p², x] = (1/2m)(−2iħp) = **−iħp/m** → d⟨x⟩/dt = (i/ħ)⟨[H, x]⟩ = ⟨p⟩/m ✓ (Ehrenfest).

steps.title: Why we can't know L_x and L_y together
steps.body: [L_x, L_y] = iħL_z ≠ 0, so only one component (conventionally L_z) is sharp along with L². That is why orbitals are labelled by l and m only.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Evaluating commutators without a test function and losing terms from the product rule.
- Writing [x, p] = −iħ (sign error).
- Assuming non-commuting operators can never share any eigenstate (they can share particular ones, e.g. l = 0 states for L_x and L_y).

activity.prompt: Using the box ground-state results σₓ = 0.1807L and σ_p = πħ/L, compute σₓσ_p in units of ħ (three decimals).

quiz.q: [x̂, p̂] equals:
quiz.why: Acting on a test function, the product rule leaves iħf, so [x̂, p̂] = iħ.

quiz.q: [x, p²] equals:
quiz.why: [x, p²] = [x, p]p + p[x, p] = 2iħp.

quiz.q: L² and L_z:
options: commute, so can be sharp together
quiz.why: [L², L_z] = 0, so states can have definite l and m simultaneously.

lessons.title: Postulates of quantum mechanics and measurement

scenes.text: Schrödinger imagined a cat in a box whose fate depends on a quantum superposition.
The measurement postulate says what happens when we open the box: one outcome, with a calculable probability.

steps.title: The postulates
steps.body:
1. **State**: a system is described by a normalised wavefunction Ψ (a vector in Hilbert space).
2. **Observables**: every observable corresponds to a Hermitian operator.
3. **Measurement outcomes**: only eigenvalues aₙ of Â can be obtained.
4. **Probabilities (Born)**: expanding Ψ = Σ cₙψₙ in eigenfunctions, P(aₙ) = |cₙ|², cₙ = ∫ψₙ*Ψ dx.
5. **Collapse**: right after the result aₙ the state is ψₙ.
6. **Evolution**: between measurements iħ∂Ψ/∂t = ĤΨ.

steps.title: Solved: superposition in a box
steps.body:
Ψ = (ψ₁ + 2ψ₂)/√5 (box eigenstates, E₂ = 4E₁).
- Normalised: (1 + 4)/5 = 1 ✓
- P(E₁) = 1/5 = 0.2, P(E₂) = 4/5 = 0.8
- ⟨E⟩ = 0.2E₁ + 0.8 × 4E₁ = **3.4E₁** (never itself measured!)
- After measuring E₂ the state is ψ₂; repeating gives E₂ with certainty.

steps.title: Solved: time evolution
steps.body: Ψ(x,t) = (1/√5)[ψ₁e^(−iE₁t/ħ) + 2ψ₂e^(−iE₂t/ħ)]. Probabilities |cₙ|² stay 0.2 and 0.8 for all t, but ⟨x⟩ oscillates at ω = (E₂ − E₁)/ħ = 3E₁/ħ.

steps.title: Dirac notation preview
steps.body: |Ψ⟩ = Σcₙ|n⟩, cₙ = ⟨n|Ψ⟩, ⟨A⟩ = ⟨Ψ|Â|Ψ⟩, orthonormality ⟨m|n⟩ = δₘₙ. Postgraduate courses use this throughout.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to normalise before squaring coefficients.
- Claiming ⟨E⟩ is a possible measurement result.
- Thinking the probabilities change in time for an energy expansion; they do not if H is time-independent.

activity.prompt: For Ψ = (ψ₁ + 2ψ₂)/√5 in an infinite well (E₂ = 4E₁), find ⟨E⟩ in units of E₁.

quiz.q: Possible results of measuring an observable are:
quiz.why: The measurement postulate restricts results to eigenvalues of the corresponding Hermitian operator.

quiz.q: For Ψ = (ψ₁ + 2ψ₂)/√5, P(E₂) is:
quiz.why: The coefficient of ψ₂ is 2/√5, and its modulus squared is 4/5.

quiz.q: Immediately after a measurement gives aₙ, the state becomes:
quiz.why: The collapse postulate projects the state onto the eigenfunction belonging to the measured eigenvalue.

questions.q: Which operator is Hermitian?
questions.why: Integration by parts shows −iħ d/dx satisfies the Hermiticity condition.
