courses.title: Unit 3 · One-dimensional potentials and tunnelling
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Quantum Mechanics and Applications)
courses.summary: Infinite square well (energies, eigenfunctions, orthonormality), finite square well and the graphical solution for bound states, potential step with reflection and transmission coefficients, rectangular barrier and quantum tunnelling with applications to α decay, tunnel diodes and the scanning tunnelling microscope.
outcomes: Solve the infinite square well and compute Eₙ = n²h²/8mL²
Explain qualitatively the bound states of a finite well and their penetration into the walls
Find R and T for a potential step and show R + T = 1
Estimate tunnelling probability T ≈ e^(−2κa) through a barrier
Relate tunnelling to α decay and STM operation

lessons.title: Particle in an infinite square well

scenes.text: QLED televisions use nanometre crystals whose colour depends only on their size.
Smaller box, higher energy levels, bluer light — the particle-in-a-box at work.

steps.title: Solution
steps.body:
V = 0 for 0 < x < L, ∞ outside → ψ = 0 at x = 0, L.
Inside: ψ″ = −k²ψ, k² = 2mE/ħ². ψ = A sin kx + B cos kx; ψ(0) = 0 → B = 0; ψ(L) = 0 → kL = nπ.

**Eₙ = n²π²ħ²/(2mL²) = n²h²/(8mL²)**, ψₙ = √(2/L) sin(nπx/L), n = 1, 2, 3, …
n = 0 is excluded (ψ ≡ 0), so the zero-point energy E₁ > 0.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- ψₙ has n − 1 nodes inside the box.
- Orthonormal: ∫ψₘψₙ dx = δₘₙ.
- Alternately even/odd about the centre.
- Level spacing grows: Eₙ₊₁ − Eₙ = (2n + 1)E₁.
- Large n: probability approaches uniform (correspondence principle).

steps.title: Solved: electron in a 1 nm box
Solved: 3-D cubic box degeneracy
steps.body: E = (h²/8mL²)(nₓ² + n_y² + n_z²). Ground (1,1,1): 3E₁. First excited: (2,1,1), (1,2,1), (1,1,2) all give 6E₁ → **three-fold degenerate**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Allowing n = 0.
- Using h instead of ħ in n²π²ħ²/2mL² (or mixing the two forms).
- Assuming equal spacing of levels (that is the oscillator, not the box).

activity.prompt: An electron in a 1.0 nm infinite well has E₁ = 0.376 eV. What is its ground-state energy (eV) if the well is narrowed to 0.5 nm?

quiz.q: Energy levels of an infinite well scale as:
quiz.why: Fitting nπ/L into k and using E = ħ²k²/2m makes Eₙ proportional to n².

quiz.q: ψ₃ for the infinite well has how many interior nodes?
quiz.why: sin(3πx/L) vanishes inside at x = L/3 and 2L/3, so it has n − 1 = 2 nodes.

quiz.q: Degeneracy of the first excited level of a cubic box is:
quiz.why: The three permutations of (2,1,1) share the same energy 6E₁.

scenes.text: Real wells are not infinitely deep. The wavefunction leaks a little into the walls.
Classically forbidden — quantum mechanically allowed, with an exponential tail.

steps.title: Setting up
steps.body:
V = −V₀ for |x| < a, 0 outside; bound states have −V₀ < E < 0.
- Inside: ψ = A cos kx (even) or A sin kx (odd), k = √(2m(E + V₀))/ħ
- Outside: ψ = Ce^(−κ|x|), κ = √(−2mE)/ħ
Match ψ and ψ′ at x = a:
- even: κ = k tan(ka); odd: κ = −k cot(ka).

steps.title: Graphical solution
steps.body:
Let z = ka, z₀ = (a/ħ)√(2mV₀). Even states: tan z = √(z₀²/z² − 1). Plot both sides; intersections give allowed energies.
- There is **always at least one** bound (even) state in 1-D, however shallow the well.
- Number of bound states ≈ the integer just above 2z₀/π.
- As V₀ → ∞, levels approach the infinite-well values for width 2a.

steps.title: Solved: penetration depth
steps.body: Electron bound 1 eV below the top of a well: κ = √(2 × 9.11×10⁻³¹ × 1.602×10⁻¹⁹)/1.055×10⁻³⁴ = 5.12×10⁹ m⁻¹. Penetration depth 1/κ ≈ **0.20 nm**. Because the wave spreads into the walls, energies are slightly lower than in an infinite well of the same width.

steps.title: Quantum-well lasers
steps.body: Thin GaAs layers sandwiched between AlGaAs form finite wells for electrons; the emitted wavelength is tuned by layer thickness. They are in DVD lasers and telecom transmitters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the exponential tail (setting ψ = 0 at the wall).
- Claiming a very shallow 1-D well has no bound state.
- Using cos for odd states.

statements.s: A 1-D finite square well always has at least one bound state.
statements.why: The even-state equation tan z = √(z₀²/z² − 1) always has a solution for 0 < z < π/2.

statements.s: In a finite well the wavefunction is exactly zero outside the well.
statements.why: It decays exponentially as e^(−κ|x|) in the classically forbidden region.

statements.s: Finite-well energies are slightly lower than those of an infinite well of the same width.
statements.why: Leaking into the walls effectively widens the well, lowering kinetic energy.

statements.s: Deepening the well can only reduce the number of bound states.
statements.why: A larger V₀ increases z₀ and so allows more bound states.

quiz.q: Outside a finite well, a bound-state ψ behaves as:
quiz.why: With E < V outside, the solutions are real exponentials and only the decaying one is normalisable.

quiz.q: As V₀ → ∞, finite-well levels approach:
quiz.why: The exponential tails shrink to nothing, recovering the hard-wall boundary conditions of the infinite well.

quiz.q: Penetration depth 1/κ increases when:
quiz.why: κ = √(2m|E|)/ħ, so a smaller binding energy |E| means a smaller κ and a longer tail.

scenes.text: A skateboarder rolling off a kerb doesn't bounce back. A quantum particle sometimes does.
Any sudden change in potential — up or down — reflects part of the wave.

steps.title: E > V₀
steps.body:
V = 0 (x < 0), V₀ (x > 0). Region I: ψ = e^(ik₁x) + r e^(−ik₁x); region II: t e^(ik₂x), k₁ = √(2mE)/ħ, k₂ = √(2m(E − V₀))/ħ.
Continuity of ψ and ψ′: r = (k₁ − k₂)/(k₁ + k₂), t = 2k₁/(k₁ + k₂).
**R = |r|² = ((k₁ − k₂)/(k₁ + k₂))²**, **T = (k₂/k₁)|t|² = 4k₁k₂/(k₁ + k₂)²**, R + T = 1.
Classically R = 0 for E > V₀.

steps.title: E < V₀
steps.body: In region II ψ = t e^(−κx): R = 1 (total reflection), yet the particle penetrates a distance ~1/κ. There is no transmitted current (real decaying exponential has J = 0).

steps.title: Solved: why the k₂/k₁ factor
steps.body: T is a ratio of probability currents J = |amplitude|² ħk/m, so transmitted current carries k₂ and incident current k₁: T = (k₂/k₁)|t|². With E = 2V₀: |t|² = (2/1.7071)² = 1.3726; T = 0.7071 × 1.3726 = 0.971 ✓.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking T = |t|² (forgets velocity change).
- Expecting zero reflection when the step goes down — reflection depends on (k₁ − k₂)², which is non-zero either way.
- Allowing a growing exponential e^(+κx) in region II.

activity.prompt: A particle with E = 4V₀/3 meets a step of height V₀ (so k₂/k₁ = 1/2). Find the reflection coefficient R (two decimals).

quiz.q: For E > V₀ at a step, quantum mechanics predicts:
quiz.why: The mismatch of wavenumbers k₁ ≠ k₂ produces a reflected wave with R = ((k₁−k₂)/(k₁+k₂))² > 0.

quiz.q: For E < V₀ the reflection coefficient is:
quiz.why: The transmitted wave is a decaying exponential carrying no current, so all incident current is reflected.

quiz.q: T at a step is (k₂/k₁)|t|² because:
quiz.why: Current J = |A|²ħk/m, so comparing currents introduces the ratio of wavenumbers.

scenes.text: In 1981 Binnig and Rohrer held a sharp tip a nanometre above a surface and measured a tiny current.
Electrons tunnelled across the vacuum gap, and the current mapped individual atoms — earning a Nobel Prize in 1986.

steps.title: Barrier transmission
steps.body:
V = V₀ for 0 < x < a, 0 elsewhere; E < V₀; κ = √(2m(V₀ − E))/ħ.
Exact: T = [1 + V₀² sinh²(κa)/(4E(V₀ − E))]⁻¹.
Thick barrier (κa ≫ 1): **T ≈ 16(E/V₀)(1 − E/V₀) e^(−2κa)**. The exponential dominates: T is extremely sensitive to a and to √(m(V₀ − E)).

steps.title: Solved: electron through a thin barrier
Applications
steps.body:
- **α decay (Gamow, 1928)**: α particles tunnel through the Coulomb barrier; small changes in energy change half-lives enormously (Geiger–Nuttall law: ²³²Th α ≈ 4.0 MeV, t½ ≈ 1.4×10¹⁰ y; ²¹²Po α ≈ 8.8 MeV, t½ ≈ 0.3 µs).
- **STM**: current ∝ e^(−2κd); a 0.1 nm change in gap changes current by roughly e^(2.05) ≈ 8×.
- Tunnel diodes, flash memory (Fowler–Nordheim tunnelling), nuclear fusion in the Sun.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Show both forms: the exact sinh² formula and the thick-barrier limit; justify the approximation by computing κa first.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using E instead of V₀ − E in κ.
- Writing e^(−κa) instead of e^(−2κa).
- Saying the particle 'borrows energy'; its energy is E throughout — tunnelling is a wave effect.

quiz.why: The exponential factor e^(−2κa) changes by orders of magnitude for small changes in width or κ.

quiz.why: α particles inside the nucleus have less energy than the Coulomb barrier height but escape by tunnelling.

quiz.why: Current ∝ e^(−2κd), so tiny height changes of atoms produce large, measurable current changes.

courses.title: Unit 4 · The quantum harmonic oscillator
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Quantum Mechanics and Applications)
courses.summary: Schrödinger equation for V = ½mω²x², dimensionless form and series/Hermite solution, energy levels (n + ½)ħω and zero-point energy, eigenfunctions and their parity, classically forbidden regions, ladder-operator method, and applications to molecular vibrations and the correspondence principle.
outcomes: Reduce the oscillator equation to Hermite's equation and derive Eₙ = (n + ½)ħω
Write and normalise the ground-state Gaussian and show it saturates ΔxΔp = ħ/2
Use ladder operators a and a† to generate states and compute matrix elements
Evaluate ⟨x²⟩, ⟨p²⟩ and probabilities beyond the classical turning points
Apply the oscillator model to vibrational spectra of diatomic molecules

lessons.title: Setting up and solving the oscillator equation

scenes.text: Zoom in close enough to the bottom of any smooth valley and it looks like a parabola.
That is why the harmonic oscillator describes molecules, crystal lattices, and even light itself.

steps.title: The equation
steps.body:
V(x) = ½mω²x² (any smooth minimum: V ≈ V₀ + ½V″(x₀)(x − x₀)², ω = √(V″/m)).
−(ħ²/2m)ψ″ + ½mω²x²ψ = Eψ.
Dimensionless: ξ = x√(mω/ħ), ε = 2E/(ħω) → ψ″ − ξ²ψ = −εψ (derivatives in ξ).

steps.title: Asymptotics and series
steps.body:
Large ξ: ψ ≈ e^(−ξ²/2). Write ψ = H(ξ)e^(−ξ²/2):
H″ − 2ξH′ + (ε − 1)H = 0 — Hermite's equation.
Power series H = Σaⱼξʲ: a_{j+2} = (2j + 1 − ε)a_j/[(j + 1)(j + 2)]. If the series does not terminate, H ~ e^(ξ²) and ψ blows up. Termination at j = n requires ε = 2n + 1:

**Eₙ = (n + ½)ħω**, n = 0, 1, 2, …

steps.title: Solved: energy spectrum
steps.body:
- Equally spaced levels, spacing ħω.
- Zero-point energy E₀ = ½ħω (no state at rest at the bottom).
- Planck's oscillators (E = nhν) missed the ½ — measurable in, for example, isotope shifts of molecular vibrations and the Casimir effect.

steps.title: Solved: HCl vibration
steps.body:
HCl vibrates at f = 8.66×10¹³ Hz.
ħω = hf = 6.626×10⁻³⁴ × 8.66×10¹³ = 5.74×10⁻²⁰ J = **0.358 eV**; zero-point energy 0.179 eV.
Absorption 0 → 1 at λ = c/f = **3.46 µm** (infrared).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the ½ in Eₙ.
- Thinking levels get closer at high n (that is hydrogen; the oscillator's are equally spaced).
- Dropping the condition that the series must terminate — that is exactly what quantises the energy.

activity.prompt: A diatomic molecule vibrates at 6.0×10¹³ Hz. What is the spacing between its vibrational levels in eV? (h = 4.136×10⁻¹⁵ eV·s)

quiz.q: Oscillator energy levels are:
quiz.why: Termination of the Hermite series requires ε = 2n + 1, giving Eₙ = (n + ½)ħω.

quiz.q: The spacing between adjacent oscillator levels is:
quiz.why: Eₙ₊₁ − Eₙ = ħω for all n, so the levels form an equally spaced ladder.

quiz.q: Zero-point energy of an oscillator is:
quiz.why: The lowest level n = 0 has energy ½ħω, consistent with the uncertainty principle.

lessons.title: Eigenfunctions, parity and the classical limit

story.title: Where the pendulum spends its time

scenes.text: A classical pendulum spends most time near its turning points, where it slows down.
The quantum ground state does the opposite — peaked at the centre. Only at high n do the two pictures agree.

steps.title: Wavefunctions
steps.body:
ψₙ(x) = (mω/πħ)^(1/4) (1/√(2ⁿn!)) Hₙ(ξ) e^(−ξ²/2).
- ψ₀ = (mω/πħ)^(1/4) e^(−mωx²/2ħ) (Gaussian)
- ψ₁ ∝ ξ e^(−ξ²/2), ψ₂ ∝ (2ξ² − 1)e^(−ξ²/2)
- Parity (−1)ⁿ: even n even, odd n odd; n nodes.

steps.title: Solved: ground-state uncertainties
steps.body:
For ψ₀: ⟨x⟩ = ⟨p⟩ = 0, ⟨x²⟩ = ħ/(2mω), ⟨p²⟩ = mωħ/2.
σₓσ_p = √(ħ/2mω × mωħ/2) = **ħ/2** — the minimum allowed. ⟨V⟩ = ⟨T⟩ = ħω/4 (virial theorem).

steps.title: Classically forbidden region
steps.body:
Classical turning point for E₀: ½mω²x₀² = ½ħω → ξ₀ = 1.
Probability |ξ| > 1 in the ground state = 1 − erf(1) = **0.157** — about 16 % of the time the particle is where classical physics forbids it.

steps.title: Correspondence principle
steps.body: For large n, |ψₙ|² oscillates rapidly but its average approaches the classical density P(x) ∝ 1/√(x₀² − x²), peaked at the turning points. A 0.1 kg mass on a 10 N/m spring with 0.1 m amplitude has n ≈ 5×10³¹ — firmly classical.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 2ⁿn! in the normalisation.
- Assuming the ground state has nodes.
- Thinking quantum probability vanishes beyond the turning point.

activity.prompt: An oscillator is in Ψ = (ψ₀ + ψ₁)/√2. What is ⟨E⟩ in units of ħω?

quiz.q: The oscillator ground state is:
quiz.why: With H₀ = 1, ψ₀ ∝ e^(−mωx²/2ħ), a Gaussian centred at the origin.

quiz.q: ψ₃ has parity:
quiz.why: ψₙ has parity (−1)ⁿ, so n = 3 is odd.

quiz.q: Probability of finding the ground-state particle beyond the classical turning points is about:
quiz.why: Integrating the Gaussian beyond |ξ| = 1 gives 1 − erf(1) ≈ 0.157.

scenes.text: Dirac found you can get every oscillator level without a single power series.
Two operators — one to step up, one to step down — do it all, and later became the language of photons.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
a = √(mω/2ħ)(x + ip/mω), a† = √(mω/2ħ)(x − ip/mω).
[a, a†] = 1. H = ħω(a†a + ½) = ħω(N + ½), N = a†a (number operator).
[H, a] = −ħωa, [H, a†] = +ħωa† → a† raises E by ħω, a lowers it.

steps.title: Action on states
steps.body:
a|n⟩ = √n |n − 1⟩, a†|n⟩ = √(n + 1) |n + 1⟩.
Ground state: a|0⟩ = 0 → first-order ODE (ξ + d/dξ)ψ₀ = 0 → ψ₀ ∝ e^(−ξ²/2).
|n⟩ = (a†)ⁿ|0⟩/√(n!).
x = √(ħ/2mω)(a + a†), p = i√(mωħ/2)(a† − a).

steps.title: Solved: ⟨x²⟩ in state n
steps.body:
x² = (ħ/2mω)(a + a†)² = (ħ/2mω)(a² + a†² + aa† + a†a).
Only aa† + a†a = 2N + 1 survives in ⟨n|…|n⟩:
**⟨x²⟩ₙ = (ħ/2mω)(2n + 1)**; similarly ⟨p²⟩ₙ = (mωħ/2)(2n + 1). So σₓσ_p = (n + ½)ħ.

steps.title: Solved: matrix elements
steps.body: ⟨n′|x|n⟩ = √(ħ/2mω)[√n δ_{n′,n−1} + √(n+1) δ_{n′,n+1}]. Non-zero only for n′ = n ± 1 → the electric-dipole selection rule Δn = ±1 for vibrational transitions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping √n and √(n + 1) factors.
- Treating a and a† as Hermitian (they are adjoints of each other, not observables).
- Forgetting the commutator when reordering aa† = a†a + 1.

activity.prompt: Find ⟨x²⟩ for the n = 2 oscillator state, in units of ħ/(mω).

quiz.q: a†|3⟩ equals:
[a, a†] equals:
quiz.why: Using [x, p] = iħ in the definitions gives aa† − a†a = 1.

quiz.q: The vibrational dipole selection rule is:
quiz.why: x connects |n⟩ only to |n ± 1⟩, so dipole transitions change n by one.

scenes.text: CO₂ and water vapour absorb Earth's infrared glow; N₂ and O₂ do not.
The reason is in their vibrational modes — quantised oscillators that must change the dipole moment to absorb.

steps.title: Diatomic molecules
steps.body:
Two atoms bound by a potential V(r) ≈ ½k(r − r₀)² near equilibrium; use reduced mass μ = m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂): ω = √(k/μ).
Absorption 0 → 1 at ħω. IR activity needs a changing dipole moment, so homonuclear N₂, O₂ are IR-inactive; HCl, CO, CO₂ (asymmetric stretch and bend) are active.

steps.title: Solved: isotope shift
steps.body: DCl (D = 2 u): μ = 70/37 u = 1.892 u. With the same k, f scales as 1/√μ: f(DCl) = 8.66×10¹³ × √(0.972/1.892) = **6.21×10¹³ Hz** — measured isotope shifts confirm the model and the zero-point energy.

steps.title: Oscillators everywhere
steps.body: Lattice vibrations (phonons) explain the heat capacity of solids (Einstein and Debye models); each mode of the electromagnetic field is an oscillator whose quanta are photons — the ½ħω per mode is the vacuum (zero-point) energy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using one atom's mass instead of the reduced mass.
- Mixing f and ω (factor 2π).
- Applying the harmonic model to high vibrational levels where anharmonicity (Morse potential) narrows the spacing.

activity.prompt: HCl absorbs at f = 8.66×10¹³ Hz. What is the absorption wavelength in micrometres (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)?

quiz.q: N₂ does not absorb IR at its vibrational frequency because:
options: its vibration does not change the dipole moment
quiz.why: A homonuclear molecule has zero dipole moment at every bond length, so its stretch cannot couple to the electric field.

quiz.q: Vibrational frequency of a diatomic molecule is ω =
quiz.why: Relative motion of two masses on a spring behaves like a single reduced mass μ = m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂).

quiz.q: Replacing H by D in HCl makes the vibrational frequency:
quiz.why: The bond's force constant stays the same while μ increases, so ω = √(k/μ) decreases.

Ground state σₓσ_p equals:
questions.why: The Gaussian ground state is a minimum-uncertainty state.

questions.q: Dimensionless variable ξ is:
questions.why: Scaling x by the oscillator length √(ħ/mω).

questions.q: Recursion for Hermite series terminates when:
questions.why: Then a_{n+2} = 0 and the polynomial is finite.
The lowering operator annihilates the ground state.

questions.q: ⟨x²⟩ in state n:
questions.why: From (a + a†)² only aa† + a†a contributes.

questions.q: HCl level spacing:
Force constant of HCl is about:
In the ground state ⟨T⟩ equals:
questions.why: Virial theorem splits E₀ = ħω/2 equally between T and V.

questions.q: H in terms of ladder operators:
questions.why: Direct substitution of x and p gives H = ħω(N + ½).

questions.q: Which molecule is IR-active?
questions.why: Heteronuclear CO has a dipole moment that changes as it vibrates.

questions.q: At large n the quantum probability density approaches:
options: the classical density peaked at turning points

courses.title: Unit 5 · Angular momentum, the hydrogen atom, revision & exam
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Quantum Mechanics and Applications)
courses.summary: Schrödinger equation in spherical coordinates and separation of variables, orbital angular momentum operators, eigenvalues l(l+1)ħ² and mħ, spherical harmonics, the radial equation and effective potential, hydrogen energies and degeneracy, ground-state probability distributions; formula sheet, previous-year-style problems and a full-paper exam.
outcomes: Separate the 3-D Schrödinger equation for a central potential
State eigenvalues of L² and L_z and describe the vector model
Write the first few spherical harmonics and interpret their shapes
Derive hydrogen energies Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV and their n² degeneracy
Compute most probable radius, ⟨r⟩ and radial probabilities for the 1s state
Revise and apply all major results of the UG Quantum Mechanics paper

lessons.title: Central potentials and separation in spherical coordinates

scenes.text: An electron around a proton feels a force that depends only on distance, not direction.
That symmetry lets us split one hard 3-D equation into three easy 1-D equations in r, θ and φ.

steps.title: Separation
steps.body:
−(ħ²/2m)∇²ψ + V(r)ψ = Eψ. Try ψ = R(r)Y(θ, φ):
- Angular: −[(1/sinθ)∂_θ(sinθ ∂_θ) + (1/sin²θ)∂²_φ]Y = l(l + 1)Y
- Further Y = Θ(θ)Φ(φ): Φ = e^(imφ), single-valuedness → m integer.
- Θ satisfies the associated Legendre equation → finite only for l = 0, 1, 2, … and |m| ≤ l.

steps.title: Spherical harmonics
steps.body:
Y_l^m(θ, φ) ∝ P_l^m(cosθ)e^(imφ), orthonormal over the sphere.
- Y₀⁰ = 1/√(4π) (s: spherical)
- Y₁⁰ = √(3/4π) cosθ (p_z: lobes along z)
- Y₁^(±1) = ∓√(3/8π) sinθ e^(±iφ)
Parity: Y_l^m(−r̂) = (−1)^l Y_l^m(r̂).

steps.title: Radial equation
steps.body:
With u(r) = rR(r):
−(ħ²/2m)u″ + [V(r) + l(l + 1)ħ²/(2mr²)]u = Eu.
The second term is the **centrifugal barrier**; together they form the effective potential. u(0) = 0 is required.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the sinθ in dΩ = sinθ dθ dφ.
- Allowing |m| > l.
- Solving for R without the u = rR substitution and losing the simple 1-D form.

activity.prompt: Evaluate Y₁⁰ = √(3/4π) cosθ at θ = 0 (three decimals).

quiz.q: m must be an integer because:
quiz.why: Requiring Φ(φ + 2π) = Φ(φ) forces e^(2πim) = 1, so m is an integer.

quiz.q: Allowed m for l = 2:
quiz.why: m runs from −l to +l, giving 2l + 1 = 5 values.

quiz.q: The centrifugal term in the radial equation is:
quiz.why: The angular part contributes l(l + 1)ħ²/(2mr²), a repulsive barrier for l > 0.

story.title: A spinning top you can't pin down

scenes.text: Classically, a spinning top has a definite axis. Quantum angular momentum doesn't.
Only its length and one component are sharp; the rest precesses on a cone.

steps.title: Operators
steps.body:
L = r × p: L_z = −iħ ∂/∂φ, L² = −ħ²[(1/sinθ)∂_θ(sinθ∂_θ) + (1/sin²θ)∂²_φ].
Commutators: [L_x, L_y] = iħL_z (cyclic), [L², L_i] = 0.
Eigenvalues: **L² Y = l(l + 1)ħ² Y, L_z Y = mħ Y**.

steps.title: Vector model
steps.body: |L| = √(l(l + 1)) ħ, L_z = mħ. L lies on a cone around z with cosθ = m/√(l(l + 1)). L can never point exactly along z (except l = 0), since then L_x and L_y would also be sharp, violating the commutation relations.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using |L| = lħ.
- Claiming L_x and L_z can be simultaneously definite.
- Forgetting the m(m ± 1) in the L± coefficient.

activity.prompt: For l = 2, m = 2, find the angle (degrees) between L and the z-axis in the vector model.

quiz.q: Eigenvalue of L² for l = 3:
quiz.why: l(l + 1)ħ² = 3 × 4 ħ² = 12ħ².

quiz.q: Which pair can be simultaneously sharp?
quiz.why: L² commutes with every component, so L² and L_z share eigenstates.

quiz.q: L_z eigenfunctions are:
quiz.why: −iħ ∂/∂φ e^(imφ) = mħ e^(imφ).

scenes.text: Bohr guessed hydrogen's energies with orbits. Schrödinger derived the same −13.6/n² eV from his equation.
But orbits became clouds: the electron's position is a probability distribution.

steps.title: Solution outline
steps.body:
V = −e²/(4πε₀r). Radial equation with ρ = 2r/(na₀); bound solutions require the series to terminate → n = 1, 2, 3, …, l = 0 … n − 1.
**Eₙ = −(me⁴/(32π²ε₀²ħ²))(1/n²) = −13.6 eV/n²**, a₀ = 4πε₀ħ²/(me²) = 0.0529 nm.
Degeneracy: Σ(2l + 1) over l = 0 … n − 1 = **n²** (2n² with spin). Accidental l-degeneracy is special to 1/r.

steps.title: Ground state 1s
steps.body:
ψ₁₀₀ = (1/√(πa₀³)) e^(−r/a₀).
Radial probability P(r) = 4πr²|ψ|² = (4r²/a₀³)e^(−2r/a₀).
- Most probable r: dP/dr = 0 → **r = a₀** (Bohr radius)
- ⟨r⟩ = **1.5 a₀**
- ⟨V⟩ = −27.2 eV, ⟨T⟩ = +13.6 eV (virial theorem)

steps.title: Solved: probability inside a₀
steps.body:
P(r < a₀) = ∫₀^{a₀} (4r²/a₀³)e^(−2r/a₀) dr. With x = 2r/a₀: (1/2)∫₀² x²e^(−x) dx = (1/2)[2 − e^(−2)(4 + 4 + 2)] = 1 − 5e^(−2) = **0.323**.
So the electron is more often *outside* the Bohr radius.

steps.title: Solved: counting n = 3 states
steps.body: l = 0 (1), l = 1 (3), l = 2 (5): 9 orbital states, 18 with spin. Labels 3s, 3p, 3d; radial nodes n − l − 1: 2, 1, 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing most probable r (a₀) with ⟨r⟩ (1.5a₀).
- Forgetting the 4πr² factor and concluding the electron is most likely at r = 0 (that is the density, not the radial probability).
- Applying n² degeneracy to multi-electron atoms (screening lifts the l-degeneracy).

activity.prompt: For the hydrogen 1s state, the probability of finding the electron within r < a₀ is 1 − 5e⁻². Give its value (three decimals).

quiz.q: Degeneracy of hydrogen level n = 4 (ignoring spin):
quiz.why: Summing 2l + 1 for l = 0 to 3 gives 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = n².

quiz.q: Most probable radius in the 1s state:
quiz.why: Maximising r²e^(−2r/a₀) gives r = a₀.

quiz.q: Number of radial nodes for the 3p state:
quiz.why: Radial nodes = n − l − 1 = 3 − 1 − 1 = 1.

lessons.title: Revision: formula sheet and previous-year-style problems

scenes.text: Quantum Mechanics feels like a new language, but the exam asks for a small set of key results.
Here they are on one page, with three exam-style problems.

steps.title: Formula sheet
steps.body:
- iħ∂Ψ/∂t = ĤΨ; p̂ = −iħ∂/∂x; J = (ħ/m)Im(Ψ*Ψ′)
- ⟨A⟩ = ∫ψ*Âψ; σ_Aσ_B ≥ ½|⟨[A,B]⟩|; [x,p] = iħ
- Box: Eₙ = n²h²/8mL², ψₙ = √(2/L) sin(nπx/L)
- Step: R = ((k₁−k₂)/(k₁+k₂))²; barrier T ≈ 16(E/V₀)(1−E/V₀)e^(−2κa)
- Oscillator: Eₙ = (n+½)ħω; a|n⟩ = √n|n−1⟩; ⟨x²⟩ = (ħ/2mω)(2n+1)
- L² → l(l+1)ħ², L_z → mħ; hydrogen Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, degeneracy n², 1s: r_mp = a₀, ⟨r⟩ = 1.5a₀

steps.title: Problem 1 (5 marks)
steps.body:
An electron is in a 0.2 nm box. Find the wavelength of the photon emitted in the 2 → 1 transition.
- E₁ = 0.376 eV × (1/0.2)² = 9.40 eV; ΔE = 3E₁ = 28.2 eV
- λ = 1240/28.2 = **44 nm** (extreme UV)

steps.title: Problem 2 (5 marks)
steps.body:
Show that ψ = Axe^(−αx²) is an eigenfunction of the oscillator Hamiltonian if α = mω/2ħ and find E.
Answer outline: compute ψ″ = A(4α²x³ − 6αx)e^(−αx²); insert into Ĥψ; the x³ terms cancel for α = mω/2ħ; remaining term gives E = 3ħα·ħ/m = **(3/2)ħω** (the n = 1 state).

steps.title: Problem 3 (long answer outline)
steps.body: 'Derive the energy levels of a particle in a 1-D box; show that ⟨x⟩ = L/2 and find σₓ for the ground state.' Steps: TISE inside, boundary conditions, kL = nπ, Eₙ; normalise; ⟨x⟩ by symmetry; ⟨x²⟩ = L²(1/3 − 1/2n²π²) → σₓ(n=1) = 0.181L.
